1.translation: One sign of relying on our deeds is a loss of hope when we stumble or make a mistake.
syarahEn: We may worship diligently while secretly feeling that the amount of worship guarantees that all our wishes will be fulfilled. When we do wrong, our hope in Allah immediately collapses. This change reveals what our hearts rely on. We feel safe because of our own achievements, then feel we have no way home when that record is damaged.

The word al-i'timad means relying on something or placing our trust in it. What is being examined is the heart's reliance, rather than the importance of good deeds. Al-raja' is hope in Allah's generosity, while al-zalal describes stumbling. The choice of the word stumbling reminds us that even someone walking along a path can fall. A fall needs to be put right, while the journey towards Allah must continue.

For example, someone may keep up the night prayer for months, then one day fall into sin. They can feel remorse, repent, and address its causes without concluding that Allah has certainly rejected them. Healthy remorse encourages a return. Despair instead drives them further away and into repeating the mistake because everything seems too late. On the other hand, success in worship should produce gratitude for Allah's help, rather than a feeling of being holier than others.

This wisdom invites us to hold two things together: a sincere commitment to obedience and an ongoing need for Allah's mercy. After a good deed, ask Him to accept it. After a mistake, ask forgiveness and promptly put our actions right. The heart is then guided by confidence that the door of return to Allah remains open to those willing to repent, rather than by pride or a shattered sense of self-worth.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, have we ever worshipped diligently and then felt certain that life would go smoothly? The moment we make a mistake, we think, “That is it. Allah surely does not want to hear my prayers anymore.” Yet we are still being given time to return. Mistakes need remorse, certainly, but hope in Allah still needs to be nurtured.

Ibn 'Ata'illah's first wisdom reminds us about a heart that relies too heavily on its own deeds. As long as we feel diligent, we become overconfident. Once we stumble, every door seems closed. It is as though our relationship with Allah rests entirely on a record of personal success. We forget that even the ability to do good comes through His help.

Imagine a father learning to guard his speech. After a week of staying calm, one afternoon he shouts at his child because he is tired. Then comes the thought, “Learning patience is pointless for me.” Dear congregation, thinking this way only prolongs the mistake. The child still needs an apology. The habit of shouting still needs work. All of that can still begin again.

Of course, we must not use the vastness of Allah's mercy as an excuse to repeat mistakes carelessly. Repentance involves real work: stopping, feeling remorse, and restoring the rights that were violated. If our words hurt someone, approach that person. If exhaustion is a cause, attend to rest and how we respond. Healthy hope gives us the energy to do that work sincerely.

Dear friends, tonight we can admit, “O Allah, I was wrong.” Follow it with a request for help, rather than ending with a sentence passed against ourselves. We are not finished simply because we failed today. While we are alive, there is an opportunity to change our steps. Choose one improvement we can make after returning home, even if it is small and nobody sees it yet.

Let us carry remorse humbly and carry hope courageously. Do not wait until we feel pure before returning to prayer. Precisely when we feel stained, we need Allah's forgiveness and guidance. May Allah help us repent honestly, correct our mistakes, and continue hoping in His mercy. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
talkEn: OPENING
Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, have we ever worshipped diligently and then felt certain that life would go smoothly? The moment we make a mistake, we think, “That is it. Allah surely does not want to hear my prayers anymore.” Yet we are still being given time to return. Mistakes need remorse, certainly, but hope in Allah still needs to be nurtured.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, imagine taking this reminder home with us. We have taken off our shoes, the gathering is over, and ordinary life begins again. That is where the lesson about having the courage to return after doing wrong will be tested. We may still face the same situation, the same people, and old habits that have not yet changed. We need to understand the message well enough to bring it into those circumstances. Listen slowly. If a sentence speaks to our situation, keep it in mind for later. We do not have to remember every explanation. One sound understanding, put sincerely into practice, is already worth working towards today.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah's first wisdom reminds us about a heart that relies too heavily on its own deeds. As long as we feel diligent, we become overconfident. Once we stumble, every door seems closed. It is as though our relationship with Allah rests entirely on a record of personal success. We forget that even the ability to do good comes through His help.

We may worship diligently while secretly feeling that the amount of worship guarantees that all our wishes will be fulfilled. When we do wrong, our hope in Allah immediately collapses. This change reveals what our hearts rely on. We feel safe because of our own achievements, then feel we have no way home when that record is damaged.

The word al-i'timad means relying on something or placing our trust in it. What is being examined is the heart's reliance, rather than the importance of good deeds. Al-raja' is hope in Allah's generosity, while al-zalal describes stumbling. The choice of the word stumbling reminds us that even someone walking along a path can fall. A fall needs to be put right, while the journey towards Allah must continue.

Dear congregation, a saying of wisdom may be very short, yet reflection reveals how deeply it touches our long-standing habits. We are seeing that here in the matter of having the courage to return after doing wrong. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Imagine a father learning to guard his speech. After a week of staying calm, one afternoon he shouts at his child because he is tired. Then comes the thought, “Learning patience is pointless for me.” Dear congregation, thinking this way only prolongs the mistake. The child still needs an apology. The habit of shouting still needs work. All of that can still begin again.

Of course, we must not use the vastness of Allah's mercy as an excuse to repeat mistakes carelessly. Repentance involves real work: stopping, feeling remorse, and restoring the rights that were violated. If our words hurt someone, approach that person. If exhaustion is a cause, attend to rest and how we respond. Healthy hope gives us the energy to do that work sincerely.

The father in that story enters the room and notices that his child has suddenly gone quiet. Usually full of questions, the child now only nods. He wants to say that he is tired, but knows the child had no say in how demanding his working day was. Dear friends, here hope has a very concrete task. He can knock, sit at the child's level, and say, “I shouted earlier. That was wrong. I am sorry.” An explanation about tiredness can come afterwards, without making the child the one to blame. The child may not smile immediately. The father can still give space and show change through how he speaks next time.
Remorse does not have to be resolved by making a child comfort the parent. Adults carry the responsibility of improving their own behaviour.

“But, dear congregation, I have apologized before and then done it again. Do I still deserve to hope?” We need to look honestly at that repetition. Perhaps a trigger remains unaddressed or we have not sincerely practised a different response. Note when our voice begins rising. Is it after work, when hungry, or when several tasks arrive together? Knowing the trigger helps us prepare a pause before causing hurt. We may seek a trusted person's help in learning to manage our responses. Admitting difficulty must still accompany an effort to stop the mistake. Do not make repetition a reason to give up, or hope a licence to keep hurting someone. Hope helps us return to work on what is still unresolved.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “What needs to be done after we hurt someone we love?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone may keep up the night prayer for months, then one day fall into sin. They can feel remorse, repent, and address its causes without concluding that Allah has certainly rejected them. Healthy remorse encourages a return. Despair instead drives them further away and into repeating the mistake because everything seems too late. On the other hand, success in worship should produce gratitude for Allah's help, rather than a feeling of being holier than others.

Dear friends, tonight we can admit, “O Allah, I was wrong.” Follow it with a request for help, rather than ending with a sentence passed against ourselves. We are not finished simply because we failed today. While we are alive, there is an opportunity to change our steps. Choose one improvement we can make after returning home, even if it is small and nobody sees it yet.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of having the courage to return after doing wrong, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

This wisdom invites us to hold two things together: a sincere commitment to obedience and an ongoing need for Allah's mercy. After a good deed, ask Him to accept it. After a mistake, ask forgiveness and promptly put our actions right. The heart is then guided by confidence that the door of return to Allah remains open to those willing to repent, rather than by pride or a shattered sense of self-worth.

For practice after returning home, choose one sentence to replace shouting. For example, “Dad is having trouble calming down. Let us pause and talk again later.” Once calm, really do return to the conversation; do not use the pause to punish through silence. If the person at fault is a child, parents can guide an apology without humiliation. We are all learning responsibility according to our age and ability. Then, in salah or supplication, bring the mistake honestly before Allah. Ask forgiveness and strength to change. We can give thanks for one small improvement while remembering that this goodness needs His help.

Now let us turn the lesson about having the courage to return after doing wrong into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about having the courage to return after doing wrong, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us carry remorse humbly and carry hope courageously. Do not wait until we feel pure before returning to prayer. Precisely when we feel stained, we need Allah's forgiveness and guidance. May Allah help us repent honestly, correct our mistakes, and continue hoping in His mercy. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مِنْ عَلَامَةِ الِاعْتِمَادِ عَلَى الْعَمَلِ
Among the signs of relying on deeds
نُقْصَانُ الرَّجَاءِ عِنْدَ وُجُودِ الزَّلَلِ.
is a decrease in hope when slipping or making a mistake.

2.translation: Your desire for tajrid, when Allah has placed you in a life requiring outward effort, is a hidden desire of the lower self. Conversely, your desire to occupy yourself with outward means, when Allah has placed you in tajrid, is a decline from lofty aspiration.
syarahEn: Some people want to leave work so they can worship continually, even though their families still need financial support. Others already have an opportunity to study and serve, yet keep pursuing new commitments because they want to appear successful. Both need to examine whether the change comes from responsibility or from personal desire dressed in the clothing of righteousness.

Al-asbab means the causes or means through which life proceeds, such as work, skills, and working relationships. Al-tajrid means being released from involvement with certain means, allowing greater concentration on devotion. In this wisdom, tajrid is not a sudden decision to abandon our obligations. Iqamah indicates being placed in a situation: we recognize the responsibility Allah presents through real circumstances, rather than through fantasies about someone else's life.

A father can draw closer to Allah by earning a lawful living, working honestly, and caring for his children. A student can draw closer through diligent study and service to the community. Their worth is not decided by who is seen more often in a place of worship. What deserves attention is whether the task is performed sincerely and religious boundaries are respected.

Circumstances may certainly change through good planning. Before making a move, examine our existing obligations, available abilities, and the effect on others. Seek advice from someone who understands our circumstances. This wisdom helps us stop idealizing another person's path and fulfil, more honestly, the opportunity for devotion that is already open before us.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, sometimes we see someone with plenty of time for the mosque and feel our own life is too ordinary. We work in the morning, care for the home in the afternoon, and are tired by evening. We think, “If I did not have all these commitments, I would surely be closer to Allah.” The question is whether the responsibility we are carrying really is a barrier to obedience.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us to understand the circumstances in which Allah has placed us. Some people's responsibilities call for outward effort. Others have room to devote more time to particular forms of service. Asbab refers to life lived through practical means, while tajrid describes being released from some of those commitments. They are not a competition in spiritual appearances.

For example, a mother opens a small food stall to help support her family. She wants to close it for the whole day to attend every religious activity. Her wish sounds good. But if the family's basic needs are neglected and debts increase, it needs examining again. Perhaps her form of devotion now is precisely to trade honestly while maintaining her obligations in worship.

“Does that mean all we need to do is work?” Our obligation to perform salah and follow religious guidance still stands, dear congregation. What changes is how we view lawful work. Accurate scales, wages paid, clean food, and friendly service are opportunities for goodness. We can study our religion at suitable times without belittling the livelihood we are responsible for providing.

Conversely, someone already given an opportunity to study also needs to use it. Do not keep daydreaming about other work simply because another person's results look dazzling. Recognize real needs, discuss decisions with the family, and make changes responsibly. This wisdom teaches appropriateness, so enthusiasm for worship does not become an excuse to escape our duties.

After returning home, try looking at our work desk afresh. There is an opportunity to honour a trust, help people, and train the heart. Ask Allah to guide our work towards goodness. May we be given clarity to recognize today's task and strength to fulfil it sincerely. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Talking about fulfilling a trust through lawful work calls for honesty, but that honesty can remain quietly within the heart. We are under no obligation to share private affairs before everyone. Simply listen, consider, and identify what can be improved. Sometimes we already know the advice, but have not made time to think about it. This gathering gives us that opportunity. We can revisit a sound understanding until it becomes clearer. Afterwards, when we face everyday situations, may we have words that help us choose our actions more calmly and responsibly.

Let us hold this understanding carefully, dear friends. Advice about fulfilling a trust through lawful work should be read alongside our obligations as servants of Allah and our responsibilities towards others. Feeling peaceful after hearing a talk is certainly pleasant. Yet sound understanding also helps us act when things no longer feel peaceful. That is why explaining the words matters. We gain something to guide our direction, rather than a beautiful impression that soon fades. If we later forget how the term sounds, remember the relationship it explains: how the heart turns to Allah and how our choices touch real life.

Accurate scales, wages paid, clean food, and friendly service are opportunities for goodness. We can study our religion at suitable times without belittling the livelihood we are responsible for providing.

Let us continue the story of the mother who runs a food stall. At dawn she is already preparing ingredients, then serving customers who are also in a hurry. A child needs breakfast, and workers depend on her business for wages. Seeing an announcement for a day-long religious lesson makes her sad because she cannot attend. Dear friends, wanting to learn is good. She can look for a recording or choose a meeting at a suitable time. But she should not belittle the duty she is fulfilling by saying, “I only sell food.” Behind that word only are clean meals prepared and family needs protected. The way she performs that task still offers much room to improve her intention and character.

“Then can we stay so busy that we never have time to learn?” We need to examine our schedule honestly, dear congregation. Sometimes the burden really is heavy; sometimes there are habits we could reduce. We can still seek an opportunity to read briefly or ask a teacher, according to our ability. What we should avoid is comparing our entire life with the best part of someone else's. Even people who seem free to attend lessons have duties we may not see. We can help each other: those with time can share notes, while those with other resources can support the activities' needs. Differences in circumstances then become an opportunity to cooperate, rather than a reason to belittle one another.

Let me ask a question, dear congregation: “How can everyday work be carried out as devotion to Allah?” Take a moment to think about it. Perhaps an answer comes straight away; perhaps a difficulty comes to mind instead. Let us hear that difficulty calmly. Good advice needs to meet the reality of life, including the limitations we face. Now imagine someone we love asking that question. Would our answer help them act, or simply leave them feeling scolded? Here we learn to convey the truth in a way that can be received. We also need honesty that gives direction when speaking to ourselves, so that understanding a problem gives us courage to begin putting it right.

A father can draw closer to Allah by earning a lawful living, working honestly, and caring for his children. A student can draw closer through diligent study and service to the community. Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about fulfilling a trust through lawful work may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Circumstances may certainly change through good planning. Before making a move, examine our existing obligations, available abilities, and the effect on others. Seek advice from someone who understands our circumstances. This wisdom helps us stop idealizing another person's path and fulfil, more honestly, the opportunity for devotion that is already open before us.

Try examining one working day from beginning to end. Where is honesty most easily tested? Perhaps when weighing goods or explaining a product's faults. Choose one improvement there. Then discuss time for worship and learning with family or colleagues so that the arrangement is realistic. If we wish to change jobs, calculate our needs and responsibilities first. A major decision can be prepared carefully. Meanwhile, fulfil the present job as well as possible. May our work desk teach us dedication, and may our limited opportunities to learn be used with full attention.

Dear congregation, if we want to take one task home from this discussion of fulfilling a trust through lawful work, choose something we can truly do. There is no need to announce it now. We can decide after getting home, when we have a fuller picture of our circumstances. Make the step small enough for us to know when it will be done. If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of fulfilling a trust through lawful work that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

After returning home, try looking at our work desk afresh. There is an opportunity to honour a trust, help people, and train the heart. Ask Allah to guide our work towards goodness. May we be given clarity to recognize today's task and strength to fulfil it sincerely. Amin.

wordsEn: tajrid; freedom from worldly preoccupations with means
phrasesEn: إِرَادَتُكَ التَّجْرِيدَ مَعَ إِقَامَةِ اللَّهِ إِيَّاكَ فِي الْأَسْبَابِ
Your desire to live in tajrid while Allah places you in a life requiring outward effort
مِنَ الشَّهْوَةِ الْخَفِيَّةِ،
is among the lower self's hidden desires.
وَإِرَادَتُكَ الْأَسْبَابَ مَعَ إِقَامَةِ اللَّهِ إِيَّاكَ فِي التَّجْرِيدِ
Conversely, your desire to occupy yourself with outward means while Allah places you in tajrid
انْحِطَاطٌ عَنِ الْهِمَّةِ الْعَلِيَّةِ.
is a decline from lofty aspiration.

3.translation: However powerfully and swiftly determination races ahead, it does not pierce the walls of the divine decree.
syarahEn: Strong determination helps us move, learn, and persevere through obstacles. Yet it does not give people power over every result. Some decisions are carefully prepared but still do not come to fruition. This wisdom puts enthusiasm in its proper place, so perseverance is accompanied by humility before Allah.

The expression sawabiq al-himam pictures determination racing ahead, like something running very fast. Aswar al-aqdar means the walls of the divine decrees. The image of walls emphasizes a limit that cannot be crossed by willpower alone. Our task is to choose and make an effort, while the outcome remains within Allah's will.

Imagine a trader who has improved the product, maintained honesty, and made a sincere effort to sell it. If sales have not increased, the way of doing business still needs reviewing. The trader also needs to guard the heart against feeling that Allah owes an outcome matching a target. Acknowledging the divine decree does not remove the need for evaluation, just as evaluation gives us no right to force a result.

When we fail, distinguish mistakes that need correcting from circumstances beyond our ability. Learn from the first and entrust the second to Allah. When we succeed, acknowledge the help that made our effort possible. Determination then becomes energy for devotion, rather than a reason to believe we control everything. We remain willing to make plans, while having the openness to accept that the best path may differ from the one we first imagined.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, sometimes a single announcement feels terribly heavy. We have studied, practised, and cut back on play. Then the exam results arrive, and our name is not on the list. Someone says, “Perhaps you did not try hard enough.” Yet they never saw the nights we went through. How do we keep going when sincere effort has not brought what we wanted?

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that however strong human determination becomes, it remains within Allah's decree. Himmah means strong resolve. That resolve matters because it moves us to act, but it does not put every outcome under our control. Ability, circumstances, opportunities, and much else lie beyond the reach of our personal decisions.

For our younger friends at school, this is no excuse to study half-heartedly. Effort still matters because that is the part for which we can take responsibility. But an exam mark should not become the measure of our entire worth. Missing out on a chosen school hurts, yet the ability to learn and opportunities to do good do not automatically disappear with one announcement.

For parents, let us be careful with our words after the results arrive. “We spent all that money, and you still failed” can burden a child who is already disappointed. We can review how the child studies without destroying the courage to try. Sit together, ask which parts were difficult, then look at the next options. Children need support so they can dare to try again in a more suitable way.

Dear friends, there is a difference between giving up and accepting the limits of an outcome. Acceptance helps us stop arguing with something that has already happened. Once calmer, we can seek advice, arrange new practice, or choose another route. If we need to cry first, that is all right. Tears do not erase sincerity. What needs protecting is the direction of our next steps.

Today, let us release the habit of treating one failure as a lifelong verdict. Our task is to learn, while Allah knows the journey we cannot yet see. May He give room to disappointed hearts, preserve love in our families, and guide our next efforts. We keep trying sincerely while asking for His help. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Yet the lesson about supporting renewed effort after disappointing exam results meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that however strong human determination becomes, it remains within Allah's decree. Himmah means strong resolve. That resolve matters because it moves us to act, but it does not put every outcome under our control. Ability, circumstances, opportunities, and much else lie beyond the reach of our personal decisions.

Strong determination helps us move, learn, and persevere through obstacles. Yet it does not give people power over every result. Some decisions are carefully prepared but still do not come to fruition. This wisdom puts enthusiasm in its proper place, so perseverance is accompanied by humility before Allah.

The expression sawabiq al-himam pictures determination racing ahead, like something running very fast. Aswar al-aqdar means the walls of the divine decrees. The image of walls emphasizes a limit that cannot be crossed by willpower alone. Our task is to choose and make an effort, while the outcome remains within Allah's will.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with supporting renewed effort after disappointing exam results. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

For our younger friends at school, this is no excuse to study half-heartedly. Effort still matters because that is the part for which we can take responsibility. But an exam mark should not become the measure of our entire worth. Missing out on a chosen school hurts, yet the ability to learn and opportunities to do good do not automatically disappear with one announcement.

For parents, let us be careful with our words after the results arrive. “We spent all that money, and you still failed” can burden a child who is already disappointed. We can review how the child studies without destroying the courage to try. Sit together, ask which parts were difficult, then look at the next options. Children need support so they can dare to try again in a more suitable way.

Imagine the atmosphere after that announcement. Family phones begin ringing. Some ask about the result; others are already comparing it with a neighbour's child. The child who studied late chooses to close the door. Parents may also feel disappointed, but adult disappointment should not all be poured onto the child. Sit nearby when the child is willing to have company. We can say, “This result is not what we hoped for. We will look at the next options once you feel a little calmer.” Those simple words make room for reality without breaking the relationship. The child knows the family's love remains, even though one target has not been reached. Sharing what was difficult then becomes more possible.

“But if we comfort children too much, they will relax and stop trying.” Dear friends, comfort and evaluation can each happen at the right time. We do not have to choose only one. When feelings are overwhelming, someone may not be ready to examine a sheet of mistakes. Once calm, look more closely together at the questions or study methods. Was the practice unsuitable? Did the child understand the material but struggle to manage time? Answers like these give us clear work to do. Simply calling a child lazy without examining the process only creates a label. We also need to acknowledge factors outside the child's control. Family support helps children try again without believing that their entire worth depends on a single result.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “What can we say to a child who has worked hard but has not been accepted into the first choice?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Imagine a trader who has improved the product, maintained honesty, and made a sincere effort to sell it. If sales have not increased, the way of doing business still needs reviewing. The trader also needs to guard the heart against feeling that Allah owes an outcome matching a target. Acknowledging the divine decree does not remove the need for evaluation, just as evaluation gives us no right to force a result.

Dear friends, there is a difference between giving up and accepting the limits of an outcome. Acceptance helps us stop arguing with something that has already happened. Once calmer, we can seek advice, arrange new practice, or choose another route. If we need to cry first, that is all right. Tears do not erase sincerity. What needs protecting is the direction of our next steps.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of supporting renewed effort after disappointing exam results, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

When we fail, distinguish mistakes that need correcting from circumstances beyond our ability. Learn from the first and entrust the second to Allah. When we succeed, acknowledge the help that made our effort possible. Determination then becomes energy for devotion, rather than a reason to believe we control everything. We remain willing to make plans, while having the openness to accept that the best path may differ from the one we first imagined.

For practice, choose one part of the learning that can be reviewed together, then set a short time to work on it. Do not immediately fill every hour with extra practice. Allow suitable rest and ask what help is needed. For those who left school long ago, this approach is also useful when supporting a family member through a selection process. Avoid promising that the next effort will certainly secure a particular place. We can promise support within our ability. The child learns that sincere effort still matters and that, when results differ, there is a way to reorganize the next steps without losing love or hope.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of supporting renewed effort after disappointing exam results again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about supporting renewed effort after disappointing exam results invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Today, let us release the habit of treating one failure as a lifelong verdict. Our task is to learn, while Allah knows the journey we cannot yet see. May He give room to disappointed hearts, preserve love in our families, and guide our next efforts. We keep trying sincerely while asking for His help. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: سَوَابِقُ الْهِمَمِ
However powerfully and swiftly resolve races forth,
لَا تَخْرِقُ أَسْوَارَ الْأَقْدَارِ.
it cannot pierce the walls of destiny's decree.

4.translation: Give yourself rest from the anxiety of managing every affair. What Another has undertaken on your behalf, do not take over and undertake for yourself.
syarahEn: The mind often becomes tired from trying to control every possibility. We calculate tomorrow's work, people's reactions, family circumstances, and even events that may never happen. Planning that should have helped turns into unending anxiety. Ibn 'Ata'illah invites us to recognize the boundary between our human task and Allah's ordering of affairs, which encompasses all of life.

Al-tadbir means managing or planning. Here, what needs calming is the heart's attempt to make every outcome certain. Arih means give rest. The invitation is gentle: an exhausted heart is allowed to stop carrying control it never possessed. Allah has already cared for so much that we could never manage ourselves.

We still make a budget, choose work, and prepare for our children's education. After taking reasonable steps, we learn not to rehearse every worry each night. A mother, for example, can support her child's learning without demanding that the child's future follow a single design. Care continues, while the educational outcome is entrusted to Allah through efforts that are continually improved.

Try writing down what can be done today and what is currently beyond reach. Attend to the first part in an orderly way. Bring the second into our supplication, then allow the body room to rest. This peace comes from recognizing our position as servants of Allah. We are entrusted to make an effort and are also allowed to feel secure in our Lord's ordering of affairs, which extends far beyond our knowledge.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, the body is lying down and the lights are off, but the mind is still holding a meeting. What if business is quiet tomorrow? What if a child becomes ill? What if the savings run out? Before one question ends, another appears. The night passes in anxiety, while tomorrow's work may be no easier because we spent the whole night thinking about it.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us to rest from the tadbir that burdens the heart. He does not mean that we should stop planning. We still prepare budgets, arrange necessities, and seek solutions. What we release is the demand that everything tomorrow must follow our arrangements. We can prepare what we need, but we do not have complete control over life.

Notice this, dear congregation. Writing a shopping list helps with a task. Replaying frightening possibilities until the early hours often only uses up our strength. Both activities take place in the mind, but their effects differ. We need to ask, “Is there an action I can take now, or am I replaying a fear about something that has not happened?”

If a simple action remains, do a reasonable amount. Prepare the paperwork, note a bill, or send a message to arrange a meeting. If nothing can yet be done, write down the issue to discuss tomorrow. Then let the body rest. We may pray in honest words, “O Allah, I am afraid. Please guide me through the part I am able to manage.”

Of course, some anxiety is severe and keeps disrupting daily life. In that situation, speaking with someone trusted or seeking professional help is a good step. Do not add another burden by accusing ourselves of weak faith. We care for our faith while also caring for our condition. Both can accompany our effort to find peace and the ability to act.

Tonight, let us learn to bring the day's work to a reasonable close. We do not have to settle our entire future before sleeping. Entrust what exceeds our ability to Allah, then prepare to fulfil our duties when morning comes. May Allah protect our homes, calm anxious hearts, and grant enough rest for us to continue our responsibilities. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Let us try a brief routine to close the day. Write down one matter already attended to and one to handle tomorrow. If a decision needs someone else's involvement, note whom we will speak with. Then offer a supplication in honest words. We may admit that we do not yet know the solution. If thoughts begin circling again, gently return our attention to the preparations already written down, without insulting ourselves. Family can also help by postponing non-urgent conversations until the agreed time. In this way, the home offers an opportunity to rest while responsibilities are still respected.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. phrasesEn: أَرِحْ نَفْسَكَ مِنَ التَّدْبِيرِ،
Rest yourself from anxious management of every affair.
فَمَا قَامَ بِهِ غَيْرُكَ عَنْكَ
What someone other than you has undertaken for you,
لَا تَقُمْ بِهِ لِنَفْسِكَ.
do not take over its management for yourself.

5.translation: Your eagerness to pursue what has been guaranteed for you, together with your neglect of what is required of you, shows that your inner sight has been veiled.
syarahEn: We readily pursue income with dedication, yet sometimes leave salah, honesty, and family rights until everything else is done. This busyness can appear reasonable because we call it earning a living. This wisdom examines our priorities: what Allah has undertaken to provide must not make us neglect what we are required to do.

Dumina, meaning has been guaranteed, refers to provision within Allah's ordering of affairs. This assurance still accompanies the command to pursue lawful means. Tuliba, meaning is required, directs attention to the devotion we must undertake. Al-basirah is inner sight: the ability to understand life's direction through the guidance of faith. When these priorities are reversed, inner sight loses its clarity.

A worker, for example, may strive to increase income. Yet additional profit should not be purchased through deception or deliberately abandoning an obligation. Provision is also more than the money that comes in. Health, sufficient time, and a well-tended family relationship affect how that income is enjoyed. A clear purpose helps us distinguish real needs from desires that keep multiplying.

Examine our daily schedule honestly. Does work have a clear place while worship always waits for spare time? Begin arranging our obligations as a fixed part of life, then organize work around them. Earning a living remains a good deed when pursued correctly. This wisdom invites us to seek a livelihood sincerely while remembering that life's purpose extends beyond satisfying a list of worldly wishes.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, orders arriving one after another certainly make a trader happy. Things need packing, messages answering, and orders delivering. Yet amid the rush we sometimes hear, “Pray later. Customers first.” One postponement becomes a habit. We are frightened of losing a single sale, yet less troubled when an obligation begins to be pushed aside.

The fifth wisdom highlights eagerness in seeking provision alongside neglect of Allah's requirements. He guarantees provision, while we are commanded to strive in the right way. That guarantee is no invitation to laziness. Its message orders our priorities so that earning a living remains within servanthood, instead of taking up all of life.

Imagine the owner of a food business approaching the busiest hour. If tasks and staggered prayer breaks are arranged from the start, service can continue. Often the problem is not a complete lack of time, but an obligation that has not been given a place in planning. We prepare ingredients days ahead, yet have not prepared a way to maintain worship while working.

“What if customers are angry about a short wait?” We can explain politely and give an estimated time. The arrangements should, of course, suit the circumstances and religious guidance. What matters is not building a business on the assumption that profit must always win over obligation. Customers also deserve honest service, rather than promises of speed that leave everyone exhausted.

Dear friends, measure today's success more broadly than the amount of money received. Check whether workers are paid, family is still cared for, and salah is maintained. The profit we appreciate should accompany an orderly life. If something has been in disarray, we can begin correcting one part of the schedule without waiting for the business to grow or circumstances to become completely relaxed.

Let us pray that those struggling to earn a living are given enough and a lawful way forward. For ourselves, ask for a heart that recognizes priorities when opportunities come. May Allah bless our efforts, protect the rights of those working with us, and help us remain obedient in both busy and spacious times. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Examine our daily schedule honestly. Does work have a clear place while worship always waits for spare time? Begin arranging our obligations as a fixed part of life, then organize work around them. Earning a living remains a good deed when pursued correctly. This wisdom invites us to seek a livelihood sincerely while remembering that life's purpose extends beyond satisfying a list of worldly wishes.

For practice, look at tomorrow's busiest period. Choose one improvement that makes an obligation easier to fulfil. It might be earlier preparation or a division of tasks that was previously unclear. Discuss the change with those involved. If the schedule has often fallen apart, review it without blaming each other. Some work really needs rearranging so the burden does not fall on one person. We also learn to accept a realistic service capacity. We need not accept every sales opportunity if promises to customers then collapse and our bodies and worship are continually neglected. Ask for lawful provision together with the ability to fulfil people's rights.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about maintaining salah when business is busy. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about maintaining salah when business is busy. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us pray that those struggling to earn a living are given enough and a lawful way forward. For ourselves, ask for a heart that recognizes priorities when opportunities come. May Allah bless our efforts, protect the rights of those working with us, and help us remain obedient in both busy and spacious times. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Yakhtaruhu means He chooses it. The difference between Allah's choice and ours explains why the answer cannot be confined to the form of our request or a timetable set by human beings.

We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

We may supplicate repeatedly, name our hopes clearly, and acknowledge sadness. But do not conclude that prayer is pointless simply because the date we imagined has passed. We ask for the good Allah chooses while caring for today's steps.

Do not let delayed giving make you despair, despite your persistent supplication.
فَهُوَ ضَمِنَ لَكَ الْإِجَابَةَ فِيمَا يَخْتَارُهُ لَكَ
For He guarantees an answer in the form He chooses for you,
لَا فِيمَا تَخْتَارُهُ لِنَفْسِكَ،
rather than the form you choose yourself.
وَفِي الْوَقْتِ الَّذِي يُرِيدُ
The answer comes at the time He wills,
لَا فِي الْوَقْتِ الَّذِي تُرِيدُ.
rather than the time you will.

7.translation: Do not let the non-fulfilment of what has been promised make you doubt His promise, even when its time has been specified. Do not let that doubt damage your inner sight and extinguish your inner light.
syarahEn: Waiting for something we believe is good often tests patience. As time passes, the heart may begin to imagine that Allah's promise does not hold. This wisdom protects us from hasty conclusions. Our limited understanding of a promise's timing and form must not become an accusation against Allah's truth.

Al-wa'd means a promise, while al-maw'ud is what has been promised. Both need to be distinguished from a personal estimate. Hopes, dreams, people's words, or feelings after supplication do not automatically become a certain promise from Allah. Qadhan describes a flaw or damage, while ikhmad means extinguishing. Doubt that is nurtured can disturb the clarity of inner sight and put out our enthusiasm for devotion.

For example, we read that Allah helps those who are mindful of Him, then imagine that this help must take the form of business success in a particular month. If the business has not succeeded, we need to examine our interpretation of that promise. Allah is not bound by the picture we added ourselves. Help may come through steadfastness, a way out we have not yet seen, or protection from a harmful step.

The practical lesson is to examine the source of our certainty before making demands. Hold to promises that truly come from revelation, understand their explanation through knowledge, and treat personal assumptions as assumptions. While waiting, continue fulfilling our duties and improve efforts that remain inadequate. Faith becomes more mature when we can say that Allah is true while our understanding can still be mistaken and needs continued guidance.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, have we ever chosen honesty and felt that we lost out? A colleague skilled at making excuses seems to receive opportunities faster, while we try to stay upright and must keep waiting. The heart asks, “They say goodness receives goodness, so why is my situation like this?” That question needs a sound understanding of Allah's promise.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us not to let faith in His promise go out simply because what we await is not yet visible. Yet we must distinguish Allah's promise from our own prediction. Sometimes we invent a formula: “If I am honest for a month, I will certainly be promoted next month.” Our homemade formula must not be treated as a promise from Allah.

Imagine an employee refusing to alter a report. Some colleagues consequently regard that person as troublesome. This is hard. Support, properly kept evidence, and a safe reporting channel may be needed. Holding to goodness still requires care in facing real circumstances. We do not have to face pressure alone without help.

Dear friends, good results do not always immediately appear as a pay rise or praise. Honesty protects us from the habit of covering a mistake with another mistake. People are also entitled to truthful reports. Reward in the Hereafter rests within Allah's knowledge and generosity. We cannot measure the whole value of obedience only through changes visible this week.

When the heart grows tired, find someone to speak with who offers strength and helps us think. Improve our working ability so honesty is accompanied by competence. Keep reasonable records of the process. Do not rush to conclude that everyone succeeds through cheating. There is still much room to pursue a livelihood properly, even if finding a healthier environment takes time.

Let us honour the promise that is our responsibility today: working faithfully and acknowledging reality truthfully. As for reward, we ask Allah with hope. May He protect those defending honesty, open lawful paths, and keep our hearts steadfast without resenting someone else's success. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

8.translation: When He opens for you a door to knowing Him, do not be overly troubled that your deeds are still few. He has only opened it because He wishes to make Himself known to you. Do you not know that this knowledge is something He brings to you, while deeds are what you offer Him? Can what you offer Him compare with what He brings to you?
syarahEn: There are times when a trial helps us recognize our own weakness and need Allah more sincerely. During that time, our additional deeds may still be few. This wisdom reminds us not to judge our entire state only by the number of acts of worship. A heart opening to know Allah is an immense gift.

Al-ta'arruf means making oneself known. In this wisdom, Allah opens a way for the servant to recognize His generosity, power, and care. Muriduhu points to what He brings to us, while muhdiha refers to the deeds we offer. These different directions teach that Allah's grace precedes our ability to respond through devotion.

Someone who is ill, for example, may not yet be able to perform additional worship as when healthy. Yet that person begins to leave arrogance behind, pray honestly, and appreciate others' help. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Listen also to the exhaustion of family members providing care. Compassion requires a realistic sharing of help so the entire burden does not fall on one person. Someone who is ill may need assistance, and the carer may also need rest. We do not know Allah's particular purpose in an illness, but we know that accompanying one another requires respect and practical care.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “How can we support someone who is ill so that they continue to feel respected?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about accepting changes in ability when the body is weak may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Knowing Allah can be examined through its fruits. Is the heart humbler, are others' rights better protected, and is obedience more beloved? A feeling of being special that only increases pride needs examining again. We do not have to announce inner experiences or assign ourselves a spiritual rank. Let us change one habit when visiting the sick. Instead of repeatedly asking why the person has not recovered, offer clear help suited to their needs. Ask when a visit would be comfortable. If bringing food, consider the needs the family has already explained. Do not force a long conversation when the person is tired. If we ourselves are ill, choose one gentle activity that still brings a sense of connection without overexertion. It might be listening briefly to recitation or offering a simple supplication. May changes in ability bring new understanding of our need for Allah and of the importance of caring for one another within the family.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of accepting changes in ability when the body is weak again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about accepting changes in ability when the body is weak. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us guard our speech when visiting the sick. Replace questions that put someone on the spot with a clear offer, such as helping with meals or taking them to an appointment. May Allah grant healing, ease pain, and strengthen the family providing care. In strength and weakness alike, may we still have the opportunity to know His generosity and experience one another's compassion. Amin.

phrasesEn: إِذَا فَتَحَ لَكَ وِجْهَةً مِنَ التَّعَرُّفِ
When He opens for you a door to knowing Him,
فَلَا تُبَالِ مَعَهَا إِنْ قَلَّ عَمَلُكَ،
do not be excessively troubled that your deeds remain few.
فَإِنَّهُ مَا فَتَحَهَا لَكَ إِلَّا وَهُوَ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَتَعَرَّفَ إِلَيْكَ.
He opens that door solely because He wishes to make Himself known to you.
أَلَمْ تَعْلَمْ أَنَّ التَّعَرُّفَ هُوَ مُورِدُهُ عَلَيْكَ
Do you not know that this knowledge is something He brings to you,
وَالْأَعْمَالُ أَنْتَ مُهْدِيهَا إِلَيْهِ،
whereas deeds are something you offer to Him?
وَأَيْنَ مَا تُهْدِيهِ إِلَيْهِ مِمَّا هُوَ مُورِدُهُ إِلَيْكَ؟
Can your offering to Him compare with what He brings to you?

9.translation: Different kinds of deeds arise from the different gifts that shape inward states.
syarahEn: Not everyone has the same opening to goodness. Some find it natural to study diligently, some have strength to serve the sick, and others readily help neighbours with their needs. These differences need not immediately become a competition. This wisdom teaches that varied deeds can grow from the different inner states and gifts of each person.

Ajnas al-a'mal means the kinds of deeds. The concern is not simply how many activities there are, but the forms of devotion. Waridat al-ahwal refers to gifts that arrive and shape the heart's states. Someone whose compassion is being strengthened may be moved to serve, while someone developing a longing for knowledge is moved to study diligently. All of this needs religious guidance.

We therefore need not copy every habit of someone we admire. A teacher's schedule differs from that of a mother caring for a baby. Shared guidance does not require every additional deed to take the same form. Obligations remain our common foundation; the space beyond them can be filled according to ability, responsibility, and the community's needs.

Try recognizing the good we can most realistically maintain, then do it without belittling others' paths. If ability changes, our form of devotion can also adjust. Someone who once taught frequently may one day spend more time caring for family. While the heart's direction is preserved, the change can remain an act of obedience. Understanding variety makes it easier to cooperate, complement one another, and give thanks that goodness comes through more than one kind of role.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, when there is a community work day at the mosque, people's roles usually differ. Some sweep, some cook, and some carry things. Others manage funds or keep children company so the work can proceed safely. Sometimes someone comments, “They have it easy, just sitting there.” Yet we may not know the task that person is doing.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains that varied deeds are connected to varied gifts and inner states. People are not always guided to perform the same form of devotion. Some have physical strength, some teach patiently, and some have financial means. These differences can complement each other if we are not busy making our own way the only measure.

Imagine everyone wanting the microphone, dear congregation. Who would tidy the cables and prepare the space? Conversely, if someone able to teach is always made to lift heavy objects, that expertise may not be used appropriately. Service requires both willingness to help and care in dividing tasks, so shared needs are met and each person's condition is respected.

“Does that mean we can choose the easiest job?” We still need honesty. Recognizing ability differs from finding excuses to avoid every responsibility. If we cannot stand for long, explain and offer help we can manage. If we are physically strong, do not wait for praise before moving. We seek benefit, rather than merely the position that looks most honoured.

Dear friends, differences also appear in additional deeds. Some enjoy reading; others diligently serve their parents. While guidance is followed and obligations maintained, we can support each other. Do not quickly dismiss a form of devotion unlike our own habits. Its benefit may be reaching people who have previously escaped our attention.

Before leaving a shared activity, try thanking someone whose work is rarely mentioned. Then ask what small task still needs help. May Allah unite our hearts in goodness, grant sincerity to everyone serving the community, and keep us from belittling one another's roles. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

Different kinds of deeds
لِتَنَوُّعِ وَارِدَاتِ الْأَحْوَالِ.
arise from diverse gifts shaping inner states.

10.translation: Deeds are outward forms that come into being. Their spirit is the presence of the secret of sincerity within them.
syarahEn: Two people can do the same activity with different purposes. One gives charity to help, while another is busy imagining the praise to come. The outward deeds both look good, yet their inner life differs. This wisdom helps us examine something that is not always visible to human judgement.

Suwar means visible forms. Deeds have forms, such as the movements of salah, giving assistance, or teaching. Arwah means spirits, used as an image for what gives those forms life. Sirr al-ikhlas points to the heart of sincerity: directing a deed towards Allah while releasing demands for human recognition. Form and spirit both need care so that devotion does not lose its purpose.

Sincerity does not always mean hiding a deed. Some good work requires reporting, announcements, or working before many people. A donation manager must still provide truthful information. What needs examining is whether openness serves the trust or becomes a stage for self-importance. Examining intention is primarily our work upon ourselves, rather than a tool for accusing someone else's heart.

Before acting, ask what purpose we want to preserve. During the deed, perform it properly even if nobody is watching. Afterwards, restrain the wish to retell it for praise. If our intention feels mixed, straighten it again while continuing the good. Sincerity is an exercise continually renewed, giving outward deeds direction while teaching the heart to be content that Allah knows.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, giving assistance nowadays may involve a camera. Documentation can help with reporting and encourage others to contribute. Yet we need to pause when a recipient begins to feel uncomfortable. We arrive with food; let us not leave with someone's dignity turned into a spectacle. Good intentions also need to become good methods.

Ibn 'Ata'illah says deeds have an outward form, while sincerity is their spirit. Outwardly, two people are both giving. Inwardly, their purposes may differ. One wants to help a brother or sister's needs; another is more concerned with appearing generous. We do not know someone else's heart, but we can examine our own.

Dear congregation, before recording a recipient's face, ask whether documentation is necessary and whether the person is truly willing. Someone needing help may struggle to refuse a giver's request. Consent must therefore be respected without pressure. Reporting can use distribution records, purchase receipts, or images protecting identity, according to the needs and responsibilities of management.

“If it is not published, will others be moved to help?” We may encourage goodness. What needs thought is the form of that invitation. Explain needs and programme results respectfully. Avoid scenes asking someone to cry again or say thank you repeatedly. Assistance should lighten burdens, including the emotional burden of dealing with the person giving.

Examine our response when our name is not mentioned too. Are we still glad the help arrived, or deeply disappointed at not appearing in the post? That disappointment can become an opportunity to straighten our intention. We need not stop helping because the intention is imperfect. Keep doing good while correcting the part of the heart that wants admiration.

Dear friends, let us keep some goodness between ourselves and Allah. When a report is necessary, prepare it truthfully and respectfully. May our giving help, may its recipients feel respected, and may our hearts be protected from seeking a stage through someone else's hardship. May Allah accept these deeds that still have so many shortcomings. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
