If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, before recording a recipient's face, ask whether documentation is necessary and whether the person is truly willing. Someone needing help may struggle to refuse a giver's request. Consent must therefore be respected without pressure. Reporting can use distribution records, purchase receipts, or images protecting identity, according to the needs and responsibilities of management.

“If it is not published, will others be moved to help?” We may encourage goodness. What needs thought is the form of that invitation. Explain needs and programme results respectfully. Avoid scenes asking someone to cry again or say thank you repeatedly. Assistance should lighten burdens, including the emotional burden of dealing with the person giving.

Imagine a volunteer bringing food parcels to someone's home. Before the parcel is handed over, the camera is already pointed at the recipient's face. The person gives a small smile, unsure whether to refuse or accept. We need sensitivity to the situation. Consent given out of fear of losing help does not necessarily show comfort. Programme coordinators can discuss reporting needs before distribution and find a way to protect identity. If a photograph is needed, explain its use clearly. Do not suddenly post private experiences that were never agreed upon. Help can reach people in an orderly way without forcing them to reveal parts of life they wish to protect.

“But donors ask for evidence.” Evidence can be prepared responsibly, dear friends. Receipt records, quantities, and expenditure can be checked as needed. We can explain why recipients' faces are not the focus of the report. Transparent management must accompany respect for human beings. Imagine someone we love receiving help. Would we be comfortable with their difficulty given an exaggerated headline to attract attention? This question helps examine our choices. We should also be careful when discussing other managers' intentions. What we can improve now is our own practice and the working arrangements for which we are responsible.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Does our documentation still leave recipients free to choose?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Sincerity does not always mean hiding a deed. Some good work requires reporting, announcements, or working before many people. A donation manager must still provide truthful information. What needs examining is whether openness serves the trust or becomes a stage for self-importance. Examining intention is primarily our work upon ourselves, rather than a tool for accusing someone else's heart.

Examine our response when our name is not mentioned too. Are we still glad the help arrived, or deeply disappointed at not appearing in the post? That disappointment can become an opportunity to straighten our intention. We need not stop helping because the intention is imperfect. Keep doing good while correcting the part of the heart that wants admiration.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about distributing assistance while protecting recipients' dignity may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Before acting, ask what purpose we want to preserve. During the deed, perform it properly even if nobody is watching. Afterwards, restrain the wish to retell it for praise. If our intention feels mixed, straighten it again while continuing the good. Sincerity is an exercise continually renewed, giving outward deeds direction while teaching the heart to be content that Allah knows.

For practice, examine one kind of assistance report we usually use. Check which personal information is actually unnecessary. If giving as an individual, try offering one act of help without demanding public thanks. Notice what happens in the heart when nobody knows. If a wish for praise appears, acknowledge it as work to be done in straightening intention. Continue helping while improving purpose and method. We want recipients to feel lighter after assistance arrives. May Allah accept our giving and protect us from taking attention through someone else's hardship.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about distributing assistance while protecting recipients' dignity. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of distributing assistance while protecting recipients' dignity. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Dear friends, let us keep some goodness between ourselves and Allah. When a report is necessary, prepare it truthfully and respectfully. May our giving help, may its recipients feel respected, and may our hearts be protected from seeking a stage through someone else's hardship. May Allah accept these deeds that still have so many shortcomings. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: الْأَعْمَالُ صُوَرٌ قَائِمَةٌ
Deeds are manifest outward forms.
وَأَرْوَاحُهَا وُجُودُ سِرِّ الْإِخْلَاصِ فِيهَا.
Their spirit is the presence of sincerity's essence within them.

11.translation: Bury your existence in the earth of obscurity. What grows without first being buried will not bear its fruit fully.
syarahEn: The drive to be known quickly can outpace our readiness. We have learned only a little, yet want to appear the most knowledgeable. We have just begun serving, yet feel anxious when our name is not mentioned. Ibn 'Ata'illah uses the image of a plant to remind us that mature growth needs a process that often remains unseen.

Al-khumul means being unknown or unobtrusive. It directs attention to willingness to learn without demanding a stage. Idfin means plant or bury, while nataj points to fruit or results. A planted seed has the opportunity to establish roots before bearing fruit. Likewise, knowledge and character need depth before carrying the attention of many people.

A prospective teacher can train through regular learning, accepting correction, and supporting a small group. Service that does not yet attract a crowd still has value. When an opportunity to appear comes, it can be used to meet a need while preserving the habit of learning. This wisdom also applies to those already well known: always leave room for deeds that never become news.

Being unknown need not become a new identity to boast about. Refusing a task the community actually needs also does not automatically demonstrate sincerity. What we practise is readiness to do good without depending on a famous name. Notice whether we still want to help when the work brings no spotlight. As the answer becomes more honest, the roots of devotion are growing. Good fruit is more likely when attention goes towards personal quality and the work's benefit.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, after just a few cooking lessons we may want to open a class immediately. After reading one book, we want everyone to turn to us for answers. Such enthusiasm can feel exciting, but a question needs asking: has our wish to be known become faster than our commitment to learning and improving our ability?

Ibn 'Ata'illah uses the image of a seed planted in the ground. Growth needs a time when something is not yet visible. Khumul means not putting ourselves forward; it is no command to hide every benefit forever. We are trained to grow sufficient roots before becoming preoccupied with displaying fruit. When responsibility expands, there is then something real to sustain it.

Imagine a young person wanting to start a tailoring business. They can begin with simple orders, practise measuring, and learn to resolve complaints. At that stage, praise may be scarce. Yet every corrected stitch is an important part of ability. If a famous name is pursued too quickly, incoming orders may exceed readiness and disappoint customers.

Dear friends, learning often tests patience because the results are not yet ready to display. We still make mistakes, ask questions, and sometimes begin again. That is all right. Someone willing to admit an inability is preserving room to grow. We need not tell a story that makes us appear expert so that our presence feels valuable before friends.

Of course, abilities the community already needs may be used and honestly introduced. What needs preserving is a match between promises and preparation. Explain what we can do, seek guidance in what we have not mastered, and accept correction. A good reputation grows more healthily through trustworthy service than through claims running far ahead of reality.

Let us give ourselves a chance to be students. Choose one ability to pursue and schedule sincere practice. May Allah protect us from rushing for recognition, bring us to good teachers, and bless the process that is not yet visible. When our contribution is needed later, may we be better prepared to serve. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.

Receiving complaints teaches listening. This preparation rarely appears in photographs, but customers feel it deeply. Matching promises to ability protects others while giving the learner room to develop.

“If we keep waiting to be ready, when will we start?” We can begin on a suitable scale, dear congregation. Not every job requires expertise beforehand, but we must be honest about the limits of our ability. Choose a task we can carry and seek guidance where a part has not been mastered. What needs examining is the wish to leap to great recognition without undergoing practice. The seed's image teaches patience in establishing a foundation. It does not require every benefit to remain hidden forever. When an ability is needed, use it faithfully. While serving, keep learning and do not be embarrassed to correct real mistakes.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “Do the promises we offer match the abilities we actually have?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

A prospective teacher can train through regular learning, accepting correction, and supporting a small group. Service that does not yet attract a crowd still has value. When an opportunity to appear comes, it can be used to meet a need while preserving the habit of learning. Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of allowing ability time to grow before seeking recognition, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Being unknown need not become a new identity to boast about. Refusing a task the community actually needs also does not automatically demonstrate sincerity. What we practise is readiness to do good without depending on a famous name. Notice whether we still want to help when the work brings no spotlight. As the answer becomes more honest, the roots of devotion are growing. Good fruit is more likely when attention goes towards personal quality and the work's benefit.

Try choosing one skill and deciding how to practise it this week. Measure progress through better work, rather than only the number of people watching. Seek specific feedback from someone knowledgeable. If the assessment is unpleasant, listen for the part we can use. Parents can help children appreciate practice that has not yet produced a trophy. We learn to say, “This part is more careful now; that part still needs another try.” Support like this makes room for real growth. May our abilities and character be more ready to carry responsibilities when they expand.

Now let us turn the lesson about allowing ability time to grow before seeking recognition into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about allowing ability time to grow before seeking recognition, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us give ourselves a chance to be students. Choose one ability to pursue and schedule sincere practice. May Allah protect us from rushing for recognition, bring us to good teachers, and bless the process that is not yet visible. When our contribution is needed later, may we be better prepared to serve. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: ادْفِنْ وُجُودَكَ فِي أَرْضِ الْخُمُولِ،
Plant your existence in the soil of obscurity.
فَمَا نَبَتَ مِمَّا لَمْ يُدْفَنْ
What grows without first being planted
لَا يَتِمُّ نَتَاجُهُ.
will not bear complete fruit.

12.translation: Nothing benefits the heart like a retreat that leads it into the field of reflection.
syarahEn: Uninterrupted busyness often leaves the heart no time to understand what it is living through. We receive much news and respond to many conversations, then lose the chance to listen to our own condition. This wisdom invites us to make time alone, bringing greater order to our thoughts and giving the heart room to reflect before Allah.

Al-'uzlah means taking some distance or being alone. Here its value is connected to fikrah, reflection. Maydan means a field or space for movement. Retreat becomes beneficial when it opens a field of contemplation: we consider life's direction, weigh choices, and recognize blessings and mistakes. Solitude filled only with daydreams or hatred does not automatically bring clarity.

It can take a simple form. We turn off phone notifications briefly, sit after salah, and review the day's events. Which conversation hurt someone? Which responsibility remains unfinished? Which blessing have we not appreciated? Concrete questions help reflection lead to action, so quiet time does not stop at enjoying an atmosphere.

Family rights and social obligations must still be respected. Solitude need not mean leaving society for a long time. For many people, a short but regular pause is more realistic. After contemplation, return with a decision we can carry out: apologizing, arranging a schedule, or reducing a disruptive habit. In this way, 'uzlah improves how we are present among people. We learn to take enough distance to return with fuller attention and a more aware heart.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, have we ever had a noisy, busy day while the heart felt empty? We wake to messages, eat while watching videos, and read comments before sleep. We know plenty of news but have no time to recognize our own state. Even when someone at home asks a question, our answer is brief because our attention remains on the screen.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains the benefit of 'uzlah that brings the heart into reflection. 'Uzlah means briefly stepping away from distracting bustle. Its purpose is to make room for clear thought. We can begin simply, without neglecting family, work, or social obligations. There is time to be present with people and time to examine our own direction in life.

Imagine ten minutes after the main work is finished. We put down the phone, stop the entertainment, and sit quietly. Ask, “Whom did I hurt earlier? Which blessing did I use well? What task do I keep avoiding?” An honest question is often more useful than adding one more advice video that is immediately forgotten.

“What if silence makes me think of more problems?” Choose a helpful approach, dear congregation. We can write, walk slowly somewhere safe, or read a few lines and reflect. It need not take long. If thoughts feel heavy and disruptive, speak to someone trusted. Quiet space need not be used to force ourselves to face every burden alone.

Dear friends, reflection shows its benefit when something follows it. After recognizing a mistake, choose one improvement. Perhaps apologize to a spouse or make time for a child. If exhaustion is what we discover, arrange help and rest. We learn to listen to our condition so we can return to relationships with others more fully.

Tonight, let us make a small but sincere pause. We do not have to be available for every notification. A heart needs care and responsibilities need thought. May Allah grant clarity in quietness, protect us from distracting busyness, and help us be more fully present for our families. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Tonight, let us make a small but sincere pause. We do not have to be available for every notification. A heart needs care and responsibilities need thought. May Allah grant clarity in quietness, protect us from distracting busyness, and help us be more fully present for our families. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَا نَفَعَ الْقَلْبَ شَيْءٌ مِثْلُ عُزْلَةٍ
Nothing benefits the heart like solitude
يَدْخُلُ بِهَا مَيْدَانَ فِكْرَةٍ.
that brings it into the field of reflection.

13.translation: How can the heart shine while the images of the world remain impressed upon its mirror? How can it journey towards Allah while still shackled by desires? How can it hope to enter nearness to Allah before purifying itself from the impurity of heedlessness? How can it hope to understand subtle mysteries before repenting of its wrongdoings?
syarahEn: The heart may know much advice yet still struggle to follow it. Sometimes the cause is not insufficient information, but an attachment that is too strong. We understand honesty's importance but fear losing profit. We know repentance matters but maintain the same habits. This wisdom pictures these obstacles through a mirror, shackles, and a state needing purification.

Mir'ah means mirror. Images of the world continually clinging to the heart's mirror make clear vision difficult. Mukabbal means shackled, explaining desire's powerful hold. Janabat al-ghaflah is an image of heedlessness that soils the inner self. This expression establishes no new rule of ritual purification; it invites us to cleanse the heart as the body is cleansed from impurity.

Cleansing begins with what is clear. To be more present in salah, reduce habits that continually drag the mind away. To understand advice, stop defending ourselves every time we are corrected. If we have taken someone's rights, restore them. A desire for deep understanding needs willingness to improve the behaviour closest to everyday life.

Repentance gives this process direction. We acknowledge a mistake, leave it, and arrange our steps to make repetition less likely. Change may be gradual, but sincerity appears in actions actually taken. Do not become so occupied with pursuing inner experiences while maintaining small lies. The heart becomes readier for guidance as its obstacles diminish. The light of understanding more readily benefits someone willing to be corrected than someone who merely wants to feel they already understand.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, sometimes the body is already on the prayer mat, but the mind is still arguing in a comment section. We repeat someone's words, prepare a reply, and imagine that person losing. Salah ends and our hand reaches for the phone again. The incident may be far from home, yet the space within the heart feels filled by that argument.

Ibn 'Ata'illah uses the image of the heart's mirror. When its surface is covered by attachments, clarity struggles to grow. He also reminds us of repentance and releasing the shackles of desire. We can bring this lesson to a habit of keeping anger that we continually feed. Each rereading of a comment gives the heat fresh fuel.

Dear friends, defending the truth may indeed be necessary. Yet we need to distinguish explaining an issue from wanting to defeat someone. Does our reply help make the matter clear? Or are we beginning to enjoy insulting? When that happens, attention has shifted. We are speaking about goodness, but our manner damages us and hurts others.

The first step can be simple: stop typing when emotions run high. Save the response, check the information, and decide whether the conversation is still worth continuing. If there is defamation or a threat, use an appropriate reporting channel. We do not have to take part in every debate. Leaving a dead-end conversation sometimes helps protect responsibilities closer to home.

“If I stay silent, will people think I lost?” Dear congregation, our life is larger than one internet group's judgement. A child awaiting attention and unfinished work have real rights over us. Give them space in our minds again. If we have already written insults, remove or correct them, then apologize as appropriate to the circumstances and their effects.

Let us cleanse the heart by reducing what continually soils it. Before the next salah, close unnecessary conversations and settle our attention for a while. May Allah guide our speech, forgive our mistakes in relationships, and give us courage to stop when anger begins taking over. We want to leave a conversation with a heart still able to listen. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “Does our reply clarify the issue or simply aim to make someone else lose?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of releasing online arguments that fill the heart, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Repentance gives this process direction. We acknowledge a mistake, leave it, and arrange our steps to make repetition less likely. Change may be gradual, but sincerity appears in actions actually taken. Do not become so occupied with pursuing inner experiences while maintaining small lies. Practise a pause before sending a comment. Read it again and ask whether we would still say it with the person sitting before us alongside their family. If needed, save the response without sending. Once calm, decide whether there is a clear benefit. Before worship, take some distance from conversations still heating the heart. If the mind returns to them, gently redirect attention without anger towards ourselves. We are improving a habit formed through repetition. May the heart gain room to hear guidance and notice the people truly present around us.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of releasing online arguments that fill the heart again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about releasing online arguments that fill the heart invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us cleanse the heart by reducing what continually soils it. Before the next salah, close unnecessary conversations and settle our attention for a while. May Allah guide our speech, forgive our mistakes in relationships, and give us courage to stop when anger begins taking over. We want to leave a conversation with a heart still able to listen. Amin.

How can the heart shine while the world's images remain attached to its mirror?
أَمْ كَيْفَ يَرْحَلُ إِلَى اللَّهِ وَهُوَ مُكَبَّلٌ بِشَهَوَاتِهِ؟
How can it journey towards Allah while shackled by desires?
أَمْ كَيْفَ يَطْمَعُ أَنْ يَدْخُلَ حَضْرَةَ اللَّهِ وَهُوَ لَمْ يَتَطَهَّرْ مِنْ جَنَابَةِ غَفَلَتِهِ؟
How can it hope to enter closeness with Allah before purifying itself of the impurity of heedlessness?
أَمْ كَيْفَ يَرْجُو أَنْ يَفْهَمَ دَقَائِقَ الْأَسْرَارِ وَهُوَ لَمْ يَتُبْ مِنْ هَفَوَاتِهِ؟
How can it hope to understand subtle secrets before repenting of its mistakes?

14.translation: The whole universe is darkness; it is illuminated through the unveiling of the signs of the presence of the Real within it. Whoever sees the universe without witnessing Him in it, beside it, before it, or after it has indeed lost those lights, and the suns of divine knowledge have been veiled by the clouds of created traces.
syarahEn: The world can be viewed as a collection of things useful only for our wishes. Food is merely something to satisfy hunger, work only a source of money, and people only helpers for our interests. This wisdom invites us to look further, until creation reminds the heart of Allah who creates and sustains it.

Zulmah means darkness. The universe is called dark when it does not lead the heart towards the meaning of its creation. Al-Haqq refers to Allah, the Real, while al-athar means the traces of creation. Shumus al-ma'arif, the suns of knowing, pictures an understanding that illuminates the heart. Language about seeing Allah in or with creation is understood as awareness of the signs of His power, without imagining Allah to be part of an object.

We can begin with what is close. A sip of water involves rain, soil, the body's ability, and help from many people. Awareness of that chain makes gratitude more alive. Seeing the body's order encourages us to care for health as a trust. Seeing someone in difficulty reminds us that the ability to help is also a gift.

Knowledge of natural causes remains useful and can enrich reflection. What we guard against is allowing knowledge to leave the heart feeling in control. We learn how things work while acknowledging our limits. Through the eyes of faith, the world becomes a place for reading guidance and practising devotion. Beauty invites gratitude as well as enjoyment; limitations remind us to seek Allah's help, as well as being something we find difficult.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, at mealtimes we often become busy judging the dishes. Too salty, not spicy enough, or too small a portion. Yet before us is a long journey we rarely consider. Rice is planted, transported, sold, and cooked. That meal arrives through many efforts whose makers we do not all know individually.

In the wisdom about the universe and the light of knowing, Ibn 'Ata'illah invites the heart to see creation while recognizing signs of Allah's power. What we see is more than something to use. Through it, we learn about the Creator's care. This does not mean Allah is inside objects; creation reminds us of Him.

Dear congregation, a plate of rice can train that way of seeing. We remember the soil that produces, available water, and a body still able to receive food. We also remember the person who prepared it. Viewed this way, everyday eating can become an opportunity to give thanks and improve how we treat the blessing before our eyes.

“If the food really does not taste good, can we say so?” Needs can certainly be expressed politely. There is a difference between giving feedback and belittling the cook. We can say, “Perhaps a little less salt tomorrow, please.” That is enough, without mocking or comparing it with someone else's cooking. Gentleness becomes more real when someone at home is tired.

Gratitude also continues in action. Take what we need, store what remains suitable, and avoid wasting food out of pride. When there is an opportunity to share, consider cleanliness and suitability. People receiving assistance deserve good food. We share to respect their needs, rather than merely passing on leftovers we no longer want to touch.

At the next meal, let us pause before complaining. Notice how much goodness brought the dish home. May Allah provide enough for families struggling for food, bless farmers and traders in their work, and make us people who value blessings. May gratitude also be felt in how we speak to the person who cooked. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

phrasesEn: الْكَوْنُ كُلُّهُ ظُلْمَةٌ وَإِنَّمَا أَنَارَهُ ظُهُورُ الْحَقِّ فِيهِ،
The whole universe is darkness; it is illuminated by the unveiling of signs of the Real's presence within it.
فَمَنْ رَأَى الْكَوْنَ وَلَمْ يَشْهَدْهُ فِيهِ أَوْ عِنْدَهُ أَوْ قَبْلَهُ أَوْ بَعْدَهُ
Whoever sees the world without witnessing Him in it, beside it, before it, or after it
فَقَدْ أَعْوَزَهُ وُجُودُ الْأَنْوَارِ،
indeed lacks those lights,
وَحُجِبَتْ عَنْهُ شُمُوسُ الْمَعَارِفِ بِسُحُبِ الْآثَارِ.
and the sun of knowledge of Allah is veiled from them by clouds of creation's traces.

15.translation: Among the signs of His absolute power, glory be to Him, is that He veils you from witnessing Him through something that has no independent existence alongside Him.
syarahEn: Sometimes work, money, or people's judgement feels so large that it absorbs all our attention. We know these are all Allah's creations, yet in practice forget Allah through busyness with creation. This wisdom presents that strangeness as a lesson about limited perception and the greatness of Allah's power.

Qahr means power that overcomes and cannot be resisted. Hajabaka means He veiled you or covered your sight. Laysa bi-mawjudin ma'ahu emphasizes that created beings have no independent existence before Allah. Creation is real as creation, but does not stand alone without His creating and sustaining it. Something wholly dependent can therefore become a veil for a heedless heart.

An example appears when someone feels an entire future is determined by one customer. Honesty begins to be compromised so the customer will not leave. A customer who is also weak and limited has taken too great a place in the heart. The remedy is restoring proper proportion: respect people, conduct business well, and place our highest trust in Allah.

A veil does not always have to be outwardly discarded. Work may remain a responsibility that must be completed. What needs changing is how the heart views it. Pause for supplication before a difficult decision, then ask whether the choice follows religious guidance. Awareness that every creature depends on Allah helps us act with greater freedom. We can relate to the world without giving it absolute power over our sense of security and the direction of our devotion.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, some people check their bank balance as soon as they wake. If the figure has risen, all of life feels secure. If it has fallen, their face stays tense all day. Money certainly needs attention because families have needs. But what if the figure on the screen begins deciding our whole sense of safety, until we struggle to enjoy anything else?

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that something dependent on Allah can veil our attention from Him. Allah's power still encompasses all creation. Wealth has no independent ability to guarantee life. We use it as a means, but the heart may mistakenly treat it as though everything will be safe simply because the amount is large enough.

Dear friends, that veil sometimes appears in small habits. We have prepared a budget but still check the balance every few minutes. We sit at the dining table while the mind keeps calculating possible losses. Family feels distant, although we claim to be thinking about their future. Unfocused worry takes away the togetherness already available.

Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, some people check their bank balance as soon as they wake. If the figure has risen, all of life feels secure. If it has fallen, their face stays tense all day. Money certainly needs attention because families have needs. But what if the figure on the screen begins deciding our whole sense of safety, until we struggle to enjoy anything else?

Dear congregation, before going further, try bringing that story closer to our own lives. We are learning about ordering our attention when a bank balance takes over our sense of safety. Perhaps a similar event passed unnoticed because our day was too full. Now we have time to look back at it calmly. If our experience differs, take the part that fits. Children at school can picture life at home; adults can recall their responsibilities. We are not looking for whoever has made the most mistakes. We want to go home with a clearer view and one action we are able to take. So let us listen while occasionally asking our own hearts a question.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that something dependent on Allah can veil our attention from Him. Allah's power still encompasses all creation. Wealth has no independent ability to guarantee life. We use it as a means, but the heart may mistakenly treat it as though everything will be safe simply because the amount is large enough.

Sometimes work, money, or people's judgement feels so large that it absorbs all our attention. We know these are all Allah's creations, yet in practice forget Allah through busyness with creation. This wisdom presents that strangeness as a lesson about limited perception and the greatness of Allah's power.

Qahr means power that overcomes and cannot be resisted. Hajabaka means He veiled you or covered your sight. Laysa bi-mawjudin ma'ahu emphasizes that created beings have no independent existence before Allah. Creation is real as creation, but does not stand alone without His creating and sustaining it. Something wholly dependent can therefore become a veil for a heedless heart.

Let us hold this understanding carefully, dear friends. Advice about ordering our attention when a bank balance takes over our sense of safety should be read alongside our obligations as servants of Allah and our responsibilities towards others. Feeling peaceful after hearing a talk is certainly pleasant. Yet sound understanding also helps us act when things no longer feel peaceful. That is why explaining the words matters. We gain something to guide our direction, rather than a beautiful impression that soon fades. If we later forget how the term sounds, remember the relationship it explains: how the heart turns to Allah and how our choices touch real life.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, that veil sometimes appears in small habits. We have prepared a budget but still check the balance every few minutes. We sit at the dining table while the mind keeps calculating possible losses. Family feels distant, although we claim to be thinking about their future. Unfocused worry takes away the togetherness already available.

What can we do? Distinguish time spent managing finances from time spent circling anxiety. Record needs and set a reasonable checking schedule. Discuss the situation with a spouse or those involved. Seek help with expenditure if needed. After taking real steps, train the heart to acknowledge that having enough still requires Allah's help.

Someone sits with family, but the same screen keeps lighting the face. The bank balance is opened again though no transaction has occurred for several minutes. When a child asks something, the answer is short. The person feels they are protecting the family's future, yet today's togetherness is slipping away. Dear friends, financial problems can indeed be heavy. We need not minimize them. Precisely because they matter, managing them needs a clear time and honest conversation. Discussing needs with those involved helps more than carrying every thought alone. After checking records, we can allow attention to return to the people sitting before us.

“If I stop checking, I am afraid I will miss something.” Create a checking method suited to the need, dear congregation. Reminders or reasonably orderly records are allowed. What this wisdom examines is a heart that seems able to breathe freely only when the figure keeps rising. Money is an important means, but that means itself depends on many circumstances. Opening the screen more often cannot give complete control. If circumstances really are urgent, seek appropriate help in organizing matters. While making an effort, also tend family relationships and worship, which cannot all be postponed until we feel wealthy.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “After recording our needs does repeatedly checking the balance still help us act?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

An example appears when someone feels an entire future is determined by one customer. Honesty begins to be compromised so the customer will not leave. A customer who is also weak and limited has taken too great a place in the heart. The remedy is restoring proper proportion: respect people, conduct business well, and place our highest trust in Allah.

We need not be embarrassed to want savings, dear congregation. Preparing for needs is a good effort. What we examine is its influence: does saving help us fulfil responsibilities, or make us constantly suspicious and reluctant to fulfil rights? Saved money needs sound management, leaving attention to Allah and family their proper place.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of ordering our attention when a bank balance takes over our sense of safety, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

A veil does not always have to be outwardly discarded. Work may remain a responsibility that must be completed. What needs changing is how the heart views it. Pause for supplication before a difficult decision, then ask whether the choice follows religious guidance. Awareness that every creature depends on Allah helps us act with greater freedom. We can relate to the world without giving it absolute power over our sense of security and the direction of our devotion.

Choose a reasonable time to examine needs and record the next step. Afterwards, try setting the phone aside while eating or talking with family. If worry returns, ask which action has not been taken. If there is no new information, return to the task at hand. This exercise does not guarantee that every difficulty disappears, but may help attention stop being continually drawn into figures. In supplication, acknowledge our need for Allah without treating savings as an absolute guarantee. May we be given enough and clarity in managing the means entrusted to us.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about ordering our attention when a bank balance takes over our sense of safety. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about ordering our attention when a bank balance takes over our sense of safety. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Today, let us choose one period with family without checking figures. Listen to their stories until they finish. We appreciate the wealth available while caring for the life it is intended to support. May Allah grant lawful provision, protect us from greed, and calm our hearts so we can use wealth wisely. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مِمَّا يَدُلُّكَ عَلَى وُجُودِ قَهْرِهِ سُبْحَانَهُ
Among the proofs of His absolute power, glorified is He,
أَنْ حَجَبَكَ عَنْهُ بِمَا لَيْسَ بِمَوْجُودٍ مَعَهُ.
is that He veils you from witnessing Him through something having no independent existence beside Him.

16.translation: How can anything be imagined to veil Him, when He is the One who makes everything manifest?
syarahEn: Everything we see has limits and depends on causes. Objects change, people grow and then weaken, and circumstances do not continue by their own will. This wisdom invites the heart to read that reality. Visible creation should remind us of Allah who brings it into existence, rather than letting attention stop at the surface.

Azhara means to make manifest or make something visible. In azhara kulla shay', everything visible is traced back to Allah's act of creation. Yahjubuhu means to veil Him from the heart's sight. The question invites reflection: how does creation become a covering when its very existence is a sign directing us towards its Creator?

When seeing a harvest, for example, we appreciate the farmer's work and study the weather's influence. At the same time, we realize that the farmer did not create the soil, seed, or ability to work. Knowledge of immediate causes can accompany awareness of Allah. Viewed this way, appreciation of human effort does not become an assumption that people stand without help.

The practical exercise is to add grateful awareness to ordinary experiences. When enjoying food, remember that the ability to obtain and digest it is also a gift. When work succeeds, acknowledge the means available before we began trying. We need not wait for an extraordinary experience to remember Allah. Creation around us already provides daily material for reflection, if attention is willing to move from the visible towards recognition of its Creator's power and generosity.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, planting something in a pot can give a slow but clear lesson. We put in a seed, water it, and wait. Tomorrow we look again; it has not grown. We feel like opening the soil to check. But digging it up every day disrupts growth. There is a part we perform and a process we must respect.

Ibn 'Ata'illah asks how creation can veil knowledge of Allah when Allah makes everything manifest. Even a simple plant's existence can remind us of His power. We prepare a place and care, but do not create life from ourselves. This awareness teaches both perseverance and humility in effort.

Dear congregation, children learning to garden can be invited to notice changes in leaves, the need for water, and light's influence. Parents need not give a complicated explanation. Simply invite them to see how life needs many connected conditions. We learn to care for creation while acknowledging Allah's generosity in providing the foundation for human effort.

This lesson also touches how we raise children. We want a child to change immediately after one reminder. If that does not happen, we keep digging up the mistake with the same questions. Yet habits require time, example, and a supportive atmosphere. Parents still guide, but cannot force all growth to follow their personal anxiety.

“If we leave them alone, will they keep making mistakes?” Caring differs from leaving someone unattended. We establish clear boundaries, repeat explanations calmly, and evaluate our guidance. If difficulties arise, seek advice from the right person. As plants need different conditions, children need attention to age and ability too. We cannot make every learning process identical.

Let us take one lesson from the pot outside: care sincerely, then watch growth patiently. May Allah guide our hands to protect life, soften our teaching, and protect children from demands beyond their capacity. May every small change make gratitude easier and our hearts humbler. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

For practice, choose one of a child's habits to support. Decide what example to give and what small help will make it easier. Then allow a chance to try without commenting on every movement. If a mistake happens, teach again the part not yet understood. Those who garden can begin by caring for one plant according to its needs. Both invite us to observe creation attentively. We do the part available, then acknowledge that life and growth require Allah's generosity. May dedication be accompanied by patience and gratitude, so effort does not become a demand to control the entire process.

Now let us turn the lesson about nurturing growth while acknowledging the limits of control into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. phrasesEn: كَيْفَ يُتَصَوَّرُ أَنْ يَحْجُبَهُ شَيْءٌ
How could anything be imagined to veil Him,
وَهُوَ الَّذِي أَظْهَرَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ؟
when He is the One manifesting all things?

17.translation: How can anything be imagined to veil Him, when He is known through everything?

Dear congregation, when a parcel arrives on time, we readily say, “Alhamdulillah.” But does the person delivering it also feel our thanks? Sometimes the courier stands at the gate while we answer irritably. We acknowledge that blessings come from Allah, yet treat harshly the person through whom they arrive.

The wisdom about Allah being known through everything invites us to see creation as a sign. Everyday encounters can open awareness of His care. Those who help remain human, with limitations. Yet through their work, our needs are met. Recognizing Allah's help should make us more courteous towards the people working to bring that goodness.

Dear friends, imagine a cleaner who arrives before a room is used. When we enter, everything is tidy. We may not know the person's name and feel cleanliness happened by itself. Yet effort, time, and a tired body stand behind that comfort. A heart aware of blessings tries to notice work often overlooked.

“What if the service really is wrong?” A complaint may be expressed clearly. Name the problem, ask about a solution, and avoid personal insults. We can be firm without stripping someone's dignity. If the mistake was not theirs, do not pour all our anger onto them. Service involves many parts, so complaints need an appropriate route.

Dear congregation, children learn this attitude from adults. If we tell them to be polite at home but shout at a parking attendant ourselves, the example becomes confusing. Try making sincere greetings and thanks a habit. We do it because human work deserves appreciation and people's rights need protecting, rather than to obtain special treatment.

The next time we meet someone helping us, look at them respectfully. Say thank you and fulfil any right that is our responsibility. May Allah bless workers whose names are often unmentioned, provide enough for their families, and make our gratitude felt through good treatment of others. Amin.

Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

When facing an event, ask what devotion is possible within it. Do we need to give thanks, help, ask forgiveness, or study more diligently? The question makes reflection bear fruit in behaviour. Nature and life experience become paths to knowing Allah when they lead us towards obedience. The heart collects more than stories about events; it learns greater awareness that life proceeds within Allah's knowledge and care.

Try remembering one job that makes our day easier but is rarely mentioned. Next time, say thank you directly or take better care of the result. If there is a complaint, prepare words naming the problem and desired resolution without insults. Invite children to notice people working behind the comfort, so they do not assume service simply appears. We still acknowledge Allah as the Giver of blessings. Precisely that acknowledgement invites us to treat the means through which blessings arrive with better manners and greater care.

Dear congregation, if we want to take one task home from this discussion of expressing gratitude by respecting those who bring blessings, choose something we can truly do. There is no need to announce it now. We can decide after getting home, when we have a fuller picture of our circumstances. Make the step small enough for us to know when it will be done. If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of expressing gratitude by respecting those who bring blessings. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

The next time we meet someone helping us, look at them respectfully. Say thank you and fulfil any right that is our responsibility. May Allah bless workers whose names are often unmentioned, provide enough for their families, and make our gratitude felt through good treatment of others. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

18.translation: How can anything be imagined to veil Him, when signs of His greatness appear in everything?

The ability to breathe, changing seasons, and the body's limitations can invite reflection. This wisdom directs attention towards every created thing so that familiarity does not rob us of wonder and gratitude.

The same applies to the body: scientific understanding can increase our responsibility to care for it. Reflection becomes more useful when followed by right action towards creation.

We can train attention by becoming less hurried. Notice one blessing usually passed over, then connect it with a real expression of gratitude. If we enjoy clean surroundings, help maintain them. If granted health, use it for good before weakness comes. Seeing Allah's signs then goes beyond expressions of wonder. Ibn 'Ata'illah invites us to see signs of Allah's greatness in everything. A faithful perspective makes room to recognize that reality extends beyond personal needs. We acknowledge the difficulty felt while learning that creation proceeds through relationships not all visible from our own front yard.

When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.

We are seeing that here in the matter of broadening our view when rain changes our plans. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.

When rain begins, someone runs to collect the washing while grumbling. Once the clothes are safe, a neighbour is seen putting out a bucket to collect water for plants. The same event meets different needs. Dear friends, we may acknowledge inconvenience without making our own interest the measure of the whole event. A wider perspective can begin once urgent needs are handled. We notice previously dry soil or water needed by many creatures. Such reflection makes room for gratitude and reminds us that shared life is far larger than the small plan we are making.

“What if the rain causes losses?” Distinguish material for personal reflection from how we support victims, dear congregation. Flooded families need safety and appropriate assistance, rather than a comment that they should see the bright side sooner. We do not know the full weight of their loss. Listening to complaints and helping with real needs is a fitting response. Meanwhile, neighbours can check drains and follow reliable information. Remembering Allah's power invites responsibility for the part we can perform. We do not use the language of tawakkul to leave problems that require shared action unattended.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “How can we recognize rain's benefits while caring for those affected?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about broadening our view when rain changes our plans may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. If granted health, use it for good before weakness comes. Seeing Allah's signs then goes beyond expressions of wonder. When it next rains, attend to safety first. Once circumstances allow, check whether a neighbour needs help. For personal reflection, recall one benefit of water rarely considered while collecting washing. Parents can discuss plants and creatures' needs with children without minimizing disaster victims' suffering. We learn to hold two concerns together: gratitude for blessings and action when difficulties arise. May rain remind us of the breadth of Allah's care and strengthen concern for the life around us.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of broadening our view when rain changes our plans again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about broadening our view when rain changes our plans. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us ask for beneficial rain and protection for those in difficulty. May Allah broaden our view so every event is not measured by our own comfort or inconvenience. May we care for the environment and come to help when water needed by life also calls for shared vigilance. Amin.

phrasesEn: كَيْفَ يُتَصَوَّرُ أَنْ يَحْجُبَهُ شَيْءٌ
How could anything be imagined to veil Him,
وَهُوَ الَّذِي ظَهَرَ فِي كُلِّ شَيْءٍ؟
when signs of His majesty appear in every thing?

19.translation: How can anything be imagined to veil Him, when He is manifest to everything? How can anything be imagined to veil Him, when He existed and was manifest before the existence of everything?
syarahEn: We know many things through a sequence in time. We see something born, develop, and end. That habit can make the mind imagine Allah as part of a sequence of objects. This wisdom restores our understanding: Allah existed before all creation, and His existence does not depend on anything newly appearing.

Al-Zahir means the Manifest, or the One who makes signs of His power apparent. Qabla wujudi kulli shay' means before the existence of everything. Qabla helps emphasize that creation does not precede Allah. Yet Allah is not measured as a creature occupying one portion of time. Time itself belongs to the created order, while Allah needs no such order to exist.

This lesson calms a heart excessively afraid of losing a means of support. Before we knew a particular job, Allah was already sustaining life. Before someone became our helper, Allah had provided many other avenues of help. We still value work and human assistance, but do not treat the loss of one means as the end of all hope.

When circumstances change, remember the difference between means that come and go and Allah who depends on none of them. Continue making an effort, receive advice, and remain open to another path. Reflection on Allah's existence before creation should bear a simple steadfastness: the heart does not make something temporary absolute. We learn to welcome help gratefully and face partings patiently, because the ground of our devotion remains even as life's forms keep changing.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, recall a childhood photograph still kept somewhere. Once we could not find our own food, did not know the way home, and could not even express needs clearly. Yet life continued through help that came. As adults, we sometimes feel every success arose from our own strength. That childhood photograph quietly challenges our arrogance.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that Allah existed before all creation. He does not depend on anything newly appearing. We, who have a beginning, need creation and care. This awareness helps us place ourselves properly, especially when we begin to feel everything only improved after we arrived and took charge.

Dear friends, families sometimes hear the words, “Without me, this home would have fallen apart.” Perhaps we have sacrificed much. That deserves appreciation and the burden needs sharing. Yet words that seem to erase every other contribution can hurt others. Much goodness came before our role, including from people no longer with us.

Looking at old photographs can be an exercise in remembering. Who cared for us? Who taught small things until we could be independent? Some relationships are warm, while some family experiences are painful. We need not force every memory to be beautiful. Simply acknowledge that today's ability to live did not arise from personal effort alone.

“Then how do we value our own hard work?” We may acknowledge our effort. That acknowledgement can accompany thanks and willingness to receive help. When leading a family, listen to input. When rest is needed, discuss sharing tasks. People aware of being supported can build life together more easily than those carrying everything while blaming others.

Let us humble our hearts by remembering how long we have been receiving. May Allah have mercy on those who cared for us, heal family wounds, and keep us from arrogance through feeling we have contributed most. As we age, may our ability to acknowledge help grow and our treatment of others become gentler. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Try remembering one act of help that enabled something we can still do today. If the person is reachable and circumstances permit, express thanks reasonably. If not, pray for their good. Within family, replace words erasing every contribution with a more honest explanation of needs. We may say we are tired and ask to share tasks without claiming to be life's only support. This change in words gives others room to take responsibility too. May remembering help make us humble and more ready to assist the generation learning to stand.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

when He is manifest to all things?
