وَهُوَ الظَّاهِرُ قَبْلَ وُجُودِ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ؟
when He existed and was manifest before all things existed?

20.translation: How can anything be imagined to veil Him, when He is more manifest than everything?
syarahEn: What is close to our eyes easily feels most real. We see accounts, positions, and people's judgements daily, so regard them as deciding life's security. This wisdom invites the heart to remember a more fundamental reality: every object and circumstance depends on Allah who creates and sustains it.

Azhar means more manifest or clearer. It highlights the clarity of guidance concerning Allah for a heart that knows Him, rather than the appearance of a form comparable with objects. Min kulli shay' means than everything. The comparison restores changing, limited creatures to their proper position before Allah, upon whom the existence of all creation rests.

Imagine someone so confident in a job position that lawful and unlawful boundaries are ignored. When that position is threatened, security collapses too. This wisdom helps the person see that a means considered utterly solid has many limits. That awareness may encourage both good work and deeper trust in Allah.

To practise this, notice what we most fear losing. Acknowledge its usefulness reasonably, then ask whether fear has displaced obligations or harmed relationships. If so, begin restoring proportion. Pray, maintain right action, and train ourselves to accept the limits of worldly means. The heart becomes calmer when its whole worth is not handed to something that can disappear. With faith, the visible is still valued without making us forget the One who sustains it.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, when a child asks, “Why should we care if nobody sees?” we have an opportunity to learn together. Many valuable things do not always appear as visible objects. Trust, affection, and responsibility are recognized through effects and actions. If we believe only in what can be displayed, life's measures become impoverished.

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes Allah as more manifest than everything. This does not mean imagining Allah as an object seen by the eye. The heart is invited to realize that creation's existence shows its need for the Creator. Allah does not depend on human recognition. We need guidance so we do not stop at viewing life only through outward forms.

Dear congregation, imagine a child returning excess change. There is no camera and perhaps no reward. Yet the action still has worth. The seller avoids a loss, the child practises honesty, and trust is preserved. If we praise only widely noticed actions, children may learn that what matters is looking good before others.

Parents can therefore ask a deeper question: “Whose rights were protected just now?” Such questions help children notice an action's consequences. We also need to give an example. Pay what is owed even when the person forgets to ask. Admit a mistake even when it has not been discovered. Teaching feels stronger when adults practise it.

“What if we are never appreciated?” Wanting appreciation is human. We may express that need properly. Yet do not let people's recognition become the sole reason for doing right. Some trusts still need protecting in an empty room and when our name is unmentioned. Allah knows what escapes human attention.

Let us perform one good deed that needs no audience. It can be as simple as returning an item or tidying facilities after use. May Allah enliven our awareness of faith, help us see meaning behind actions, and teach our children through honest examples. May what is hidden from people remain well guarded before Him. Amin.

Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, when a child asks, “Why should we care if nobody sees?” we have an opportunity to learn together. Many valuable things do not always appear as visible objects. Trust, affection, and responsibility are recognized through effects and actions. If we believe only in what can be displayed, life's measures become impoverished.

Dear congregation, before going further, try bringing that story closer to our own lives. We are learning about maintaining goodness even when nobody sees. Perhaps a similar event passed unnoticed because our day was too full. Now we have time to look back at it calmly. If our experience differs, take the part that fits. Children at school can picture life at home; adults can recall their responsibilities. We are not looking for whoever has made the most mistakes. We want to go home with a clearer view and one action we are able to take. So let us listen while occasionally asking our own hearts a question.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes Allah as more manifest than everything. This does not mean imagining Allah as an object seen by the eye. The heart is invited to realize that creation's existence shows its need for the Creator. Allah does not depend on human recognition. We need guidance so we do not stop at viewing life only through outward forms.

What is close to our eyes easily feels most real. We see accounts, positions, and people's judgements daily, so regard them as deciding life's security. This wisdom invites the heart to remember a more fundamental reality: every object and circumstance depends on Allah who creates and sustains it.

Azhar means more manifest or clearer. It highlights the clarity of guidance concerning Allah for a heart that knows Him, rather than the appearance of a form comparable with objects. Min kulli shay' means than everything. The comparison restores changing, limited creatures to their proper position before Allah, upon whom the existence of all creation rests.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with maintaining goodness even when nobody sees. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, imagine a child returning excess change. There is no camera and perhaps no reward. Yet the action still has worth. The seller avoids a loss, the child practises honesty, and trust is preserved. If we praise only widely noticed actions, children may learn that what matters is looking good before others.

Parents can therefore ask a deeper question: “Whose rights were protected just now?” Such questions help children notice an action's consequences. We also need to give an example. Pay what is owed even when the person forgets to ask. Admit a mistake even when it has not been discovered. Teaching feels stronger when adults practise it.

That child receives too much change. The seller is already serving someone else and seems unaware of the mistake. The child could go home without correction. Yet the child pauses, counts again, and returns the excess. Dear friends, parents can use this simple event to talk about rights. Do not hurry to photograph it and make praise the centre of the story. Ask what prompted the return. Listen, then explain that the money still belonged to someone else even though the seller forgot. The child learns the connection between action and responsibility, including when recognition from others is unavailable.

“Without praise, will the child remain motivated?” Reasonable appreciation is still allowed, dear congregation. We can say we are pleased that honesty was preserved. What we avoid is making every good action feel entitled to a stage. Adults learn the same lesson. We pay obligations when someone forgets to ask and admit errors before discovery. Trust does not always take the form of an object, but honesty's effects can be felt. Discussion about signs leading to knowledge of Allah also needs correct understanding. We recognize guidance through creation without equating Allah with a form that can be pointed out before our eyes.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Whose rights still need protecting when nobody knows what we do?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Imagine someone so confident in a job position that lawful and unlawful boundaries are ignored. When that position is threatened, security collapses too. This wisdom helps the person see that a means considered utterly solid has many limits. That awareness may encourage both good work and deeper trust in Allah.

“What if we are never appreciated?” Wanting appreciation is human. We may express that need properly. Yet do not let people's recognition become the sole reason for doing right. Some trusts still need protecting in an empty room and when our name is unmentioned. Allah knows what escapes human attention.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about maintaining goodness even when nobody sees may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

To practise this, notice what we most fear losing. Acknowledge its usefulness reasonably, then ask whether fear has displaced obligations or harmed relationships. If so, begin restoring proportion. Pray, maintain right action, and train ourselves to accept the limits of worldly means. The heart becomes calmer when its whole worth is not handed to something that can disappear. With faith, the visible is still valued without making us forget the One who sustains it.

For practice, choose one small obligation easily postponed because nobody is watching. Fulfil it properly without waiting for repeated reminders. When supporting children, ask whose rights will be protected, then demonstrate through our own action. There is no need to set a trap to test a child's honesty. We build habits through trustworthy relationships. After doing good, direct thanks to Allah who grants ability. May attention to what is not displayed broaden our measure of goodness beyond the number of people who know about it.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about maintaining goodness even when nobody sees. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of maintaining goodness even when nobody sees. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us perform one good deed that needs no audience. It can be as simple as returning an item or tidying facilities after use. May Allah enliven our awareness of faith, help us see meaning behind actions, and teach our children through honest examples. May what is hidden from people remain well guarded before Him. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: كَيْفَ يُتَصَوَّرُ أَنْ يَحْجُبَهُ شَيْءٌ
How could anything be imagined to veil Him,
وَهُوَ أَظْهَرُ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ؟
when He is more manifest than all things?

21.translation: How can anything be imagined to veil Him, when He is the One and nothing accompanies Him?
syarahEn: We declare that Allah is One, yet the heart sometimes divides its highest trust among many things. Money is thought certain to save us, a particular person always able to help, and personal ability treated as an absolute guarantee. This wisdom invites us to put the heart's reliance in order so that affirming tawhid truly affects how we live.

Al-Wahid means the One. Laysa ma'ahu shay' emphasizes that nothing accompanies Allah as a rival or independently existing power. Creatures exist because they are created and continually need Him. Their existence therefore adds nothing to Allah's power and diminishes none of His oneness. Tawhid preserves the fundamental distinction between the Creator and everything created.

In daily life, we still use money, consult experts, and receive help from friends. These are means worth appreciating. What we preserve is the conviction that means have no absolute power. A doctor seeks to treat according to knowledge, while healing is still sought from Allah. This awareness also makes us humbler when we are the person asked for help.

Try examining a decision we find hardest to make. Are we abandoning what is right through fear of losing one means of support? If so, return attention to Allah and seek a lawful way still possible. Strengthening tawhid does not mean ceasing to relate to people. It makes those relationships healthier, because respect does not become servitude and need does not drive us to sacrifice principles Allah has commanded.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, sometimes we are excessively afraid of someone. A manager can decide a work assessment, a major customer reduce orders, or an influential person close an opportunity. We say, “If that person dislikes me, I am finished.” Such fear can make us sacrifice boundaries we already understand well.

The wisdom about Allah's oneness reminds us that nothing is His rival. People have limited authority and still depend on Allah. Awareness of tawhid helps us respect someone's role without regarding that person as absolute ruler over our entire future. We seek a way carefully while keeping the heart's reliance on Allah.

For example, a worker is asked to approve an untruthful report and fears losing a job. That fear is real, so we should not lightly say, “Just refuse.” Evidence, support, and livelihood planning may be needed. Yet amid that effort, do not let the assumption that one person controls everything make every boundary feel permissible to cross.

Dear friends, tawhid can strengthen a quiet courage. We assess choices, seek advice, and find an appropriate way to express an objection. If there are threats, protection should be sought through available channels. We do not have to challenge recklessly to prove faith. Courage can also take the form of small, orderly steps taken with trusted people.

Examine the sentence often appearing in the heart. Do we say, “My provision lies only in that person's hands”? Replace it with a more accurate acknowledgement: the person has a role, while Allah remains the source of help. This perspective does not instantly remove problems, but may open the mind to choices previously hidden by fear.

Let us ask for courage to preserve what is right and wisdom in pursuing it. May Allah protect people under pressure, provide for their families, and bring them safe support. May our respect for people remain within proper bounds, so the heart does not lose its freedom to obey Him. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, we need to respect the situation's weight. Support can begin by listening to facts and helping identify safe choices. The worker can seek appropriate assistance, understand the proper task, or carefully prepare livelihood plans. We do not demand a shouted challenge to prove courage. Tawhid helps the heart avoid making one person the absolute owner of the future. From that conviction, orderly steps can be sought without justifying a wrongful command.

Acknowledging its limits helps us think more clearly than endlessly repeating, “My life is certainly over.” If there is a real threat, protection should still be sought from authorities or appropriate support. Do not carry everything alone when help is available. We also need care in advising someone vulnerable. Words easily spoken from safety may not be enough to help a person under pressure.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “What can help us preserve boundaries when we fear someone powerful?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of facing human influence without treating it as control over everything, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Try writing the issue factually: what request was made, which part is wrong, and what help is needed. Use the record within our authority and needs, rather than spreading private faults carelessly. Then identify one suitable person to consult. In supplication, ask for courage accompanied by wisdom. Those holding positions should examine whether others feel safe bringing a valid objection to us. Power is a trust to exercise with good manners, because those working under us retain rights and dignity.

Now let us turn the lesson about facing human influence without treating it as control over everything into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about facing human influence without treating it as control over everything, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us ask for courage to preserve what is right and wisdom in pursuing it. May Allah protect people under pressure, provide for their families, and bring them safe support. May our respect for people remain within proper bounds, so the heart does not lose its freedom to obey Him. Amin.

How could anything be imagined to veil Him,
وَهُوَ الْوَاحِدُ الَّذِي لَيْسَ مَعَهُ شَيْءٌ؟
when He is One and nothing accompanies Him?

22.translation: How can anything be imagined to veil Him, when He is nearer to you than everything?
syarahEn: When facing a problem, we can feel completely alone. Even those closest may not understand, while the mind finds nowhere to rest. This wisdom reminds us that no part of our condition escapes Allah's knowledge. His nearness opens room for honest supplication and fulfilling responsibilities without feeling abandoned.

Min kulli shay' means than everything, including the means we have considered most understanding of us. Even someone who loves us deeply remains limited in knowledge and ability.

Someone struggling to speak about sadness can begin speaking to Allah through supplication. Beautiful sentences are not required for exhaustion to be known. Afterwards, support can still be sought from family or someone with expertise. Awareness of Allah gives an inward foundation to the effort of finding appropriate help.

This nearness also nurtures responsibility. Actions hidden from people remain known to Allah, so we learn honesty without supervision. Thus the wisdom contains both reassurance and training in good manners. We may feel weak without hiding it before Allah, while still striving to improve our actions. A heart aware of this loving watchfulness can move through life more openly, humbly, and sincerely.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, our phones offer an option to delete messages. A small mistake in sending, and we quickly find the button. Yet that ease can make us feel all speech can be put right by removing the trace. The reader may already be hurt. There are also hidden conversations unknown to family that still affect our honesty.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us of Allah's nearness to His servants. This is not a physical distance like that between objects. We recognize His knowledge, watchfulness, and help encompassing our condition. Private space therefore remains a place for honouring a trust. When no person sees, our responsibility to Allah does not disappear.

Dear congregation, we can practise this through speech in small conversations. Before sending, ask whether the information is true, necessary, and addressed to the right person. If it is only material for laughter, better withhold it.

“What if I have already sent it?” Stop its spread and correct false information. If someone is affected, seek to repair the harm as circumstances allow. Do not merely hope others forget while maintaining the same habit. We can learn to apologize without adding excuses that shift blame to the person hurt by our words.

Awareness of Allah's watchfulness should guide us, rather than leave us continually terrorized by fear. We can still repent and improve choices. Private space can even be where goodness grows: praying for someone, sending help, or offering sincere support. The same phone can nurture relationships when the heart becomes more careful.

Tonight, let us examine one conversation that needs stopping or improving. May Allah help us guard speech in public and private, conceal faults for which we repent, and grant courage to repair mistakes' effects. May nearness to Him make us more honest, gentle, and responsible towards others. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

For practice, choose one kind of message to check more carefully before forwarding from now on. If unsure about truth or benefit, withhold it first. If harm has already been caused, seek a way to apologize and repair it without widening its spread. Parents can model mistakes in sending or accusing: admit them calmly, then correct them. We want children to see that responsibility remains even when a mistake can be hidden from some people. May private conversations become safer spaces and our speech leave fewer wounds.

Dear congregation, if we want to take one task home from this discussion of preserving honesty in hidden conversations, choose something we can truly do. There is no need to announce it now. We can decide after getting home, when we have a fuller picture of our circumstances. Make the step small enough for us to know when it will be done. If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of preserving honesty in hidden conversations that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Tonight, let us examine one conversation that needs stopping or improving. May Allah help us guard speech in public and private, conceal faults for which we repent, and grant courage to repair mistakes' effects. May nearness to Him make us more honest, gentle, and responsible towards others. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

How could anything be imagined to veil Him,
وَهُوَ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ؟
when He is nearer to you than all things?

23.translation: How can anything be imagined to veil Him, when without Him nothing would exist?
syarahEn: We readily see a connection between effort and results, then feel that everything proceeds through its own strength. Yet long before effort begins, there are a body, time, materials, and abilities we did not create. This wisdom directs attention towards all existence's dependence on Allah, down to its most basic foundation.

Lawlahu means were it not for Him. Ma kana wujudu kulli shay' means there would be no existence of anything. The construction emphasizes that creatures cannot bring themselves into being. Even after creation, they are never independent of Allah's care. Human success at work takes place within a life already granted.

This reflection can change how we speak about achievement. A person may acknowledge working hard and taking responsibility for choices. At the same time, they remember learning opportunities, health, and help that made the work possible. That acknowledgement restrains arrogance without extinguishing the desire to develop.

If we feel we contributed most, pause and recall who and what helped the work happen. Then look deeper: all those means also depend on Allah. Respond with practical gratitude by using ability honestly and benefiting others. We become more open to correction when we understand that we are not the source of every good. Devotion grows more healthily because achievement is received as a trust to care for.

Dear congregation, only when the tap stops do we realize how many tasks depend on water. Bathing is delayed, washing piles up, and cooking becomes difficult. While water flows, we rarely think about it. Sometimes it is wasted because we assume it is always available. Something close can lose its place in our gratitude through frequent use.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that all existence needs Allah. Without Him, creation would not exist. Nor do creatures become independent after being created. This awareness invites us to notice needs continually accompanying life, including through very ordinary means. We care for water while acknowledging that human ability still requires Allah's sustaining care.

Dear friends, gratitude for water can begin with how we use it. Close the tap when there is enough, repair leaks, and avoid polluting water sources. If facilities are shared, think of the next user. A clean wudu area helps someone else worship. These simple actions show gratitude's direct connection with responsibility.

“I pay for my own water. Why should its use be limited?” Payment gives a right of use according to the arrangements, but does not remove the responsibility to preserve blessings. Other people's needs connect with the same environment. Children also learn from our habits. Seeing taps left open daily can teach them that waste is normal and needs no thought.

Dear congregation, we need not wait for shortage to begin caring. When the means are available, that is a good time to improve habits. If a neighbour lacks water, help can match our ability and local needs. Ask first, then assist usefully. Do not let a wish to help ignore their circumstances.

Tomorrow, when opening the tap, remember that our life is continually sustained. May Allah provide enough for those lacking clean water, bless people supplying facilities for them, and protect us from waste. May dependence on Allah make our hands more careful with the blessings within reach. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

In the matter of caring for water we often assume will always be available, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

The step is simple but helps gratitude appear in action. May we be given wisdom in using available blessings and care for those whose needs connect with the same source.

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about caring for water we often assume will always be available invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. wordsEn: and were it not for Him
phrasesEn: كَيْفَ يُتَصَوَّرُ أَنْ يَحْجُبَهُ شَيْءٌ
How could anything be imagined to veil Him,
وَلَوْلَاهُ مَا كَانَ وُجُودُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ؟
when without Him nothing would exist?

24.translation: How astonishing that existence should appear within non-existence! How can what has a beginning remain before the One whose existence has no beginning?
syarahEn: Everything we possess once did not exist. Our bodies were not present before birth, abilities form through a process, and ownership can change hands. Allah differs from all these creatures with a beginning. This wisdom invites us to weigh that distinction so the world's apparent greatness does not make the heart forget the source of its existence.

Al-hadith means something new or having a beginning. Al-qidam refers to Allah's attribute of having no beginning. Al-'adam means non-existence. The image of existence appearing within non-existence emphasizes the wonder of creation: what has no existence of its own is brought into being. Creatures remain real as creation, but cannot be placed on a level with Allah who needs no creator.

Its effect is felt in how we regard wealth, position, or bodily strength. All have a beginning, change, and may end. Recognizing these limits helps us use blessings appropriately. We may nurture a growing business without staking honesty as though the business alone determines life's worth.

Reflect on one thing we once did not have, which then arrived through many causes. Did it make us more grateful or feel more powerful? This question brings a seemingly lofty discussion into everyday life. Knowing the distinction between Creator and creation should produce humility. We appreciate blessings while present, fulfil their associated rights, and learn to accept change with awareness that no human possession has absolute permanence or independence.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, there is a small moment when we look in the mirror and find a new grey hair. We laugh, yet quietly feel time moving quickly. Once we ran everywhere; now the body tires more easily. Ageing can make people fear losing worth, especially if appreciation has seemed dependent on appearance and strength.

Ibn 'Ata'illah distinguishes creatures with a beginning from Allah who has no beginning. We change because we are limited. Allah does not undergo creatures' changes and needs. This lesson in tawhid helps us accept that being human means growth as well as diminishing ability. We care for ourselves without demanding the body remain in one state forever.

Dear congregation, accepting age does not mean neglecting health. We still move according to ability, eat reasonably, and seek help when needed. Yet hating every sign of ageing can leave life continually fighting the mirror. A changing face does not erase experience, affection, or opportunities for good still available today.

For younger people, avoid using parents' age to belittle them. If they understand a device more slowly, explain patiently. Once we learned many things through their repetition. Family relationships grow warm when changing ability receives adjustment rather than mockery. We too are moving towards greater age.

“What if I feel no longer needed?” Try discussing the need to be involved. We could share experience, accompany grandchildren, tend plants, or help activities suited to our strength. A role can change without losing meaning. We need not force ourselves to do everything as before to remain valued in family and community.

Let us look more kindly at bodily change. May Allah bless the years still available, help us care for health, and preserve relationships between generations. May the strong be gentle in supporting others and those growing weak still feel respected. We live our limited time through devotion that remains possible. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

phrasesEn: يَا عَجَبًا كَيْفَ يَظْهَرُ الْوُجُودُ فِي الْعَدَمِ،
How astonishing that existence should appear within non-existence!
أَمْ كَيْفَ يَثْبُتُ الْحَادِثُ مَعَ مَنْ لَهُ وَصْفُ الْقِدَمِ؟
How can something originated endure before the One whose attribute is beginninglessness?

25.translation: Whoever wishes to bring into a moment something other than what Allah has manifested in it has left no ignorance within himself unexpressed.
syarahEn: Some exhaustion comes from a problem, and additional exhaustion comes from continually refusing the reality that it has happened. We repeat if only without finding an action to take. Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that wanting to force the present into a completely different reality can reveal ignorance of our position.

Al-jahl means ignorance or failure to recognize the limits of knowledge. Yuhditha means to bring something about. Al-waqt refers to the moment being lived. This wisdom addresses a heart wanting to produce reality according to its wishes when an event has already arrived. The expression leaving no ignorance is a strong rebuke to making personal desire absolute before Allah's decree.

For example, goods have already been damaged through improper storage. We still need to find the cause and improve the procedure. Yet remaining angry because today is not the day we wanted merely uses up energy. Acceptance begins by acknowledging that the damage really exists, then choosing a useful response. If someone made a mistake, their responsibility still needs resolving.

Accepting an event does not mean approving injustice or ceasing to change circumstances. Seeing reality clearly enables us to protect victims, repair losses, and prevent repetition. What we release is an inward argument with a past that cannot be repeated. We ask for strength, acknowledge limits, and take available steps. Patience then becomes conscious action, rather than merely suppressing complaints without direction.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, have we prepared a family outing carefully, only for circumstances to change suddenly? Food is cooked and children have woken early, but heavy rain makes the road unsuitable. Someone immediately becomes angry with everyone. Yet the family is disappointed too. An event changing the plan is then followed by words making the atmosphere at home heavier.

Ibn 'Ata'illah rebukes the desire to force a moment to show something different from the reality Allah has brought. We often struggle to accept that an event has already happened. The heart keeps shouting, “It should not be like this!” Energy is spent protesting circumstances while an opportunity to respond better passes unused before us.

Dear friends, accepting reality begins by naming it honestly. Today it is raining; the journey needs postponing. Then consider available actions. Perhaps the food can be enjoyed together at home. Perhaps a new time can be chosen after checking conditions. Disappointment may still be felt, but we need not surrender all our behaviour to it.

“If we accept everything, will we become passive?” We may still improve plans and work for change. What we accept is present reality as our starting point. If preparation was negligent, examine that once things are calm. Blaming a child for a cancelled event does not make the road safe. Action needs directing towards an issue we can actually address.

This lesson looks small, dear congregation, yet is very useful in family life. Many arguments grow because we are unprepared to accept small disruptions. When an adult can say, “We are disappointed; now let us find another option,” a child learns to face change. The child sees that plans matter and also witnesses love continuing when plans change.

Let us train the heart through one change faced today. Pause before responding, then choose helpful words. May Allah protect our families when travelling, open our hearts when plans are delayed, and grant wisdom to arrange new steps. May accepting reality become easier without our ceasing to make an effort. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah rebukes the desire to force a moment to show something different from the reality Allah has brought. We often struggle to accept that an event has already happened. The heart keeps shouting, “It should not be like this!” Energy is spent protesting circumstances while an opportunity to respond better passes unused before us.

Some exhaustion comes from a problem, and additional exhaustion comes from continually refusing the reality that it has happened. We repeat if only without finding an action to take. Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that wanting to force the present into a completely different reality can reveal ignorance of our position.

Al-jahl means ignorance or failure to recognize the limits of knowledge. Yuhditha means to bring something about. Al-waqt refers to the moment being lived. This wisdom addresses a heart wanting to produce reality according to its wishes when an event has already arrived. The expression leaving no ignorance is a strong rebuke to making personal desire absolute before Allah's decree.

Let us hold this understanding carefully, dear friends. Advice about ordering our response when a family outing must change should be read alongside our obligations as servants of Allah and our responsibilities towards others. Feeling peaceful after hearing a talk is certainly pleasant. Yet sound understanding also helps us act when things no longer feel peaceful. That is why explaining the words matters. We gain something to guide our direction, rather than a beautiful impression that soon fades. If we later forget how the term sounds, remember the relationship it explains: how the heart turns to Allah and how our choices touch real life.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, accepting reality begins by naming it honestly. Today it is raining; the journey needs postponing. Then consider available actions. Perhaps the food can be enjoyed together at home. Perhaps a new time can be chosen after checking conditions. Disappointment may still be felt, but we need not surrender all our behaviour to it.

“If we accept everything, will we become passive?” We may still improve plans and work for change. What we accept is present reality as our starting point. If preparation was negligent, examine that once things are calm. Blaming a child for a cancelled event does not make the road safe. Action needs directing towards an issue we can actually address.

The child has a little bag ready and food is on the table. When the journey is cancelled, disappointment brings tears. Adults who are also disappointed easily answer, “Stop making this harder.” Yet the child needs help accepting change. Dear friends, we can state reality simply and explain the safety reason. Then offer genuinely available choices: eat the food together or do an activity at home. Small choices help the family move from a cancelled plan into today. We do not promise a replacement event before checking time and ability, so disappointment is not followed by another unfulfilled promise.

“If I did most of the preparation, surely being upset is natural?” The feeling is understandable, dear congregation. Time and effort have been spent. We may say so without identifying a family member as the cause of weather. If real negligence occurred, discuss that once things settle. An event that cannot now be changed needs to become the starting point for the next decision. We still assess conditions and prepare another plan. Acceptance makes it more possible to use energy for relationships and safe choices, instead of exhausting it by demanding that today become a different event.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “What can still be protected when today's picnic plan cannot go ahead?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, goods have already been damaged through improper storage. We still need to find the cause and improve the procedure. Yet remaining angry because today is not the day we wanted merely uses up energy. Acceptance begins by acknowledging that the damage really exists, then choosing a useful response. If someone made a mistake, their responsibility still needs resolving.

This lesson looks small, dear congregation, yet is very useful in family life. Many arguments grow because we are unprepared to accept small disruptions. When an adult can say, “We are disappointed; now let us find another option,” a child learns to face change. The child sees that plans matter and also witnesses love continuing when plans change.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of ordering our response when a family outing must change, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Accepting an event does not mean approving injustice or ceasing to change circumstances. Seeing reality clearly enables us to protect victims, repair losses, and prevent repetition. What we release is an inward argument with a past that cannot be repeated. We ask for strength, acknowledge limits, and take available steps. Patience then becomes conscious action, rather than merely suppressing complaints without direction.

When the next plan changes, practise a helpful first sentence. For example, “We are disappointed, but today we need to postpone the journey.” Allow family members to express feelings without laughing at one another. Then consider one activity still enjoyable together. For children, adults' example will speak more strongly than an instruction to be patient. We may look disappointed while still guarding our words. May home become a place for learning to face change honestly, so difficult circumstances need not be made worse by hurtful treatment.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about ordering our response when a family outing must change. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about ordering our response when a family outing must change. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us train the heart through one change faced today. Pause before responding, then choose helpful words. May Allah protect our families when travelling, open our hearts when plans are delayed, and grant wisdom to arrange new steps. May accepting reality become easier without our ceasing to make an effort. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

All ignorance is gathered within
مَنْ أَرَادَ أَنْ يُحْدِثَ فِي الْوَقْتِ
someone who wants to bring about at a given time
غَيْرَ مَا أَظْهَرَهُ اللَّهُ فِيهِ.

26.translation: Postponing deeds until free time arrives is among the follies of the lower self.
syarahEn: We often promise to begin more regular worship once work is finished, the children grow up, or finances settle. In reality, one commitment usually replaces another. This wisdom reminds us that waiting for perfect spaciousness can be a subtle way of continually postponing a step already possible.

Ihalah means deferring or moving an action to another time. Al-faragh is spaciousness or free time. Ru'unat al-nafs points to the folly and immaturity of personal desire. The term reveals how the lower self can use reasonable-sounding excuses to avoid discipline. We feel we are waiting for an opportunity while continually passing over small opportunities.

A worker may not be able to read religious books for hours. Yet a few pages after salah or listening to a lesson at a scheduled time may be possible. Someone wishing to give charity can also begin according to ability. A modest beginning is more useful than a grand plan forever moved into the future.

Some circumstances genuinely require adjustment, such as illness or urgent responsibilities. What needs examining is the pattern of postponement. Choose a realistic deed, set its time, and do it before adding another target. If missed, return at the next opportunity without making a small failure an excuse to stop. The heart is trained through repeated action. Spaciousness often arises after life is organized, so we need not wait for every matter to be settled before beginning the journey towards Allah.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, have we intended to call our parents and then said, “Later, when I have more time”? Days pass and new work arrives. The imagined free time still does not appear. What we wanted to ask may have been simple: have they eaten, how are they feeling, and what do they need? Closeness is sometimes postponed by plans waiting too much for perfect circumstances.

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes postponing deeds until spare time appears as a folly of the lower self. We assume a good opportunity will arrive as abundant time and a light mind. In reality, life often stays busy. If goodness may begin only when every matter is finished, other people's rights will keep receiving what is left over.

Dear congregation, a brief call can mean more than a lengthy intention never acted on. We need not prepare an exceptional conversation. Listen to stories that may be repeated, ask clearly about needs, and arrange help if necessary. For complicated relationships, steps can suit circumstances and healthy boundaries. Improvement need not be forced all at once.

“What if I truly am busy?” Try making a small, reasonable time, perhaps after dinner or before leaving. If we cannot talk yet, send a message and decide when to call. What we preserve is a sincere place for the relationship within life, rather than a vague promise that the next commitment can always displace.

Parents awaiting news can also express needs without accusing a child of lacking love. “Mum would be happy to hear your voice for a little while” is often easier to receive than lengthy sarcasm. Relationships are tended by both sides in manageable ways. We learn to be present and to express our hopes gently.

Tonight, choose one person we have long wanted to contact. Take a possible step before the intention disappears again. May Allah have mercy on our parents, make room for maintaining family ties, and heal strained relationships. May simple goodness gain a real place in our schedule from today. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Choose a realistic time to call and make a note if we forget easily. Ask clearly about needs, then avoid promising help beyond our ability. If parents have died or cannot be contacted, we can pray and fulfil other responsibilities suited to the circumstances. Postponing good deeds until free time appears
مِنْ رُعُونَاتِ النَّفْسِ.
is among the lower self's follies.

27.translation: Do not ask Him to remove you from one state so He may employ you in devotion in another. If He wishes you to serve, He can employ you without changing your state.
syarahEn: We sometimes imagine obedience would be easier if our home, work, or family circumstances changed. That picture makes today's devotion feel less meaningful. This wisdom invites us to see the doors already available. Allah can use us for good through the circumstances we are living, even before a major change occurs.

Hal means the state accompanying a person. Yasta'milaka means to employ you in a task or service. It shifts attention from personal comfort towards benefit we can offer. Ikhraj means taking out or moving. The message is not to make changed circumstances an absolute condition for willingness to obey and serve.

An employee may want to leave the office to spend more time giving religious reminders. Before that decision, responsibilities can be fulfilled in the present place: preserving honesty, treating colleagues well, and helping create a fair workplace. Someone supporting parents can also serve through patient care, even as opportunities to attend public activities diminish.

Change may still be planned when beneficial and without neglecting duties. This wisdom primarily trains the heart not to keep making goodness dependent on an imagined life. Ask what today's clearest task is, then do it with renewed intention. If another path opens, receive it with careful consideration. If not, devotion need not stop. Ordinary-seeming circumstances can nurture sincerity when we are willing to fulfil responsibilities that really exist.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, someone caring for a family member sometimes feels left behind. Friends are active in many activities while that person must look after someone ill or accompany a small child. The thought comes, “When will I have a more useful life?” Yet at home there is a human being benefiting daily from that attention and effort.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us not always to ask for changed circumstances before we can serve. Allah can employ a servant in goodness without changing the whole setting of life. This wisdom helps us see nearby responsibilities. A wish for great service needs appreciation for real needs already before us.

Dear friends, helping someone take medicine, cleaning a bed, or listening to complaints can feel repetitive. Few people praise it. Yet these activities protect someone's dignity and comfort. We need not wait for a public stage to acknowledge that service's worth. Home is also where we learn patience, care, and love for people.

“Does that mean family carers may not have other wishes?” Of course they may. Exhaustion needs attention and duties need sharing. Ask relatives to take turns, arrange rest, or seek help according to means. This wisdom must not be used to make one person carry everything. Valuing service also means caring for the person doing it so their strength is not exhausted.

Dear congregation, other family members can help through clear actions. Do not merely say, “Be patient,” then leave without asking about needs. Take a task, deliver food, or give the carer a chance to go out briefly. When burdens are shared, service becomes more manageable. Compassion is directed towards the person providing care as well as the person who is ill.

Let us look again at the quiet work in our own homes. A responsibility may have become so ordinary that we forget to appreciate it. May Allah strengthen family carers, heal the sick, and soften relatives' hearts to help one another. May we serve through present circumstances while continuing to nurture good hopes. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us look again at the quiet work in our own homes. A responsibility may have become so ordinary that we forget to appreciate it. May Allah strengthen family carers, heal the sick, and soften relatives' hearts to help one another. May we serve through present circumstances while continuing to nurture good hopes. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: لَا تَطْلُبْ مِنْهُ أَنْ يُخْرِجَكَ مِنْ حَالَةٍ
Do not ask Him to take you out of one state
لِيَسْتَعْمِلَكَ فِيمَا سِوَاهَا،
so He may employ you in devotion in another.
فَلَوْ أَرَادَكَ لَاسْتَعْمَلَكَ مِنْ غَيْرِ إِخْرَاجٍ.
If He wishes, He can employ you without changing your state.

28.translation: Whenever a traveller's aspiration wishes to stop at something unveiled along the path, the calls of reality remind him: what you seek is still ahead. Whenever the outward beauty of created things presents itself, their reality calls out: we are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.
syarahEn: On the journey of improving ourselves, we may become captivated by a certain peace, people's praise, or an inner experience that feels special. All can easily be taken as signs that the goal is reached. Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds the heart not to stop at what merely appears along the way. Devotion's goal remains Allah.

Himmah means determination or the direction of aspiration. Hawatif al-haqiqah pictures reality's calls reminding us of the journey's direction. Zawahir al-mukawwanat means creation's attractive outward appearances. Calling creation a trial invites examination of whether its attraction helps obedience or takes over the goal. A beautiful experience gives no certainty about someone's rank before Allah.

For example, someone beginning regular dhikr feels an unfamiliar peace. It may be appreciated, while obligations, character, and family rights still need protecting. If that peace diminishes one day, dhikr need not be abandoned. Devotion matures when it does not depend entirely on pleasant feelings.

The same applies to knowledge and social influence. More followers or wider discussions do not automatically mean a closer heart. Notice clearer fruits: willingness to receive correction, greater compassion, and honesty in responsibilities. If an inner experience causes confusion, discuss it with a trustworthy teacher. We may enjoy gifts while continuing to walk, without making them a permanent resting place. Experience then retains its position as a means supporting devotion, rather than a substitute for the goal.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, after a lesson the heart sometimes feels warm. We cry, write down beautiful words, and want to change. That deserves gratitude. Yet days later, behaviour returns to normal. We seek another event to feel the same thing. The question is: where has the lesson that moved us yesterday gone?

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds the traveller not to stop at something unveiled or beautiful along the way. Inner experience is not devotion's final goal. We still need to journey towards Allah through real obedience. Pleasant feelings may encourage us, but should not become the sole measure of success in religious learning.

Dear congregation, suppose advice about guarding speech touches us. On returning home, what is needed may be more than another quotation on our status. A family member needs to hear a change in tone. If we still interrupt stories and shout, that is the next task. Knowledge finds a place when habits begin improving in daily encounters.

“If I do not feel moved, does that mean the lesson is useless?” Not necessarily. Some lessons enter quietly and their effects appear later. We do not have to chase tears to feel close to Allah. Listen sincerely, understand the meaning, and practise the appropriate part. A maintained small change deserves gratitude even without drama.

Dear friends, after a lesson, try choosing one task for the week. Perhaps let a spouse finish speaking before answering. Note when it works and when we are provoked. If we fail, learn the cause and try again. This helps the lesson move from notes into real relationships, allowing others to feel the benefit of what we hear.

Let us ask Allah for a heart that is moved and a willingness to act. May He accept our learning, protect us from becoming addicted merely to atmosphere, and help us improve behaviour. May the lessons we attend make home warmer, speech more guarded, and responsibilities more sincerely fulfilled. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about turning inspiration from a lesson into changed action meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.

We still need to journey towards Allah through real obedience. Pleasant feelings may encourage us, but should not become the sole measure of success in religious learning.

A beautiful experience gives no certainty about someone's rank before Allah.

Dear congregation, a saying of wisdom may be very short, yet reflection reveals how deeply it touches our long-standing habits. We are seeing that here in the matter of turning inspiration from a lesson into changed action. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, suppose advice about guarding speech touches us. On returning home, what is needed may be more than another quotation on our status. A family member needs to hear a change in tone. If we still interrupt stories and shout, that is the next task. Knowledge finds a place when habits begin improving in daily encounters.

“If I do not feel moved, does that mean the lesson is useless?” Not necessarily. Some lessons enter quietly and their effects appear later. We do not have to chase tears to feel close to Allah. Listen sincerely, understand the meaning, and practise the appropriate part. A maintained small change deserves gratitude even without drama.

Someone returns from a lesson with many quotations saved, eager to share them on the journey. Yet on entering home, something is untidy and the voice rises again. Dear friends, there the lesson finds its nearest task. Quotations may be shared, but family also needs to receive benefit through how we speak. We can pause and improve the sentence just spoken. That small event need not prove the entire lesson pointless. It shows precisely what needs practice, giving enthusiasm a clearer direction than merely seeking the next moving atmosphere.

“If I do not cry during a lesson, is my heart hard?” We cannot judge every state of the heart through tears, dear congregation. Some understand quietly. Others are easily moved but still need to learn follow-through. Both need to examine meaning and action. Do not force feelings to resemble someone else's experience. We can ask what is clearer after listening and what action is our responsibility. A pleasant spiritual experience deserves gratitude without becoming a certain measure of rank. We still need guidance and sincerity to practise what we understand.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “After being moved by advice about speech which words will we improve at home?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone beginning regular dhikr feels an unfamiliar peace. It may be appreciated, while obligations, character, and family rights still need protecting. If that peace diminishes one day, dhikr need not be abandoned. Devotion matures when it does not depend entirely on pleasant feelings.

Dear friends, after a lesson, try choosing one task for the week. Perhaps let a spouse finish speaking before answering. Note when it works and when we are provoked. If we fail, learn the cause and try again. This helps the lesson move from notes into real relationships, allowing others to feel the benefit of what we hear.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about turning inspiration from a lesson into changed action may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

The same applies to knowledge and social influence. More followers or wider discussions do not automatically mean a closer heart. Notice clearer fruits: willingness to receive correction, greater compassion, and honesty in responsibilities. If an inner experience causes confusion, discuss it with a trustworthy teacher. We may enjoy gifts while continuing to walk, without making them a permanent resting place. Experience then retains its position as a means supporting devotion, rather than a substitute for the goal.

Choose one sentence of advice from this lesson and connect it to a habit. If the theme is guarding speech, try listening to a family member until the end before answering. Notice what usually makes us interrupt. After trying, evaluate calmly. We may open old notes and revisit the lesson, so knowledge already received is not always covered by new quotations. For those teaching, questions about action matter too. May knowledge give direction to daily life and enthusiasm for learning bring benefits felt by those closest to us.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of turning inspiration from a lesson into changed action again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about turning inspiration from a lesson into changed action. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us ask Allah for a heart that is moved and a willingness to act. May He accept our learning, protect us from becoming addicted merely to atmosphere, and help us improve behaviour. May the lessons we attend make home warmer, speech more guarded, and responsibilities more sincerely fulfilled. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَا أَرَادَتْ هِمَّةُ سَالِكٍ أَنْ تَقِفَ عِنْدَمَا كُشِفَ لَهَا
Whenever a traveller's aspiration wishes to stop at something unveiled to them,
إِلَّا وَنَادَتْهُ هَوَاتِفُ الْحَقِيقَةِ الَّذِي تَطْلُبُهُ أَمَامَكَ،
reality's call reminds them: what you seek is still ahead.
وَلَا تَبَرَّجَتْ ظَوَاهِرُ الْمُكَوَّنَاتِ إِلَّا وَنَادَتْكَ حَقَائِقُهَا
Whenever creation's outward beauty displays itself, its reality calls:
إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ فِتْنَةٌ فَلَا تَكْفُرْ.
we are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.

29.translation: Your asking from Him may reveal doubt about Him. Your seeking Him may reveal that your heart is still absent from Him. Your seeking other than Him shows how little shame you feel before Him. Your asking from other than Him shows your distance from Him.
syarahEn: Supplication is an important part of servanthood. Yet the way the heart asks can differ. Some ask with trust; others secretly accuse Allah of not attending to their needs. This wisdom addresses that inward condition so the requests we utter improve our relationship with Allah rather than fill with mistaken demands.

Talabuka minhu means your asking from Him, while ittiham means accusation or suspicion. This rebuke needs reading alongside the teaching to supplicate, including Wisdoms 6 and 112. What is examined is a request arising from accusation. Ghaybah indicates the heart's absence, while bu'd means distance. Both describe the servant's awareness, rather than Allah being distant in spatial terms.

We may ask for provision while certain that Allah knows our state. We may also seek human help through lawful means. What needs guarding is treating people as independently powerful, or concluding that all help has ended when assistance is not obtained. Our relationship with means must remain within tawhid.

Before asking, examine the inner language accompanying supplication. Are we entrusting our needs or demanding that our own will be fulfilled? Acknowledge weakness, ask for good, and accept that the answer's form may exceed our knowledge. If disappointment arises, bring it honestly into prayer too. This wisdom teaches the manners of asking, so need becomes a way back to Allah and the heart better recognizes its limits.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, some prayers come with sadness. Others quietly turn into accusation. We say, “O Allah, why am I left like this? Have I not tried?” The pain is real, yet the heart needs guarding so requests do not keep filling with the assumption that Allah forgets or does not know our condition.

Ibn 'Ata'illah's wisdom about asking speaks to a subtle state of the heart. He corrects demandingness and attention disconnected from Allah. The message does not forbid supplication, because asking is part of worship. We learn instead to ask honestly while acknowledging that Allah's knowledge and wisdom extend far beyond how we understand one problem.

Dear friends, consider a family facing an urgent bill. We may name the amount needed, acknowledge fear, and ask for a way out. Then contact those concerned, discuss ability to pay, and seek proper help. We do not have to hide needs from people. What needs preserving is the heart's reliance and a way of asking that respects others' rights and limits.

“What if I have already become angry in prayer?” Pause, then continue by asking for guidance. We can say, “O Allah, I do not yet understand. Please protect my heart and show me a good step.” Simple words like these help us come as we are without nurturing accusations that make the relationship feel more distant and resistant.

Dear congregation, some are afraid to pray because their sentences seem unbeautiful. Yet what we need is no performance of verbal skill. We bring needs humbly to Allah. The manners of supplication can be learned gradually while we acknowledge feelings and pursue a solution. If the burden is heavy, a trusted person's support may also help.

Let us examine the request we repeat most often. Include a request for clarity of heart, rather than only changed circumstances. May Allah ease our needs, forgive words overstepping proper bounds, and guide the efforts underway. May supplication be a warm place of return for a tired heart. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, our ages and experiences differ. Some of us are only beginning to look after ourselves; others have carried the needs of a family for years. Yet we are all still learning about bringing needs into supplication without nurturing accusations. So let us not feel that we are too late for this discussion. Those who are older can still discover a new understanding, and children can still bring serious questions. Let us listen with an open heart. If an example does not match our circumstances exactly, notice the attitude being discussed. Often, beneath differences in work or age, there is a habit of the heart that many of us recognize.

Dear friends, after hearing that explanation, give our minds room to connect its meaning with actual events. We need not use the lesson about bringing needs into supplication without nurturing accusations as a label for judging people's inner states. We see only part of their lives. For ourselves, this advice can become an honest question. What am I hoping for? What am I neglecting? Our answer may not be complete today. That is all right. What matters is being willing to learn sincerely, examine our understanding, and follow sound guidance when seeking to change our daily habits.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, consider a family facing an urgent bill. We may name the amount needed, acknowledge fear, and ask for a way out. Then contact those concerned, discuss ability to pay, and seek proper help. We do not have to hide needs from people.
