Please protect my heart and show me a good step.” Simple words like these help us come as we are without nurturing accusations that make the relationship feel more distant and resistant.

A family facing bills may sit together after the children sleep. The amount needed feels larger than available means. In such circumstances, supplication may come haltingly. Dear friends, we may name needs honestly and admit not knowing a way out. We need not pretend calm to deserve to pray. Yet examine the assumption that Allah does not know or has forgotten our state. It can increase distance within our own awareness. We can ask, “O Allah, we are afraid and do not yet understand. Guide us in attending to our responsibilities and open a good way forward.”

“But does the wisdom not rebuke asking?” Read the rebuke in full, dear congregation. The sequence of wisdoms also encourages continued supplication. What is examined is a heart accusing Allah and feeling all arrangements must submit to its wishes. We may still ask for provision, help, or ease. Afterwards, take appropriate steps and respect the limits of those asked for help. Do not use religion's name to pressure someone to give beyond ability. A good request accompanies proper manners towards Allah and responsibility in human relationships.

Now try answering silently, dear friends: “How can we admit fear before Allah while preserving the manners of supplication?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. May a gathering like this send us home with the courage to learn, rather than merely the ability to comment on other people's lives.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

We may ask for provision while certain that Allah knows our state. We may also seek human help through lawful means. What needs guarding is treating people as independently powerful, or concluding that all help has ended when assistance is not obtained. Our relationship with means must remain within tawhid.

Dear congregation, some are afraid to pray because their sentences seem unbeautiful. Yet what we need is no performance of verbal skill. We bring needs humbly to Allah. The manners of supplication can be learned gradually while we acknowledge feelings and pursue a solution. If the burden is heavy, a trusted person's support may also help.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of bringing needs into supplication without nurturing accusations, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Before asking, examine the inner language accompanying supplication. Are we entrusting our needs or demanding that our own will be fulfilled? Acknowledge weakness, ask for good, and accept that the answer's form may exceed our knowledge. If disappointment arises, bring it honestly into prayer too. This wisdom teaches the manners of asking, so need becomes a way back to Allah and the heart better recognizes its limits.

Try naming one need in supplication with simple words. Then write one step still possible. If it concerns an obligation to someone, discuss ability honestly and avoid deliberately making an insincere promise. When emotions peak, pause before continuing conversation or prayer. We can return to asking for guidance without forcing every feeling to become calm immediately. May asking become a way to recognize our need for Allah more deeply and help us handle problems with proper manners and right effort.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about bringing needs into supplication without nurturing accusations will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. What we want to nurture is a willingness to do our part properly and in an orderly way, even when the results still take time to appear.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of bringing needs into supplication without nurturing accusations that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Let us examine the request we repeat most often. Include a request for clarity of heart, rather than only changed circumstances. May Allah ease our needs, forgive words overstepping proper bounds, and guide the efforts underway. May supplication be a warm place of return for a tired heart. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: طَلَبُكَ مِنْهُ اتِّهَامٌ لَهُ،
Your asking from Him may reveal doubt concerning Him.
وَطَلَبُكَ لَهُ غَيْبَةٌ مِنْكَ عَنْهُ،
Your seeking Him may reveal your heart's absence from Him.
وَطَلَبُكَ لِغَيْرِهِ لِقِلَّةِ حَيَائِكَ مِنْهُ،
Your seeking other than Him reveals little modesty before Him.
وَطَلَبُكَ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ لِوُجُودِ بُعْدِكَ عَنْهُ.
Your asking from other than Him reveals distance from Him.

30.translation: Not a single breath leaves you without a decree of His being carried out within you.
syarahEn: We usually recognize life's importance when facing illness, loss, or a great threat. Yet Allah's care is present in the nearest, most repeated event: the breath moving in and out. This wisdom invites us to see life down to a very subtle unit, so dependence on Allah appears beyond moments of distress alone.

Nafas means a single breath. Tubdihi points to the breath we release, while qadar means a decree with a particular measure. Yumdihi means He carries it out or brings it into effect. Together, the words show that life does not proceed outside Allah's knowledge and decree. Even what is most ordinary to us has a measure and limits we do not fully control.

This reflection can reduce the habit of treating time carelessly. We need not fill every second with demanding activity. Rest, work, and conversation with family can have worth when done properly. What needs reducing is heedlessness through which time keeps passing without awareness of responsibilities and actions' effects.

When life feels too full, pause to recognize that we are receiving a new opportunity. Use it for one clear improvement, such as restraining hurtful words or fulfilling a delayed obligation. The next breath is not guaranteed by our ability. This awareness is intended to nurture gratitude and attention, rather than panic. We live the day more fully because we understand that the life we are using is a continually renewed gift.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, in a waiting room we often feel time is being stolen. Our number is far away, the phone grows hot, and we keep looking at the clock. Wanting to finish quickly is natural. Yet if waiting is filled with scolding staff and complaining about everyone, exhaustion grows before our main matter even reaches its turn.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that every breath carries Allah's decree within us. Passing time remains part of life, including while waiting. We may not choose the circumstances, but can still choose part of our response. This awareness helps us see opportunities for goodness beyond times when the schedule follows our wishes.

Dear congregation, a queue holds small, clear responsibilities. Respect the order, make room for those entitled to priority, and ask politely for information. If the process fails, complaints may follow the proper channel. We can seek good service without making another working person the outlet for all our private frustration.

“What if the wait is really long?” Seek information, assess needs, and decide among possible choices. If waiting remains necessary, use some time beneficially. We can read, make quiet dhikr, or check that a companion has eaten. Attend to safety and staff calls. Not every pause must be filled with a screen or conversation that makes the atmosphere hotter.

Dear friends, a child waiting with us is watching our example. If we push ahead and then tell the child to be patient, the lesson becomes confused. When we explain the rules calmly, the child learns respect for others' rights. Boring waiting time can become practice in shared life, even as we still hope the matter is handled as well as possible.

Let us guard the next breath with better words. May Allah ease the affairs of those awaiting news or service, grant patience to staff, and protect the vulnerable. May we not lose good character simply because a schedule moves more slowly than we wish. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Yet if waiting is filled with scolding staff and complaining about everyone, exhaustion grows before our main matter even reaches its turn.

Dear congregation, before going further, try bringing that story closer to our own lives. We are learning about using waiting time with order and good manners. Perhaps a similar event passed unnoticed because our day was too full. Now we have time to look back at it calmly. If our experience differs, take the part that fits. Children at school can picture life at home; adults can recall their responsibilities. We are not looking for whoever has made the most mistakes. We want to go home with a clearer view and one action we are able to take. So let us listen while occasionally asking our own hearts a question.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that every breath carries Allah's decree within us. Passing time remains part of life, including while waiting. We may not choose the circumstances, but can still choose part of our response. This awareness helps us see opportunities for goodness beyond times when the schedule follows our wishes.

We usually recognize life's importance when facing illness, loss, or a great threat. Yet Allah's care is present in the nearest, most repeated event: the breath moving in and out. This wisdom invites us to see life down to a very subtle unit, so dependence on Allah appears beyond moments of distress alone.

Nafas means a single breath. Tubdihi points to the breath we release, while qadar means a decree with a particular measure. Yumdihi means He carries it out or brings it into effect. Together, the words show that life does not proceed outside Allah's knowledge and decree. Even what is most ordinary to us has a measure and limits we do not fully control.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with using waiting time with order and good manners. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, a queue holds small, clear responsibilities. Respect the order, make room for those entitled to priority, and ask politely for information. If the process fails, complaints may follow the proper channel. We can seek good service without making another working person the outlet for all our private frustration.

“What if the wait is really long?” Seek information, assess needs, and decide among possible choices. If waiting remains necessary, use some time beneficially. We can read, make quiet dhikr, or check that a companion has eaten. Attend to safety and staff calls. Not every pause must be filled with a screen or conversation that makes the atmosphere hotter.

In that waiting room, staff call numbers while several people look tired. Some have children; others struggle to sit for long. Dear friends, we can examine nearby needs before adding complaints. Ensure those we accompany are as comfortable as we can make them. If information is unclear, ask staff briefly. Do not push ahead because our own affair feels most urgent. Follow any applicable priority arrangements. Waiting may be inconvenient, yet there is still an opportunity to respect others' rights and reduce shared tension.

“If the service is poor, must we simply be told to be patient?” Complaints may be made, dear congregation. We can record the problem and use an appropriate channel. Distinguish improving service from releasing every frustration onto the nearest person. The staff member at the desk may not control the whole process. Ask about their authority and explain needs clearly. If waiting takes longer, consider genuinely available options. The wisdom about breath reminds us that life continues, including when our agenda is delayed. We can still choose a responsible attitude within an unwanted pause.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “What can we still do well before our turn arrives?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

This reflection can reduce the habit of treating time carelessly. We need not fill every second with demanding activity. Rest, work, and conversation with family can have worth when done properly. What needs reducing is heedlessness through which time keeps passing without awareness of responsibilities and actions' effects.

Dear friends, a child waiting with us is watching our example. If we push ahead and then tell the child to be patient, the lesson becomes confused. When we explain the rules calmly, the child learns respect for others' rights. Boring waiting time can become practice in shared life, even as we still hope the matter is handled as well as possible.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about using waiting time with order and good manners may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

When life feels too full, pause to recognize that we are receiving a new opportunity. Use it for one clear improvement, such as restraining hurtful words or fulfilling a delayed obligation. The next breath is not guaranteed by our ability. This awareness is intended to nurture gratitude and attention, rather than panic. We live the day more fully because we understand that the life we are using is a continually renewed gift.

For the next queue, prepare simple necessities to make waiting more orderly. Attend to calls and do not become so absorbed in a screen that the turn is missed. If reading or making quiet dhikr, avoid disturbing others. Those with children can offer age-appropriate explanations and safe activities. If irritation arises, ask what action truly helps. We need not like every delay, but can prevent it being followed by violated rights or hurtful words. May every period of time find room for goodness.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about using waiting time with order and good manners. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of using waiting time with order and good manners. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us guard the next breath with better words. May Allah ease the affairs of those awaiting news or service, grant patience to staff, and protect the vulnerable. May we not lose good character simply because a schedule moves more slowly than we wish. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَا مِنْ نَفَسٍ تُبْدِيهِ
There is not a single breath you exhale
إِلَّا وَلَهُ قَدَرٌ فِيكَ يُمْضِيهِ.
without a decree of His being carried out in you.

31.translation: Do not wait for all affairs and commitments to end. That attitude will prevent you from maintaining awareness of His watchfulness in the state in which He has now placed you.
syarahEn: We often wait for every matter to be settled before feeling able to draw closer to Allah. Yet life almost always brings something new. If the heart's presence must wait for busyness to end, devotion is continually postponed. This wisdom teaches that present circumstances can become a place for remembering Allah and fulfilling a trust.

Faragh al-aghyar means the ending of dealings with everything other than Allah. Al-muraqabah is awareness that Allah knows and watches us. Muqimuka means He places you. The word placement invites us to see daily circumstances as a space of responsibility. Awareness of Allah needs training precisely within those circumstances, rather than only when everything is calm.

A trader can maintain muraqabah through accurate scales. A teacher does so by preparing lessons and not belittling pupils. Someone caring for family can remember Allah through patience with recurring needs. Work becomes part of devotion when its intention, method, and boundaries follow religious guidance.

Dedicated time for worship and learning still needs arranging. Yet do not regard the rest of the day as separate from our relationship with Allah. Begin a task with supplication, preserve honesty throughout it, then end with gratitude and review. When attention wanders, gently return it without awaiting a new atmosphere. Nearness of heart grows through practice accompanying life. Busyness then does not automatically obstruct devotion, because within it we learn to be aware servants.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, work sometimes feels far from worship. In the mosque, we remember to guard ourselves. Back at work, the thought becomes, “What matters is getting the report done.” Arrival time is then recorded earlier, unfinished work marked complete, or shortcomings deliberately concealed to avoid questions.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us not to wait for every commitment to end before maintaining muraqabah. Muraqabah is awareness that Allah knows our state. It is trained precisely within what we are doing. We do not have to leave the workplace to begin obeying. Honesty in today's records is already a real space for devotion.

Dear friends, figures in reports connect with people's rights. Managers make decisions using that information. A colleague may have to finish something we marked complete. Falsified records can have effects reaching further than the momentary safety we gain. Administration that appears trivial therefore needs care too.

“If I am honest, will I look incapable?” A missing skill can still be learned when the situation is truthfully explained. We can state completed parts, emerging obstacles, and the help needed. This acknowledgement takes courage but offers a chance to improve the process. Concealing difficulty makes help arrive too late.

Dear congregation, Allah's watchfulness also comforts someone whose work is rarely seen. Our care is still known even without praise today. Keep documenting work well and discuss rights appropriately. Hoping for Allah's judgement does not require silence when there is injustice or a division of tasks needing improvement.

Tomorrow, before pressing send, read our report again. Ensure the words match reality. May Allah protect workers' trusts, grant courage to acknowledge shortcomings, and bless efforts to improve ability. May everyday busyness increase awareness of Him, because within it many small choices shaping honesty are taking place. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We need to understand the message well enough to bring it into those circumstances. Listen slowly. If a sentence speaks to our situation, keep it in mind for later. We do not have to remember every explanation. One sound understanding, put sincerely into practice, is already worth working towards today.

In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.

Imagine work unfinished while the report column calls for a completion mark. Afraid of being judged slow, we mark it without explaining the real situation. The next colleague assumes their part is ready and takes a mistaken step. Dear friends, one small mark can transfer difficulty to someone else. We need to see people behind administration. A record is more than a task to pass a manager's questions. It carries shared information. Writing the state truthfully opens a chance for assistance and adjustment. We can state progress without hiding what still needs work.

“What if the manager only wants to hear that everything is done?” Handle that pressure carefully, dear congregation. Find a factual way to explain obstacles through work channels. If necessary, seek support from a trustworthy party. We do not guarantee an easy response to honesty. Yet false information may make the problem harder to repair. Awareness that Allah knows helps preserve actions under pressure, including outside the atmosphere of a lesson. Leaders should make room for difficulties to be reported without immediate humiliation. Healthy working habits also need fairness from those receiving reports.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “Can others make a sound decision from the report we write?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

A trader can maintain muraqabah through accurate scales. A teacher does so by preparing lessons and not belittling pupils. Someone caring for family can remember Allah through patience with recurring needs. Work becomes part of devotion when its intention, method, and boundaries follow religious guidance.

Keep documenting work well and discuss rights appropriately. Hoping for Allah's judgement does not require silence when there is injustice or a division of tasks needing improvement.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of preserving truth in work records, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Dedicated time for worship and learning still needs arranging. Yet do not regard the rest of the day as separate from our relationship with Allah. In the next report, check one part easily written according to hope rather than reality. Separate completed work from work underway. Explain necessary help clearly enough. If a mistake was made, correct it properly so information used by others becomes accurate again. Students can practise by honestly acknowledging friends' contributions in group work. May awareness of Allah accompany ordinary-looking tasks, and may our records be trustworthy to those depending on them.

Now let us turn the lesson about preserving truth in work records into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about preserving truth in work records, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Tomorrow, before pressing send, read our report again. Ensure the words match reality. May Allah protect workers' trusts, grant courage to acknowledge shortcomings, and bless efforts to improve ability. Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: لَا تَتَرَقَّبْ فُرُوغَ الْأَغْيَارِ،
Do not await the end of every affair and preoccupation.
فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ يَقْطَعُكَ عَنْ وُجُودِ الْمُرَاقَبَةِ
That attitude prevents maintaining awareness of His watchfulness
لَهُ فِيمَا هُوَ مُقِيمُكَ فِيهِ.
in the state where He has placed you now.

32.translation: Do not be surprised by difficulties while living in this worldly abode. It only displays what accords with its nature and character.
syarahEn: We can be deeply shocked when hardship comes, as though life has departed from what it should be. Yet the world contains change, limitation, and parting. Ibn 'Ata'illah recalls the nature of this temporary home so the heart does not demand continual comfort. Sound understanding helps us face problems more calmly.

Al-akdar means murkiness or things disturbing tranquillity. Hadhihi al-dar refers to the abode in which we now live. Mustahaqqu wasfiha points towards what accords with the world's nature. Difficulty is described as normal for this world because every creature has limits, rather than because we are commanded to leave suffering without trying to relieve it.

When plans change or relationships encounter problems, sadness is still allowed. Feeling sad does not demonstrate a failure of faith. What can be trained is the response afterwards: seeking causes, asking help, and taking useful steps. Expecting life always to match our wishes often adds to an already heavy hurt.

For someone supporting others in difficulty, this wisdom is best used first to order ourselves. Presence, practical help, and willingness to listen are often needed more than quickly telling someone to accept the divine decree. We remember the world's nature while practising compassion. Pleasure is appreciated without being considered permanent, and difficulty faced without being considered the whole of life. From this understanding grows patience that keeps moving, because we understand the journey's terrain and do not lose direction when the road becomes hard.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, some months seem to test patience at home. The roof leaks, the washing machine stops, and the vehicle develops a problem too. We stare at expenses and sigh, “Why all at once?” A family member asking a little question gets scolded, although equally confused by the same situation.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that difficulty is part of worldly life's nature. The world contains change, breakdown, and continually arriving needs. Understanding this does not make damage pleasant. Yet it helps the heart stop treating every disruption as something that should be impossible in our family's life.

Dear congregation, things we use require maintenance. When they break, first assess needs and safety. What needs immediate repair and what can wait? Check costs reasonably and avoid forcing every replacement at once. Seek advice from someone knowledgeable so panic alone does not drive decisions.

“What if the money is not there yet?” Explain the situation calmly to family. Choose a safe temporary approach, rearrange expenditure, and seek help if needed. Not every difficulty must be solved alone. Yet do not rush into payment promises we cannot meet simply to look as though everything remains fine before neighbours.

Dear friends, what most needs protecting is often the relationship at home. A broken machine can be repaired, but harsh words can remain longer. We can say, “I am worried about the cost. Please give me a moment so I can speak calmly.” Acknowledging our state helps family understand a need without becoming the target of anger.

Let us learn to prepare for disruptions that reasonably occur. In easier times, maintain belongings and set aside what circumstances allow. In tight times, prioritize needs and guard speech. May Allah provide enough for our households, bring honest help, and enable us to strengthen each other when work and costs arrive together. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of organizing household needs when breakdowns come together that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Let us learn to prepare for disruptions that reasonably occur. In easier times, maintain belongings and set aside what circumstances allow. In tight times, prioritize needs and guard speech. May Allah provide enough for our households, bring honest help, and enable us to strengthen each other when work and costs arrive together. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: لَا تَسْتَغْرِبْ وُقُوعَ الْأَكْدَارِ مَا دُمْتَ فِي هَذِهِ الدَّارِ،
Do not be surprised by hardships while living in this worldly abode.
فَإِنَّهَا مَا أَبْرَزَتْ إِلَّا مَا هُوَ مُسْتَحِقُّ وَصْفِهَا وَوَاجِبُ نَعْتِهَا.
The world only manifests what accords with its nature and character.

33.translation: A goal you seek through reliance on your Lord will not be blocked. A goal you seek through reliance on yourself will not become easy.
syarahEn: A goal can consume our energy when every outcome is thought to depend on our own ability. We want everything perfect, struggle to accept shortcomings, and readily blame ourselves when obstructed. This wisdom places effort within a relationship with Allah, giving dedication a firmer reliance than confidence in personal ability.

Matlab means a goal or something sought. Bi-rabbika means through reliance on your Lord, while bi-nafsika means through reliance on yourself. The different attachments of the preposition show the direction of the heart's trust. Relying on Allah includes asking help, taking a proper path, and accepting that success's form remains within His wisdom.

Someone establishing a business needs to calculate costs, study customer needs, and maintain quality. Supplication does not replace that work. Yet all can be done without considering oneself the absolute controller. If the path changes, there remains room to learn. If success comes, it need not lead to looking down on those not given the same opportunity.

This wisdom does not promise every personal target will come about as planned. It teaches how to pursue goals properly and care for the heart along the way. Seek guidance before beginning, examine methods, and keep correcting shortcomings. When results differ from wishes, bring the experience back to Allah. Effort becomes healthier because courage accompanies humility. We sincerely perform our responsibility while accepting that help may come through a path we do not yet understand.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, when asked to organize a neighbourhood event, we sometimes immediately say, “Relax, I can handle it all.” Schedules are arranged, messages sent, and work taken home. Days later we are overwhelmed but embarrassed to admit it. We reject help, then become angry at working alone. Dedication becomes a burden we have enlarged ourselves.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches the importance of pursuing goals through reliance on Allah. We use available abilities while acknowledging our need for help. Excessive self-reliance makes us feel we must master everything. When reality becomes more complicated, the heart readily breaks or seeks someone to blame for the limitations appearing.

Dear friends, tawakkul in organizing a committee can be very practical. Begin with supplication, map the work, and divide tasks according to ability. Explain obstacles before they grow large. Ask about parts not yet mastered. Willingness to learn does not diminish a leader's responsibility. People find helping easier when circumstances are openly explained and the work's direction is reasonably clear.

“If we rely on Allah, will the event certainly succeed?” We still do not control every outcome. Weather, health, and other circumstances can change. We pursue a good aim through proper means. If the plan needs adjustment, make it calmly. Faith does not require a promise that every detail will follow our wishes exactly.

Dear congregation, examine how we treat helpers too. Do not demand they depend on us while we claim reliance on Allah. Give sufficient information, respect their time, and acknowledge shared work. When mistakes occur, resolve the problem without humiliation. Healthy cooperation can be part of the help we ask for.

Let us reduce the words, “I must be able to do everything.” Replace them with dedication to our own part and willingness to receive help. May Allah bless our community activities, protect organizers from arrogance, and preserve fellowship through work. May success bring gratitude and shortcomings willingness to learn together. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
talkEn: OPENING

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about organizing activities through reliance on Allah and shared work meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with organizing activities through reliance on Allah and shared work. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, tawakkul in organizing a committee can be very practical. Begin with supplication, map the work, and divide tasks according to ability. Explain obstacles before they grow large. If the plan needs adjustment, make it calmly. Faith does not require a promise that every detail will follow our wishes exactly.

That event leader receives messages from every direction. Someone asks about food, another needs a confirmed time, and equipment is incomplete. Wanting to appear capable, the answer to each question is, “Already handled,” although it is not. Dear friends, this habit makes help difficult to receive. Others do not know where help is needed. The leader can change approach by explaining the state of work and who handles each task. Not every matter must pass through one pair of hands. Clarity enables cooperation and reduces guesswork. Leadership's dedication also appears in willingness to receive proper assistance and maintain trustworthy communication.

“If I admit I do not know, people may lose trust.” Trust needs reality, dear congregation. Admitting one part is not mastered and finding the right person is more responsible than giving false certainty. Relying on Allah invites us to ask for help and use means properly. Dividing tasks is part of that effort. We still anticipate change without promising a perfect event. If weather or other circumstances change, decisions adjust to purpose and safety. Helpers also deserve respect, because they are not tools for proving a leader always succeeds.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “Can the courage to acknowledge limitations help a committee?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone establishing a business needs to calculate costs, study customer needs, and maintain quality. Supplication does not replace that work. Yet all can be done without considering oneself the absolute controller. If the path changes, there remains room to learn. If success comes, it need not lead to looking down on those not given the same opportunity.

When mistakes occur, resolve the problem without humiliation. Healthy cooperation can be part of the help we ask for.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of organizing activities through reliance on Allah and shared work, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

This wisdom does not promise every personal target will come about as planned. It teaches how to pursue goals properly and care for the heart along the way. Seek guidance before beginning, examine methods, and keep correcting shortcomings. When results differ from wishes, bring the experience back to Allah. Effort becomes healthier because courage accompanies humility. We sincerely perform our responsibility while accepting that help may come through a path we do not yet understand.

Before the next meeting, write unfinished work and the help needed. Explain early so people have time to respond. Once tasks are divided, provide clarity and room to carry them out without taking every detail back again. Afterwards, review the process factually and thank helpers. If mistakes occurred, admit our own part. May working together teach that effort requires trustworthiness, while the heart continues asking Allah through good results and plans needing change.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of organizing activities through reliance on Allah and shared work again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about organizing activities through reliance on Allah and shared work invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us reduce the words, “I must be able to do everything.” Replace them with dedication to our own part and willingness to receive help. May Allah bless our community activities, protect organizers from arrogance, and preserve fellowship through work. May success bring gratitude and shortcomings willingness to learn together. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَا تَوَقَّفَ مَطْلَبٌ أَنْتَ طَالِبُهُ بِرَبِّكَ،
An aim pursued in reliance on your Lord will not be thwarted.
وَلَا تَيَسَّرَ مَطْلَبٌ أَنْتَ طَالِبُهُ بِنَفْسِكَ.
An aim pursued relying on yourself will not become easy.

34.translation: Among the signs of success at the journey's end is returning to Allah from its beginning.
syarahEn: Much work begins with great enthusiasm, then loses direction when success or obstacles appear. We think busily about the end result but pay less attention to the initial foundation. This wisdom reminds us that how we begin matters greatly to the journey. Returning to Allah from the start helps keep aims and steps rightly directed.

Al-najah means success, while al-nihayat points to a journey's endings. Al-ruju' ila Allah means returning to Allah through intention, supplication, and submission. Al-bidayat means beginnings. Their relationship emphasizes establishing a sound reliance before busyness takes over attention.

For example, before opening an educational activity, examine the benefit we wish to give and our ability to fulfil the trust. We ask for help, make a reasonable plan, and ensure working methods do not violate others' rights. This foundation needs remembering as the activity grows, so success is not narrowly measured by praise or participant numbers alone.

A good beginning can also be renewed. If work was once pursued with mixed intentions, we need not wait to start an entire life from zero. Pause, correct direction, and improve mistaken methods. Returning to Allah is a movement of the heart that can be repeated. With this foundation, final success is understood as a journey drawing closer to devotion. We learn to preserve our relationship with Allah from the first step, then bring it into the small decisions shaping the journey's quality.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, when opening a business, conversation usually moves quickly to capital, location, and profit. All matter. Yet have we sat with a prospective partner and asked, “Which methods will we preserve when business is quiet?” A question before beginning can protect the relationship when money and pressure begin speaking too.

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes returning to Allah from the beginning as a good sign for the journey's end. Beginning with Allah means arranging both intention and method. An opening supplication needs decisions respecting religious guidance and human rights. We do not want enthusiasm for earning to produce steps that disregard honesty from the outset.

Dear congregation, before trading, agree on duties, profit-sharing, and recording money. Examine materials and services to be offered. If a contractual matter is unclear, study it with competent help. Do not rely on embarrassment about discussing matters with a close friend. Clarity helps friendship last when business circumstances are not always pleasant.

“If we discuss too much, when will we begin?” We need not know everything first. Begin at a manageable scale while clarifying essentials. There is a difference between courage to act and deliberately ignoring a visible issue. Customer promises, workers' wages, and entrusted money need thought from the start because they concern other people's rights.

Dear friends, returning to Allah also means readiness to correct direction. If a method proves harmful, do not persist merely because we have begun. Admit it, stop what is wrong, and seek repair. Healthy business requires self-evaluation. We want provision enjoyed with a calmer heart, so family receives an example as well as money.

Let us bring the intention to earn into concrete decisions. Before opening the business door, ensure our promises can be accounted for. May Allah bless the beginnings of our businesses, keep us from fraud, and bring trustworthy partners. May seeking a livelihood also become a path of learning obedience to Him. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

When business is quiet, do not suddenly cross boundaries previously considered important. Discussion of lawful methods therefore needs a place before pressure arrives. We ask Allah for success while preparing a business path respecting buyers, partners, and workers.

Now try answering silently, dear friends: “What agreements need discussing before money and pressure begin influencing friendship?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. May a gathering like this send us home with the courage to learn, rather than merely the ability to comment on other people's lives.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Try asking about one thing we have merely assumed both sides understand. Discuss calmly and record agreement as needed. If circumstances change, use the agreed communication route. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about building a business on clarity and lawful methods, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. phrasesEn: مِنْ عَلَامَاتِ النُّجْحِ فِي النِّهَايَاتِ
Among the signs of success at the journey's end
الرُّجُوعُ إِلَى اللَّهِ فِي الْبِدَايَاتِ.
is returning to Allah from its beginning.

35.translation: Whoever has a radiant beginning will also have a radiant end.
syarahEn: A good beginning is often marked by honest intention, willingness to learn, and attention to proper methods. Yet its light may fade if kept only as a memory. This wisdom invites us to tend the quality of the beginning so enthusiasm for devotion retains direction as the journey lengthens and circumstances change.

Ashraqat means shone or became bright. Bidayatuhu points to its beginning, and nihayatuhu to its ending. Light describes an initial state illuminated by faith and sincerity. Its connection to the ending is no reason to feel assured of salvation simply because we once began beautifully. The light needs preserving through obedience and continued improvement.

A student of religion may begin humbly, then become proud as knowledge grows. A social programme organizer may begin wanting to help, then be drawn into competition for recognition. In such circumstances, remembering the first intention is useful when followed by corrected actions. We return to accepting correction and examining the benefit others actually receive.

Tending it can be simple: establish regular review and seek advice from someone willing to remind us. Notice small deeds we once performed readily. Are we now willing only when they benefit our name? The question helps examine the heart's direction. A bright journey is built through repeated decisions, rather than the experience of beginning alone. We ask Allah to preserve sincerity from start to finish while continuing the practical means that keep devotion healthy.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, the first day of a course or job is usually full of enthusiasm. Books are tidy, the schedule saved, and we arrive early. Weeks later, habits loosen. Tasks are postponed and excuses increase. Sometimes we need a way to preserve an already good beginning more than a large new burst of motivation.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches a connection between a luminous beginning and a luminous end. We are not receiving a guarantee of a smooth road. The lesson is to arrange the journey's foundation through right intention and action. Initial habits maintained can sustain us when excitement becomes ordinary.

Dear friends, when learning a new ability, choose a realistic schedule. Twenty sincere minutes daily may be more useful than a long target that lasts briefly. Prepare equipment, decide a place, and identify the main distraction. If the phone often distracts, move it away during practice. Dedication needs a form our body and circumstances can sustain.

“What if everything has already become a mess?” We can still make a new beginning in the part needing improvement. Identify the most urgent task, seek explanation if unclear, and begin there. Do not spend every bit of energy hating ourselves for falling behind. Shame can be directed into responsibility rather than made an excuse to stop learning.

Dear congregation, those supporting learners also need to value the process. Do not praise only large results while overlooking consistent small practice. Ask what has been learned and which difficulty arose. Such support helps a child or colleague feel safe admitting shortcomings. Foundations can then be improved before problems pile up and courage diminishes.

Let us choose one initial habit to tend for a week. Make it simple enough to do honestly. May Allah bless learning time, protect motivation from excessive demands, and grant perseverance until its benefit is felt. May each beginning lead towards better work and a humbler heart. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Advice about preserving a good start in learning through realistic habits should be read alongside our obligations as servants of Allah and our responsibilities towards others. Feeling peaceful after hearing a talk is certainly pleasant. Yet sound understanding also helps us act when things no longer feel peaceful. That is why explaining the words matters. We gain something to guide our direction, rather than a beautiful impression that soon fades. If we later forget how the term sounds, remember the relationship it explains: how the heart turns to Allah and how our choices touch real life.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, when learning a new ability, choose a realistic schedule. Twenty sincere minutes daily may be more useful than a long target that lasts briefly. Prepare equipment, decide a place, and identify the main distraction. If the phone often distracts, move it away during practice. Dedication needs a form our body and circumstances can sustain.

“What if everything has already become a mess?” We can still make a new beginning in the part needing improvement. Identify the most urgent task, seek explanation if unclear, and begin there. Do not spend every bit of energy hating ourselves for falling behind. Shame can be directed into responsibility rather than made an excuse to stop learning.

On the first day, every tool is neatly arranged. We imagine long practice each evening. Days later work increases and the lengthy schedule feels impossible. Dear friends, we can adjust the amount of practice before abandoning everything. Choose a time fitting real life. Prepare equipment so starting does not always require a long search. If screens are the main distraction, create distance during practice. These small things give dedication a form. We need not wait for the first day's feelings to sit and learn again. Progress can grow through reasonable repetition and attention to obstacles that actually arise.

“I am already behind and embarrassed to begin again.” Shame may be acknowledged without being given authority over every decision, dear congregation. Ask which task most needs doing and which explanation remains unclear. Contact a teacher if needed. A good beginning deserves gratitude, but does not guarantee every subsequent stage will automatically be orderly. It needs maintaining through action. Parents can also help children arrange reasonable practice rather than repeat commands to be more enthusiastic. Check whether the schedule makes sense and the child knows how to begin the work requested.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “What makes a study schedule manageable after the first enthusiasm fades?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

A student of religion may begin humbly, then become proud as knowledge grows. A social programme organizer may begin wanting to help, then be drawn into competition for recognition. In such circumstances, remembering the first intention is useful when followed by corrected actions. We return to accepting correction and examining the benefit others actually receive.

Dear congregation, those supporting learners also need to value the process. Do not praise only large results while overlooking consistent small practice. Ask what has been learned and which difficulty arose. Such support helps a child or colleague feel safe admitting shortcomings. Foundations can then be improved before problems pile up and courage diminishes.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of preserving a good start in learning through realistic habits, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Tending it can be simple: establish regular review and seek advice from someone willing to remind us. Notice small deeds we once performed readily. Are we now willing only when they benefit our name? The question helps examine the heart's direction. A bright journey is built through repeated decisions, rather than the experience of beginning alone. We ask Allah to preserve sincerity from start to finish while continuing the practical means that keep devotion healthy.

For practice, choose a short period to try for several days. Specify the task so time is not entirely spent deciding what to study. Afterwards, see whether the amount needs adjusting. If a day is missed, return at the next scheduled time without making lateness a reason to close the book forever. We may also appreciate modest progress. May a beginning illuminated by good intention continue to receive care, and may learning habits benefit us through dedication we can sustain.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about preserving a good start in learning through realistic habits. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about preserving a good start in learning through realistic habits. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us choose one initial habit to tend for a week. Make it simple enough to do honestly. May Allah bless learning time, protect motivation from excessive demands, and grant perseverance until its benefit is felt. May each beginning lead towards better work and a humbler heart. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَنْ أَشْرَقَتْ بِدَايَتُهُ
Whoever has a radiant beginning
أَشْرَقَتْ نِهَايَتُهُ.
will also have a radiant end to their journey.

36.translation: What is stored in the hidden depths of the inner self will appear in its outward reality.
syarahEn: Something continually nurtured in the heart usually seeks a way to appear. Hatred may emerge as sarcasm, a wish for praise in storytelling, and affection through small attentions. This wisdom invites care for behaviour's source, so improvement extends beyond appearances before people.

Ghayb al-sara'ir means the unseen depths of inward secrets. Shahadat al-zawahir points to outward reality that can be witnessed. Ustudi'a means entrusted or stored. The choice of storing shows that what settles within influences what appears. Improving the heart and improving behaviour therefore need to reinforce each other.

For example, we want to speak more gently to family. Adjusting our tone is useful, but we also need to examine the assumption that we are always right. If that source of arrogance is preserved, gentleness easily disappears when tired. Learning to respect family needs instead helps an attitude change last longer.

This wisdom is primarily a tool for self-examination. One mistake by someone else gives no certain knowledge of their entire heart. We can observe our own patterns: which words often emerge in anger, and what feeling precedes them? Correct hurtful actions and tend the inner self through supplication, repentance, and good habits. Harmony between inward and outward grows through willingness to be honest, so goodness is more than a performance and gradually becomes part of how we live.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, some jokes make everyone laugh except their target. A friend buys something new and we immediately mock it. A relative receives good news and we find a flaw. After the person is offended, we say, “Only joking.” But is it truly only a joke, or is envy seeking a way out?

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that what is stored inwardly leaves traces in outward behaviour. We must not guess another's heart from one incident. For ourselves, however, words can offer material for examination. Repeated expressions often indicate something needing attention, including feeling threatened by someone else's happiness.

Dear congregation, imagine a younger sibling finding a good job. We smile along but keep inserting comments about shortcomings. Perhaps we have long felt compared by family. That wound needs acknowledging, but the sibling need not become its outlet. We can discuss the habit of comparison with the appropriate people without spoiling the good news being received.

“What if envy arises on its own?” An initial feeling sometimes comes uninvited. What we can train is our response afterwards. Restrain belittling comments, pray for good, and notice an unmet personal need. We may want to develop. Pursue that reasonably without making another person's success something that must be reduced.

Dear friends, apologies need clarity too. Avoid blaming someone for being supposedly too sensitive. Acknowledge our part: “That remark hurt. I will be more careful.” Then demonstrate change. Others need not forget immediately, but we can begin showing that their dignity matters more than defending a joke that wounded them.

Let us guard the heart's doorway through more conscious speech. If we cannot yet praise freely, at least avoid hurting. May Allah cleanse envy, heal relationships between siblings, and enable us to share joy in others' blessings. May what is stored within become better, so what leaves the tongue brings calm too. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

When the next good news comes, try offering congratulations without inserting the person's flaws. If a real issue needs discussing, choose a separate time and a clear reason. Examine family habits of comparison too and seek a more respectful conversation. For ourselves, write one step towards development we can pursue. Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. phrasesEn: مَا اسْتُودِعَ فِي غَيْبِ السَّرَائِرِ
What is stored in the depths of inner secrets
ظَهَرَ فِي شَهَادَةِ الظَّوَاهِرِ.
will appear in outward reality.

37.translation: How different is one who understands everything by beginning with Allah from one who seeks evidence for Allah. One who begins with Him has assigned truth to its rightful possessor and established a matter from its source. Seeking evidence for Him arises because the heart has not yet arrived at Him. Otherwise, when was He absent that evidence for Him was needed? When was He distant that created traces were needed to lead to Him?
syarahEn: Some come to know Allah by reflecting on creation and seeking proofs. Others have a faith so alive that they read every event with awareness of Allah. This wisdom discusses those different conditions of the heart. Both need careful understanding so we appreciate learning and do not belittle the use of reason.

Yastadillu 'alayhi means seeking evidence for Him through signs in creation. Yastadillu bihi describes someone beginning from knowledge of Allah to understand life. Wusul means arrival, in the sense of mature knowing within the heart, rather than movement to a location. The term explains depth of awareness without granting people knowledge encompassing Allah's reality.

A student first understands that the universe's order points to a Creator. As faith and devotion are maintained, that awareness can increasingly accompany work and trials. The entire proof need not be rebuilt every time the person prays. A conviction learned begins becoming a foundation for life whose influence is felt in action.

Keep studying proofs and asking when something is unclear. Reason properly used helps distinguish guidance from fantasy. At the same time, tend deeds so knowledge extends beyond discussion. The nearest measure is greater honesty, submission, and compassion. This wisdom invites faith to grow, so what was once known only through lessons gradually accompanies daily life, without making us feel entitled to measure others' hearts.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, some children's questions make adults nervous. “Why do we believe in Allah?” Unprepared, we sometimes answer, “Do not ask strange questions.” The child becomes quiet, but silence may not mean understanding. Perhaps the lesson learned is that confusion about faith must be hidden to avoid making parents angry.

Ibn 'Ata'illah discusses the journey from seeking evidence for Allah towards viewing life with awareness of faith. Human paths of understanding differ. Some need explanation; others have learned to draw lessons from daily life. We need not belittle an honest question. Growing knowledge should help the heart know Allah more deeply and become more willing to obey.

Dear friends, when a child asks, listen first for the meaning. Perhaps a friend's conversation or a thought about creation prompted it. Answer with correct, simple, age-appropriate language. If we do not know, we may say we will seek an explanation. Parents lose no authority by acknowledging knowledge's limits. Children instead see honesty before what is not yet understood.

“What if the question is very difficult?” Record it and ask a teacher with knowledge and a good way of supporting children. Avoid pictures of Allah resembling objects or a human body. Tawhid requires care. A hurried explanation merely to end a conversation can create longer confusion for a child.

Dear congregation, after obtaining an answer, invite the child to see faith's connection with behaviour. Believing Allah knows us guides honesty during play. Acknowledging His generosity teaches thanks and sharing. The conversation then becomes more than a puzzle to win. Children learn that faith directs the life they are living with others.

Let us make home safe for learning. We preserve sound belief through knowledge, patience, and a lived example. May Allah guide our children's questions, bring wise teachers, and protect parents from words that kill the courage to learn. As our family knows Him more, may we become more honest and loving towards one another. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
