الْمُسْتَدِلُّ بِهِ عَرَفَ الْحَقَّ لِأَهْلِهِ فَأَثْبَتَ الْأَمْرَ مِنْ وُجُودِ أَصْلِهِ،
Those starting from Him have assigned truth to its owner, then established a matter from its source.
وَالِاسْتِدْلَالُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ عَدَمِ الْوُصُولِ إِلَيْهِ،
Seeking evidence of Him arises because the heart has not yet arrived at Him.
وَإِلَّا فَمَتَى غَابَ حَتَّى يُسْتَدَلَّ عَلَيْهِ،
Otherwise, when was He absent so as to need proof of Him?
وَمَتَى بَعُدَ حَتَّى تَكُونَ الْآثَارُ هِيَ الَّتِي تُوصِلُ إِلَيْهِ؟
When was He distant so that creation's traces were needed to lead to Him?

38.translation: Let the one with abundance spend from that abundance: this is the likeness of those who have arrived at Him. As for the one whose provision is restricted: this is the likeness of those still journeying towards Him.
syarahEn: People's ability to explain and guide differs. Some have broad learning and maturity in facing circumstances; others are still strengthening their own foundations. This wisdom uses abundant provision as an image to remind us that giving knowledge and guidance should follow the ability actually possessed.

Dhu sa'ah means one possessing abundance. Liyunfiq means let them spend or give. In this spiritual reading, abundance images breadth of understanding. Al-sa'irun refers to those still journeying. They may still benefit others, but need to recognize limits and not force explanations they do not themselves understand.

Someone new to learning may encourage family to maintain salah or share a clear lesson. Yet a complicated question not yet mastered should be referred to someone more knowledgeable. Admitting we do not know is part of trustworthiness. Conversely, someone with broader ability should use that abundance to help, rather than merely enjoy being consulted.

This image also teaches gentleness towards a person's learning stage. Do not burden beginners beyond readiness or consider simple deeds meaningless. Begin with the clearest need, explain in understandable language, and open a path for further learning. Giving within ability preserves both benefit and the sound handling of knowledge. We keep helping while remaining humble that understanding needs continued development and accountability.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, have we taught a parent to use a phone and needed to repeat the explanation? We have just shown one button and the question begins again. Unconsciously our voice rises: “I just explained that!” Yet when we learned simple things, that parent may also have repeated them many times with considerable effort.

Ibn 'Ata'illah uses abundance and restriction to explain different states on the journey of knowing Allah. People give according to the ability received. A lesson we can carry is respect for stages of understanding. Those who understand have an opportunity to help; those still learning need guidance in a form they can receive.

Dear congregation, when explaining a device, divide steps into small parts. Show one action, invite a try, and wait. If needed, write instructions in readable letters. Do not take the phone too quickly saying, “Here, I will do it.” The matter may finish sooner, but the opportunity to learn independence is also lost and confidence may diminish.

“What if time is tight?” Explain politely that we will help at a specified time. For urgent needs, complete them first with enough explanation. Afterwards, still provide an opportunity to learn. We need not always have unlimited energy, but limits can be expressed without humiliating someone who needs help understanding something new.

Dear friends, differences of ability appear in many matters. Young people may recognize apps faster, while parents have experiences we do not possess. Relationships become warmer when differences help us support each other. Do not make one skill a reason to feel superior, because life keeps giving chances to be the person who does not know.

Let us choose patience in the next explanation. Notice the face of the person we support, rather than only the button we want pressed quickly. May Allah open the hearts of children and parents, protect families from mockery, and bless knowledge shared gently. May those who understand become humbler and those learning remain respected. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about patiently teaching our parents to use a phone meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.

Dear congregation, a saying of wisdom may be very short, yet reflection reveals how deeply it touches our long-standing habits. We are seeing that here in the matter of patiently teaching our parents to use a phone. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, when explaining a device, divide steps into small parts. Show one action, invite a try, and wait. If needed, write instructions in readable letters. Do not take the phone too quickly saying, “Here, I will do it.” The matter may finish sooner, but the opportunity to learn independence is also lost and confidence may diminish.

We need not always have unlimited energy, but limits can be expressed without humiliating someone who needs help understanding something new.

A parent holds the phone, trying to remember a button just shown. We wait briefly, then want to take over. The task may finish faster, but the steps remain unclear. Dear friends, explain one action at a time. Show, allow a try, then wait without complaint. A brief note with large enough writing may help. Ask whether the explanation is comfortable to follow. Do not treat repetition as proof of laziness. Experience with devices and ability to see print may differ from what we take for granted.

“What if I am in a hurry?” Express the time limit politely, dear congregation. For an urgent matter, we may complete it first with sufficient explanation. Afterwards, keep another time for learning. Helpers' limits deserve respect, but how they are expressed can still protect feelings. Nor should we give instructions we do not understand ourselves out of embarrassment. If something is confusing, seek accurate information. Abundant knowledge offers a chance to benefit others within ability. Those still learning can also help honestly without forcing explanations beyond their preparation.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “Does our way of helping give our parents an opportunity to learn independently?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone new to learning may encourage family to maintain salah or share a clear lesson. Yet a complicated question not yet mastered should be referred to someone more knowledgeable. Admitting we do not know is part of trustworthiness. Conversely, someone with broader ability should use that abundance to help, rather than merely enjoy being consulted.

Relationships become warmer when differences help us support each other. Do not make one skill a reason to feel superior, because life keeps giving chances to be the person who does not know.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about patiently teaching our parents to use a phone may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

This image also teaches gentleness towards a person's learning stage. Do not burden beginners beyond readiness or consider simple deeds meaningless. Begin with the clearest need, explain in understandable language, and open a path for further learning. Giving within ability preserves both benefit and the sound handling of knowledge. We keep helping while remaining humble that understanding needs continued development and accountability.

Next time, choose the phone function most needed. Teach patiently and let the parent repeat it independently. Keep instructions somewhere easy to find if wanted. If tiredness begins, stop kindly and continue at an agreed time. Remember how much repetition we once received when learning simple things. May this little knowledge become a way of honouring parents, and may our ease not make us forget respect for someone learning.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of patiently teaching our parents to use a phone again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about patiently teaching our parents to use a phone. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us choose patience in the next explanation. Notice the face of the person we support, rather than only the button we want pressed quickly. May Allah open the hearts of children and parents, protect families from mockery, and bless knowledge shared gently. May those who understand become humbler and those learning remain respected. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: لِيُنْفِقْ ذُو سَعَةٍ مِنْ سَعَتِهِ
Let someone possessing abundance spend from their abundance:
الْوَاصِلُونَ إِلَيْهِ،
this is the likeness of those who have arrived at Him.
وَمَنْ قُدِرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقُهُ
As for someone whose provision is restricted:
السَّائِرُونَ إِلَيْهِ.
this is the likeness of those still travelling towards Him.

39.translation: Those still journeying are guided by the lights of turning towards Him. Those who have arrived receive the lights of encounter. The first are still led by light; for the second, those lights are granted to them. For they are directed only towards Allah, rather than anything else. Say Allah, then leave them to play in their empty discussions.
syarahEn: Early in the journey, a person often needs repeated reminders to pray, arrange intention, and return to Allah. Through practice, awareness can become more settled. This wisdom describes that growth through light, helping us understand that devotion involves a process and Allah's help precedes the depth of human experience.

Anwar al-tawajjuh means the lights of the heart's turning. Tawajjuh emphasizes the direction of attention being ordered. Anwar al-muwajahah describes the lights of encounter: the heart's increasingly living knowledge. Belonging to Allah indicates devotion no longer continually controlled by other interests. Encounter here does not imagine bodies meeting or equate Allah with creatures.

A beginner can maintain worship times and reduce distractions. Success need not be measured by experiences of those described as mature. Each stage has real work. Even someone feeling closer remains obliged to preserve religious guidance and others' rights. An inner experience bearing no fruit in character needs examining again.

The invitation to say Allah and leave empty discussion directs us towards a focused heart. Reduce conversations merely prolonging self-defence or competition for position. Use time for worship, learning, and genuinely needed service. Discussion of light thus returns to daily practice. We ask for help in preserving the heart's direction while accepting faith's growth under Allah's guidance through continued obedience, without demanding a particular experience.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, a lively religious gathering can awaken enthusiasm. Beautiful recitation, many friends, and the heart readily moved towards good. Yet returning to the small neighbourhood prayer room, everything seems less attractive. Gradually we want to attend only when the atmosphere suits our tastes. Is our worship's direction shifting?

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains that those still journeying are led by lights of the heart's turning. As they grow, attention becomes more directed towards Allah. This image helps us understand that initial enthusiasm needs nurturing towards steadfastness. We may enjoy a good atmosphere without making all willingness to obey depend on feelings arising from a particular place.

Dear friends, a small prayer room may have ordinary speakers and few worshippers. Yet neighbours there need togetherness. Our presence can sustain activities, tidy the place, or accompany someone lonely. Some benefit comes without excitement. We learn to see tasks available in our nearest community.

“Does that mean large lessons are forbidden?” Of course not. We receive knowledge and encouragement from many good places. What we examine is what follows. Does encouragement make us readier to fulfil obligations and improve character? If only the list of places visited grows, we can reorder that learning journey's purpose.

Dear congregation, when the atmosphere feels ordinary, try remaining present according to ability and need. Help one task without awaiting a request. Listen to someone not skilled at telling stories. The heart is trained so devotion does not always need great stimulation. Motivation may rise and fall, but direction can be preserved through simple decisions honestly maintained.

Let us ask Allah to preserve our worship's purpose. May the places we study bring benefits reaching home and community. May we appreciate an encouraging atmosphere while remaining obedient when circumstances feel ordinary. May our steps become more directed towards Him and more useful to those around us. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

The lighting is ordinary and the recitation less beautiful than yesterday's. Stopping there feels unappealing. Dear friends, here we can examine purpose. Communities have different needs and abilities. Nor may we determine someone's heart from a chosen gathering. Now try answering silently, dear friends: “Does a lesson's atmosphere help us be more fully present in our own community?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. May a gathering like this send us home with the courage to learn, rather than merely the ability to comment on other people's lives.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of preserving worship's direction after encouragement from a lively gathering, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. We ask for help in preserving the heart's direction while accepting faith's growth under Allah's guidance through continued obedience, without demanding a particular experience.

Choose one benefit from a lesson to carry into the home community. Perhaps help tidy a place or attend an activity genuinely needing support. Act within ability without regarding ourselves as every matter's saviour. If facilities are lacking, discuss improvements with their managers. We may still learn from various good gatherings. May the learning journey improve the heart's direction, so encouragement becomes more than a memory of atmosphere and benefits worship and everyday relationships.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about preserving worship's direction after encouragement from a lively gathering will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. What we want to nurture is a willingness to do our part properly and in an orderly way, even when the results still take time to appear.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of preserving worship's direction after encouragement from a lively gathering that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

wordsEn: belong to Allah; are directed towards Allah
phrasesEn: اهْتَدَى الرَّاحِلُونَ بِأَنْوَارِ التَّوَجُّهِ،
Those still travelling receive guidance through the light of the heart's turning towards Him.
وَالْوَاصِلُونَ لَهُمْ أَنْوَارُ الْمُوَاجَهَةِ،
Those who have arrived receive the light of encounter.
فَالْأَوَّلُونَ لِلْأَنْوَارِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ الْأَنْوَارُ لَهُمْ،
The first group is still guided by light; for the second, lights are bestowed for them.
لِأَنَّهُمْ لِلَّهِ لَا لِشَيْءٍ دُونَهُ،
For they are directed only towards Allah rather than anything besides Him.
قُلِ اللَّهُ ثُمَّ ذَرْهُمْ فِي خَوْضِهِمْ يَلْعَبُونَ.
Say Allah, then leave them playing in their idle talk.

40.translation: Your desire to know the faults hidden within you is better than your desire to uncover unseen matters veiled from you.
syarahEn: Curiosity may lead to knowledge, but can become a preoccupation with matters that do not help self-improvement. We want others' secrets or extraordinary experiences while allowing hurtful habits and the wish for praise to remain. This wisdom returns attention to the knowledge most urgently needed.

Al-'uyub means faults or personal shortcomings. Al-ghuyub means hidden unseen matters. These similar-sounding words have very different directions. Batana fika points to something hidden within you, while hujiba 'anka indicates something veiled from you. We are invited to prioritize knowledge of shortcomings we are responsible for improving.

For example, someone is interested in discovering whether they possess a special spiritual experience, while family is often wounded by their words. The more urgent lesson is understanding why they readily belittle people and practising better speech. That knowledge may attract little attention, but its benefit to shared life is very real.

Take one pattern that often brings regret. Ask when it appears, what triggers it, and who is affected. Seek feedback from someone trustworthy, then plan improvement. Knowing our faults is not intended to nurture self-hatred. It opens repentance and growth. The heart is readier for guidance when the desire to be corrected exceeds the wish to appear to possess abilities others lack.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, we can spend much time wanting to know the future. Will provision flow? What does that person really intend? Some seek fortune-telling and match various signs. Meanwhile, clear matters before us remain delayed: lying habits, unreturned money, or words continually hurting family.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that wanting to know our own faults is better than pursuing unseen matters hidden from us. Some knowledge is beyond our reach. Conversely, some shortcomings are clear and improvement can begin. The heart becomes more responsible when attention moves towards work actually within our task.

Dear congregation, suppose we fear business becoming quiet and grow busy seeking lucky signs. Yet expenditure is not recorded and customer complaints unanswered. A more useful step is organizing accounts and improving service. We still supplicate and seek guidance while using abilities Allah has granted to handle what is real.

“What if I want to know so I can prepare?” Preparation can use verifiable information, reasonable planning, and advice from someone understanding the issue. We need not claim knowledge of what is hidden. Human knowledge has limits deserving respect. Acknowledging them helps more honest decisions and prevents us being easily tossed about by people's claims.

Dear friends, self-examination also needs gentleness and direction. Do not turn it into insulting ourselves all night. Choose one harmful behaviour, recognize its cause, and decide an improvement. If assessment is difficult, seek trustworthy feedback. We seek clarity for better steps, rather than a list of flaws that makes us feel worthless.

Let us reduce one useless guessing activity and use the time to fulfil a trust. May Allah protect us from misleading knowledge, grant courage to admit mistakes, and guide sincere improvement. May attention to our own faults make us humbler and less occupied with other people's hidden lives. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Al-'uyub means faults or personal shortcomings. Al-ghuyub means hidden unseen matters. These similar-sounding words have very different directions. Batana fika points to something hidden within you, while hujiba 'anka indicates something veiled from you. We are invited to prioritize knowledge of shortcomings we are responsible for improving.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with improving real shortcomings before pursuing hidden information. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, suppose we fear business becoming quiet and grow busy seeking lucky signs. Yet expenditure is not recorded and customer complaints unanswered. A more useful step is organizing accounts and improving service. We still supplicate and seek guidance while using abilities Allah has granted to handle what is real.

“What if I want to know so I can prepare?” Preparation can use verifiable information, reasonable planning, and advice from someone understanding the issue. We need not claim knowledge of what is hidden. Human knowledge has limits deserving respect. Acknowledging them helps more honest decisions and prevents us being easily tossed about by people's claims.

A business owner opens various predictions of good fortune while customer complaints remain unanswered. The wish is to know whether next week will be busy, but this week's records are unfinished. Dear friends, attention can return to what is clear. We can inspect goods, answer questions, and arrange expenses. Testable information helps preparation. Unfounded claims about hidden things may instead drag decisions off course. Human knowledge's limits need acknowledgement. We ask Allah for guidance while using abilities already available, rather than waiting for unseen certainty beyond our power.

“I only want to know so I do not take a wrong step.” Readiness can be pursued reasonably, dear congregation. Seek relevant information and ask someone understanding the issue. Distinguish a possibility considered from certainty we do not have. At the same time, notice any personal shortcoming deliberately avoided. Sometimes discussing destiny is easier than returning money or admitting a lie. The wisdom directs attention towards work that is our responsibility. We need not know the entire future to begin correcting today's wrong action.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “What can be improved now when we are too busy guessing the future?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone is interested in discovering whether they possess a special spiritual experience, while family is often wounded by their words. The more urgent lesson is understanding why they readily belittle people and practising better speech. That knowledge may attract little attention, but its benefit to shared life is very real.

Dear friends, self-examination also needs gentleness and direction. Do not turn it into insulting ourselves all night. Choose one harmful behaviour, recognize its cause, and decide an improvement. If assessment is difficult, seek trustworthy feedback. We seek clarity for better steps, rather than a list of flaws that makes us feel worthless.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about improving real shortcomings before pursuing hidden information may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Take one pattern that often brings regret. Ask when it appears, what triggers it, and who is affected. Seek feedback from someone trustworthy, then plan improvement. Knowing our faults is not intended to nurture self-hatred. It opens repentance and growth. The heart is readier for guidance when the desire to be corrected exceeds the wish to appear to possess abilities others lack.

Write one real issue continually postponed while attention seeks signs. Choose a step whose result can be checked, such as completing records or honestly answering a complaint. If a claim makes us afraid or hurried, do not decide immediately. Seek correct explanation and hold to religious guidance. Families should avoid using predictions to label children. May we receive clarity to distinguish knowledge's limits from responsibilities already clear, and courage to improve ourselves before becoming busy guessing what is hidden.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about improving real shortcomings before pursuing hidden information. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of improving real shortcomings before pursuing hidden information. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us reduce one useless guessing activity and use the time to fulfil a trust. May Allah protect us from misleading knowledge, grant courage to admit mistakes, and guide sincere improvement. May attention to our own faults make us humbler and less occupied with other people's hidden lives. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: تَشَوُّفُكَ إِلَى مَا بَطَنَ فِيكَ مِنَ الْعُيُوبِ
Your desire to know your hidden faults
خَيْرٌ مِنْ تَشَوُّفِكَ إِلَى مَا حُجِبَ عَنْكَ مِنَ الْغُيُوبِ.
is better than your desire to unveil unseen matters concealed from you.

41.translation: The Real is not veiled. You are the one veiled from witnessing Him. If something veiled Him, it could cover Him. If He had a covering, that covering would limit His existence. Whatever limits something has power over it. Yet He is the One who has absolute power over all His servants.
syarahEn: When feeling close to Allah is difficult, we easily imagine Allah moving away or becoming covered by something. This wisdom corrects that perspective. Allah is not limited by creation. What needs examining is our own heart, because heedlessness and attachment can veil awareness of His guidance.

Al-mahjub means the veiled one. Ibn 'Ata'illah directs it towards the servant whose perception is not yet clear. Satir means a covering, while hasir means a limiter. The explanation emphasizes that Allah is not ruled by anything enclosing or limiting Him. Al-Qahir indicates Allah's absolute power over all servants, so no creature stands above His power.

For example, someone continually fills attention with competition and human judgement. During worship, thoughts still circle personal position. A supposedly more special place may not be needed. Perhaps what is needed more is organizing habits, reducing useless busyness, and returning attention to the clearest devotion.

Change begins by recognizing an obstacle we can improve. If someone's rights are withheld, fulfil them. If lying is habitual, stop and repair its effects. If basic knowledge is unclear, learn regularly. This wisdom moves our work from imagining Allah's condition to caring for our own. We ask for help in cleansing the heart and take steps following guidance. Hope becomes more alive because the veil is understood as the servant's state, still capable of guidance, rather than a deficiency in Allah.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, have we seen a room as blurry and then found our own glasses dirty? We could blame lighting, walls, or weather. Once lenses are cleaned, things look different. This small experience helps examine how we view life. Sometimes attention and habits of judgement within us need improving first.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains that Allah is not covered by creation. The veil lies in the servant's perception. We do not imagine Allah as an object hidden behind something. The heart is invited to recognize how heedlessness leaves signs of goodness and guidance unnoticed. We become so occupied with flaws that available blessings are hard to acknowledge.

Dear friends, consider saying, “Nobody in this house cares.” There may be a real unmet need requiring expression. Yet examine whether small family attentions are always rejected because their form differs from expectation. Some show affection through action while we count only the words we want to hear.

“Does that mean every problem is my fault?” Certainly not. Mistreatment still needs recognizing and handling. Examining our perception is no reason to erase another person's responsibility. We simply make room for fairer assessment: what truly hurts, what needs explaining, and what goodness has been missed through deep disappointment.

Dear congregation, try words that name needs clearly. Instead of accusing everyone of not caring, state the help needed. Then listen to their responses. Relationships often gain another opportunity when we stop demanding mind-reading. If conversation is difficult, a wise person's support can help make the process safer.

Let us cleanse our way of seeing through supplication and honesty. May Allah help us recognize blessings without concealing wounds and admit shortcomings without losing dignity. May our families learn to hear each other. May clearer perception open better actions and warmer relationships. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We are seeing that here in the matter of examining our perspective without erasing reality. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Someone hopes a family member will say particular caring words. When the words do not come, the conclusion is nobody cares. Yet food may have been prepared or a task quietly helped. Dear friends, a need for words may still be expressed. Yet we can open our eyes to existing forms of care. Conversation then need not begin with a sweeping accusation. We can say, “I appreciate that help, and I would also like to be listened to briefly.” Clearer words give family a chance to understand needs without erasing goodness expressed differently.

“What if the person truly treats me badly?” Self-examination does not erase others' actions, dear congregation. Violence or harmful treatment needs recognizing and handling with suitable assistance. The glasses image simply asks whether our view is fair enough. We distinguish facts, feelings, and guesses about intention. Do not use it to make someone blame themselves for everything. The explanation of the heart's veil also concerns the servant's limited knowing. Allah is not limited by objects or covered by creatures; what needs improvement is how the heart receives guidance.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “Is there goodness we have missed because its form differs from our hopes?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone continually fills attention with competition and human judgement. During worship, thoughts still circle personal position. A supposedly more special place may not be needed. Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of examining our perspective without erasing reality, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Change begins by recognizing an obstacle we can improve. If someone's rights are withheld, fulfil them. If lying is habitual, stop and repair its effects. If basic knowledge is unclear, learn regularly. This wisdom moves our work from imagining Allah's condition to caring for our own. We ask for help in cleansing the heart and take steps following guidance. Hope becomes more alive because the veil is understood as the servant's state, still capable of guidance, rather than a deficiency in Allah.

Choose one disappointing event. State what truly occurred and what we concluded ourselves. If a need remains unexpressed, find a calm time to speak. Acknowledge real goodness without covering the painful part. If support is needed, seek someone trustworthy. This exercise helps fuller listening before judgement. May the heart gain clarity to see blessings, recognize problems, and act fairly towards ourselves and others.

Now let us turn the lesson about examining our perspective without erasing reality into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about examining our perspective without erasing reality, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us cleanse our way of seeing through supplication and honesty. May Allah help us recognize blessings without concealing wounds and admit shortcomings without losing dignity. May our families learn to hear each other. May clearer perception open better actions and warmer relationships. Amin.

phrasesEn: الْحَقُّ لَيْسَ بِمَحْجُوبٍ،
The Real is not veiled.
وَإِنَّمَا الْمَحْجُوبُ أَنْتَ عَنِ النَّظَرِ إِلَيْهِ،
It is you who are veiled from witnessing Him.
إِذْ لَوْ حَجَبَهُ شَيْءٌ لَسَتَرَهُ،
If anything veiled Him, it could cover Him.
وَلَوْ كَانَ لَهُ سَاتِرٌ لَكَانَ لِوُجُودِهِ حَاصِرٌ،
If He had a covering, that covering would limit His existence.
وَكُلُّ حَاصِرٍ لِشَيْءٍ فَهُوَ لَهُ قَاهِرٌ،
Whatever limits something has power over it.
وَهُوَ الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ.
Yet He is the All-Dominant over all His servants.

42.translation: Leave every human quality that contradicts your servanthood. You will then be ready to answer the call of the Real and draw near to His presence.
syarahEn: Being human means having needs, emotions, and limitations. These need not all be hated. Yet some ways of treating ourselves contradict being servants, such as feeling entitled to belittle people or rejecting truth out of pride. This wisdom invites us to release qualities that undermine devotion.

Al-bashariyyah refers to human qualities. Munaqid li-'ubudiyyatika clarifies the scope: qualities contradicting servanthood. The command to leave therefore does not mean erasing hunger, sadness, or the need for rest. Mujiban means one answering a call, while qariban means near. Nearness grows as our responses increasingly follow Allah's guidance.

When angry, for example, emotion may arise naturally. Our task is to prevent anger becoming insult or violence. When wanting appreciation, we can acknowledge it without making praise a condition for helping. Training the heart works on how we direct needs, rather than pretending to have none.

Choose one quality often harming relationships, such as difficulty accepting correction. Practise a small response: listen to the end, delay self-defence, and examine what is true. Accompany it with supplication and apology where needed. Servanthood becomes real through attitudes others can feel. We need not wait for every bad quality to vanish before beginning obedience. By repeatedly answering goodness's call, the heart learns humility and greater readiness for guidance.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, someone very friendly with neighbours may change behind the steering wheel. Being overtaken brings anger, a prolonged horn, and complaints heard by the family. Roads can be tiring. Yet tiredness does not permit disregarding others' safety and dignity.

Ibn 'Ata'illah invites us to leave qualities contradicting servanthood. This does not erase human needs such as rest or irritation. What needs improvement is arrogance, anger overstepping limits, and always wanting to win. Daily travel can expose these when we feel our interests must come first for every road user.

Dear congregation, imagine a driver slowing to find an address. We do not know the situation but assume deliberate obstruction. Immediately provoking an argument increases risk. Keep a safe distance and follow the rules. If a violation is dangerous, use the appropriate reporting route. We need not create fresh danger to release personal annoyance.

“What if someone treats me harshly?” Prioritize safety. Avoid replies that escalate tension, find safety if necessary, and seek help suited to the circumstances. Restraint does not approve wrongdoing. We are preventing one bad incident becoming a greater loss for ourselves, family, and those nearby.

Dear friends, change can begin before departure. Allow more time, check our physical state, and do not force travel when severely tired. If taking a child, explain that rules apply to us too. Good manners become clearer when children see adults respect queues, give way, and admit mistakes without excuses.

Let us bring travel supplications into responsible driving. May Allah protect us on the road, soften our hearts when provoked, and guard against arrogance endangering others. May safe arrival accompany guarded speech and treatment of road users as fellow humans with destinations of their own. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Let us bring travel supplications into responsible driving. May Allah protect us on the road, soften our hearts when provoked, and guard against arrogance endangering others. May safe arrival accompany guarded speech and treatment of road users as fellow humans with destinations of their own. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: اخْرُجْ مِنْ أَوْصَافِ بَشَرِيَّتِكَ عَنْ كُلِّ وَصْفٍ مُنَاقِضٍ لِعُبُودِيَّتِكَ،
Leave every human quality contrary to your servanthood.
لِتَكُونَ لِنِدَاءِ الْحَقِّ مُجِيبًا
You will thus be ready to answer the Real's call
وَمِنْ حَضْرَتِهِ قَرِيبًا.
and draw near to His presence.

43.translation: The root of every act of disobedience, heedlessness, and desire is being pleased with the lower self. The root of every act of obedience, vigilance, and restraint is not being pleased with it.
syarahEn: Feeling already good can close the door to improvement. When corrected, we immediately prepare reasons. When wrong, attention shifts towards others' mistakes. Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that satisfaction with the lower self roots many deviations, because the heart loses willingness to be examined and directed.

Al-rida 'an al-nafs means being pleased with or justifying oneself. The issue is satisfaction that no longer acknowledges shortcomings. Al-yaqazah means vigilance or wakefulness. Al-'iffah points to restraint from what is inappropriate. Vigilance grows when we realize personal desires need guidance and can bring misleading excuses.

Someone may say harsh speech aims to educate, while actually wanting to win the conversation. Another may consider busyness devotion while neglecting dependants. Examining these possibilities does not mean suspecting every intention until paralysed. Simply leave room to ask whether the action truly matches the reason given.

Accepting ourselves as valuable human beings can accompany acknowledging mistakes. We need not insult ourselves to become humble. What is needed is courage to correct actions, apologize, and receive advice. Make time to review one event that hurt someone. Listen to its impact before explaining our intention. Dissatisfaction with the lower self then becomes energy for improvement, so obedience grows from a heart willing to learn and not finished being corrected.

Dear congregation, has a spouse said, “Lately your voice is always raised when we talk”? Before the sentence ends, our defence is prepared. We recall every task performed and reply with their shortcomings. A conversation about one habit becomes a contest over who is most wrong and who has contributed most.

Ibn 'Ata'illah warns of being satisfied with the lower self. If we always consider ourselves right, improvement struggles to enter. The dissatisfaction meant is willingness to correct behaviour, rather than self-hatred. We still respect our dignity while acknowledging speech or action needing further practice.

Dear friends, criticism is not always well expressed. We may ask for a calmer time and manner. Afterwards, examine its content honestly. Is any part true? If every comment is rejected because its giver also has flaws, we will always find a reason never to change.

“If I stay quiet, will I seem to admit every accusation?” Listening does not mean agreeing with everything. We can say, “Let me listen first. Then I would like to explain where I see things differently.” This leaves room for both sides. If behaviour hurts or threatens, safety remains first and help may be needed for a safe discussion.

Dear congregation, afterwards choose one observable change. Perhaps stop interrupting at dinner. Ask family to remind us in an agreed way. When reminded, try not to retaliate immediately. The exercise may seem small, but relationships gain hope when feedback produces genuinely different behaviour maintained the next day.

Let us bring a heart still willing to learn into the home. May Allah protect us from feeling always right, grant gentleness in advising, and help us receive useful advice. May those closest not need to wait for perfection before feeling our honest and continuing efforts to improve. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We recall every task performed and reply with their shortcomings. A conversation about one habit becomes a contest over who is most wrong and who has contributed most.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about hearing correction before preparing a defence meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.
CORE WISDOM

The dissatisfaction meant is willingness to correct behaviour, rather than self-hatred. We still respect our dignity while acknowledging speech or action needing further practice.

Al-'iffah points to restraint from what is inappropriate. Vigilance grows when we realize personal desires need guidance and can bring misleading excuses.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with hearing correction before preparing a defence. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, criticism is not always well expressed. We may ask for a calmer time and manner. Afterwards, examine its content honestly. Is any part true? If every comment is rejected because its giver also has flaws, we will always find a reason never to change.

“If I stay quiet, will I seem to admit every accusation?” Listening does not mean agreeing with everything. We can say, “Let me listen first. Then I would like to explain where I see things differently.” This leaves room for both sides. If behaviour hurts or threatens, safety remains first and help may be needed for a safe discussion.

A spouse has just said our voice is often raised. We remember this morning's incident, yet the mind immediately seeks a list of tasks completed. Dear friends, a record of service does not always answer a problem of tone. We can hear one complaint to the end. If its delivery is heated, clearly ask for a calmer time. Then return to its content. Did words truly wound? Is tiredness making shouting easier? Specific questions help more than a contest over sacrifice. A relationship gains a chance when one habit is discussed without turning an entire life into a field of defence.

“If some accusations are wrong, must I admit them?” We may distinguish what is true from what differs, dear congregation. Listening does not remove our right to explain. State facts calmly without adding fresh attacks. If discussion is unsafe or threatening, seek appropriate help rather than forcing a private conversation. The wisdom rebukes self-justification that rejects all correction. It does not ask us to accept every accusation. We learn to allow truth room, including when brought by someone with shortcomings. This willingness can begin with one unhurried response.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “Can we examine advice without immediately answering with its giver's flaws?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone may say harsh speech aims to educate, while actually wanting to win the conversation. Another may consider busyness devotion while neglecting dependants. Examining these possibilities does not mean suspecting every intention until paralysed. Simply leave room to ask whether the action truly matches the reason given.

Dear congregation, afterwards choose one observable change. Perhaps stop interrupting at dinner. Ask family to remind us in an agreed way. When reminded, try not to retaliate immediately. The exercise may seem small, but relationships gain hope when feedback produces genuinely different behaviour maintained the next day.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of hearing correction before preparing a defence, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Accepting ourselves as valuable human beings can accompany acknowledging mistakes. We need not insult ourselves to become humble. What is needed is courage to correct actions, apologize, and receive advice. Make time to review one event that hurt someone. Listen to its impact before explaining our intention. Dissatisfaction with the lower self then becomes energy for improvement, so obedience grows from a heart willing to learn and not finished being corrected.

For practice, choose a response making room to listen. For example, “I would like to understand the example you mean.” Afterwards, acknowledge what is true and choose a possible improvement. If a difference needs explaining, do so without mockery. Next time, notice whether those affected begin to feel change. We need not receive all criticism perfectly before learning can begin. May vigilance towards ourselves help preserve speech and receive beneficial advice.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of hearing correction before preparing a defence again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about hearing correction before preparing a defence invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us bring a heart still willing to learn into the home. May Allah protect us from feeling always right, grant gentleness in advising, and help us receive useful advice. May those closest not need to wait for perfection before feeling our honest and continuing efforts to improve. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: أَصْلُ كُلِّ مَعْصِيَةٍ وَغَفْلَةٍ وَشَهْوَةٍ الرِّضَا عَنِ النَّفْسِ،
The root of all disobedience, heedlessness, and desire is satisfaction with the lower self.
وَأَصْلُ كُلِّ طَاعَةٍ وَيَقَظَةٍ وَعِفَّةٍ عَدَمُ الرِّضَا مِنْكَ عَنْهَا.
The root of all obedience, vigilance, and self-restraint is dissatisfaction with it.

44.translation: Keeping company with someone without learning who is not pleased with himself is better for you than keeping company with a learned person pleased with himself. What use is knowledge to a learned person pleased with himself? And what blameworthy ignorance remains in someone without learning who continually corrects himself?
syarahEn: Broad knowledge does not necessarily make truth easy to receive. Someone with limited knowledge may instead possess humility encouraging our improvement too. This wisdom examines the quality of influence in friendship. Good friends help us be honest with ourselves, making relationships places of growth.

Jahilan means someone without learning, while 'aliman means a learned person. The contrast is sharpened by yarda 'an nafsih, being pleased with oneself. The rebuke centres on one's attitude towards oneself. This wisdom does not belittle knowledge; it warns that knowledge loses benefit when used to justify arrogance and close opportunities for correction.

When choosing close friends, notice how they face mistakes. Are they willing to apologize? Can advice be received without always answering with insults? Those acknowledging limits and willing to learn can provide a healthy environment. Someone knowledgeable but always defensive may train us to consider self-justification intelligence.

We still need to learn from knowledgeable, trustworthy people. Friendship and scholarly guidance can complement each other. At the same time, examine our own influence on friends. Do not make mistakes look acceptable simply because we can assemble reasons. Dare to say we do not know and accept valid correction. Knowledge benefits more when accompanied by humility, so relationships strengthen honesty and open a desire for continued learning.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, pleasant companions are usually easy to seek. They agree with stories, laugh along, and defend us in anger. Yet another friend may not always feel comfortable, saying, “Think again; our words went too far.” After hearing that, do we still want closeness or begin moving away?

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that a friend willing to correct themselves is better than a learned person complacent about themselves. Knowledge matters and needs pursuing. The message concerns our attitude towards truth. Intelligence may lose benefit when used to justify every error, while humility opens continued learning and improvement.

Dear congregation, suppose we want to retaliate against a colleague by spreading damaging stories. A friend stops us and suggests a better approach. We may feel disappointed and undefended. Yet that friend is protecting us from a regrettable decision. Good friendship has courage to protect, including through advice unpleasant to hear.

“What if a friend criticizes until it becomes belittling?” Distinguish that. Good advice respects dignity and circumstances. We may set boundaries against mockery or pressure. We seek someone honest and caring, rather than always finding faults to feel superior. We also need to become that kind of friend for others.

Dear friends, when advising, ask whether the time is right. State the issue clearly without uncovering an entire history of mistakes. Leave room for explanation, then consider improvement together. When corrected ourselves, give thanks before busily seeking a reply. This habit gives friendship a safe place to grow in honesty and mutual respect.

Recall a friend who protected us through advice. Contact them and express appreciation if possible. May Allah bring trustworthy friends, guard our speech when reminding, and keep friendship from a habit of justifying each other's mistakes. May closeness increase courage for goodness and self-improvement. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

phrasesEn: وَلَأَنْ تَصْحَبَ جَاهِلًا لَا يَرْضَى عَنْ نَفْسِهِ خَيْرٌ لَكَ
Befriending someone without learning but dissatisfied with themselves is better for you
مِنْ أَنْ تَصْحَبَ عَالِمًا يَرْضَى عَنْ نَفْسِهِ،
than befriending a learned person satisfied with themselves.
فَأَيُّ عِلْمٍ لِعَالِمٍ يَرْضَى عَنْ نَفْسِهِ،
What benefit is knowledge to a learned person satisfied with themselves?
وَأَيُّ جَهْلٍ لِجَاهِلٍ لَا يَرْضَى عَنْ نَفْسِهِ؟
Conversely, what blameworthy ignorance remains in someone without learning who continually corrects themselves?

45.translation: The ray of inner sight shows you His nearness. The essence of inner sight shows you the disappearance of attention to yourself through witnessing His existence. The reality of inner sight shows only His existence, without attention to your own existence or non-existence.
syarahEn: When beginning self-improvement, we often pay great attention to personal progress. We count deeds, assess concentration in worship, and compare today with yesterday. This may help, but can also keep ourselves at the centre. This wisdom describes the heart's growth towards deeper knowledge of Allah.

Shu'a' al-basirah is the ray of inner sight, 'ayn al-basirah its essence, and haqq al-basirah its increasingly complete depth. 'Adamaka, your non-existence, is read as the disappearance of self-glorifying attention when the heart acknowledges Allah's power. Creatures remain present as creation and responsible for obligations; this language does not erase that reality.

For example, someone initially feels proud of maintaining worship. Through learning, health, time, and Allah's assistance are recognized as enabling it. Pride gradually becomes gratitude. With maturity, the person grows busier fulfilling a trust than wondering whether they appear to possess a high spiritual rank.

We need not assign ourselves a numbered level or claim a particular state. The nearby measure is diminishing arrogance and better treatment of others. If worship makes belittling people easier, something needs examining. Continue learning, praying, and doing clear good. This wisdom guides attention from admiration for personal achievement towards a more honest acknowledgement of Allah's gifts.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, after helping an activity, we sometimes keep examining people's impressions. Did I look capable? Did anyone notice? Were my words considered good? The activity is over, yet in our minds we still stand in the room awaiting applause that never arrives.

Ibn 'Ata'illah discusses degrees of the heart's sight. With knowledge of Allah, self-glorifying attention diminishes. Witnessing in the heart does not mean people become God or creatures lose responsibility. We learn to acknowledge Allah's power until our own contribution no longer continually fills every space of attention in devotion.

Dear friends, imagine taking a neighbour to hospital. Afterwards, what is most useful is ensuring the person has support and clear next needs. If attention is consumed by awaiting acknowledgement of our contribution, helping feels heavy. We start calculating whether the thanks are enough and a small good deed becomes an emotional bill.

“Wanting appreciation is natural, is it not?” Indeed. We may acknowledge that need and discuss sharing burdens. Yet it must not govern every action. Practise returning attention to the benefit someone needs. If energy is limited, state limits clearly. We need not continually sacrifice ourselves to look good and secretly resent insufficient praise.

Dear congregation, a simple exercise after helping is to check completion, give thanks for the ability, and continue life. Correct shortcomings if any. We need not keep replaying our own image mentally. The person helped has needs of their own. We make room for service to end reasonably and the relationship to remain light.

Let us ask for a heart broader than the wish to be the centre of attention. May Allah accept our help, forgive mixed intentions, and assist us in reducing pride. As we know His generosity more, may we more readily serve others' benefit without continually counting how visible we are. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
