Creatures remain present as creation and responsible for obligations; this language does not erase that reality.

Let us hold this understanding carefully, dear friends. Advice about focusing attention on benefit while helping should be read alongside our obligations as servants of Allah and our responsibilities towards others. Feeling peaceful after hearing a talk is certainly pleasant. Yet sound understanding also helps us act when things no longer feel peaceful. That is why explaining the words matters. We gain something to guide our direction, rather than a beautiful impression that soon fades. If we later forget how the term sounds, remember the relationship it explains: how the heart turns to Allah and how our choices touch real life.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, imagine taking a neighbour to hospital. Afterwards, what is most useful is ensuring the person has support and clear next needs. If attention is consumed by awaiting acknowledgement of our contribution, helping feels heavy. We start calculating whether the thanks are enough and a small good deed becomes an emotional bill.

“Wanting appreciation is natural, is it not?” Indeed. We may acknowledge that need and discuss sharing burdens. Yet it must not govern every action. Practise returning attention to the benefit someone needs. If energy is limited, state limits clearly. We need not continually sacrifice ourselves to look good and secretly resent insufficient praise.

After taking the neighbour somewhere, someone repeatedly checks the residents' group, hoping for a mention in a thank-you message. When none comes, help once readily given feels heavy. Dear friends, this feeling can offer a chance to redirect attention. Ask again about the neighbour's needs: is someone accompanying them, does the return journey need arranging? If our energy is spent, state limits kindly. We need not take every matter to preserve a helper's image. Clear benefit and honest limits help more than sacrifice secretly becoming a bill demanding continual recognition.

“I am human too; I want appreciation.” We may acknowledge that need, dear congregation. We can discuss shared burdens and hope for mutual respect. Yet do not make recipients responsible for our entire sense of worth. They may be tired or occupied with their own problem. Sincerity needs practice while goodness continues. The wisdom's language about attention to self disappearing also needs proper reading. Human responsibility remains. We are not erasing our existence, but learning not to place personal pride at the centre of every action. Allah's help is acknowledged as the foundation of our ability to assist.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Has the person been helped or is our attention still caught on recognition?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone initially feels proud of maintaining worship. Through learning, health, time, and Allah's assistance are recognized as enabling it. Pride gradually becomes gratitude. With maturity, the person grows busier fulfilling a trust than wondering whether they appear to possess a high spiritual rank.

Dear congregation, a simple exercise after helping is to check completion, give thanks for the ability, and continue life. Correct shortcomings if any. We need not keep replaying our own image mentally. The person helped has needs of their own. We make room for service to end reasonably and the relationship to remain light.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of focusing attention on benefit while helping, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

We need not assign ourselves a numbered level or claim a particular state. The nearby measure is diminishing arrogance and better treatment of others. If worship makes belittling people easier, something needs examining. Continue learning, praying, and doing clear good. This wisdom guides attention from admiration for personal achievement towards a more honest acknowledgement of Allah's gifts.

For practice, decide the help's aim beforehand. Afterwards, check whether it was achieved without continually measuring praise. If rest is needed, arrange it honestly. If the heart resents being unmentioned, bring that feeling into supplication and straighten intention without sarcastic remarks to the recipient. We can keep one act of help as something few need know. May attention return more readily to others' needs, so goodness does not become a tool for demanding thanks according to our taste.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about focusing attention on benefit while helping. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about focusing attention on benefit while helping. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us ask for a heart broader than the wish to be the centre of attention. May Allah accept our help, forgive mixed intentions, and assist us in reducing pride. As we know His generosity more, may we more readily serve others' benefit without continually counting how visible we are. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: شُعَاعُ الْبَصِيرَةِ يُشْهِدُكَ قُرْبَهُ مِنْكَ،
The inner eye's ray shows you His nearness.
وَعَيْنُ الْبَصِيرَةِ يُشْهِدُكَ عَدَمَكَ لِوُجُودِهِ،
The essence of inner sight shows attention to yourself vanishing through witnessing His existence.
وَحَقُّ الْبَصِيرَةِ يُشْهِدُكَ وُجُودَهُ لَا عَدَمَكَ وَلَا وُجُودَكَ.
The reality of inner sight shows only His existence, without attention to your existence or non-existence.

46.translation: Allah was, and nothing was with Him. Even now, He remains as He was.
syarahEn: Allah gains no greatness because the world is created and loses none when creatures end. All creation needs Him, while He needs no creation. This wisdom strengthens tawhid in a short sentence, so our relationship with Allah is not imagined like relationships between creatures completing each other's deficiencies.

Kana Allah means Allah was. La shay'a ma'ahu emphasizes that nothing accompanies Him independently or as a rival. Wa huwa al-ana directs attention to the present: creation's existence does not alter Allah's perfection. He remains independent of creatures, space, and the changes characteristic of our lives.

This lesson orders how we worship. Allah does not become more perfect through our obedience. Devotion benefits the servant helped to obey. Understanding this prevents deeds becoming bargaining tools for Allah to fulfil wishes. Salah and service to others are performed as obligations and gratitude for gifts already received.

When pride arises about contributing much to religion or community, remember how many abilities still depend on Allah's help. Good work remains valued and needs completing, but gives no right to feel needed by God. This awareness produces humility preserving deeds. We work more sincerely through knowing our position, then ask that limited devotion be accepted by Allah who needs nothing.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, moving home often makes much feel unfamiliar. Roads differ, neighbours are unknown, and family habits need rearranging. Some move for a good opportunity; others must adjust costs. Amid change, the heart may say, “My life used to feel more whole.” We miss a place and the safety once accompanying it.

Ibn 'Ata'illah affirms that Allah existed independently of creation and remains as He is. His oneness and perfection do not change when creatures' circumstances change. This lesson gives the heart a hold when surroundings shift. The old home may be missed, yet servanthood to Allah remains open in a new place and different circumstances.

Dear congregation, settling in may involve simple things. Learn the area, seek necessary information, and gradually build neighbourly relationships. Arrange a suitable prayer space, however simple. We need not wait for every piece of furniture to establish good habits. Some routines can come with us, such as family supplication or listening to children's stories after their activities.

“What if a child keeps wanting the old home?” Listen to that loss. Do not force immediate happiness because adults have decided. Explain the move's reasons according to age and involve the child in arranging a small area. Change becomes more manageable when feelings are acknowledged and there is something the child can choose.

Dear friends, allow ourselves time too. Memories need not be erased for us to move forward. We can retain good relationships with the old community while beginning to be present now. Pray for former neighbours and seek one chance to greet new ones. Life continues through encounters that may initially feel awkward.

Let us ask for steadiness amid relocation. May Allah bless our homes, protect families adjusting, and open good fellowship. May we realize a changed address does not close devotion's door. Wherever we live, we can still honour responsibilities and learn to love the people we meet. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

phrasesEn: كَانَ اللَّهُ وَلَا شَيْءَ مَعَهُ،

Even now He remains as He always was.

47.translation: Do not let your aspiration pass beyond Him towards another. For hopes need not pass beyond the Most Generous.
syarahEn: At times the heart pursues human approval until its relationship with Allah is forgotten. We want acceptance, help, or recognition and feel obliged to please anyone considered influential. This wisdom directs our aspirations towards Allah so needing people does not remove inward freedom.

Niyyatu himmatik means the direction of resolve or the aim sincerely sought. Al-Karim refers to Allah, the Most Generous, whose generosity is vast. Al-amal means hopes. The image of hopes not passing beyond the Most Generous explains why Allah deserves our highest reliance. We need not seek an imagined power more decisive than His generosity and might.

We may still propose cooperation, seek work, or ask people for advice. All must remain within proper limits. If a relationship demands deception or belittling others, hope needs reordering. Losing one opportunity does not mean losing every door to help, since the person offering it also has limits.

Before deciding to gain something, ask what we are truly pursuing. Does the need make us violate a principle we know is right? If so, pause to pray and seek another lawful path. Directing hope to Allah helps us ask reasonably and receive refusal without losing dignity. The heart becomes calmer because the whole future is not handed to one person's acceptance, while effort remains respectful and sincere.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, parents naturally hope children grow well and love family. Yet sacrifice sometimes becomes calculation: “I raised this child; later they must repay me exactly as I want.” Different choices then feel like betrayal. Relationships grow heavy because love carries an emotional bill never clearly expressed.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us not to let the heart's aim pass beyond Allah, the Most Generous. Hope in His generosity is not exhausted by human limits. Family rights and duties remain. Yet all happiness and the meaning of service should not rest on one person's ability to fulfil our own picture of the return we should receive.

Dear friends, adult children have abilities, responsibilities, and paths needing discussion. If parents require financial help or company, state it concretely. Avoid disguising needs in long sarcasm about past sacrifice. Clear conversation gives children a chance to understand and arrange help according to their real circumstances.

“Does that mean children may forget their parents' service?” Dutifulness must certainly be preserved. We are ordering two directions: children learn respect and parents broader hope. Negligence or mistreatment needs proper discussion. Hoping in Allah does not leave rights ignored; it gives a hold so the heart is not drowned in human disappointment.

Dear congregation, self-care and broader meaningful activities also help parents. Friends, community, and service remain possible according to ability. Life need not stop while waiting for a child to provide happiness. We keep praying for their good while tending a more orderly daily life and a relationship filled with more than demands or guilt.

Let us bring family sacrifice before Allah with expansive hope. May He guide children towards dutifulness, provide enough for parents, and soften conversations at home. May love grow through honestly expressed needs and help within ability. May we respect each other while retaining reliance on Him. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

48.translation: Do not present to another a need that He has brought to you. How can another remove what He Himself has placed? One unable to remove a need from himself: how can he remove it from someone else?
syarahEn: When a need feels urgent, all hope may be placed in someone thought able to resolve it. If they cannot help, the heart collapses. This wisdom reminds us that human helpers also have needs and limits. Requests through means therefore need the heart's dependence on Allah.

Hajah means need. Muriduha points to Him who brings that need into our life. Rafi'an means one lifting or removing. The sequence emphasizes that creatures do not independently control themselves, let alone every circumstance of others. Human assistance can truly help, but its ability remains among the means Allah provides.

For example, someone in financial difficulty may seek work, advice, or available assistance. They are not commanded to reject all help. What needs guarding is need becoming a conviction that a particular person can certainly guarantee life. Awareness of means' limits makes requests more reasonable and gratitude greater when help arrives.

Bring needs to Allah through honest supplication, then pursue proper avenues of help. Explain enough, avoid manipulation, and accept when someone truly cannot assist. If helping, offer our best ability without feeling supremely powerful. Need can then bring servanthood to Allah together with human compassion. The heart has firm reliance while social relationships remain alive through cooperation, responsibility, and respect for each other's limits.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, some facing health problems feel reluctant to seek help and say, “I simply surrender to Allah.” Others place every hope in one doctor as though healing were certainly held in that person's hands. We need to order the relationship between supplication, effort, and respect for human ability.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that creatures also need help themselves. No human can independently guarantee every need of another. This message preserves the heart's reliance on Allah. We may still, and need to, use proper means, including treatment, consultation, or support for difficulties requiring expertise.

Dear congregation, consulting a health professional does not mean insufficient tawakkul. We use abilities and means available. Listen to explanations, ask about what is unclear, and follow guidance suited to the situation. If another opinion is needed, seek it properly. Supplication accompanies effort, sparing us a false choice between them.

“What if help has not brought the hoped-for result?” We may be sad and ask about next steps. Yet avoid assuming people can certainly control everything. They work within knowledge's and ability's limits. If negligence is suspected, investigate through proper channels. Fair judgement needs information, rather than only anger at an outcome differing from personal hopes.

Dear friends, supporting family can help record questions, arrange transport, or accompany explanations. Do not make a sick person feel guilty for needing much assistance. We all have times when we cannot manage alone. Human help can be a very real path of goodness, provided it comes without demands, excessive promises, or disregard for the recipient's dignity.

Let us ask for healing and wisdom in pursuing effort. May Allah bless health professionals, strengthen family carers, and provide enough for those struggling with care costs. May we receive assistance respectfully, use means responsibly, and continue acknowledging all life within His power and care. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about using human assistance while continuing to hope in Allah meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.
CORE WISDOM

Dear congregation, a saying of wisdom may be very short, yet reflection reveals how deeply it touches our long-standing habits. We are seeing that here in the matter of using human assistance while continuing to hope in Allah. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, consulting a health professional does not mean insufficient tawakkul. We use abilities and means available. A family accompanies someone needing examination. One seeks information, another arranges travel, and another prays anxiously. Dear friends, these activities can support each other. We may ask competent professionals for explanation and state what is unclear. Asking need not feel like insufficient surrender. Conversely, human ability must not be treated as controlling every result. We respect the work and acknowledge limits. Hope can remain strong without demanding certainty nobody can promise. Supplication makes room for the heart's needs, while effort attends to available means.

“If the outcome differs from hope, who is at fault?” Disappointment alone cannot decide, dear congregation. Many circumstances need understanding. If there are service questions, seek explanation through appropriate channels. Fair assessment needs information. A family's sadness also deserves hearing without immediately being labelled weak faith. We can accompany them and help with next steps. The wisdom reminds us that creatures have no independent power over every need. This acknowledgement orders the heart's reliance while human responsibility is properly examined and useful assistance still used.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “How can supplication and effort work together when a family needs health assistance?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone in financial difficulty may seek work, advice, or available assistance. They are not commanded to reject all help. We all have times when we cannot manage alone. Human help can be a very real path of goodness, provided it comes without demands, excessive promises, or disregard for the recipient's dignity.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about using human assistance while continuing to hope in Allah may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Bring needs to Allah through honest supplication, then pursue proper avenues of help. Explain enough, avoid manipulation, and accept when someone truly cannot assist. If helping, offer our best ability without feeling supremely powerful. Need can then bring servanthood to Allah together with human compassion. The heart has firm reliance while social relationships remain alive through cooperation, responsibility, and respect for each other's limits.

For practice, choose one unclear question and record it before consultation. When supporting family, help listen without replacing professional explanations with personal guesses. Express needs honestly and seek support within ability. In supplication, ask for assistance and guidance in attending to available steps. We need not create a choice as though only prayer or effort were permitted. May Allah open a good way, strengthen anxious hearts, and help us appreciate means without making them absolute reliance.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of using human assistance while continuing to hope in Allah again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about using human assistance while continuing to hope in Allah. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us ask for healing and wisdom in pursuing effort. May Allah bless health professionals, strengthen family carers, and provide enough for those struggling with care costs. May we receive assistance respectfully, use means responsibly, and continue acknowledging all life within His power and care. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: لَا تَرْفَعَنَّ إِلَى غَيْرِهِ حَاجَةً هُوَ مُورِدُهَا عَلَيْكَ،
Do not present to anyone besides Him a need He Himself has brought to you.
فَكَيْفَ يَرْفَعُ غَيْرُهُ مَا كَانَ هُوَ لَهُ وَاضِعًا؟
How can anyone besides Him remove what He Himself has placed?
مَنْ لَا يَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ يَرْفَعَ حَاجَةً عَنْ نَفْسِهِ
Someone unable to remove need from themselves,
فَكَيْفَ يَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَهَا عَنْ غَيْرِهِ رَافِعًا؟
how can they remove it from another?

49.translation: If you do not yet think well of Him because of the beauty of His attributes, think well of Him because of His dealings with you. Has He not always treated you well? Has He bestowed anything upon you but gifts?
syarahEn: In hardship, memory often narrows to what has not been given. Past help and remaining blessings become less visible. Ibn 'Ata'illah invites us to reopen that memory. Recognizing Allah's goodness throughout life helps the heart think well of Him while today's circumstances remain beyond our understanding.

Husn al-zann means thinking well. Husnu wasfih points to the beauty of Allah's attributes, while mu'amalatuhu ma'aka refers to His dealings with you. This wisdom offers a nearby path: if understanding of His attributes is not yet deep, reflect on gifts experienced. Minan means gifts, reminding us that life has long received blessings not all specifically requested.

We have passed through times that felt blocked, then found help along an unexpected path. We also receive everyday blessings, such as the ability to learn and someone willing to listen. Remembering these does not erase today's sadness. It offers a fuller view so one difficulty does not become the measure of our entire relationship with Allah.

Write down help we can clearly remember. Notice who became its means and how gratitude can become action. Then state present needs in supplication without hiding their weight. Thinking well does not mean certainty that every wish will be fulfilled. It means continuing to trust Allah's generosity while acknowledging limited understanding. That trust gives energy to strive and remain open to different forms of help.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, when one problem remains unresolved, the mind readily fills with, “My life is always difficult.” The journey seems to contain only closed doors. Yet sitting briefly may reveal someone who helped, a need once met, or hardship already overcome. Memory sometimes shrinks when facing disappointment.

Ibn 'Ata'illah invites us to improve our opinion of Allah by recalling generosity accompanying life. Recognizing His perfect attributes needs knowledge and the heart's growth. Remembering help received can be a nearby beginning. We learn to view one issue within a larger journey, so today's circumstances do not immediately exhaust hope.

Dear friends, try writing three remembered instances of help. They need not be great events. Perhaps a neighbour brought food during busyness, a teacher offered another learning opportunity, or a relative listened to an overwhelmed heart. This writing does not prove sadness forbidden. We simply allow sadness not to cover every memory of goodness that came.

“What if my past contains many wounds too?” We need not turn wounds into beautiful stories. Acknowledge pain and seek help for healing. At the same time, if one kindness can be recognized, allow it a place. The heart may hold sadness and thanks without forcing either to disappear immediately.

Dear congregation, follow remembering with action. Thank someone still reachable. If there is a present need, ask clearly for help. We are not returning to the past to live there. We take provision to face today more courageously and avoid hastily concluding that help can never come again.

Let us pray with our whole journey, including what remains unclear. May Allah open hearts, heal wounds, and guide difficult steps. May memories of His generosity help us think well while continuing effort. May we also have opportunities to become a means of help for those in need. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Perhaps a neighbour once helped with food or a teacher allowed a lesson to be repeated. Dear friends, that event does not cancel today's difficulty. Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. If you do not yet think well of Him through the beauty of His attribute,
فَحَسِّنْ ظَنَّكَ بِهِ لِوُجُودِ مُعَامَلَتِهِ مَعَكَ،

50.translation: How astonishing is someone who flees what he can never escape, yet seeks what cannot remain with him! Truly, it is not outward eyes that are blind, but the hearts within the breasts.
syarahEn: People may avoid responsibility to Allah while pursuing what they will certainly leave behind. We postpone repentance for work, honesty for profit, and worship for comfort. This wisdom reveals the strangeness of that choice: what cannot be avoided is shunned, while what cannot be kept is continually pursued.

Yahrubu means fleeing. La infikaka lahu 'anhu indicates what cannot be escaped: dependence on and return to Allah. La baqa'a lahu ma'ahu emphasizes that created pleasures will not always accompany us. Ta'ma al-qulub describes blindness of hearts: losing the ability to see priorities while outward eyes still function.

For example, someone protects profit by deceiving customers. Temporary extra money is gained, but a trust for which an account will be required is damaged. What is missing from sight is a longer measure. This wisdom invites consideration of consequences beyond momentary satisfaction, without rejecting every lawful enjoyment.

Examine one pursuit that keeps displacing obligations. Ask how long it can accompany us and what follows from the way it is obtained. Reorder priorities so worldly needs accompany preparation for the Hereafter. We may work, enjoy family, and reasonably maintain comfort. The heart needs to remember the direction of return, using the temporary as provision. With that clarity, effort no longer makes us flee the devotion giving meaning to the entire journey.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, buying something new often excites us. We research for days, compare prices, and carefully preserve packaging. Meanwhile, certainties such as death and accountability receive little time for thought. We diligently chase what will part from us while readily avoiding what we cannot avoid.

Ibn 'Ata'illah calls this astonishing. People flee what will certainly reach them and pursue what cannot always accompany them. The lesson does not forbid useful possessions. It reminds us not to let pleasure in temporary things consume attention until duties and provision for the Hereafter always come last.

Dear congregation, suppose we want to replace a vehicle. Calculate need and ability. Yet examine unfinished obligations too. A debt may need paying or entrusted belongings returning. Do not be so careful checking a vehicle's condition while less sincerely examining others' rights still in our care.

“Will remembering death make life gloomy?” Proper remembrance can help us value time. We become readier to end needless arguments and more careful with promises. Joy can still be enjoyed. Awareness of limited time gives reason to use opportunities more fully, rather than continually postponing relationships needing care.

Dear friends, discuss important matters calmly with family as needed. Put records of obligations and document storage in order. If a question of rights is unclear, seek competent explanation. Such actions make responsibilities easier to continue. We do not know when the journey ends, but can reduce what remains in disorder.

Let us enjoy the lawful without forgetting our return to Allah. May He bless provision, help fulfil obligations, and protect the heart from distracting attachments. May remaining time serve worship and good relationships. When buying something new, may we also remember one long-delayed trust to put right. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

When replacing a vehicle, we may know many details by heart. The engine is inspected, colours compared, and purchase plans repeatedly discussed. Meanwhile, an entrusted item remains unreturned because it can wait. Dear friends, attending to needs is not forbidden. Yet obligations deserve the same care. Someone awaiting a right also has a life. Remembering death helps us see time beyond control. We can enjoy blessings while organizing duties, so joy is not built on others' rights repeatedly postponed without sound reason.

“Thinking about death often makes me afraid.” Fear can be directed towards useful attention, dear congregation. We need not fill every moment with paralysing images. Remember life's limited opportunity, then examine a trust needing fulfilment. Resolve unnecessary quarrels and be more present with family. If thoughts of death become deeply disruptive, seek suitable support. This reminder aims to help responsible living. We may still laugh, plan needs, and enjoy the lawful while remembering return to Allah.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Which obligation needs attention before we become busy seeking the next purchase?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone protects profit by deceiving customers. Temporary extra money is gained, but a trust for which an account will be required is damaged. What is missing from sight is a longer measure. This wisdom invites consideration of consequences beyond momentary satisfaction, without rejecting every lawful enjoyment.

Dear friends, discuss important matters calmly with family as needed. Put records of obligations and document storage in order. If a question of rights is unclear, seek competent explanation. Such actions make responsibilities easier to continue. We do not know when the journey ends, but can reduce what remains in disorder.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about remembering our return while enjoying blessings responsibly may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Examine one pursuit that keeps displacing obligations. Ask how long it can accompany us and what follows from the way it is obtained. Reorder priorities so worldly needs accompany preparation for the Hereafter. We may work, enjoy family, and reasonably maintain comfort. The heart needs to remember the direction of return, using the temporary as provision. With that clarity, effort no longer makes us flee the devotion giving meaning to the entire journey.

Look at one shopping wish list and one list of obligations. Check whether a right should be settled first. If unable to fulfil everything, explain honestly and arrange proper steps. Do not promise merely to finish the conversation quickly. Families can practise reminding each other about borrowed belongings without humiliation. May awareness of time's limits increase care for trusts, and may today's blessings bring us nearer gratitude and accountability.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about remembering our return while enjoying blessings responsibly. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of remembering our return while enjoying blessings responsibly. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us enjoy the lawful without forgetting our return to Allah. May He bless provision, help fulfil obligations, and protect the heart from distracting attachments. May remaining time serve worship and good relationships. When buying something new, may we also remember one long-delayed trust to put right. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: الْعَجَبُ كُلُّ الْعَجَبِ مِمَّنْ يَهْرُبُ مِمَّا لَا انْفِكَاكَ لَهُ عَنْهُ،
How astonishing is someone fleeing what they cannot escape,
وَيَطْلُبُ مَا لَا بَقَاءَ لَهُ مَعَهُ،
yet seeking what cannot remain with them forever.
فَإِنَّهَا لَا تَعْمَى الْأَبْصَارُ
Indeed, it is not outward eyes that are blind,
وَلَكِنْ تَعْمَى الْقُلُوبُ الَّتِي فِي الصُّدُورِ.
but hearts within chests.

51.translation: Do not merely move from one created realm to another. Otherwise you resemble a mill donkey that keeps walking, yet reaches the very place from which it began. Move from created things towards the Creator. Indeed, to your Lord is the final end of all aims.
syarahEn: Outward change sometimes leaves the heart's aim unchanged. We leave work wanting praise, then enter religious activity with the same desire. The activity changes but the centre remains ourselves. This wisdom invites examination of direction so change truly brings us closer to Allah.

Al-akwan means created realms, while Al-Mukawwin points to the Creator bringing them all into being. Himar al-raha, the mill donkey, images circular movement returning to its starting place. The animal keeps stepping without changing destination. So does a heart changing objects of desire without improving its reliance and intention.

Someone once chasing position at work may later chase position in a religious gathering. If competition for a name and pride remain the goal, the move has not reached the root. Improvement means making new work a trust, accepting correction, and remaining willing to perform unseen tasks.

Moving towards Allah means ordering intention and life to follow His pleasure. We still live among creation and use necessary means. What changes is their place within the heart. Ask what disappoints us when our name is unmentioned or a task brings no spotlight. Honest answers show direction still needing correction. The journey becomes more meaningful when outward steps accompany inward change, so energy is not spent circling the need for recognition.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, have we thought, “Once promoted, I will be at peace”? After promotion, peace lasts briefly. Another position then becomes the next pursuit. We work harder while contentment recedes. Like changing rooms while carrying the same leak, the problem enters the new place and wets life again.

Ibn 'Ata'illah pictures moving between worldly interests as a mill animal turning in circles. There is much movement, but direction remains around the same centre. He invites the heart beyond attachment towards Allah. Work continues while devotion's purpose is examined, so it does not always end in personal pride.

Dear friends, promotion may be pursued when beneficial and within ability. Ask why. Do we want better service, enough for family, or merely to appear above someone? Intentions can mix. Admitting them offers correction, preventing work being ruled by competition that never truly ends.

“If I still want to develop, am I attached to the world?” Development can be well directed. Specify the benefit and boundaries to preserve. For example, we will not take colleagues' rights or neglect family for position. Such limits give a clearer direction than merely pursuing something appearing higher than the present.

Dear congregation, imagine the job title removed from our card. What goodness would we still want to do? The answer may reveal work nearer to devotion. Perhaps mentoring a new colleague, improving service, or keeping decisions fair. We learn to value benefit so a change of position is not our sole source of worth.

Let us bring aspirations before Allah with continually examined intentions. May He bless growing ability, protect us from competition exhausting the heart, and help us stop when ambition crosses rights. May each change in work bring real benefit and nearness to Him, giving our steps clearer purpose. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We may still face the same situation, the same people, and old habits that have not yet changed. We need to understand the message well enough to bring it into those circumstances. Listen slowly. If a sentence speaks to our situation, keep it in mind for later. We do not have to remember every explanation. One sound understanding, put sincerely into practice, is already worth working towards today.

We are seeing that here in the matter of ordering our purpose when a new position has not brought peace. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

For example, we will not take colleagues' rights or neglect family for position. Such limits give a clearer direction than merely pursuing something appearing higher than the present.

Someone finally gains a long-desired position. Relief lasts several weeks. Then another person appears in a higher position and inadequacy returns. Dear friends, examine the pattern before setting another target. Perhaps benefit genuinely needs expanding; perhaps the heart chases continually shifting recognition. Both motives may mix. Acknowledging this need not stop work. We can give a clearer aim: which responsibility can be carried and who should benefit? This measure directs work without continual comparison pulling it away.

“Does wanting promotion mean I am ungrateful?” Development may be pursued properly, dear congregation. Examine methods and boundaries. Do not take colleagues' rights or sacrifice duties to appear higher. A position also brings work, so weigh our ability to carry it. The wisdom about circular movement addresses a heart changing objects without correcting reliance. Some continually change positions while worth must still be proved daily by defeating others. The lesson invites ordering direction before energy is exhausted again chasing a measure that never stops moving.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “What are we truly seeking when the next position feels urgently necessary?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone once chasing position at work may later chase position in a religious gathering. If competition for a name and pride remain the goal, the move has not reached the root. Improvement means making new work a trust, accepting correction, and remaining willing to perform unseen tasks.

Dear congregation, imagine the job title removed from our card. What goodness would we still want to do? The answer may reveal work nearer to devotion. Perhaps mentoring a new colleague, improving service, or keeping decisions fair. We learn to value benefit so a change of position is not our sole source of worth.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of ordering our purpose when a new position has not brought peace, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.

Before setting a target, write the benefit sought and one boundary we will not cross. Ask whether a real need is neglected through attention absorbed by status. Seek honest feedback from someone understanding the work. Then develop ability systematically. We keep asking Allah for enough and for guidance. May changed positions bring accountable benefit and the heart find direction deeper than a continual need to be seen as superior.

Now let us turn the lesson about ordering our purpose when a new position has not brought peace into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about ordering our purpose when a new position has not brought peace, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us bring aspirations before Allah with continually examined intentions. May He bless growing ability, protect us from competition exhausting the heart, and help us stop when ambition crosses rights. May each change in work bring real benefit and nearness to Him, giving our steps clearer purpose. Amin.

phrasesEn: لَا تَرْحَلْ مِنْ كَوْنٍ إِلَى كَوْنٍ
Do not merely move from one created world to another.
فَتَكُونَ كَحِمَارِ الرَّحَى يَسِيرُ
Then you are like a mill donkey continually walking,
وَالْمَكَانُ الَّذِي ارْتَحَلَ إِلَيْهِ هُوَ الَّذِي ارْتَحَلَ مِنْهُ،
yet arriving where it originally departed.
وَلَكِنِ ارْحَلْ مِنَ الْأَكْوَانِ إِلَى الْمُكَوِّنِ،
Move from all creation towards the Creator.
وَأَنَّ إِلَى رَبِّكَ الْمُنْتَهَى.
Indeed, with your Lord is the final destination.

52.translation: Consider his saying, may Allah send blessings and peace upon him: whoever migrates to Allah and His Messenger, their migration is truly to Allah and His Messenger. Whoever migrates for worldly gain or to marry a woman, their migration is only to what they intended. Understand his saying, may blessings and peace be upon him, and reflect on this matter if you possess understanding.
syarahEn: Hijrah concerns both a place left and an aim sought. Two people can make the same move with different purposes. Through the Prophet's saying about migration, Ibn 'Ata'illah invites examination of intention so life changes truly connect with devotion to Allah.

Hijrah means moving or leaving one state for another. Ila Allahi wa rasulih shows obedience directed to Allah and His Messenger's guidance. Yusibuha means obtaining what is sought. This choice emphasizes that a person's journey follows its intention. Visible change alone therefore does not sufficiently explain its inward worth.

Seeking work, building a family, and moving home can be lawful needs. What needs examining is the honesty of purpose and method. Do not use devotion's name to hide interests we will not admit. Conversely, daily needs can have worship's value when rightly intended and pursued according to guidance.

Before major change, write the most real reasons. Are we seeking greater obedience, escaping responsibility, or chasing fresh recognition? Mixed intentions can be straightened through willingness to admit and improve them. Afterwards, keep examining their fruits in obligations and character. Healthy hijrah makes us more responsible. We leave more than an old place: we also learn to release bad habits that once accompanied our steps.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, when someone begins improving, visible changes are often discussed first. Different clothes, changed company, and posts filled with advice. We should support that good intention. Yet the journey needs to reach what is less visible: honesty, responsibility, and treatment of those once hurt by our actions.

Ibn 'Ata'illah invites attention to the Prophet's saying about hijrah and its purpose. Intention gives movement meaning. People may move into new circumstances, yet the heart's goal needs examining. We want change to bring devotion to Allah and the Messenger's guidance, rather than stop at worldly gain or a particular group's acceptance.

Dear congregation, suppose someone regularly attends lessons but still delays debt while avoiding the person asking for repayment. Some work cannot be replaced by a new appearance. They need to explain ability, arrange honest payments, and stop false promises. Religious change should help those around us receive rights and feel greater responsibility.

“If my past has many mistakes, will people trust me?” Trust takes time. We cannot demand people immediately forget experiences. Make real improvements and allow them to assess the process. Do not use hijrah to close discussion of mistakes' effects. Repentance helps us courageously face responsibility, even along an uncomfortable path.

Dear friends, family and companions should avoid mocking beginners. They may still stumble and lack consistency. Support the good and respectfully remind them of what needs improvement. We may appreciate the process without allowing rights to be ignored. Warm support often helps more than demanding immediate perfection after someone expresses a wish to change.

Let us renew our journey's purpose. May Allah preserve hijrah's intention, help us restore rights, and guide change until it is felt in daily character. May learners not despair when still untrusted and supporters receive wisdom. We want to continue with humility and responsibility. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Let me ask a question, dear congregation: “Whose rights need restoring so others can feel our change too?” Take a moment to think about it. Perhaps an answer comes straight away; perhaps a difficulty comes to mind instead. Let us hear that difficulty calmly. Good advice needs to meet the reality of life, including the limitations we face. Now imagine someone we love asking that question. Would our answer help them act, or simply leave them feeling scolded? Here we learn to convey the truth in a way that can be received. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. phrasesEn: وَانْظُرْ إِلَى قَوْلِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ
Consider his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.
فَمَنْ كَانَتْ هِجْرَتُهُ إِلَى اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ
Whoever's migration is towards Allah and His Messenger,
فَهِجْرَتُهُ إِلَى اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ،
their migration is truly towards Allah and His Messenger.
وَمَنْ كَانَتْ هِجْرَتُهُ إِلَى الدُّنْيَا يُصِيبُهَا أَوِ امْرَأَةٍ يَتَزَوَّجُهَا
Whoever migrates to obtain worldly gain or marry a woman,
فَهِجْرَتُهُ إِلَى مَا هَاجَرَ إِلَيْهِ.
their migration reaches only the purpose they intended.
فَافْهَمْ قَوْلَهُ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلَاةُ وَالسَّلَامُ
Understand his saying, blessings and peace be upon him,
وَتَأَمَّلْ هَذَا الْأَمْرَ إِنْ كُنْتَ ذَا فَهْمٍ.
and reflect on this matter if you possess understanding.

53.translation: Do not keep company with someone whose state does not lift you and whose words do not guide you to Allah.
syarahEn: Company shapes what feels normal. In one environment, honesty feels valued. In another, belittling people and delaying duties are ordinary. This wisdom invites closeness that keeps the heart alive, especially with people whose behaviour encourages us and whose words direct us towards Allah.

Haluhu means the person's state or behaviour. Yunhiduka means lifting and moving you. Maqaluhu means their speech, and yadulluka means showing the way. State and speech together emphasize that a friend's influence extends beyond advice. Work, family treatment, and responses to mistakes also teach us daily.

A good friend need not always speak about religion. Faithfulness to promises, willingness to listen, and courage to admit mistakes can strengthen devotion. Conversely, beautiful advice loses influence when accompanied by belittling habits. We need to assess repeated influence while acknowledging everyone's shortcomings.

Caring for our company is no reason to become hostile to those needing guidance. We can still be kind and help within ability. Yet the closeness most shaping our hearts needs conscious choice. Spend time with those making us more honest, diligent, and responsible. Be that friend for others too. Friendship becomes a gift when meeting brings courage to do goodness previously felt difficult.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, friendship groups can have a contagious atmosphere. One begins gossip and another adds a story. One suggests postponing work and everyone follows. It initially feels close, but afterwards the heart is hotter and tasks further behind. We need to ask where this closeness is taking our habits.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us to choose friends whose states and words guide towards Allah. Friendship is assessed through more than lively conversation. We also notice its effect on honesty, worship, and responsibility. Good friends can still joke, but closeness helps us become more trustworthy and willing to improve.

Dear friends, examine what often follows socializing. Are apologies easier or excuses cleverer? Are existing promises still respected? These questions concern our choices, rather than publicly identifying bad friends. We do not know entire hearts, but can recognize habits needing limits.

“If I leave the group, will I be thought arrogant?” Begin by reducing harmful conversations, redirecting topics, or politely stating limits. If the situation continually leads to wrong, distance may be needed. Not every relationship needs ending with an argument. Remain friendly while choosing healthier involvement for ourselves and our responsibilities.

Dear congregation, seek strengthening friends and become one too. Invite useful activity, do not mock someone wanting change, and stop private faults becoming stories. We need not preach at length in every conversation. Sometimes a simple, “Shall we discuss something else?” helps change everyone's direction.

Let us appreciate friends preserving goodness in our lives. May Allah bring a healthy environment, grant courage for boundaries, and protect friendship from slander and gossip. May togetherness make us more responsible, so benefits brought home are felt by family too. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about choosing involvement in friendships that shape habits meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with choosing involvement in friendships that shape habits. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, examine what often follows socializing. Are apologies easier or excuses cleverer? Are existing promises still respected? These questions concern our choices, rather than publicly identifying bad friends. We do not know entire hearts, but can recognize habits needing limits.

“If I leave the group, will I be thought arrogant?” Begin by reducing harmful conversations, redirecting topics, or politely stating limits. If the situation continually leads to wrong, distance may be needed. Not every relationship needs ending with an argument. Remain friendly while choosing healthier involvement for ourselves and our responsibilities.

A group conversation begins with light jokes. Then someone mentions a private fault and others add stories. We hesitate to stop, afraid of spoiling closeness. Dear friends, friendship's influence works through small habits here. We can refrain from adding stories and redirect discussion if possible. If there is a legitimate need for help, direct it appropriately without widening exposure. Notice time too: a family promise or work task may be long delayed. Closeness needs boundaries so relationships are not always paid for with negligence later regretted alone.

“If I keep distance, will they call me arrogant?” State limits warmly, dear congregation. Not every adjustment needs announcing as judgement on every member. Reduce harmful involvement and seek surroundings supporting better habits. We may refuse clearly wrong invitations. Maintain manners and do not retaliate by spreading bad stories about the group. The wisdom invites examination of how friends' states and words affect our direction. It helps us choose involvement, rather than claim knowledge of entire hearts or consider ourselves the purest among them.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “After a group conversation are we readier for our duties or increasingly heedless?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

A good friend need not always speak about religion. Faithfulness to promises, willingness to listen, and courage to admit mistakes can strengthen devotion. Conversely, beautiful advice loses influence when accompanied by belittling habits. We need to assess repeated influence while acknowledging everyone's shortcomings.

Dear congregation, seek strengthening friends and become one too. Invite useful activity, do not mock someone wanting change, and stop private faults becoming stories. We need not preach at length in every conversation. Sometimes a simple, “Shall we discuss something else?” helps change everyone's direction.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of choosing involvement in friendships that shape habits, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Caring for our company is no reason to become hostile to those needing guidance. We can still be kind and help within ability. Yet the closeness most shaping our hearts needs conscious choice. Spend time with those making us more honest, diligent, and responsible. Be that friend for others too. Friendship becomes a gift when meeting brings courage to do goodness previously felt difficult.

Notice one conversation most often taking time. Set a realistic limit and prepare how to refuse bad invitations. Meanwhile, preserve relationships helping us be more honest and responsible. We also try to become friends who respect promises and do not pressure others into gossip. Parents can guide children without immediately labelling all their friends. May company become a space for reminders and benefit, rather than a shared habit continually distancing us from responsibilities.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of choosing involvement in friendships that shape habits again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about choosing involvement in friendships that shape habits invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us appreciate friends preserving goodness in our lives. May Allah bring a healthy environment, grant courage for boundaries, and protect friendship from slander and gossip. May togetherness make us more responsible, so benefits brought home are felt by family too. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: لَا تَصْحَبْ مَنْ لَا يُنْهِضُكَ حَالُهُ
Do not keep company with someone whose state does not inspire you
وَلَا يَدُلُّكَ عَلَى اللَّهِ مَقَالُهُ.
and whose words do not guide you towards Allah.

54.translation: You may be doing wrong, yet your companionship makes you see yourself as good because you associate with someone whose state is worse than yours.
syarahEn: We may feel already good simply by being among people making more mistakes. Such comparison comforts, but does not always reflect reality. This wisdom returns improvement's measure to sound guidance and our own responsibility, rather than a friend's weakness.

Musi'an means someone doing wrong. Al-ihsan points to goodness as seen in one's own judgement. Suhbatuka means your companionship, while aswa'a halan means worse in state. These words explain how an environment changes assessment. Our mistake appears light because our comparison is someone crossing limits further.

For example, someone considers their speech courteous because friends insult more frequently. Yet daily sarcasm still hurts family. Comparing degrees of error does not resolve its effects. Ask instead whether the words are right and how to repair affected relationships.

Seek an environment helping growth while preserving compassion for those still learning. Do not use their weakness to elevate ourselves. Nor need we continually compare with apparently perfect figures until hope is lost. Use clear measures: obligations, character, and others' rights. Improvement appears in courage to acknowledge mistakes once defended. Friendship can then support without becoming a mirror deliberately chosen to make us always look best.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, a frequent defence is, “I may be like that, but others are worse.” We arrive a little late and point to a frequently absent friend. We discuss someone and compare ourselves with a slanderer. Our own shortcomings then feel unnecessary to correct because a comparison can always be found.

Ibn 'Ata'illah warns that someone may wrongly judge themselves good through company worse in state. Environment affects our measures. If standards continually fall, the heart readily feels safe. We need a proper measure and willingness to examine our own actions without hiding in someone else's faults.

Dear congregation, imagine a student copying one answer and saying, “My friend copied everything.” Comparison does not change the borrowed answer. The task is admitting it, learning what is not mastered, and improving the approach to exams. Children also need safety in asking help before difficulty drives them towards wrong choices.

“What if I simply want to feel there is still good in me?” We may acknowledge our goodness without obtaining it through belittling others. We can say, “Some parts I have done, and some need improving.” This is more honest than constructing worth through deliberate comparison with someone appearing worse.

Dear friends, use news of another's mistake as a reminder, rather than self-elevation. We may not face the same test. Avoid mockery and examine boundaries needing care in our own lives. If tasked with assessing conduct, use evidence and fair rules. Judgement must not become a stage for displaying personal superiority.

Let us stop one excuse saying, “At least I am better.” May Allah grant courage to admit shortcomings, protect us from false security, and guide real improvement. May we see our goodness gratefully and mistakes responsibly, without needing someone else's wrongdoing to feel worthy of respect. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

If an example does not match our circumstances exactly, notice the attitude being discussed. Often, beneath differences in work or age, there is a habit of the heart that many of us recognize.

Does this explanation make our responsibilities clearer? Are other people's rights still protected? Questions like these help us read advice with a humble heart and a mind willing to learn.

A student taking one friend's answer feels the mistake small because someone else copied everything. Adults can repeat that pattern when delaying promises or gossiping. Dear friends, comparison shifts discussion from our action to others' mistakes. Bring it back with, “My part still needs improvement.” This admission does not mean the whole self is bad. Some goodness deserves gratitude and an action requires responsibility. Worth need not be built by finding someone crossing boundaries further than us.

“Without comparison, how do we know progress?” We may assess action through proper measures, dear congregation: whether work is our own and promises are increasingly kept. We can also compare with previous habits. Avoid a deliberately chosen comparison making faults seem unnecessary to address. Environment affects judgement, so repeated mistakes can feel ordinary. Keep company helping us accept correction. When supporting a child, allow help-seeking before difficulty prompts a wrong method. Honesty needs an opportunity to learn.

Now try answering silently, dear friends: “Does someone else's mistake make our own mistake right?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. May a gathering like this send us home with the courage to learn, rather than merely the ability to comment on other people's lives.
PERSONAL REFLECTION
