Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about admitting shortcomings without seeking a worse comparison may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. For practice, identify our most frequent defensive sentence. When it returns, pause and name the actual action needing examination. Choose an appropriate improvement. We need not name a comparison or humiliate ourselves publicly. If someone is affected, attend to their rights properly. May courage to admit shortcomings grow with healthy self-respect, so change no longer waits until we become worse than someone else.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about admitting shortcomings without seeking a worse comparison will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. What we want to nurture is a willingness to do our part properly and in an orderly way, even when the results still take time to appear.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about admitting shortcomings without seeking a worse comparison, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us stop one excuse saying, “At least I am better.” May Allah grant courage to admit shortcomings, protect us from false security, and guide real improvement. May we see our goodness gratefully and mistakes responsibly, without needing someone else's wrongdoing to feel worthy of respect. Amin.

phrasesEn: رُبَّمَا كُنْتَ مُسِيئًا
Sometimes you are doing wrong,
فَأَرَاكَ الْإِحْسَانَ مِنْكَ صُحْبَتُكَ
but your companionship makes you see yourself as already good,
إِلَى مَنْ هُوَ أَسْوَأُ حَالًا مِنْكَ.
because your companion's state is worse than yours.

55.translation: A deed emerging from a heart detached from the world is not small in worth. A deed emerging from a heart captivated by the world is not great in worth.
syarahEn: The amount of visible activity does not necessarily reveal purity of purpose. Small help may be given freely, while great activity fills with a wish for recognition. This wisdom examines the heart's direction so dedication is not measured only by easily displayed size.

Zahid means someone not enslaved by worldly attachment. Zuhd need not mean poverty or abandoning possessions. Raghib here points to a heart intensely drawn to worldly gain. Baraza, emerging or coming forth, connects deeds with their inward source. Deeds carry traces of the heart producing them, so intention's quality also needs care.

A wealthy person can practise zuhd by using wealth properly without sacrificing principles for more possessions. Conversely, someone with little may remain ruled by greed. This wisdom is therefore primarily our own mirror. We do not know others' entire intentions through the size of their assistance alone.

Act within ability and improve quality. Do not belittle small help when useful and properly given. Fulfil large responsibilities in order and openly to examination. Tend willingness to do good without reward in reputation. A heart freer from the world can give more honestly. From that state, deeds gain weight not necessarily proportional to the stage's size or number watching.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, some simple gifts feel very warm. Perhaps only a parcel of food, given without making us feel inferior. Other large help leaves recipients fearful because the favour is continually mentioned. A relationship's worth is more than the quantity of goods. The giver's attachment shapes the recipient's experience too.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that deeds from a heart of zuhd are not considered small in worth. Zuhd means not being enslaved by ownership, rather than abandoning all wealth. Someone may have little yet be deeply attached, or have much and use it responsibly. We cannot assess the inner state solely from a wallet or appearance.

Dear friends, imagine a neighbour helping carry shopping, then continuing work. Assistance feels light because no demand follows for every wish to be fulfilled. We can practise this in giving help. Ask needs, give within ability, and explain limits if any. Do not conceal conditions and reveal them after someone feels indebted.

“What if our help is misused?” We may improve distribution and set reasonable boundaries. Sincerity does not require ignoring a trust or evidence of misuse. Yet help genuinely given without conditions should not become a tool to control recipients' choices. They retain dignity and rights over their lives, including the right to disagree with the giver.

Dear congregation, if we can offer only a little, do not quickly belittle the opportunity. Physical help, accurate information, or listening time may be very useful according to need. Do it well and preserve prior obligations. We need not force giving to match others while neglecting the family dependent on us.

Let us learn to give with a lighter heart. May Allah provide for those in need, bless wealth used for good, and protect us from controlling through favours. May our small help arrive respectfully, bring real benefit, and leave no emotional burden for its recipients. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Do it well and preserve prior obligations. We need not force giving to match others while neglecting the family dependent on us.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of giving help without adding hidden conditions, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Act within ability and improve quality. Do not belittle small help when useful and properly given. Fulfil large responsibilities in order and openly to examination. Tend willingness to do good without reward in reputation. A heart freer from the world can give more honestly. From that state, deeds gain weight not necessarily proportional to the stage's size or number watching.

Examine one intended act of assistance. Explain necessary limits or terms from the start. If unconditional, keep later words from turning it into pressure. Allow recipients to express needs and choices. Those receiving still preserve thanks and responsible use. May even small help give safety and relationships grow warmer through mutual respect, rather than one person continually feeling under a debt of gratitude.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about giving help without adding hidden conditions. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about giving help without adding hidden conditions. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us learn to give with a lighter heart. May Allah provide for those in need, bless wealth used for good, and protect us from controlling through favours. May our small help arrive respectfully, bring real benefit, and leave no emotional burden for its recipients. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَا قَلَّ عَمَلٌ بَرَزَ مِنْ قَلْبٍ زَاهِدٍ،
A deed from a heart detached from the world is not small in value.
وَمَا كَثُرَ عَمَلٌ بَرَزَ مِنْ قَلْبٍ رَاغِبٍ.
A deed from a heart captivated by the world is not great in value.

56.translation: Good deeds result from good inward states. Good inward states arise from firmness in the station Allah has granted.
syarahEn: Good habits last more readily when supported by a healthy heart. Teaching with compassion produces different treatment of pupils from teaching merely to appear powerful. This wisdom connects actions' quality with the inner source, then reminds us that inward maturity also needs Allah's help.

Husn al-a'mal means goodness of deeds, while husn al-ahwal means goodness of inward states. Al-tahaqquq means firmness or something truly becoming established. The expression about a granted station invites devotion suited to the circumstances Allah gives. Such spiritual terms need not become titles for ranking ourselves against others.

For example, someone wants more patience serving family. Restraining speech needs practice, but so does examining the sense of contributing most that makes service feel like others' debt. Remembering the ability to help as a gift can reduce inward demands. This change of perspective helps good action last without continual thanks.

Outward and inward improvement can proceed together. Set a clear action, such as keeping a promise, and tend intention through supplication and review. If we fail, seek causes without immediately abandoning hope. Ask for help in steadying the heart within the devotion entrusted to us. This wisdom makes us attentive to behaviour's source. Deeds are not merely tidied externally, but grown from a heart learning gratitude, receiving guidance, and not making personal ability absolute.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, housework may be the same while our way of doing it differs. With a calm heart, dirty dishes are washed ordinarily. With stored resentment, plates sound louder and every question irritates. Family may be confused, not knowing which problem entered the kitchen with us.

Ibn 'Ata'illah connects good deeds with good inward states and growth Allah grants. Outward behaviour needs care for the heart. Demanding patient appearances is insufficient while exhaustion and anger remain ignored. Honest recognition of our state helps appropriate action and asking help with a clear need.

Dear congregation, before work after a heavy day, pause if possible. Ask, “With whom am I angry? Do I need food, rest, or conversation?” The answer does not justify harshness. We seek causes precisely so those uninvolved do not bear effects of an unattended burden.

“What if the work cannot wait?” Do the most urgent part and state the need briefly. For example, “I am very tired. Could you help set the table?” A clear request helps more than expecting everyone to guess, then becoming angry at their failure. Discuss shared tasks when reasonably calm so exhaustion does not repeat without change.

Dear friends, inward care also comes through maintained worship, safe conversation, and gradual willingness to forgive. Seek appropriate support for serious relationship problems. Everything need not be solved in one night. What matters is stopping the assumption that the heart's state has no connection with daily treatment of those living with us.

Let us tend behaviour's source, rather than only its final appearance. May Allah open the hearts of those managing homes, grant sufficient energy, and help families share burdens fairly. When exhaustion comes, may needs be expressed without harm. May everyday work nurture compassion felt together. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

What matters is being willing to learn sincerely, examine our understanding, and follow sound guidance when seeking to change our daily habits.

If possible, pause and recognize the nearest need. Have we not eaten, or does a work issue fill the mind? Then make a clear request, perhaps for help setting the table. A brief explanation can help more than deliberately loud objects. We remain responsible for treating those who do not know the burden carried.

“I am already tired; must I still explain?” Explaining may indeed feel heavy, dear congregation. Task-sharing should therefore also be discussed at a reasonably calm time. Do not always wait until everyone's energy is gone. Other family members need active attention rather than expecting one person to remind everyone about all work. The wisdom about inward states reveals their effect on action. Yet do not use ikhlas to close discussion of unshared burdens. The heart receives care and working arrangements improve so goodness at home gains practical support.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “What needs expressing when a burdened heart enters the kitchen?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Choose one task most often causing tension. Discuss responsibility and when help is needed. Prepare brief words expressing tiredness without blame. If we have shouted, admit it and correct speech. Give children age-appropriate tasks and clear instructions. Housework connects with relationships, so its manner needs attention too. May exhaustion receive care and families increasingly help one another before raised voices become accepted language.

Now let us turn the lesson about recognizing exhaustion before releasing it through housework into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about recognizing exhaustion before releasing it through housework invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us tend behaviour's source, rather than only its final appearance. May Allah open the hearts of those managing homes, grant sufficient energy, and help families share burdens fairly. Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: حُسْنُ الْأَعْمَالِ نَتَائِجُ حُسْنِ الْأَحْوَالِ،
Good deeds result from good inner states.
وَحُسْنُ الْأَحْوَالِ مِنَ التَّحَقُّقِ فِي مَقَامَاتِ الْإِنْزَالِ.
Good inner states arise from firmness in the station Allah grants.

57.translation: Do not abandon dhikr because your heart is not yet present with Allah while remembering Him. Heedlessness that leaves remembrance altogether is more serious than heedlessness while still remembering. May He raise you from heedless remembrance to wakeful remembrance, from wakeful remembrance to remembrance with presence of heart, and from presence to remembrance in which attention disappears from everything other than Allah. That is not difficult for Allah.
syarahEn: During dhikr, the mind may wander to work or family problems. We then feel remembrance is useless without concentration. Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us not to make insufficient presence a reason to stop. Remembrance still accompanied by heedlessness can remain a path of training towards better attention.

Ghaflah means heedlessness. Yaqazah is awareness or wakefulness, while hudur means presence of heart. These stages describe growing attention. Disappearance from everything other than the One remembered explains the heart's focus on Allah, without removing life's responsibilities. We still follow worship's guidance and need not force a particular spiritual experience.

If attention shifts during dhikr, gently return to the words and meaning. Choose a calmer time, understand the recitation, and reduce avoidable distractions. Do not assess the whole practice by one experience. Some days are easy and others hard, while faithfulness retains its training value.

The form and number of dhikr follow correctly understood guidance. Avoid adding burdens until obligations or health are neglected. Begin with a maintainable habit and ask Allah to bring the heart into it. If interrupted, return without waiting for perfect conditions. This wisdom nurtures active hope: we keep the door of deeds open while acknowledging deep knowing as a gift sought through practice, patience, and Allah's help.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, have we begun dhikr and suddenly remembered the washing? After a few recitations, thoughts move to bills and tomorrow's work. Noticing, we feel disappointed: “Pointless. My mouth moves but the heart wanders everywhere.” Recitation is then abandoned entirely. We imagine full presence must come immediately for a practice to deserve continuation in daily life.

Ibn 'Ata'illah specifically reminds us not to abandon dhikr because presence is inconsistent. Heedlessness without any remembrance can be more serious than heedlessness while still trying to remember. We hope Allah helps attention grow. Training needs sincere practice without making initial shortcomings an excuse to stop.

Dear friends, small steps can help. Choose a known recitation, learn its meaning, and read at a reasonable pace. If attention wanders, gently return it. Do not scold ourselves every time thoughts leave. Like someone learning to listen, we repeatedly invite the heart home to what we intend to attend to.

“What if life is very busy?” Prioritize obligations and choose a suitable time. Maintain a simple guided practice while respecting safety and tasks requiring concentration. Do not force a particular number merely to feel successful. Sincerity also appears in learning correct recitation and understanding what we ask Allah.

Dear congregation, dhikr is no competition to prove inner experience. We need not claim a special state. Notice whether remembrance helps restrain bad speech or regain calm before acting. If effects are not visible, keep learning and examine practice. Change of heart often needs perseverance not striking from one day to the next.

Let us preserve chances to remember Allah even while attention needs training. May He accept imperfect recitation, guide easily distracted hearts, and help us understand its meaning. May dhikr enliven our relationship with Him and help us be more fully present in daily duties and relationships. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

phrasesEn: لَا تَتْرُكِ الذِّكْرَ لِعَدَمِ حُضُورِكَ مَعَ اللَّهِ فِيهِ،
Do not abandon dhikr because your heart is not yet present with Allah during remembrance.
لِأَنَّ غَفْلَتَكَ عَنْ وُجُودِ ذِكْرِهِ أَشَدُّ مِنْ غَفْلَتِكَ فِي وُجُودِ ذِكْرِهِ،
Heedlessness that leaves remembrance entirely is more serious than heedlessness while still remembering.
فَعَسَى أَنْ يَرْفَعَكَ مِنْ ذِكْرٍ مَعَ وُجُودِ غَفْلَةٍ إِلَى ذِكْرٍ مَعَ وُجُودِ يَقَظَةٍ،
May He raise you from heedless dhikr to dhikr accompanied by awareness.
وَمِنْ ذِكْرٍ مَعَ وُجُودِ يَقَظَةٍ إِلَى ذِكْرٍ مَعَ وُجُودِ حُضُورٍ،
Then from aware dhikr to dhikr accompanied by presence of heart.
وَمِنْ ذِكْرٍ مَعَ وُجُودِ حُضُورٍ إِلَى ذِكْرٍ مَعَ غَيْبَةٍ عَمَّا سِوَى الْمَذْكُورِ،
Then from dhikr with presence of heart to dhikr in which attention vanishes from everything besides Allah.
وَمَا ذَلِكَ عَلَى اللَّهِ بِعَزِيزٍ.
That is not difficult for Allah.

58.translation: Among the signs of a dead heart are feeling no sadness for obedience missed and no remorse for a wrong committed.
syarahEn: A sensitive heart feels loss when goodness is abandoned and remorse when it causes hurt. These feelings invite improvement. This wisdom warns against every mistake feeling normal, until we see no reason to change or restore violated rights.

Mawt al-qalb means death of the heart, an image of lost spiritual sensitivity. Al-huzn points to sadness for missed obedience, while al-nadam means remorse for mistakes. Both have value when moving us towards repair. Use this rebuke for self-examination, rather than deciding others' inward states from appearances.

For example, someone grows used to ignoring promises until apologies no longer seem necessary. The mistake may look small through frequency. Precisely that repetition needs attention. Sensitivity can be revived by acknowledging effects on others, compensating losses if any, and learning promises suited to ability.

Sensitivity need not appear as tears or strong emotion. Deciding to stop hurting and fulfil duties again is an important sign. If the heart feels dry, still do clear good, supplicate, and seek supportive company. Avoid turning remorse into self-hatred until energy is lost. The heart is tended through real repentance and repeated good habits. Gradually we learn obedience's worth again and stop treating mistakes as something to preserve.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, the first time we hurt someone, we usually feel uneasy. Repeatedly doing it can diminish that feeling. We shout and immediately eat as though nothing happened. Someone still holds back tears while everything feels ordinary to us. Reduced sensitivity needs attention before the habit is considered an unchangeable character trait.

Ibn 'Ata'illah names as signs of a dead heart no sadness for missed goodness and no remorse for wrong. We carry this as self-examination, rather than a verdict on others' hearts. Ask whether we remain willing to recognize actions' effects and take responsibility for repair.

Dear congregation, imagine an adult mocking a child's ability before family. Everyone laughs and the child is quiet. Afterwards, we say the child must be strong for the world. Yet home should be safe for learning. If words hurt, admit it without telling the child to find them funny. An adult's courageous apology can teach precious responsibility.

“What if I feel no guilt?” Begin with observable consequences. Listen to the affected person's explanation without rushing to interrupt. Feelings may lag, but actions can still change. Stop mockery, improve correction, and seek help if anger is hard to control. Strong remorse need not precede stopping hurt.

Dear friends, sensitivity is also nurtured by space after an event. Ask what happened within us and the relationship. Record repeated triggers if needed. Do not cover discomfort with fresh busyness every time. Brief examination helps recognize patterns and arrange more real change than a mere promise to improve.

Let us ask for hearts still willing to be corrected. May Allah soften us, protect families from harshness, and grant courage to acknowledge speech's impact. May growing remorse lead to repair, so loved ones no longer continually await changes promised but not sincerely made. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
talkEn: OPENING

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, the first time we hurt someone, we usually feel uneasy. Repeatedly doing it can diminish that feeling. We shout and immediately eat as though nothing happened. Someone still holds back tears while everything feels ordinary to us. Reduced sensitivity needs attention before the habit is considered an unchangeable character trait.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about restoring sensitivity to hurtful words meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah names as signs of a dead heart no sadness for missed goodness and no remorse for wrong. We carry this as self-examination, rather than a verdict on others' hearts. Ask whether we remain willing to recognize actions' effects and take responsibility for repair.

A sensitive heart feels loss when goodness is abandoned and remorse when it causes hurt. These feelings invite improvement. This wisdom warns against every mistake feeling normal, until we see no reason to change or restore violated rights.

Mawt al-qalb means death of the heart, an image of lost spiritual sensitivity. Al-huzn points to sadness for missed obedience, while al-nadam means remorse for mistakes. Both have value when moving us towards repair. Use this rebuke for self-examination, rather than deciding others' inward states from appearances.

Dear congregation, a saying of wisdom may be very short, yet reflection reveals how deeply it touches our long-standing habits. We are seeing that here in the matter of restoring sensitivity to hurtful words. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, imagine an adult mocking a child's ability before family. Everyone laughs and the child is quiet. Afterwards, we say the child must be strong for the world. Yet home should be safe for learning. If words hurt, admit it without telling the child to find them funny. An adult's courageous apology can teach precious responsibility.

“What if I feel no guilt?” Begin with observable consequences. Listen to the affected person's explanation without rushing to interrupt. Feelings may lag, but actions can still change. Stop mockery, improve correction, and seek help if anger is hard to control. Strong remorse need not precede stopping hurt.

A child is quiet when abilities are mocked before family. Adults assume silence means no problem and repeat the joke next time. Dear friends, notice effects not loudly expressed. A child may fear spoiling the atmosphere or lack words to explain. Invite gentle conversation and listen without defending our joke. If the words hurt, admit it clearly. Do not make the child responsible for proving sufficient strength. Adults remain responsible for correction preserving dignity and the chance to learn.

“If I do not yet feel guilty, is an apology false?” Begin with the facts and effects, dear congregation. Feelings sometimes follow slowly. Yet we can stop mockery and improve speech. Acknowledging wrong words need not await tears or dramatic remorse. Listen to those affected and identify necessary repair. Death of the heart is a rebuke for examining our sensitivity, rather than a label for anyone looking calm. Actions can improve while we ask for a heart more receptive to guidance.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “Does the person we joke with truly feel safe saying they are hurt?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone grows used to ignoring promises until apologies no longer seem necessary. The mistake may look small through frequency. Precisely that repetition needs attention. Sensitivity can be revived by acknowledging effects on others, compensating losses if any, and learning promises suited to ability.

Dear friends, sensitivity is also nurtured by space after an event. Ask what happened within us and the relationship. Record repeated triggers if needed. Do not cover discomfort with fresh busyness every time. Brief examination helps recognize patterns and arrange more real change than a mere promise to improve.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about restoring sensitivity to hurtful words may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Sensitivity need not appear as tears or strong emotion. Deciding to stop hurting and fulfil duties again is an important sign. If the heart feels dry, still do clear good, supplicate, and seek supportive company. Avoid turning remorse into self-hatred until energy is lost. The heart is tended through real repentance and repeated good habits. Gradually we learn obedience's worth again and stop treating mistakes as something to preserve.

Recognize one sharp sentence that leaves our mouth too readily. Prepare a replacement correction naming behaviour without belittling the person. If public mockery is habitual, stop its spread and seek proper repair. Family can make a habit of listening when someone expresses discomfort. Do not turn that objection into the next joke. May home be safe for learning and dulled sensitivity receive care through guarding speech and courageously accepting our actions' effects.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of restoring sensitivity to hurtful words again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about restoring sensitivity to hurtful words. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us ask for hearts still willing to be corrected. May Allah soften us, protect families from harshness, and grant courage to acknowledge speech's impact. May growing remorse lead to repair, so loved ones no longer continually await changes promised but not sincerely made. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مِنْ عَلَامَاتِ مَوْتِ الْقَلْبِ عَدَمُ الْحُزْنِ عَلَى مَا فَاتَكَ مِنَ الْمُوَافَقَاتِ،
Among the signs of a dead heart is no sadness over missed obedience
وَتَرْكُ النَّدَمِ عَلَى مَا فَعَلْتَهُ مِنْ وُجُودِ الزَّلَّاتِ.
and no regret for slips committed.

59.translation: Do not magnify your sin until it prevents a good opinion of Allah Most High. Whoever knows their Lord sees their sin as small beside the vastness of His generosity.
syarahEn: Sin needs remorse, but remorse can become despair if we see only the mistake's size. Someone feels too damaged to return and moves further from Allah's help. This wisdom directs the heart to see sin alongside His immense generosity, so guilt opens repentance's path.

La ya'zum means let it not become so great in your sight. Tasudduka, preventing you from thinking well, explains the rebuke's scope. Karamih points to Allah's generosity. Sin is small compared with His vast grace, rather than trivial as an action. The comparison preserves hope so the wrongdoer remains willing to leave error and repair its effects.

Someone who lied can admit the lie, stop the habit, and restore harmed rights. Feeling pure need not precede returning to worship. At the same time, hope for forgiveness must not excuse deliberately repeating the act. Repentance's sincerity appears in steps taken after remorse arises.

If memories of error keep pressing, direct attention to a duty possible now. Ask forgiveness, repair one real thing, and accept trustworthy help if needed. We may neither declare our acceptance certain nor close Allah's vast mercy with despairing conclusions. This wisdom helps us walk humbly: honestly acknowledging wrong while trusting that return to Allah is a path worth taking.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, someone wants to resume salah but fears friends knowing the past will call them hypocritical. Another wants to apologize but thinks the sins too many. Good intention remains hidden. They feel unworthy to approach Allah, as though a bad record erased every chance to return and improve.

Ibn 'Ata'illah warns against sin's greatness obstructing a good opinion of Allah. The message guards against despair of His generosity. Sin remains wrong and effects need handling. Yet we cannot claim to know forgiveness impossible. Allah knows His servants and opens repentance's path to be pursued sincerely.

Dear friends, return can begin with a duty understood today. Learn what is unknown, seek supportive company, and stop harmful actions. Where human rights are involved, seek proper restoration. Not everything ends with relief after prayer. Real work remains part of responsibility towards others.

“What if people will not yet forgive?” We cannot force them. Admit wrong without demanding they immediately comfort our hearts. Continue repair and respect necessary boundaries. Repentance is a lived direction, rather than a method for instantly erasing past effects from everyone's memory. Trust often needs time and felt evidence.

Dear congregation, when seeing someone begin returning, do not busily recall faults for amusement. Support goodness without ignoring victims' rights needing repair. We can want improvement for the wrongdoer and protection for the wounded. Wise support helps responsible change, rather than only making someone appear accepted without facing remaining issues.

Let us bring the past before Allah with honest acknowledgement. May He forgive sins, steady repentance, and open ways to repair violated rights. May shame no longer extinguish hope. We can begin one act of obedience today and seek help to maintain it tomorrow. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Learn unknown parts with good guidance. We need not wait for the whole past to feel light before praying. Meanwhile, sincerely attend to unrestored human rights. This does not make wrongdoing trivial to repeat. We acknowledge it seriously while trusting repentance worth pursuing as long as life gives room.

Now try answering silently, dear friends: “How can we return to worship while respecting those previously harmed?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. In the matter of beginning return without erasing past responsibility, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Choose one duty to maintain today and one obligation whose resolution needs learning. Seek supportive company without demands to appear perfect. If belittling comments come, focus on repair and seek support if needed. We also learn respectful reception of someone returning. Do not make change seem reserved for people with orderly pasts. May Allah help honest return and grant strength for its accompanying responsibilities.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about beginning return without erasing past responsibility will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. What we want to nurture is a willingness to do our part properly and in an orderly way, even when the results still take time to appear.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of beginning return without erasing past responsibility that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Let us bring the past before Allah with honest acknowledgement. May He forgive sins, steady repentance, and open ways to repair violated rights. May shame no longer extinguish hope. We can begin one act of obedience today and seek help to maintain it tomorrow. Amin.

phrasesEn: لَا يَعْظُمْ الذَّنْبُ عِنْدَكَ عَظَمَةً تَصُدُّكَ عَنْ حُسْنِ الظَّنِّ بِاللَّهِ تَعَالَى،
Do not magnify your sin until it prevents you thinking well of Allah Most High.
فَإِنَّ مَنْ عَرَفَ رَبَّهُ اسْتَصْغَرَ فِي جَنْبِ كَرَمِهِ ذَنْبَهُ.
Those knowing their Lord see their sin as small beside the vastness of His generosity.

60.translation: No sin is small when you face His justice. No sin is great when you face His grace.
syarahEn: People easily assess sin too lightly or too heavily. Some dismiss an error as small; others consider forgiveness impossible because it is great. This wisdom places both before Allah's justice and grace, keeping the heart vigilant while retaining hope.

Saghirah means a minor sin and kabirah a major sin. 'Adluhu points to Allah's justice, and fadluhu to His grace. A sin's smallness gives no right to feel secure before His justice. Conversely, its greatness does not limit His generosity towards a returning servant. This expression trains perspective without removing religious teachings about wrongdoing and responsibility.

For example, dismissing hurtful speech may permit continued harm because it is considered only joking. Remembering Allah's justice awakens responsibility. Someone regretting a serious wrong instead needs remembrance of His grace to avoid surrender. Repentance and repair remain work to do.

Practise both attitudes together. Do not preserve a mistake because it seems light, and do not let guilt close the way home. Ask forgiveness, repair consequences, and continue obedience humbly. We do not control Allah's decision concerning us. Vigilance guards our steps, while hope preserves energy to continue. Together they keep devotion alive, avoiding both heedlessness and despair that can equally distance us from improvement.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, some take office belongings saying, “Only a little.” A few sheets, stationery, or materials for private use. Because the value is small, asking seems unnecessary. Yet trustworthiness is not determined only by price. We need to know whether the owner or authorized party permits the use.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that no sin is small before Allah's justice and none exceeds His generosity. We train care about wrongdoing and hope for forgiveness. Do not dismiss an action as small or close return's door once a mistake has happened.

Dear congregation, shared work needs clear usage boundaries. If a policy permits particular use, follow its terms. If unsure, ask. We need not complicate what is clear, but common practice must not be our sole reason. Frequent action is not necessarily agreed by the rights-holder.

“What if I took something without permission?” Examine what can be restored. Return or replace appropriately and seek explanation if unsure how. Act honestly without adding lies to preserve appearance. Acknowledged error opens repair of a trust. Shame is uncomfortable, but can accompany courage to bear consequences of our choices.

Dear friends, this applies at home too. Siblings' belongings and shared property deserve respect. Children learn boundaries through adults asking before use. We want honesty growing through visible action, rather than advice about sin alone. Responsibility is clearer when practised in nearby, simple affairs.

Let us stop one justification using only. May Allah protect against belittling rights, open repair, and accept sincere repentance. May His generosity nurture hope moving us towards improvement, and awareness of His justice bring greater care in using what is not personally ours. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of preserving a trust in belongings considered low in value. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us stop one justification using only. May Allah protect against belittling rights, open repair, and accept sincere repentance. May His generosity nurture hope moving us towards improvement, and awareness of His justice bring greater care in using what is not personally ours. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: لَا صَغِيرَةَ إِذَا قَابَلَكَ عَدْلُهُ،
No sin is small when you face His justice.
وَلَا كَبِيرَةَ إِذَا وَاجَهَكَ فَضْلُهُ.
No sin is great when you face His bounty.

61.translation: No deed is more likely to be accepted than one you no longer regard with admiration and consider small.
syarahEn: After doing something good, our attention easily returns to ourselves. We count our sacrifices, remember praise, or feel entitled to special treatment. This wisdom invites us to protect our deeds from excessive self-admiration, so that devotion does not become a reason to make demands on people or feel entitled before Allah.

Arja lil-qabul means more likely to be accepted. Yaghibu 'anka shuhuduhu describes the absence of attention that constantly admires one's own deeds. Yuhtaqaru means considered small in one's own eyes. What we diminish is our sense of having earned special credit, while continuing to take responsibility for improving our deeds. We still need to learn the right way and do our work as well as possible.

Someone helping their family can meet a need without repeatedly reminding everyone how much they have sacrificed. An activity coordinator still prepares reports and evaluates results, but uses reporting to fulfil a trust rather than build a sense of being the most deserving. We examine this distinction mainly through our intentions and the way we treat others after doing good.

If a desire for praise appears, acknowledge it as something that still needs training. Return your attention to the benefit of the work and ask Allah to accept it. Remember that many blessings make our deeds possible in the first place. Do not abandon all good simply because your intention feels imperfect; keep correcting it as you continue. Healthy humility makes us grateful for the opportunity and more open to correction. In this way, our deeds are better protected from the arrogance that can spoil their fruits.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, recording good habits can help us become more consistent. We mark the readings we have completed and the activities we have attended. But there is a danger when that record becomes a reason to feel more entitled to respect. We see someone less consistent and think, “I am clearly better.” A useful tool turns into material for self-praise.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us about deeds we do not continually regard with admiration. We hope for their acceptance while recognizing their shortcomings. Considering our deeds small does not mean belittling worship or giving up our efforts. We maintain humility so that a record of achievement does not make us forget Allah's help or our need to keep improving our intentions and behaviour.

Dear friends, imagine someone who regularly joins mosque activities but becomes irritated when their suggestions are not followed. They bring a list of their contributions into every conversation. Yet consultation still requires sound reasons and respect for people's rights. Frequent attendance does not give anyone permission to speak harshly or assume every decision must follow their personal wishes.

“If I do not appreciate my own efforts, will I lose motivation?” We may be grateful for our perseverance and use records to evaluate ourselves. However, distinguish gratitude from feeling entitled to a higher position. Ask whether those good habits have helped us listen more patiently, judge more honestly, and act more responsibly when working with others.

Dear congregation, after completing a good deed, make a habit of asking Allah to accept it. Our attention still wanders and our intentions are still mixed. Acknowledging this need not make us gloomy. It gives us a reason to keep learning without feeling we have finished. Someone who has done less still deserves respect, because we do not know all the struggles they face in daily life.

Let us use a record of deeds as a mirror for practice rather than a tool for ranking people. May Allah accept our little good, forgive our many shortcomings, and protect our hearts from arrogance that grows after doing good. May our perseverance bring gentleness, so that those around us feel its benefit without having to bear the pride we display. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

One sound understanding, put sincerely into practice, is already worth working towards today.

Dear congregation, a saying of wisdom may be very short, yet reflection reveals how deeply it touches our long-standing habits. We are seeing that here in the matter of using a record of deeds to learn without feeling superior. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, imagine someone who regularly joins mosque activities but becomes irritated when their suggestions are not followed. They bring a list of their contributions into every conversation. Yet consultation still requires sound reasons and respect for people's rights. Frequent attendance does not give anyone permission to speak harshly or assume every decision must follow their personal wishes.

However, distinguish gratitude from feeling entitled to a higher position. Ask whether those good habits have helped us listen more patiently, judge more honestly, and act more responsibly when working with others.

During a mosque consultation, someone feels their opinion must be accepted because they attend most often. When someone objects, they list the activities they have managed. Dear friends, contributions deserve appreciation, but shared decisions still require sound reasons. Many marks on a record of good deeds do not automatically give us the right to speak harshly. We can be grateful for perseverance while still listening. Try noticing whether the activities you join help you become more trustworthy when opinions differ. This question offers a measure closer to good character than simply counting attendance. The record becomes a tool for self-improvement rather than a rank everyone must acknowledge.

“If I do not look at the results of my efforts, I may lose motivation.” We may evaluate our progress, dear congregation. Notice habits that have become more consistent and areas still needing care. Gratitude acknowledges Allah's help in our ability to do good. A sense of having earned special credit makes us demand a privileged position among people. We can distinguish the two by our response when praise is absent or an opinion is corrected. The wisdom about deeds likely to be accepted does not ask us to act carelessly. Quality still needs attention. What we soften is the attention that constantly admires itself, giving devotion more room than the need to feel superior.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “Do our good habits help us listen to other people more readily?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone helping their family can meet a need without repeatedly reminding everyone how much they have sacrificed. An activity coordinator still prepares reports and evaluates results, but uses reporting to fulfil a trust rather than build a sense of being the most deserving. We examine this distinction mainly through our intentions and the way we treat others after doing good.

It gives us a reason to keep learning without feeling we have finished. Someone who has done less still deserves respect, because we do not know all the struggles they face in daily life.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of using a record of deeds to learn without feeling superior, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

If a desire for praise appears, acknowledge it as something that still needs training. Return your attention to the benefit of the work and ask Allah to accept it. Remember that many blessings make our deeds possible in the first place. Do not abandon all good simply because your intention feels imperfect; keep correcting it as you continue. Healthy humility makes us grateful for the opportunity and more open to correction. In this way, our deeds are better protected from the arrogance that can spoil their fruits.

Look at one record of good habits you regularly use. Add an evaluation question about its effect on your relationships, without passing a final judgement on yourself. If you often attend to help, also check whether you respect the rights of those who disagree. If you begin bringing a list of contributions into a conversation, pause and return to the issue being discussed. May our aids to worship make us both more consistent and humble, and may the perseverance Allah grants us nurture a willingness to serve without demanding a higher place.

Now let us turn the lesson about using a record of deeds to learn without feeling superior into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about using a record of deeds to learn without feeling superior, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us use a record of deeds as a mirror for practice rather than a tool for ranking people. May Allah accept our little good, forgive our many shortcomings, and protect our hearts from arrogance that grows after doing good. May our perseverance bring gentleness, so that those around us feel its benefit without having to bear the pride we display. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: لَا عَمَلَ أَرْجَى لِلْقَبُولِ مِنْ عَمَلٍ
No deed is more likely to be accepted than one
يَغِيبُ عَنْكَ شُهُودُهُ وَيُحْتَقَرُ عِنْدَكَ وُجُودُهُ.
you no longer regard with admiration and consider small.

62.translation: He brings you a spiritual gift so that, through it, you may come and draw near to Him.
syarahEn: Sometimes the heart is suddenly moved to repent, becomes calmer in supplication, or grows more sensitive to other people's needs. Such changes can be opportunities to draw nearer to Allah. This wisdom reminds us to respond to that good influence with action, so that a gift does not remain merely an enjoyable experience.

Al-warid means something that comes to the heart: an inner prompting or spiritual gift. Awrada means He causes it to come, while waridan 'alayhi describes a servant coming and drawing near to Him. This play on the direction of the words explains the relationship between gift and response: Allah's gift comes to move the servant towards devotion. A warid differs from a wird, a devotional practice performed regularly.

For example, a piece of advice makes us want to repair our relationship with a relative. We should show gratitude for that stirring of the heart by getting in touch, apologizing, or fulfilling a neglected right. If we only retell it as a beautiful experience, the opportunity for repair may pass. A practical response helps more mature habits grow.

We do not need to insist that every feeling is a special spiritual experience. Examine its direction through religious guidance and its fruits in action. A prompting that leads to arrogance or neglect of obligations needs further examination. When your heart is receptive to advice, use the opportunity to take one clear step towards good. When that feeling fades, continue the practice you have begun. In this way, we treat the gift as an invitation to draw near, while faithful practice keeps the journey going after our mood changes.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, sometimes in a quiet moment we suddenly remember someone we once hurt. After years of feeling right, our heart softens that evening. We want to get in touch, but pride quickly appears: “They will think they have won.” A good prompting that visits briefly can disappear if we keep nurturing the self-defence that first drove the relationship apart.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains that a gift coming to the heart invites a servant to draw nearer to Allah. A warid refers to something bestowed, rather than an experience we can force to appear whenever we wish. When awareness arises that leads towards good, welcome it through appropriate action. Do not merely enjoy the emotion while leaving responsibility postponed without taking a step.

Dear congregation, apologizing requires consideration for the person we approach. If communication is safe and appropriate, state the wrong clearly. Avoid beginning with a long explanation that actually defends yourself. We might say, “I realize that what I said then was hurtful.” Then give them room to respond. They do not have to feel at peace immediately simply because we are finally ready to speak.

“What if contacting them reopens a wound?” Seek advice from someone wise who understands the situation. Some forms of repair require a different approach or another person's help. The aim is to address the harm, rather than merely remove our guilt. The boundaries and safety of the person affected must be respected. We learn responsibility without making our personal regret the centre of the entire process.

Dear friends, we can also act on the urge to apologize by stopping the same behaviour. If the issue was sharing someone's private story, guard your next conversation. If it was a promise, begin by keeping small commitments. Consistent change helps a relationship gain a new foundation, even if it may not return to how it once was. We do our part while asking for Allah's help.

Let us not be too quick to close a heart that is being softened. May Allah guide good intentions into practical repair, give us courage to admit mistakes, and restore those we have hurt. May the gift of awareness pass through us as more than a feeling, bringing more honest steps in our relationship with Him and with one another. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired.
