phrasesEn: إِنَّمَا أَوْرَدَ عَلَيْكَ الْوَارِدَ
He brings you a spiritual gift
لِتَكُونَ بِهِ عَلَيْهِ وَارِدًا.
so that through it you may come and draw near to Him.

63.translation: He brings you a spiritual gift to free you from the power of all besides Him and release you from enslavement to created things.
syarahEn: The heart can feel bound by things we use in everyday life. Praise must always arrive, possessions must keep increasing, or a particular person must always approve of us. When those conditions are not met, life seems to fall apart. This wisdom explains one fruit of spiritual gifts: freedom from dependence that dominates our inner life.

Al-aghyar means everything besides Allah. Riqq al-athar describes enslavement to the traces of creation. Yuharriraka means to set you free, while yatasallamaka points towards releasing you from a power that holds you. The language of enslavement is used because the heart can lose its freedom to choose what is right when it is too afraid of losing approval, profit, or comfort.

For example, someone finds it difficult to refuse a wrongful request because they fear being disliked. As they learn to strengthen their reliance on Allah, they begin to refuse politely. They still respect people, but no longer surrender their principles to people's opinions. Relationships become more honest because respect does not depend on agreeing to every wish.

This freedom does not remove our social needs or make us belittle human help. We still cooperate and thank those who assist us. What lessens is the inner demand that created beings must provide an absolute guarantee. Practise by making one right decision even if it brings no praise. Ask for help so that your heart is not enslaved by its own desires. The benefit of the gift becomes clearer when we can better fulfil our trusts, accept differences, and do good without constantly needing recognition.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, some shopping begins with a need, and some begins with a sale sign. We had not thought about the item yesterday, but today buying it feels essential because time is running out. Regret follows payment. We work to earn money, then it slips away easily because we fear missing something whose benefit to our lives is not yet clear.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains that Allah's gifts free the heart from enslavement to possessions and worldly impulses. We still use things, but we do not have to obey every desire to own them. The heart's freedom becomes apparent when we can consider calmly and say, “Enough.” A desire passes, while our decisions still follow our needs and the responsibilities entrusted to us.

Dear friends, before buying, try pausing. Ask whether the item will be used, whether you already have something that serves its purpose, and whether money remains after essential needs are met. If you are unsure, leave it for now. The usefulness of something beneficial can usually still be assessed once the rush has eased. We do not have to decide while a countdown is putting our attention under pressure.

“What if the price goes up later?” It might. But money we do not spend on something unnecessary remains useful too. We can fulfil obligations or give ourselves more room for unexpected needs. This calculation does not make us stingy. We are learning to use our provision to support life, rather than keep drawing ourselves back into the same regret after shopping.

Dear congregation, families can make a simple agreement about purchases outside routine needs. Discuss limits according to your means, rather than following the standards of another household. Children can also learn the difference between wanting and needing without being shamed. Adults must set an example, because it is difficult to teach self-control while always giving in to every offer on our screens.

Let us try one day without buying anything we do not yet need. Notice that a desire can subside even when we do not fulfil it. May Allah bless our provision, protect our families from spending beyond our means, and grant us contentment. May wealth be a means of helping us fulfil life's responsibilities, while the heart remains free to choose what brings greater benefit. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
talkEn: OPENING
Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, some shopping begins with a need, and some begins with a sale sign. We had not thought about the item yesterday, but today buying it feels essential because time is running out. Regret follows payment. We work to earn money, then it slips away easily because we fear missing something whose benefit to our lives is not yet clear.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about pausing before a discount determines our shopping choices meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains that Allah's gifts free the heart from enslavement to possessions and worldly impulses. We still use things, but we do not have to obey every desire to own them. The heart's freedom becomes apparent when we can consider calmly and say, “Enough.” A desire passes, while our decisions still follow our needs and the responsibilities entrusted to us.

The heart can feel bound by things we use in everyday life. Praise must always arrive, possessions must keep increasing, or a particular person must always approve of us. When those conditions are not met, life seems to fall apart. This wisdom explains one fruit of spiritual gifts: freedom from dependence that dominates our inner life.

Al-aghyar means everything besides Allah. Riqq al-athar describes enslavement to the traces of creation. Yuharriraka means to set you free, while yatasallamaka points towards releasing you from a power that holds you. The language of enslavement is used because the heart can lose its freedom to choose what is right when it is too afraid of losing approval, profit, or comfort.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with pausing before a discount determines our shopping choices. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, before buying, try pausing. Ask whether the item will be used, whether you already have something that serves its purpose, and whether money remains after essential needs are met. If you are unsure, leave it for now. The usefulness of something beneficial can usually still be assessed once the rush has eased. We do not have to decide while a countdown is putting our attention under pressure.

“What if the price goes up later?” It might. But money we do not spend on something unnecessary remains useful too. We can fulfil obligations or give ourselves more room for unexpected needs. This calculation does not make us stingy. We are learning to use our provision to support life, rather than keep drawing ourselves back into the same regret after shopping.

A countdown appears on the screen, and an item that seemed ordinary yesterday suddenly feels important. We imagine regretting it if we do not buy. Dear friends, we can pause that sense of urgency. Close the page briefly and look at the needs already on your list. Will the item be used? Is there something at home that works adequately? We do not need to hate promotions to learn to choose. A discount can help with a clear need. However, we should not surrender the whole decision to time pressure. Money that remains available also serves obligations and needs that may matter more than an item first considered a few minutes ago.

“What if it really is more expensive later?” That is possible, dear congregation. We weigh usefulness and affordability, rather than guarantee that every decision will secure the lowest price. Buying something unnecessary can also increase spending despite an attractive discount. The wisdom about the heart's freedom invites us to see whether we can still choose calmly. Do not make possessions the measure of success or acceptance among friends. We may enjoy what is lawful within our means. What we nurture is freedom to decline an offer that does not meet our needs, without feeling that every opportunity in life has disappeared when the sale ends.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “Do we need the item, or are we only afraid of losing the discount?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone finds it difficult to refuse a wrongful request because they fear being disliked. As they learn to strengthen their reliance on Allah, they begin to refuse politely. They still respect people, but no longer surrender their principles to people's opinions. Relationships become more honest because respect does not depend on agreeing to every wish.

Dear congregation, families can make a simple agreement about purchases outside routine needs. Discuss limits according to your means, rather than following the standards of another household. Children can also learn the difference between wanting and needing without being shamed. Adults must set an example, because it is difficult to teach self-control while always giving in to every offer on our screens.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of pausing before a discount determines our shopping choices, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

This freedom does not remove our social needs or make us belittle human help. We still cooperate and thank those who assist us. What lessens is the inner demand that created beings must provide an absolute guarantee. Practise by making one right decision even if it brings no praise. Ask for help so that your heart is not enslaved by its own desires. The benefit of the gift becomes clearer when we can better fulfil our trusts, accept differences, and do good without constantly needing recognition.

With the next offer, try allowing time to check your needs and budget. If unsure, leave the item for now without paying immediately. Invite the family to distinguish necessary items from things they merely want at that moment. If you have already bought something and regret it, consider what responsible steps remain possible, without covering it up with another purchase. May we use our provision more consciously, and may promotional notifications no longer constantly govern our contentment. We learn to appreciate the usefulness of things while retaining direction over our choices.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of pausing before a discount determines our shopping choices again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about pausing before a discount determines our shopping choices invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us try one day without buying anything we do not yet need. Notice that a desire can subside even when we do not fulfil it. May Allah bless our provision, protect our families from spending beyond our means, and grant us contentment. May wealth be a means of helping us fulfil life's responsibilities, while the heart remains free to choose what brings greater benefit. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
wordsEn: and so it may free you
phrasesEn: أَوْرَدَ عَلَيْكَ الْوَارِدَ
He brings you a spiritual gift
لِيَتَسَلَّمَكَ مِنْ يَدِ الْأَغْيَارِ
to release you from the power of everything besides Him
وَلِيُحَرِّرَكَ مِنْ رِقِّ الْآثَارِ.
and free you from enslavement to created things.

64.translation: He brings you a spiritual gift to take you out of the prison of fixation on yourself and into the spaciousness of the heart's witnessing.
syarahEn: Thinking excessively about ourselves can make life feel narrow. We constantly assess how we appear, how much we are valued, and whether others consider us successful. Even worship can become material for measuring our own specialness. This wisdom invites the heart towards a broader concern: devotion to Allah.

Sijn wujudik means the prison of your own existence. The prison metaphor highlights attention confined to self-interest and self-image. Fada' shuhudik means the spaciousness of the heart's witnessing. It refers to an awareness that increasingly recognizes Allah's help and power, so that the self is no longer always at the centre. Created beings still exist and remain responsible, while excessive self-importance is gradually loosened.

Someone serving at an event may be busy calculating whether their contribution has been recognized. When attention returns to the needs of those being served, the work becomes more meaningful. They may still set limits on their energy and ask for a fair division of tasks. What changes is their reason for working, so that their entire mood no longer hangs on praise.

Try doing one good deed without turning it into a way of judging your own standing. Pay attention to those who benefit and to the quality of the work, then be grateful for the help that made its completion possible. If the desire for recognition appears, bring it into your supplication without hiding it from yourself. The heart grows spacious when we do not have to be the centre of every event. From there, our relationships with Allah and with people can feel lighter, because devotion is no longer constantly burdened by the wish to prove who we are.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, may Allah honour us, sometimes we bring a suggestion to a meeting that we believe is excellent. As soon as the participants choose another approach, we feel upset. We become passive, secretly hoping their decision fails so that we can say, “I told you so.” A shared concern becomes a matter of proving that we should have been the centre of attention.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that a gift draws a servant nearer by freeing them from the prison of self-absorption. We do not need to imagine ourselves disappearing as human beings. We are training ourselves to become less attached to feeling the most important. In shared work, this lesson helps us pay attention to needs and aims, so that personal pride does not keep obstructing our willingness to help.

Dear congregation, if our suggestion is not chosen, we may calmly ask for an explanation. Perhaps there is information we do not yet know. If the choice remains within proper bounds, help it succeed. We can record points for evaluation without waiting for someone to fail. There is a difference between remaining alert and nurturing a desire for a colleague to be proved wrong in public.

“What if the decision really is dangerous or unjust?” Concerns need to be stated clearly through an appropriate approach. Letting go of ego does not mean allowing wrongdoing. Explain the reasons, consequences, and possible improvements. If needed, use a channel with authority. Guard the purpose of your objection so that it serves protection and justice, rather than merely retaliation because your suggestion was rejected.

Dear friends, after the meeting, examine the small conversations we create. Do not gather a group to mock those who disagree. If there is important information, share it with the relevant people. We want our workplace or neighbourhood to be a space where people can think together. That grows more easily when participants do not have to win every time to remain willing to contribute.

Let us practise saying, “I will help with the part entrusted to me.” May Allah make our hearts spacious when opinions differ, protect consultation from arrogance, and give us courage to defend what is right politely. May our abilities serve our shared aims, so that others still feel safe expressing an opinion in our presence. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

The meeting decides on a different approach. We close our notebook in disappointment and begin answering only as much as necessary. Inside, there is a small hope that their choice will fail. Dear friends, we can recognize this feeling before it becomes an action. We may ask about the reasons for the decision and check information we do not yet know. If the choice is still sound and safe, support its implementation according to your role. Do not withhold important help simply to prove your own suggestion was better. The activity's purpose involves many people's needs. They should not bear the consequences of a contest of pride that we could address through conversation and examination of our intentions.

“What if the decision is seriously wrong?” State your concerns with reasons that can be examined, dear congregation. Distinguish a choice that does not suit your preferences from an action that endangers people or neglects rights. If necessary, use a channel with authority. Freedom from ego does not ask us to allow injustice. We guard the purpose and manner of raising concerns. We do not need to enjoy someone else's failure. The image of the prison of the self helps us recognize attention confined by the need to win. A spacious heart helps us return to shared benefit while properly fulfilling our responsibility to raise concerns.

Now try answering silently, dear friends: “Do we still want the activity to succeed even when the approach differs from our suggestion?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. May a gathering like this send us home with the courage to learn, rather than merely the ability to comment on other people's lives.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about continuing to help when our own suggestion is not chosen may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Try doing one good deed without turning it into a way of judging your own standing. Pay attention to those who benefit and to the quality of the work, then be grateful for the help that made its completion possible. If the desire for recognition appears, bring it into your supplication without hiding it from yourself. The heart grows spacious when we do not have to be the centre of every event. From there, our relationships with Allah and with people can feel lighter, because devotion is no longer constantly burdened by the wish to prove who we are.

For practice, choose one shared decision that did not meet your hopes. Check whether an important concern remains unspoken or whether you are simply disappointed your suggestion was not used. If you need to raise a concern, prepare clear reasons. If the decision remains reasonable, ask what help you can offer. Afterwards, evaluate without words that celebrate a colleague's mistakes. May consultation become a place to learn to listen, and may our abilities keep benefiting others even when our own names and ideas are not the centre of attention.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about continuing to help when our own suggestion is not chosen will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. What we want to nurture is a willingness to do our part properly and in an orderly way, even when the results still take time to appear.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about continuing to help when our own suggestion is not chosen, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

phrasesEn: أَوْرَدَ عَلَيْكَ الْوَارِدَ
He brings you a spiritual gift
لِيُخْرِجَكَ مِنْ سِجْنِ وُجُودِكَ
to bring you out of the prison of fixation on yourself
إِلَى فَضَاءِ شُهُودِكَ.
into the spaciousness of the heart's witnessing.

65.translation: Lights are the mounts of hearts and their innermost secrets.
syarahEn: The journey of self-improvement requires more than a passing impulse. We need guidance to recognize the direction, strength to do what is right, and clarity when choices feel complicated. This wisdom describes that help as light that carries the heart and its inner depths towards devotion.

Al-anwar means lights. Mataya means mounts, used as a metaphor for a means that carries someone on a journey. Al-qulub means hearts, while al-asrar refers to the deepest secrets of the inner self. Light here can be understood through the guidance of faith and the understanding Allah nurtures. We do not have to imagine it as a flash visible to the eyes.

When we understand advice and then find the courage to correct a mistake, guidance has brought practical benefit. Someone who used to lie easily begins to feel the need for honesty even at the cost of embarrassment. Someone usually busy defending themselves begins to listen. These changes deserve more attention than pursuing an extraordinary experience that leaves behaviour unchanged.

Therefore, ask for light by nurturing clear means: learning, maintaining worship, repenting, and using knowledge for good. Do not assume you possess a special distinction simply because you once had a powerful feeling. Examine whether your heart is becoming humbler and your trusts are better kept. Just as a mount carries its rider forward, guidance should lead us to action. We nurture light through a proper response, so that knowledge does not remain an ornament of the mind and the heart's journey continues to find direction.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, when the electricity goes out, we usually do not immediately walk quickly through a dark room. We look for a lamp or switch on a torch, then watch our path. Yet in life's problems, we sometimes do the opposite. The heart is confused, but we rush a decision simply to end uncertainty. Only afterwards do we see consequences we had not considered carefully enough.

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes light as the heart's mount. Light helps the journey by bringing clarity. We can learn to seek sound guidance before acting. Religious knowledge, verifiable information, and trustworthy advice help us distinguish between choices. We ask for Allah's guidance while using the ability He has given us to understand our circumstances.

Dear friends, suppose a job offer sounds very profitable but its details are vague. Do not ask only people certain to agree. Read the duties and terms, check who is making the offer, then seek advice from someone who understands the field. If anything conflicts with religious guidance or people's rights, that issue needs resolving before we go further.

“If I spend too long considering it, will the opportunity disappear?” Real deadlines do exist. However, pressure to decide immediately without an explanation also deserves attention. Ask for essential information and assess your ability to bear the risks. We do not have to accept every offer because we fear no other opportunity will come. A responsible decision needs sufficient reasons, even though we can never control the entire future.

Dear congregation, light also needs care after we choose. Keep learning and remain open to correction. If new information appears, review your steps honestly. Correcting a decision does not diminish our dignity. That willingness helps our journey stay directed by reality and guidance, rather than by pride in defending something that turns out to harm ourselves and others.

Let us ask for clarity before asking for speed. May Allah illuminate our hearts with guidance, bring us trustworthy advisers, and protect us from decisions made in panic. May each step include a sincere effort to understand our circumstances, so that courage grows together with care and practical responsibility. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

The job offer sounds attractive, but the duties and terms are unclear. The person offering it asks for an immediate answer. Dear friends, we can appreciate an opportunity while asking for essential explanations. Ask what work is required and what boundaries need observing. Do not seek opinions only from people certain to say yes. Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “What information is still needed so that the decision is not driven only by haste?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

When we understand advice and then find the courage to correct a mistake, guidance has brought practical benefit. Someone who used to lie easily begins to feel the need for honesty even at the cost of embarrassment. Someone usually busy defending themselves begins to listen. These changes deserve more attention than pursuing an extraordinary experience that leaves behaviour unchanged.

Dear congregation, light also needs care after we choose. Keep learning and remain open to correction. If new information appears, review your steps honestly. Correcting a decision does not diminish our dignity. That willingness helps our journey stay directed by reality and guidance, rather than by pride in defending something that turns out to harm ourselves and others.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of seeking guidance before making a decision in confusion, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Therefore, ask for light by nurturing clear means: learning, maintaining worship, repenting, and using knowledge for good. Do not assume you possess a special distinction simply because you once had a powerful feeling. Examine whether your heart is becoming humbler and your trusts are better kept. Just as a mount carries its rider forward, guidance should lead us to action. We nurture light through a proper response, so that knowledge does not remain an ornament of the mind and the heart's journey continues to find direction.

Try writing down the decision you face, then separate known information from assumptions. Seek explanations for the points that matter. If you do not understand something, say so honestly. Once you have considered enough, take a step within your ability and keep asking Allah for guidance. Family members asked for an opinion can help with clarifying questions rather than pressure to choose according to their own preferences. May confusion receive the light of guidance, and may decisions be reached through efforts we can take responsibility for.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about seeking guidance before making a decision in confusion. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about seeking guidance before making a decision in confusion. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us ask for clarity before asking for speed. May Allah illuminate our hearts with guidance, bring us trustworthy advisers, and protect us from decisions made in panic. May each step include a sincere effort to understand our circumstances, so that courage grows together with care and practical responsibility. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: الْأَنْوَارُ مَطَايَا
Lights are the mounts
الْقُلُوبِ وَالْأَسْرَارِ.
of hearts and inner secrets.

66.translation: Light is the army of the heart, just as darkness is the army of the lower self. When Allah wishes to help His servant, He supports them with armies of light and cuts off the support of darkness and everything that distances them from Him.
syarahEn: Within us there is often a struggle between guidance and uncontrolled desire. We know we need to apologize, but pride holds us back. We want to be honest, but profit is tempting. This wisdom uses the language of armies to describe that struggle, while reminding us that victory requires Allah's help.

Jund means an army or supporting force. Al-nur is the light that helps the heart recognize its direction, while al-zulmah describes darkness that feeds heedlessness. Al-madad means strengthening assistance. This language invites us to notice what we keep feeding each day: awareness that guides us, or habits that strengthen wrongful desires.

For example, anger easily grows when we repeatedly revisit conversations that stir hatred. Conversely, calmly hearing an explanation and remembering the consequences of our words can help restrain our actions. Our surroundings, reading, and habits influence the strength of our choices. We are responsible for arranging the means within our control while asking for Allah's help.

Choose one habit that often weakens your self-control, then reduce its opportunities to enter. Replace it with an activity that supports clarity, such as learning or fulfilling responsibilities in an orderly way. If you slip, do not simply blame the circumstances; look for an opening that still allows the mistake to recur. This wisdom invites us to struggle consciously. Hope in Allah's help goes together with closing harmful paths, making it easier for the heart to choose good when facing repeated temptations.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, have you ever opened your phone briefly and ended up feeling angry? One video provokes anger; the next adds suspicion. We end up looking more harshly at those around us, although they have done nothing. What we watch can help shape our inner state, especially when consumed continually without a pause or examination.

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes light as a helper of the heart, while darkness strengthens the impulses of the lower self. We learn to pay attention to what enters us. If anger receives new fuel every day, restraint can become harder. Asking for Allah's help needs to be accompanied by willingness to stop something that repeatedly strengthens a damaging habit.

Dear congregation, this does not mean closing our eyes to society's problems. We still need important information through reliable sources. But there is a difference between understanding an issue and continually enjoying material that encourages insults. Ask whether a video helps us take useful action or merely makes it easier to hate people we have never met.

“If I stop watching, will I miss the news?” Set a time and choose your sources. We do not need to accept every clip forwarded to us. Check before sharing, especially when someone's or a group's reputation is involved. If your heart is already heated, pause. Have a drink, finish a task, and return to assess things with calmer attention. Sharing quickly matters less than getting the content right.

Dear friends, fill the space you leave with something helpful. You might talk directly with family, learn a skill, or follow reading that guides good character. This does not guarantee we will never become angry again. However, we are reducing material that amplifies anger and adding support for better choices. Small habits repeated over time influence the way we are present with others.

Let us examine one source that keeps making our hearts harsh. Reduce your engagement if it brings no benefit. May Allah guard our hearing and sight, help us examine reports fairly, and protect our families from anger brought home through a screen. May what we receive each day help brighten the heart and guard our speech. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.

The lesson about guarding the information intake that shapes anger may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Choose one screen habit you want to change. Set a realistic pause and use that time for a task or relationship you have neglected. If an emotional clip arrives, seek context before judging. Within the family, discuss ways to remind one another without mockery. We can also admit having shared false information and correct it appropriately. May our attention have room to receive guidance, and may concern grow into useful action rather than anger continually fed through a screen.

Now let us turn the lesson about guarding the information intake that shapes anger into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about guarding the information intake that shapes anger invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. phrasesEn: النُّورُ جُنْدُ الْقَلْبِ
Light is the army of the heart,
كَمَا أَنَّ الظُّلْمَةَ جُنْدُ النَّفْسِ،
just as darkness is the army of the lower self.
فَإِذَا أَرَادَ اللَّهُ أَنْ يَنْصُرَ عَبْدَهُ
When Allah wishes to help His servant,
أَمَدَّهُ بِجُنُودِ الْأَنْوَارِ
He supports them with armies of light
وَقَطَعَ عَنْهُ مَدَدَ الظُّلَمِ وَالْأَغْيَارِ.
and cuts off the support of darkness and everything distancing them from Him.

67.translation: Light unveils. The inner eye judges. The heart turns towards or turns away.
syarahEn: Knowing that something is true does not always make us follow it immediately. We may understand the consequences of lying yet still choose to lie for fear of losing an advantage. This wisdom distinguishes the roles of illumination, judgement, and the heart's will. That distinction helps us see what still needs improvement when knowledge has not become action.

Al-kashf means unveiling: something previously unclear becomes apparent. Al-hukm means judging or reaching a decision about what is understood. Al-iqbal means acceptance or turning towards, while al-idbar means turning away. Light gives clarity, the inner eye judges, and the heart determines its response. Therefore, adding information alone is insufficient if other desires still dominate our choices.

For example, we already know that certain words hurt our spouse. That knowledge needs to lead to acknowledging the action is wrong, followed by a decision to restrain and correct it. If every piece of advice meets only a defence, willingness to accept it may be the obstacle. We need to look honestly at the advantage we still wish to preserve through that habit.

After receiving a lesson, choose one action that shows acceptance. If it is difficult, divide it into smaller steps and ask someone to help remind you. Pray for the heart to find it easier to follow the truth it knows. This wisdom helps connect knowledge with responsibility. Clarity is a gift that calls for a response, so that increased knowledge does more than improve our speaking ability: it also improves the decisions we make in life.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, we all know rubbish belongs in a bin. Even a young child can answer that question. Yet after an event, food wrappers sometimes remain on the chairs. The knowledge is there, but our choices have not followed. This simple issue shows that knowing what is right does not automatically make us willing to do it when the choice appears.

Ibn 'Ata'illah distinguishes the roles of light, inner sight, and the heart. Something illuminates, something recognizes, and then the heart turns towards or away. The lesson is to carry understanding through into a decision. If we know an action is good, ask what prevents us from doing it. Do not keep adding knowledge while leaving the nearest choices to run as usual.

Dear friends, after eating in a public place, look at the table before leaving. Which things are still being used, and which rubbish needs throwing away? If the venue requires items to be left for staff, follow its procedure neatly. We are training attention to the next users and those who clean. We do not want our own comfort always to leave avoidable trouble for someone else.

“Are there not staff paid to do that?” Their work still deserves respect. We can help through orderly behaviour without taking over duties they need to perform themselves. Avoid leaving spills or dangerous objects without telling anyone. This small responsibility is a practical way to show that knowledge about cleanliness and respect for people truly has a place in our decisions.

Dear congregation, children follow examples more easily than scolding. Invite them to tidy up together and briefly explain the benefit. Adults need to do the same when no child is watching. Good character is not only a performance while teaching. We are developing a habit that can be trusted in company and in private, at home and in shared places.

Let us choose one good thing we know that has not yet become a habit. Put it into practice at the nearest opportunity. May Allah give us clarity to recognize what is right, willingness to choose it, and perseverance in simple actions. May our knowledge go beyond giving good answers and bring benefit that people around us can feel. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

68.translation: Do not rejoice in obedience because you feel it comes from yourself. Rejoice because it is a gift from Allah to you. Say: In Allah's bounty and mercy, let them rejoice. That is better than what they accumulate.
syarahEn: We may feel happy when we maintain worship or complete beneficial service. What needs examination is the source of that happiness. Are we grateful for being helped, or admiring ourselves as better people? This wisdom directs our joy towards Allah's gifts so that success does not damage humility.

La tufrihka al-ta'ah reminds us not to let obedience delight us because we regard it solely as the result of our own strength. Barazat minka means it emerged from you, while barazat min Allahi ilayka returns the ability to obey to its source as Allah's gift to you. Fadl and rahmah refer to bounty and mercy. This perspective turns happiness into gratitude that strengthens devotion.

Someone who manages to rise for night prayer can be grateful for the health, time, and ease they have received. That awareness makes them gentler towards those still struggling to establish the habit. They may still invite others and set an example, but do not use their deeds as a reason to belittle anyone. Healthy joy increases the desire to continue doing good and helping others.

After completing a deed, make a habit of giving thanks and asking Allah to accept it. Remember, too, the people whose help served as a means, and offer appropriate appreciation. If your ability diminishes one day, do not feel that your entire worth has disappeared. Do what remains possible while asking for help. This wisdom makes joy steadier, because the heart enjoys the opportunity to serve without constantly maintaining an image of someone who is always strong, most diligent, or most deserving of credit.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, some members of the congregation begin learning to read the Qur'an as adults. Their tongues are still unfamiliar with the sounds and lines need repeating. When they finally complete one page, they feel delighted. Others have read fluently since childhood but rarely open the Qur'an. An ability we take for granted sometimes only feels precious when we see someone struggling to learn it from the beginning.

Ibn 'Ata'illah directs the joy of those who obey towards Allah's generosity in helping them. We rejoice in being given a way to do good, while still acknowledging the effort involved. This attention protects perseverance from feeling superior. Teachers, opportunities, health, and much help come before our ability to complete a deed well.

Dear congregation, if your reading is still hesitant today, do not let someone else's ability become a reason for shame. Find a patient teacher and explain your situation honestly. Adapt practice to your ability and maintain it gradually. Those who read fluently can help without mockery. We want a learning space where people feel brave enough to improve their reading, rather than fear being considered too late.

“Is it wrong to be happy because I succeeded?” That happiness can be received with gratitude. Direct it towards acknowledging that Allah gives the opportunity and help to learn. Thank your teacher and maintain your practice. Avoid using achievement to compare your worth with someone still struggling. Greater knowledge should make our support gentler and more sensitive to a learner's needs.

Dear friends, parents can praise a child's effort without using it to belittle their friends. We can say today's practice looked more consistent. Then invite gratitude and continued learning. The child receives the message that ability is a trust to be used, so that happiness over progress grows alongside respect for others whose journey may differ.

Let us appreciate one ability to obey that we still possess. May Allah protect learners, bless teachers, and ease the tongues being trained. May joy over progress bring perseverance rather than arrogance. May we always remember that every page read is possible through opportunities and help that deserve sincere gratitude. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about being grateful for the ability to read the Qur'an while continuing to learn meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.

Dear congregation, a saying of wisdom may be very short, yet reflection reveals how deeply it touches our long-standing habits. We are seeing that here in the matter of being grateful for the ability to read the Qur'an while continuing to learn. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, if your reading is still hesitant today, do not let someone else's ability become a reason for shame. Find a patient teacher and explain your situation honestly. An adult learner slowly repeats a line. When they finally manage it, their face lights up. Someone already fluent may consider it ordinary. Dear friends, we can learn to appreciate the size of a step according to each person's journey. That learner is overcoming embarrassment and making time amid a busy life. A teacher can encourage them through clear correction and patience. There is no need to compare them with another learner. Small successes deserve room for gratitude, followed by continued practice. An ability that once seemed very difficult can grow through Allah's help and support that gives someone courage to keep learning.

“Am I not too old to begin?” The opportunity available can be used now, dear congregation. Explain your ability to the teacher and choose suitable guidance. We do not have to pretend to be fluent to avoid embarrassment. Those already able should not use their own ease as the measure of someone else's effort. Joy at being able to read is welcome. This wisdom directs it: we are grateful for Allah's gift rather than treating ability solely as proof of personal greatness. With this understanding, success nurtures appreciation for teachers and gentleness in supporting others, because we remember everyone once needed teaching.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “What turns learning success into gratitude rather than a reason to belittle those still reading hesitantly?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone who manages to rise for night prayer can be grateful for the health, time, and ease they have received. That awareness makes them gentler towards those still struggling to establish the habit. They may still invite others and set an example, but do not use their deeds as a reason to belittle anyone. Healthy joy increases the desire to continue doing good and helping others.

The child receives the message that ability is a trust to be used, so that happiness over progress grows alongside respect for others whose journey may differ.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about being grateful for the ability to read the Qur'an while continuing to learn may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

After completing a deed, make a habit of giving thanks and asking Allah to accept it. Remember, too, the people whose help served as a means, and offer appropriate appreciation. If your ability diminishes one day, do not feel that your entire worth has disappeared. Do what remains possible while asking for help. This wisdom makes joy steadier, because the heart enjoys the opportunity to serve without constantly maintaining an image of someone who is always strong, most diligent, or most deserving of credit.

Choose a realistic practice time and one passage to read with guidance. If something is unclear, ask without shame. After receiving correction, repeat slowly and maintain continuity according to your ability. Family can support this by providing a comfortable atmosphere rather than commenting on every error in public. If already fluent, use the ability more earnestly and help when asked. May improving recitation bring gratitude to Allah and make the learning environment welcoming to anyone who wants to begin.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of being grateful for the ability to read the Qur'an while continuing to learn again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about being grateful for the ability to read the Qur'an while continuing to learn. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us appreciate one ability to obey that we still possess. May Allah protect learners, bless teachers, and ease the tongues being trained. May joy over progress bring perseverance rather than arrogance. May we always remember that every page read is possible through opportunities and help that deserve sincere gratitude. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: لَا تُفْرِحْكَ الطَّاعَةُ لِأَنَّهَا بَرَزَتْ مِنْكَ،
Do not rejoice in obedience because you feel it comes from yourself.
وَافْرَحْ بِهَا لِأَنَّهَا بَرَزَتْ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِلَيْكَ،
Rejoice because obedience is Allah's gift to you.
قُلْ بِفَضْلِ اللَّهِ وَبِرَحْمَتِهِ فَبِذَلِكَ فَلْيَفْرَحُوا
Say: In Allah's bounty and mercy, let them rejoice.
هُوَ خَيْرٌ مِمَّا يَجْمَعُونَ.
That is better than what they accumulate.

69.translation: He frees those travelling the path and those who have arrived at Him from fixation on their own deeds and inner states. Those travelling have not yet established complete sincerity with Allah in those deeds and states. As for those who have arrived, witnessing Him diverts their attention from all of these.
syarahEn: After doing good, we can become too busy assessing our own achievements. At another stage, someone may even be more interested in their peace or inner experience than in the devotion that is the aim. This wisdom invites the heart to avoid fixation on deeds and feelings, keeping its attention on Allah, who helps the entire journey.

Ru'yat a'malihim means seeing or attending to their own deeds. Shuhud ahwalihim refers to attention to inner states. Al-sidq means earnest sincerity. Ghayyabahum describes attention being diverted, so that they do not continually admire themselves. This language does not remove the need to evaluate behaviour; it frees the heart from pride revolving around personal achievement.

A beginner needs to examine whether their intention remains mixed with a desire for praise. Someone who has practised for a long time also needs to avoid making peaceful experiences into a special identity. Both can return to a simple question: are today's responsibilities being fulfilled properly, and are other people's rights being met?

Evaluate honestly and sufficiently. After learning the lesson, continue the work without constantly calculating your spiritual standing. If the heart feels light, be grateful and use it for good. If it feels heavy, maintain obligations and the deeds within your ability. Our purpose is to answer the call to devotion rather than preserve a feeling of success. By letting go of fixation on deeds and states, the heart has more room to recognize Allah's help and is readier to receive guidance when the journey does not meet our hopes.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, sometimes someone loves describing their experiences of worship. They once felt extraordinary peace, joined a lengthy programme, or completed a demanding practice. The story is repeated continually. Yet when a small duty appears today, they feel they have already done plenty. An experience that should strengthen the next step becomes a place to rest too long.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds those journeying towards Allah not to remain absorbed in admiring their deeds and inner states. Those still learning need help, while growing understanding reduces self-aggrandizing attention. We still value good experiences, but do not turn them into proof that all the work of self-improvement is complete and correction is no longer needed.

Dear friends, suppose someone often talks about their enthusiasm for worship during a particular month. Afterwards, promises to people remain neglected. What is needed now is to fulfil today's trust. A memory of a good period may remind us of our ability to persevere, but it cannot replace the responsibility waiting now. Those around us need change they can feel in everyday encounters.

“Are we not allowed to share experiences?” We may, if it benefits others and is presented honestly. Examine the listener's needs and your own intention. Do not exaggerate a state to be considered close to Allah. Nor must we explain everything we feel. Some experiences are better kept private while seeking guidance from the right person, especially when we do not yet understand their meaning.

Dear congregation, when praised for piety, return attention to your duties. Ask what still needs care. If someone points out a shortcoming, listen without bringing an old story as a defence. Spiritual progress should open willingness to improve. We do not know Allah's final judgement, so hope for acceptance remains accompanied by humility and effort to improve deeds that still have many shortcomings.

Let us allow good experiences to support the next step. May Allah protect us from claims beyond reality, accept the worship we have performed, and guide today's obligations. May we have less need to tell stories about closeness to Him because the benefit of devotion is increasingly felt in honesty, trustworthiness, and the way we respect people. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

In conversation, someone repeatedly describes a time when their worship was especially enthusiastic. Listeners nod, but a simple promise has remained unfulfilled for several days. Dear friends, good memories may encourage us. Yet the person awaiting the promise still needs action today. We can pause the story and attend to what remains unfinished. This wisdom warns about attention too busy looking at our deeds and states. We still evaluate actions, but need not constantly stand before a memory to admire it. Now try answering silently, dear friends: “Do memories of past deeds help us fulfil the trust waiting now?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. May a gathering like this send us home with the courage to learn, rather than merely the ability to comment on other people's lives.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of carrying experiences of worship into today's responsibilities, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. Try recalling one lesson from your most memorable experience of worship. Connect it to a task waiting now. If the lesson concerns earnestness, use it to keep a promise. If it concerns gentleness, bring it into a family conversation. We do not have to announce that connection to others. Let its benefit appear through action. May good memories help the journey continue, and may the heart receive today's responsibilities more lightly without continually demanding recognition for experiences already past.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about carrying experiences of worship into today's responsibilities will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. What we want to nurture is a willingness to do our part properly and in an orderly way, even when the results still take time to appear.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of carrying experiences of worship into today's responsibilities that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

phrasesEn: قَطَعَ السَّائِرِينَ لَهُ وَالْوَاصِلِينَ إِلَيْهِ عَنْ رُؤْيَةِ أَعْمَالِهِمْ وَشُهُودِ أَحْوَالِهِمْ،
He frees those travelling the path and those who have arrived at Him from fixation on their own deeds and inner states.
أَمَّا السَّائِرُونَ فَلِأَنَّهُمْ لَمْ يَتَحَقَّقُوا الصِّدْقَ مَعَ اللَّهِ فِيهَا،
Travellers have not yet established sincerity with Allah in those deeds and states.
وَأَمَّا الْوَاصِلُونَ فَلِأَنَّهُ غَيَّبَهُمْ بِشُهُودِهِ عَنْهَا.
For those who have arrived, witnessing Him diverts attention from all these.

70.translation: The branches of humiliation grow only from the seed of greed.
syarahEn: Greed can make someone capable of preserving their honour willingly do things that degrade them. They flatter excessively, deceive, or abandon principles because they feel they must obtain something. This wisdom reveals the relationship between uncontrolled desire and humiliation growing in our attitudes and decisions.

Aghsan al-dhull means branches of humiliation. Badhr al-tama' means the seed of greed. The image of a tree explains that degrading behaviour has a root that needs examination. As long as the seed is nurtured, branches can appear in different forms. Al-tama' is more than having needs: it is excessive desire that dominates judgement and demands fulfilment without measure.

For example, someone accepts work involving deception because they fear losing the chance of quick money. Another keeps seeking an influential person's attention while neglecting real responsibilities. In both cases, desire has taken control. Improvement requires more than hiding the behaviour, because the feeling of having to obtain something is still working within the heart.

Recognize the desire that makes it difficult to say enough. Arrange needs reasonably, pursue lawful means, and practise accepting delay without sacrificing principles. Give thanks for what is already available so that attention does not remain fixed on what is lacking. We may still have ambitions and improve our livelihood. Dignity is preserved when ambition does not enslave us to results. By reducing greed, we become freer to act honestly and better able to respect ourselves and others.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, some people want to belong to a circle so much that they will agree to anything. Asked to belittle someone, they join the laughter. Treated improperly, they fear stating a boundary. They feel that if this group rejects them, they will have nowhere else. An overwhelming wish for acceptance can make us tolerate treatment that continually hurts.

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes humiliation growing from the seed of greed. Greed concerns more than money. The heart can desire position, attention, or recognition so intensely that personal boundaries are sacrificed. This lesson invites honest attention to our needs, so that wanting something does not allow others to control choices contrary to guidance and human dignity.

Dear congregation, we all need friendship. However, a healthy relationship should not ask us to hurt people to prove loyalty. If a group continually tests us through degrading demands, reconsider the benefit of that closeness. We may politely refuse particular activities. If refusal provokes threats, seek support from someone safe and able to help.

“What if I end up alone after refusing?” That fear needs acknowledgement. Gradually build other relationships through good activities, supportive family, or healthier learning environments. Everything will not feel familiar immediately. But courage to maintain boundaries creates opportunities for friendships that do not require us to keep paying for acceptance with our principles and peace of mind.

Dear friends, parents and teachers can help by listening without ridicule. When a child describes peer pressure, do not immediately call them weak. Ask what happened and help prepare a safe response. A child needs to know they have somewhere to return, so rejection by one group does not feel like the end of their entire life. Practical support can reduce the fear that has made them feel forced to join in.

Let us pray for hearts strong enough to preserve dignity. May Allah bring us relationships of mutual respect, reduce our greed for recognition, and give us courage to refuse harmful treatment. May the need for acceptance go together with the ability to uphold what is right, so that friendship becomes a place of growth rather than a source of fear continually maintained. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
