Dear congregation, before going further, try bringing that story closer to our own lives. We are learning about maintaining boundaries when the desire for acceptance begins to degrade us. Perhaps a similar event passed unnoticed because our day was too full. Now we have time to look back at it calmly. If our experience differs, take the part that fits. Children at school can picture life at home; adults can recall their responsibilities. We are not looking for whoever has made the most mistakes. We want to go home with a clearer view and one action we are able to take. So let us listen while occasionally asking our own hearts a question.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes humiliation growing from the seed of greed. Greed concerns more than money. The heart can desire position, attention, or recognition so intensely that personal boundaries are sacrificed. This lesson invites honest attention to our needs, so that wanting something does not allow others to control choices contrary to guidance and human dignity.

Greed can make someone capable of preserving their honour willingly do things that degrade them. They flatter excessively, deceive, or abandon principles because they feel they must obtain something. This wisdom reveals the relationship between uncontrolled desire and humiliation growing in our attitudes and decisions.

Aghsan al-dhull means branches of humiliation. Badhr al-tama' means the seed of greed. The image of a tree explains that degrading behaviour has a root that needs examination. As long as the seed is nurtured, branches can appear in different forms. Al-tama' is more than having needs: it is excessive desire that dominates judgement and demands fulfilment without measure.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with maintaining boundaries when the desire for acceptance begins to degrade us. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, we all need friendship. However, a healthy relationship should not ask us to hurt people to prove loyalty. If a group continually tests us through degrading demands, reconsider the benefit of that closeness. We may politely refuse particular activities. If refusal provokes threats, seek support from someone safe and able to help.

“What if I end up alone after refusing?” That fear needs acknowledgement. Gradually build other relationships through good activities, supportive family, or healthier learning environments. Everything will not feel familiar immediately. But courage to maintain boundaries creates opportunities for friendships that do not require us to keep paying for acceptance with our principles and peace of mind.

Someone is invited to laugh at a weaker member. They feel uncomfortable but fear becoming the next target. Eventually, they smile along. Dear friends, group pressure can be heavy, especially for someone who badly needs a place to belong. We can support them without assuming refusal is always easy. Choose a safe refusal and seek a trustworthy person if threats arise. A good relationship should not continually demand proof of loyalty through humiliation. We may want friends while retaining the right to say no to wrongdoing. That choice can open room for a more respectful environment.

“What if they abandon me after I refuse?” Fear of being alone needs attention, dear congregation. Gradually build other relationships through good activities and safe people. We do not have to end every connection with an argument. Some boundaries can be stated and some involvement reduced. The wisdom about the seed of greed invites us to examine desires that come to dominate judgement. The need for friendship is natural, but acceptance by one group must not become the only condition for a worthwhile life. We ask Allah for help while seeking support that helps preserve dignity and safety.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Does the friendship ask us to hurt other people to prove loyalty?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, someone accepts work involving deception because they fear losing the chance of quick money. Another keeps seeking an influential person's attention while neglecting real responsibilities. In both cases, desire has taken control. Improvement requires more than hiding the behaviour, because the feeling of having to obtain something is still working within the heart.

Dear friends, parents and teachers can help by listening without ridicule. When a child describes peer pressure, do not immediately call them weak. Ask what happened and help prepare a safe response. A child needs to know they have somewhere to return, so rejection by one group does not feel like the end of their entire life. Practical support can reduce the fear that has made them feel forced to join in.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about maintaining boundaries when the desire for acceptance begins to degrade us may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Recognize the desire that makes it difficult to say enough. Arrange needs reasonably, pursue lawful means, and practise accepting delay without sacrificing principles. Give thanks for what is already available so that attention does not remain fixed on what is lacking. We may still have ambitions and improve our livelihood. Dignity is preserved when ambition does not enslave us to results. By reducing greed, we become freer to act honestly and better able to respect ourselves and others.

Choose one important boundary in your social life. Prepare a short refusal and identify someone who can help if the group's response is harmful. Parents can listen to children's experiences without immediately scolding them for not yet daring to refuse. Help prepare steps suited to their age and circumstances. We also examine whether we have pressured friends to do something uncomfortable. May closeness grow through safety and respect, so that the need for acceptance does not make us continually sacrifice principles or self-respect.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about maintaining boundaries when the desire for acceptance begins to degrade us. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of maintaining boundaries when the desire for acceptance begins to degrade us. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us pray for hearts strong enough to preserve dignity. May Allah bring us relationships of mutual respect, reduce our greed for recognition, and give us courage to refuse harmful treatment. May the need for acceptance go together with the ability to uphold what is right, so that friendship becomes a place of growth rather than a source of fear continually maintained. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَا بَسَقَتْ أَغْصَانُ الذُّلِّ
The branches of humiliation do not rise
إِلَّا عَلَى بِذْرِ طَمَعٍ.
except from the seed of greed.

71.translation: Nothing drags you along as powerfully as empty imagining.
syarahEn: Not everything we imagine about the future rests on a strong foundation. Some hope encourages preparation, while some imagining makes us feel we will obtain results without following the right path. This wisdom reminds us how powerfully fantasy can pull people along, even when reality has given signs to stop and reassess.

Al-wahm means an assumption or imagining without a firm foundation. Qadaka means it drags or leads you. This choice of words shows that unfounded thinking can take over the direction of action. When desire is too strong, we easily interpret every sign as support while overlooking information that actually reveals weaknesses in the plan.

For example, someone believes an offer will certainly make them rich quickly, yet is reluctant to examine the business and its risks. They prefer hearing success stories to understanding the responsibilities involved. Imagining the outcome weakens judgement. The same can happen in service when we imagine many benefits but reject the small tasks needed to bring them about.

Test hope with simple questions: what evidence can be checked, what steps are required, and who can give an honest assessment? Accept answers that are not always pleasing. Pray for good without treating personal wishes as certainties. Healthy hope makes us more diligent and open to learning. When empty imagining is reduced, the heart is freer to face reality and less easily led by promises that merely suit its preferences.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, one unanswered message can send our thoughts a long way. “They must be angry.” A few minutes later, “Perhaps I do not matter to them.” Yet the person may be working or may have left their phone behind. We have no information, but our heart is already responding to a story of its own making, spoiling the whole day without an actual conversation having taken place.

Ibn 'Ata'illah warns about wahm that can drag someone along. Wahm is an assumption that gains strength as though already real. We can use this lesson to examine the habit of guessing. The anxious feeling is real, but the content of the assumption may be untrue. Separating the two helps us choose a fairer response to ourselves and others.

Dear friends, when a message remains unanswered, first assess the need. If urgent, use an appropriate way to contact them and explain clearly why it matters. If it is not urgent, allow reasonable time. Avoid sending a string of accusations simply to ease momentary anxiety. Other people have work and limits on their attention that deserve respect, even when we strongly want immediate certainty.

“What if they often ignore me?” Discuss the pattern that actually occurs when things are calm. State your needs and realistic expectations, then listen to their circumstances. You can agree on ways to update each other about important matters. A conversation grounded in events is more useful than an accusation based on one sign on a screen. If a relationship keeps causing harm, reasonable limits on involvement can be considered.

Dear congregation, while waiting, return attention to your own tasks. Put the phone down briefly and do something clear. We do not have to keep checking to maintain a relationship. If this kind of anxiety frequently disrupts your life, speak with someone you trust or seek appropriate support. Some patterns can be understood and trained without insulting ourselves for supposedly overthinking.

Let us hold back one negative conclusion until we have enough information. May Allah clear our thinking, protect relationships from hasty accusations, and help us express needs politely. May we distinguish fear from reality, so our decisions are not continually dragged along by stories that may never have happened. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

If the relationship keeps causing harm, consider limits on involvement. The wisdom about assumptions helps us see how thoughts without firm foundations can direct action. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of distinguishing information from assumptions when a message goes unanswered, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

The next time a message remains unanswered, pause before adding a comment. Ask whether you have explained an urgent need. If a conversation about the relationship's pattern is required, choose a time when both can listen. Those receiving important messages can try to provide updates within their ability so that others do not keep guessing. We learn to maintain clarity in both directions. May conversation become safer, and may a mind that does not know the full circumstances avoid taking over too quickly in the way we treat those we love.

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about distinguishing information from assumptions when a message goes unanswered, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us hold back one negative conclusion until we have enough information. May Allah clear our thinking, protect relationships from hasty accusations, and help us express needs politely. May we distinguish fear from reality, so our decisions are not continually dragged along by stories that may never have happened. Amin.

phrasesEn: مَا قَادَكَ شَيْءٌ
Nothing drags you along so powerfully
مِثْلُ الْوَهْمِ.
as empty imagining.

72.translation: You are free of whatever you no longer covet. You are a slave to whatever you greedily desire.
syarahEn: We often measure freedom by how many choices we have. Yet someone can have many choices while remaining enslaved to one desire. They cannot rest until praised, accepted, or in possession of a particular item. This wisdom shows that inner freedom is closely connected to managing expectations and releasing greed.

Hurr means free, while 'abd means servant or slave. Ayis here refers to no longer hanging one's hopes on a created thing, rather than despairing of Allah's mercy. Tami' describes someone who intensely desires something. The comparison between freedom and slavery explains how an object of desire can dominate decisions when we feel unable to live without it.

For example, someone finds it difficult to refuse a wrongful invitation because they want their group to keep accepting them. As they learn that the group's approval does not determine the whole value of life, their decisions become freer. They may still have friends and desire good relationships, but need not sacrifice principles to be considered agreeable all the time.

Choose one desire that most often controls your mood. Practise delaying its fulfilment, assessing the need, and accepting the possibility of not obtaining it. Use what you already have more consciously. This practice does not extinguish ambition; it helps us pursue goals without losing control of our methods. Reliance on Allah makes the heart more spacious by returning created things to their proper measure. We can receive blessings gratefully and face their absence without feeling we must sell our honesty or dignity.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, may Allah honour us, meeting friends should be enjoyable. Yet sometimes we return home burdened because the venue costs far beyond our spending ability. We order anxiously and hide it with a smile. We do not really want the food; we fear being considered on a different level. A warm relationship feels expensive because pride sits at the same table.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that we are free of what we do not covet, and bound to what we chase intensely. The heart gains room when it can assess needs without always seeking permission from people's opinions. We may still enjoy company, but need not sacrifice obligations to maintain a particular image of our financial circumstances.

Dear congregation, we can say, “I need to watch my budget this month. How about choosing somewhere simpler?” That sentence belittles no one. We respectfully explain our situation and offer a way to keep meeting. Good friends usually care more about our presence than the price of our order. If someone mocks us, treat that as information about the quality of the relationship being built.

“What if I feel embarrassed to admit I cannot afford it?” Embarrassment can arise. Begin with a simple boundary without revealing every financial detail. We have a right to privacy. What matters is not continually making purchases that harm the family simply to avoid a brief conversation. Courage to state a boundary today can prevent a much longer burden afterwards.

Dear friends, those with more means should be sensitive to a friend's circumstances. Do not force everyone to follow your choice. If you wish to pay for them, make that clear and preserve their dignity. We can enjoy meeting in many simple places. Closeness grows from attention, time, and listening; it should not be available only to those who can pay the same amount.

Let us preserve companionship without allowing pride to direct spending. May Allah grant contentment, bless every family's provision, and make our friendships spacious. May we be brave enough to be honest about limits and gentle in accepting others' limits. May meetings bring warmth that remains after returning home, without leaving fear of tomorrow's needs. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Within the family, discuss shared needs so personal decisions do not neglect household responsibilities. May honesty make relationships lighter, and may we dare to enjoy company within our means without continually paying for pride through a lasting burden.

Dear congregation, if we want to take one task home from this discussion of stating spending limits while preserving closeness, choose something we can truly do. There is no need to announce it now. We can decide after getting home, when we have a fuller picture of our circumstances. Make the step small enough for us to know when it will be done. If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of stating spending limits while preserving closeness that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Let us preserve companionship without allowing pride to direct spending. May Allah grant contentment, bless every family's provision, and make our friendships spacious. May we be brave enough to be honest about limits and gentle in accepting others' limits. May meetings bring warmth that remains after returning home, without leaving fear of tomorrow's needs. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: أَنْتَ حُرٌّ مِمَّا أَنْتَ عَنْهُ آيِسٌ
You are free of what you no longer covet.
وَعَبْدٌ لِمَا أَنْتَ لَهُ طَامِعٌ.
You become a slave to what you greedily desire.

73.translation: Whoever does not draw near to Allah through the gentleness of His gifts will be drawn towards Him through the chains of trials.
syarahEn: Some people draw nearer to Allah when receiving blessings. Others only begin listening to their hearts after facing difficulty. This wisdom invites us to recognize different ways devotion can be awakened, so that ease does not make us heedless and trials are not read entirely as a closed path to Allah.

Mulatafat al-ihsan describes the gentleness of gifts inviting the heart. Salasil al-imtihan means chains of trials. The chain metaphor shows the force of experiences that interrupt old habits and make us see our limits. This language gives us no certain knowledge of Allah's particular reason behind someone's suffering. Primarily, it invites us to read our own experiences more honestly.

Someone busy chasing profit may begin rearranging priorities after their business is disrupted. However, they need not conclude that every loss must be caused by a particular sin. More useful are clear lessons: improving working methods, protecting the family's rights, and returning to seek help. Both blessings and difficulties can receive an appropriate response of devotion.

While enjoying ease, make gratitude and listening to advice habitual, so the heart does not wait for a severe event before changing. During a trial, seek necessary help and allow yourself reasonable space to grieve. When supporting others, offer assistance and compassion rather than accusations. This wisdom preserves the possibility of returning to Allah in varied circumstances. The call to good can be answered now, through blessings still present and lessons we can take from difficulty.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, sometimes the body has repeatedly signalled fatigue, yet we keep pushing. Meals become irregular, rest is reduced, and family reminders are dismissed as nagging. Only after activities are disrupted do we say, “If only I had been more careful yesterday.” An event that stops our busyness can make us hear something long drowned out by the desire to keep going.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that people may be invited to return through gentle blessings as well as difficult circumstances. We use this wisdom for self-examination. Do not make it a reason to declare someone's illness a punishment. We do not know Allah's particular purpose in every event, while someone who is ill still needs care, support, and practical compassion.

Dear friends, while healthy, we have an opportunity to arrange habits. Rest according to need, manage work, and seek advice from a healthcare professional if symptoms arise. Caring for the body does not make us less diligent. We are maintaining a means of fulfilling our trusts. Family also deserves our company when we can still listen, rather than always receiving energy and emotions already exhausted by work.

“What if necessity forces me to work long hours?” Everyone's circumstances differ. We are not blaming those with limited choices. Seek possible small steps and available support. Discuss sharing the burden when an opportunity appears. Those with more room can help, perhaps by taking a particular task or giving a break to a relative continually struggling to earn a living.

Dear congregation, if you are ill now, focus your energy on seeking care and fulfilling obligations according to guidance. We do not have to find a beautiful story in pain immediately. Lessons may come slowly. We can begin by accepting help and noticing habits that need improvement when circumstances allow. Give yourself time for the process without adding accusations whose truth we do not know.

Let us welcome reminders before busyness takes all our attention. May Allah grant health, ease workers' burdens, and help us care responsibly for our bodies. May existing blessings make us willing to hear advice, and may difficulty never extinguish hope of returning to Him with better steps. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
talkEn: OPENING

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about listening to the body's needs before busyness forces us to stop meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with listening to the body's needs before busyness forces us to stop. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Discuss sharing the burden when an opportunity appears. Those with more room can help, perhaps by taking a particular task or giving a break to a relative continually struggling to earn a living.

Family reminds us to rest, but we answer that there is still much work. Days later, the body is more tired and our voice rises more easily. Dear friends, gentle reminders often lose to the desire to keep going. We can pause to notice basic needs neglected along the way. Bodily care supports our ability to fulfil responsibilities. Not everyone has much freedom over time, so steps need adapting. Those with more room can take some tasks to give a relative a break. We do not want health advice to turn into accusation against people pressed by necessity. Care should add practical support for the ability to look after oneself.

“If I reduce work, what about household needs?” That question deserves serious thought, dear congregation. We can seek possible ways to share burdens and ask competent professionals about symptoms. We need not make a major decision from one general piece of advice. This wisdom invites honest reading of our experiences, including trials that reveal limits. We must not declare someone's illness a particular punishment or assume they have managed life badly. What we can do is help meet needs and remind respectfully. Learning to listen to the body goes together with efforts suited to circumstances.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “What small step remains possible to care for our energy today?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone busy chasing profit may begin rearranging priorities after their business is disrupted. However, they need not conclude that every loss must be caused by a particular sin. More useful are clear lessons: improving working methods, protecting the family's rights, and returning to seek help. Both blessings and difficulties can receive an appropriate response of devotion.

Lessons may come slowly. We can begin by accepting help and noticing habits that need improvement when circumstances allow. Give yourself time for the process without adding accusations whose truth we do not know.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of listening to the body's needs before busyness forces us to stop, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

While enjoying ease, make gratitude and listening to advice habitual, so the heart does not wait for a severe event before changing. During a trial, seek necessary help and allow yourself reasonable space to grieve. When supporting others, offer assistance and compassion rather than accusations. This wisdom preserves the possibility of returning to Allah in varied circumstances. The call to good can be answered now, through blessings still present and lessons we can take from difficulty.

Choose one habit most possible to improve without neglecting dependants. Discuss rest needs or task sharing with those involved. If symptoms arise, seek appropriate help rather than continuing to guess alone. Family offering reminders should provide clear support to make advice easier to follow. We also need to ensure time together is not always filled with leftover anger from work. May Allah grant sufficiency, protect those continually struggling to earn a living, and help us care for the body as a precious trust.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of listening to the body's needs before busyness forces us to stop again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about listening to the body's needs before busyness forces us to stop invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us welcome reminders before busyness takes all our attention. May Allah grant health, ease workers' burdens, and help us care responsibly for our bodies. May existing blessings make us willing to hear advice, and may difficulty never extinguish hope of returning to Him with better steps. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَنْ لَمْ يُقْبِلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ بِمُلَاطَفَاتِ الْإِحْسَانِ
Whoever does not draw near to Allah through the gentleness of His gifts
قُيِّدَ إِلَيْهِ بِسَلَاسِلِ الِامْتِحَانِ.
will be drawn towards Him through the chains of trials.

74.translation: Whoever fails to thank Allah for a blessing opens the way for its disappearance. Whoever gives thanks secures the blessing with its tether.
syarahEn: Blessings that remain with us easily feel ordinary. We use health without care, enjoy help without thanks, and assume opportunities will always be available. This wisdom reminds us of the relationship between gratitude and preserving blessings. What needs nurturing is more than happiness at receiving: it includes how we use the gift.

Yashkur means to give thanks, while al-ni'am means blessings. Zawal means loss or disappearance. Qayyadaha bi-'iqaliha describes tethering something, like securing a mount so it does not escape. Gratitude is likened to a tether because it directs blessings towards their proper purposes and prevents us damaging them through neglect or misuse.

Someone grateful for health tries to care for the body and use it to fulfil responsibilities. Someone grateful for knowledge keeps learning and shares responsibly. Someone grateful for help maintains the relationship without treating the helper as obliged to be constantly available. Gratitude takes a form suited to the blessing received, so the heart's acknowledgement bears fruit in action.

Do not turn this wisdom into a formula for accusing someone who loses something of insufficient gratitude. Life contains many circumstances unknown to us. Use its advice to improve your own attitude. Choose one blessing often taken for granted, then determine how to care for and use it. Gratitude gives fuller attention to Allah's gifts. We learn to enjoy them reasonably, observe the rights accompanying them, and accept change without erasing thanks for benefits previously received.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, a book can benefit many people when cared for. Someone borrows, reads, and returns it. The next person receives the same opportunity. Yet one person who stores it carelessly or fails to return it can stop that benefit. Shared blessings need habits of care, so they continue providing room to learn for others who also wish to use them.

Ibn 'Ata'illah connects gratitude with preserving blessings. Thanks to Allah should appear in their use. We do not understand gratitude as a guarantee that an item can never break or disappear. We learn that neglecting a trust can open the way to loss, while care is part of trying to preserve the benefit still available.

Dear congregation, when borrowing a book, record its return date and keep it somewhere safe. If you need longer, ask permission. If it is damaged, explain honestly and discuss responsibility. Do not disappear until the owner has to chase you. Clarity helps people remain comfortable lending shared items, so benefit does not stop because trust is continually eroded by neglect.

“If it is inexpensive, does it really need such care?” We are also protecting rights and trust. A small book may matter to someone who needs it. Children can learn this attitude without excessive fear. Show them how to care for it and help remember the date. If a mistake happens, support them in acknowledging and correcting it, so responsibility is understood as action they can take.

Dear friends, the same principle applies to classroom facilities, sports equipment, and mosque items. We are grateful for convenience and consider the next user. If able, help tidy up or report damage to the manager. Do not wait until everything is ruined before complaining. Shared benefit is easier to preserve when everyone takes a reasonable part in maintenance.

Let us check whether a borrowed item remains at home. Return it or contact its owner today. May Allah help us thank Him for blessings through trustworthiness, bless community facilities, and preserve mutual trust. May what we use remain beneficial for the next person, so its goodness can continue to be shared. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

A book is borrowed with the intention of finishing it. As activities increase, it slips among other belongings and the return date passes. The owner feels awkward asking. Dear friends, we can support trust by keeping a record from the beginning. Store the book safely and ask permission if more time is needed. If damage occurs, explain without avoiding it. Caring for an item preserves another person's opportunity to learn. We need not wait for a book to be expensive before considering this trust important. Someone is waiting for the same benefit, and our neglect may interrupt its flow for longer.

“What if the damage was accidental?” Even an accident needs honest explanation, dear congregation. Discuss how to take responsibility according to the circumstances. Do not add a lie for fear of embarrassment. The lender can also respond fairly and provide clarity from the beginning. This wisdom describes gratitude as a tether for blessings. Care is one expression: we use something for its purpose and protect its benefit from damage through neglect. This does not mean every loss must result from insufficient gratitude. We direct advice towards our own habits and still acknowledge the limits of our knowledge about events.

Now try answering silently, dear friends: “Is the item we borrowed still ready for the next person to use?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. May a gathering like this send us home with the courage to learn, rather than merely the ability to comment on other people's lives.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about caring for borrowed books so their benefit continues will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about caring for borrowed books so their benefit continues, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us check whether a borrowed item remains at home. Return it or contact its owner today. phrasesEn: مَنْ لَمْ يَشْكُرِ النِّعَمَ فَقَدْ تَعَرَّضَ لِزَوَالِهَا،
Whoever fails to thank Allah for blessings opens the way to their disappearance.
وَمَنْ شَكَرَهَا فَقَدْ قَيَّدَهَا بِعِقَالِهَا.
Whoever gives thanks secures them with their tether.

75.translation: Beware of His continued kindness to you while you continue to act badly towards Him. It may be istidraj for you. We shall draw them on gradually from where they do not know.
syarahEn: An easy life does not always make a person more aware. Sometimes someone continues profiting while feeling free to violate a trust. Seeing no immediate consequence, they assume everything they do must be right. This wisdom invites caution about that conclusion, so enjoyment does not lull the heart's sensitivity to sleep.

Istidraj means being drawn on gradually, leaving a wrongdoer lulled into complacency without realizing where the consequences lead. Dawam refers to something continuing, while isa'ah means wrongdoing. Their relationship reveals a state in which gifts remain enjoyed while disobedience is maintained. The concern is that opportunities for self-improvement become ever more distant because everything feels fine.

For example, a business grows despite earning profit in ways that harm people. That growth cannot prove deception is justified. Standards of right and wrong still return to religious guidance and rights that must be protected. Wealth or comfort gives no certain knowledge of someone's standing with Allah.

Examine how ease affects our lives. Does it help protect obligations and extend benefit, or increase our boldness in overlooking wrongdoing? If there is a violation, stop and repair its effects without waiting for disaster. At the same time, do not guess other people's state from visible blessings alone. This wisdom primarily awakens us to practise gratitude properly. Ease becomes an opportunity to improve devotion, so we are not deceived by pleasant outward circumstances while responsibilities are increasingly abandoned.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, there is a dangerous business assumption: “If my goods sell, my methods must be right.” Defects are then hidden, exaggerated promises continue, and customer complaints are treated as interruptions. We make results a defence of our methods. Yet a large income does not automatically explain whether people's rights have been protected or neglected.

Ibn 'Ata'illah warns about istidraj, when ease accompanies heedlessness and someone feels safe. This message calls for watchfulness over ourselves. We must not casually label another person's success istidraj. What needs examination is the reality of our own behaviour: is a violation continually justified simply because its harmful consequences are not visible yet?

Dear friends, suppose an item has a defect but the photograph is arranged so buyers cannot see it. Transactions remain numerous. Busy sales do not change the obligation to provide accurate information. Stop the misleading approach, correct the description, and address complaints that are your responsibility. Provision received with gratitude should accompany earnest protection of rights rather than serve as a reason for continued dishonesty.

“What if honesty makes people decide not to buy?” Some may choose another item. However, buyers have a right to know its condition before deciding. We can improve quality and explain benefits that actually exist. A business should grow through service, rather than through information deliberately leading people to decide without understanding important limitations of the goods or services offered.

Dear congregation, invite colleagues to examine sales habits. Are there promises that cannot be kept? Are complaints recorded and answered? Such evaluation helps prevent profit from making us complacent. If rules or contractual matters remain unclear, seek explanation from a competent person. Do not choose an answer merely because it most easily justifies a habit already making money.

Let us ask for provision alongside hearts willing to be examined. May Allah bless honest businesses, protect customers from deception, and help us stop wrongful methods. May ease make us more obedient and sensitive to people's rights, so success does not remove the courage to improve ourselves. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
talkEn: OPENING
Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, there is a dangerous business assumption: “If my goods sell, my methods must be right.” Defects are then hidden, exaggerated promises continue, and customer complaints are treated as interruptions. We make results a defence of our methods. Yet a large income does not automatically explain whether people's rights have been protected or neglected.

Dear congregation, before going further, try bringing that story closer to our own lives. We are learning about examining business methods even when sales are busy. Perhaps a similar event passed unnoticed because our day was too full. Now we have time to look back at it calmly. If our experience differs, take the part that fits. Children at school can picture life at home; adults can recall their responsibilities. We are not looking for whoever has made the most mistakes. We want to go home with a clearer view and one action we are able to take. So let us listen while occasionally asking our own hearts a question.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah warns about istidraj, when ease accompanies heedlessness and someone feels safe. This message calls for watchfulness over ourselves. We must not casually label another person's success istidraj. What needs examination is the reality of our own behaviour: is a violation continually justified simply because its harmful consequences are not visible yet?

An easy life does not always make a person more aware. Sometimes someone continues profiting while feeling free to violate a trust. Seeing no immediate consequence, they assume everything they do must be right. This wisdom invites caution about that conclusion, so enjoyment does not lull the heart's sensitivity to sleep.

Istidraj means being drawn on gradually, leaving a wrongdoer lulled into complacency without realizing where the consequences lead. Dawam refers to something continuing, while isa'ah means wrongdoing. Their relationship reveals a state in which gifts remain enjoyed while disobedience is maintained. The concern is that opportunities for self-improvement become ever more distant because everything feels fine.

Let us hold this understanding carefully, dear friends. Advice about examining business methods even when sales are busy should be read alongside our obligations as servants of Allah and our responsibilities towards others. Feeling peaceful after hearing a talk is certainly pleasant. Yet sound understanding also helps us act when things no longer feel peaceful. That is why explaining the words matters. We gain something to guide our direction, rather than a beautiful impression that soon fades. If we later forget how the term sounds, remember the relationship it explains: how the heart turns to Allah and how our choices touch real life.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, suppose an item has a defect but the photograph is arranged so buyers cannot see it. Transactions remain numerous. Busy sales do not change the obligation to provide accurate information. Stop the misleading approach, correct the description, and address complaints that are your responsibility. Provision received with gratitude should accompany earnest protection of rights rather than serve as a reason for continued dishonesty.

“What if honesty makes people decide not to buy?” Some may choose another item. However, buyers have a right to know its condition before deciding. We can improve quality and explain benefits that actually exist. A business should grow through service, rather than through information deliberately leading people to decide without understanding important limitations of the goods or services offered.

A product photograph looks good because a defective part is deliberately hidden. Orders keep coming and the owner feels the approach has proved successful. Dear friends, buyers decide from the information provided. Busy sales do not change their right to know important conditions. We can correct descriptions and explain benefits actually available. If a complaint falls within our responsibility, handle it properly. A business can improve through quality and service. We need not preserve misleading information simply because it previously earned money. While resources remain available, there is an opportunity to improve before harm to others increases.

“What if honesty makes buyers leave?” They have a right to weigh their choices, dear congregation. We can improve quality or find buyers suited to the item's actual condition. The obligation to explain does not disappear through fear of reduced sales. The wisdom about istidraj warns against feeling safe when gifts continue but wrongdoing is maintained. Use it to examine yourself. Do not look at another person's busy business and declare they are experiencing istidraj. We do not know their full circumstances. What is clear is the part of our business needing care so profit does not become a reason to justify violations.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Does a high number of transactions remove the obligation to explain product defects?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, a business grows despite earning profit in ways that harm people. That growth cannot prove deception is justified. Standards of right and wrong still return to religious guidance and rights that must be protected. Wealth or comfort gives no certain knowledge of someone's standing with Allah.

Dear congregation, invite colleagues to examine sales habits. Are there promises that cannot be kept? Are complaints recorded and answered? Such evaluation helps prevent profit from making us complacent. If rules or contractual matters remain unclear, seek explanation from a competent person. Do not choose an answer merely because it most easily justifies a habit already making money.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of examining business methods even when sales are busy, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Examine how ease affects our lives. Does it help protect obligations and extend benefit, or increase our boldness in overlooking wrongdoing? If there is a violation, stop and repair its effects without waiting for disaster. At the same time, do not guess other people's state from visible blessings alone. This wisdom primarily awakens us to practise gratitude properly. Ease becomes an opportunity to improve devotion, so we are not deceived by pleasant outward circumstances while responsibilities are increasingly abandoned.

Choose one product description or service promise needing review. Check whether important information has deliberately been obscured. Correct it appropriately and discuss standards with those helping the business. If a buyer has been harmed, attend to responsibility according to the circumstances. Family can support courage to be honest without promising sales will rise immediately. May profit come with gratitude and watchfulness, so business opportunities become a place to fulfil rights rather than continually conceal wrongful methods.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about examining business methods even when sales are busy. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about examining business methods even when sales are busy. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us ask for provision alongside hearts willing to be examined. May Allah bless honest businesses, protect customers from deception, and help us stop wrongful methods. May ease make us more obedient and sensitive to people's rights, so success does not remove the courage to improve ourselves. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
wordsEn: We shall draw them on gradually
phrasesEn: خَفْ مِنْ وُجُودِ إِحْسَانِهِ إِلَيْكَ وَدَوَامِ إِسَاءَتِكَ مَعَهُ
Beware of His continued kindness while you continue wrongdoing towards Him.
أَنْ يَكُونَ ذَلِكَ اسْتِدْرَاجًا لَكَ،
It may be istidraj for you.
سَنَسْتَدْرِجُهُمْ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ.
We shall draw them on gradually through a path they do not know.

76.translation: Among a disciple's follies is to behave badly, then, when punishment is delayed, say: If this were bad conduct, support would surely have been cut off and I would have been distanced. Yet support may have been cut off without their noticing, even if only through being denied further gifts. They may have been placed at a distance without knowing, even if only through being left to follow their own desires.
syarahEn: We sometimes feel safe after wrongdoing because life continues as usual. Work is uninterrupted, the body healthy, and worship continues. Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that harmful consequences do not always arrive as visible loss. The heart can also weaken as sensitivity and the desire to improve diminish.

Su' al-adab means bad conduct: a response unsuited to one's position as a servant. Al-imdad is the assistance sustaining devotion. Man' al-mazid means withholding an increase in gifts, while yukhalliyaka describes being left to follow one's desires. These terms direct attention to the quality of our relationship with Allah rather than simply the smooth running of worldly affairs.

Someone may remain busy in good activities yet become less willing to accept advice and more likely to hurt others. If we only count activities, that change escapes evaluation. We need to examine whether deeds still improve character or are being used to cover self-justification. Watchfulness helps us return before a harmful pattern is considered normal.

However, do not treat every feeling of fatigue or loss of enthusiasm as certain punishment from Allah. The body, life's burdens, and surrounding circumstances also need attention. Examine known mistakes, repent, and address their causes. Maintain needed rest and support too. This wisdom nurtures seriousness without asking us to guess the unseen. We are responsible for clear conduct and actions, while continually asking for help so the heart is not left submerged in directionless desires.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, sometimes we hurt someone and think, “If it were wrong, there would already be consequences.” Because work continues and the person stays silent, we feel safe. Belittling words are repeated. We forget that consequences do not always appear as a major event. Trust can slowly disappear and relationships grow distant without much sound.

Ibn 'Ata'illah rebukes someone who considers bad conduct harmless because its recompense is not yet apparent. Heedlessness can make a person insensitive to inner losses already occurring. This wisdom invites examination before waiting for an event considered a sign. We have no basis to determine an event's unseen cause, but clearly wrongful behaviour still needs stopping.

Dear congregation, suppose a parent repeatedly embarrasses a child before relatives. The child still obeys, so the parent thinks the method works. Yet the child begins keeping stories private and avoids asking advice. Silence does not measure whether those words hurt. We need to view a relationship through safety, willingness to speak, and how we receive explanations differing from our wishes.

“What if the child needs correction?” Correction can still be clear and preserve dignity. Name the behaviour needing change, explain why, and allow an opportunity to understand. Do not turn a particular mistake into a label that their entire self is bad. We want children to learn responsibility, so closeness need not be sacrificed for obedience driven only by fear.

Dear friends, if we usually wait for protests, try asking first: “Was the way I spoke earlier too harsh?” Listen without demanding an answer that comforts us. An adult's acknowledgement can reopen conversation. If the relationship is already difficult, suitable support may be needed. We can still begin by stopping behaviour we already recognize as harmful.

Let us improve conduct without waiting for something shocking. May Allah preserve the heart's sensitivity, forgive mistakes in raising children, and give courage to acknowledge the effects of our actions. May our families have safe room to speak. May calm circumstances never make us neglect examining the rights and feelings of those living closest to us. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, imagine taking this reminder home with us. We have taken off our shoes, the gathering is over, and ordinary life begins again. That is where the lesson about recognizing the effects of words before waiting for a major reprimand will be tested. We may still face the same situation, the same people, and old habits that have not yet changed. We need to understand the message well enough to bring it into those circumstances. Listen slowly. If a sentence speaks to our situation, keep it in mind for later. We do not have to remember every explanation. One sound understanding, put sincerely into practice, is already worth working towards today.

For ourselves, this advice can become an honest question. What am I hoping for? What am I neglecting? Our answer may not be complete today. That is all right. What matters is being willing to learn sincerely, examine our understanding, and follow sound guidance when seeking to change our daily habits.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, suppose a parent repeatedly embarrasses a child before relatives. The child still obeys, so the parent thinks the method works. Yet the child begins keeping stories private and avoids asking advice. Silence does not measure whether those words hurt. Do not turn a particular mistake into a label that their entire self is bad. We want children to learn responsibility, so closeness need not be sacrificed for obedience driven only by fear.

A child still follows instructions but shares school stories less often. The parent assumes they are simply growing older. Perhaps so; perhaps there is fear after repeated humiliation. Dear friends, we need to ask without immediately treating an assumption as certain. Make room to listen and do not use a shared story as material for the next joke. Visible obedience does not explain the whole sense of safety in a relationship. We can improve correction before waiting for a major argument. Name a particular behaviour and give an opportunity to understand. The child still learns responsibility while knowing they do not have to be degraded for advice to be considered firm.

“If no harm has appeared, why change?” We cannot always see consequences immediately, dear congregation. Trust can diminish slowly without an announcement. Actions therefore still need sound guidance as their measure, rather than merely smooth affairs. This wisdom invites examination of conduct and warns against feeling safe simply because no reprimand has come. Nor may we treat every person's difficulty as certain punishment. Advice is directed to our choices: do our words respect rights, and will we listen when told someone is hurt? Those answers are closer to responsibility we can act on.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “Does a child's silence really show that our way of correcting them does not hurt?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone may remain busy in good activities yet become less willing to accept advice and more likely to hurt others. If we only count activities, that change escapes evaluation. We need to examine whether deeds still improve character or are being used to cover self-justification. Watchfulness helps us return before a harmful pattern is considered normal.

Dear friends, if we usually wait for protests, try asking first: “Was the way I spoke earlier too harsh?” Listen without demanding an answer that comforts us. An adult's acknowledgement can reopen conversation. If the relationship is already difficult, suitable support may be needed. We can still begin by stopping behaviour we already recognize as harmful.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about recognizing the effects of words before waiting for a major reprimand may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

However, do not treat every feeling of fatigue or loss of enthusiasm as certain punishment from Allah. The body, life's burdens, and surrounding circumstances also need attention. Examine known mistakes, repent, and address their causes. Maintain needed rest and support too. This wisdom nurtures seriousness without asking us to guess the unseen. We are responsible for clear conduct and actions, while continually asking for help so the heart is not left submerged in directionless desires.

Try asking the family about one speaking habit that needs improvement, at a safe and calm time. Listen without immediately calling for a defence. If something is true, choose a visible change. Avoid judging a child's entire self through one mistake. Adults may also seek help when anger is difficult to manage. May we not wait to lose closeness before caring for conduct, and may home give room to honesty that weaker members do not always find easy to express.

Now let us turn the lesson about recognizing the effects of words before waiting for a major reprimand into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about recognizing the effects of words before waiting for a major reprimand invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us improve conduct without waiting for something shocking. May Allah preserve the heart's sensitivity, forgive mistakes in raising children, and give courage to acknowledge the effects of our actions. May our families have safe room to speak. May calm circumstances never make us neglect examining the rights and feelings of those living closest to us. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
wordsEn: a disciple; a traveller on the path
phrasesEn: مِنْ جَهْلِ الْمُرِيدِ أَنْ يُسِيءَ الْأَدَبَ فَتُؤَخَّرَ الْعُقُوبَةُ عَنْهُ،
Among a disciple's follies is bad conduct followed by delayed punishment.
فَيَقُولَ لَوْ كَانَ هَذَا سُوءَ أَدَبٍ لَقُطِعَ الْإِمْدَادُ وَأُوجِبَ الْإِبْعَادُ،
They say: If this were bad conduct, help would have been cut off and I would have been distanced.
فَقَدْ يُقْطَعُ الْمَدَدُ عَنْهُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَشْعُرُ،
Yet help may already be cut off without their awareness,
وَلَوْ لَمْ يَكُنْ إِلَّا مَنْعُ الْمَزِيدِ،
even if only through withholding further gifts.
وَقَدْ يُقَامُ مَقَامَ الْبُعْدِ وَهُوَ لَا يَدْرِي،
They may already have been placed at a distance without knowing,
وَلَوْ لَمْ يَكُنْ إِلَّا أَنْ يُخَلِّيَكَ وَمَا تُرِيدُ.
even if only through being left to follow their own desires.

77.translation: When you see a servant whom Allah has established in regular devotional practice and continues to sustain in it with His help, do not belittle what their Lord has bestowed simply because you do not see the signs of those who know Him or the radiance of those who love Allah. Without a spiritual gift arriving, no regular devotional practice would be performed.
syarahEn: Some people appear simple in their devotion. They maintain prayer, recite dhikr, and keep daily practices without many stories about inner experiences. We may wrongly belittle that perseverance because we see no supposedly special signs. This wisdom reminds us that the ability to remain steadfast is itself a gift deserving respect.

Al-awrad is the plural of wird, a practice maintained regularly. Al-warid refers to a gift coming to the heart and moving it towards devotion. Sima means a sign, while bahjah refers to a radiance of joy or cheerfulness. The absence of a particular visible sign gives us no right to conclude someone receives no spiritual help.

For example, a worker maintains daily recitation among their responsibilities. They cannot explain Sufi terminology eloquently, yet gradually become more patient and honest. Such perseverance has real value. We need not demand that everyone display the same experience, speaking style, or expression as our imagined spiritual figures.

For yourself, maintain practices within your ability according to guidance. If pleasant feelings have not arrived, do not immediately judge the practice useless. Notice its effect on obligations and character. For others, offer appreciation without exaggerating their rank. This wisdom teaches respect for gifts in quiet forms. Allah's help may be recognized through unobtrusive faithfulness, so devotion is not narrowly measured by the ability to tell stories about the heart or extraordinary experiences.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, someone arrives early at the prayer room every day. Their recitation and movements are simple, and they leave afterwards without much talk. We rarely notice them. Sometimes we even think, “Their learning is ordinary; they do not know much.” Yet we do not know the struggle to maintain that habit or the help accompanying it day after day.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us not to belittle someone who diligently maintains a wird even when signs of spiritual distinction are not apparent. Perseverance in devotion itself deserves appreciation. We do not determine people's inner ranks. Visible knowledge and speaking ability may be useful, but give us no right to dismiss earnestness carried on without an attention-grabbing appearance.

Dear friends, perhaps that person must arrange time around demanding work. Perhaps they have just begun learning and still repeat the same recitation to get it right. We need not invent a story about them. Simply acknowledge how much we do not know. The proper attitude is to respect, greet, and help if there is a need we can appropriately meet.

“What if their recitation is still incorrect?” Help can be offered gently and appropriately. Ask whether they are willing to learn, choose a time that preserves dignity, and never make a mistake into a joke. We respect perseverance while supporting improvement. People accept explanations more readily when treated as fellow learners rather than a bad example displayed before the congregation.

Dear congregation, this wisdom also helps those who feel their deeds are too ordinary. You need not wait for a special experience to appreciate the opportunity for obedience you are maintaining. Keep learning guidance, improve shortcomings, and ask Allah for acceptance. We do not know the full value of a good habit faithfully practised when life is difficult and support feels scarce.

Let us greet one person we have previously overlooked. May Allah bless the perseverance of little-known servants, ease learning, and guard us against hasty judgement. May places of worship respect every member of the congregation, so those still learning hesitantly dare to attend and nurture their devotion earnestly. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
