“What if a recitation error needs correction?” Help may still be offered appropriately, dear congregation. Ask about willingness to learn and choose circumstances preserving dignity. Do not make the mistake a public display. Appreciate perseverance while supporting the quality of worship. This wisdom distinguishes regular practice from the gift moving the heart. A particular sign remaining unseen is no basis for declaring someone receives no help. We learn enough humility to acknowledge our judgement's limits, then attend to what is practical: mutual respect, sound learning, and help within our ability.

Let me ask a question, dear congregation: “What do we not know about the struggle of someone whose worship appears simple?” Take a moment to think about it. Perhaps an answer comes straight away; perhaps a difficulty comes to mind instead. Let us hear that difficulty calmly. Good advice needs to meet the reality of life, including the limitations we face. Now imagine someone we love asking that question. Would our answer help them act, or simply leave them feeling scolded? Here we learn to convey the truth in a way that can be received. We also need honesty that gives direction when speaking to ourselves, so that understanding a problem gives us courage to begin putting it right.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, a worker maintains daily recitation among their responsibilities. They cannot explain Sufi terminology eloquently, yet gradually become more patient and honest. Such perseverance has real value. We need not demand that everyone display the same experience, speaking style, or expression as our imagined spiritual figures.

Dear congregation, this wisdom also helps those who feel their deeds are too ordinary. You need not wait for a special experience to appreciate the opportunity for obedience you are maintaining. Keep learning guidance, improve shortcomings, and ask Allah for acceptance. We do not know the full value of a good habit faithfully practised when life is difficult and support feels scarce.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of respecting perseverance that does not stand out, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

For yourself, maintain practices within your ability according to guidance. If pleasant feelings have not arrived, do not immediately judge the practice useless. Notice its effect on obligations and character. For others, offer appreciation without exaggerating their rank. This wisdom teaches respect for gifts in quiet forms. Allah's help may be recognized through unobtrusive faithfulness, so devotion is not narrowly measured by the ability to tell stories about the heart or extraordinary experiences.

At the next gathering, try greeting a member of the congregation rarely spoken to. There is no need to ask about private experiences or give a title that makes them uncomfortable. Build simple companionship. If asked to help with learning, act within your knowledge and find a suitable teacher for what lies beyond it. For yourself, maintain beneficial practices without demanding everyone know about them. May quiet perseverance receive support, and may we avoid measuring human worth only through what attracts attention.

Dear congregation, if we want to take one task home from this discussion of respecting perseverance that does not stand out, choose something we can truly do. There is no need to announce it now. We can decide after getting home, when we have a fuller picture of our circumstances. Make the step small enough for us to know when it will be done. If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of respecting perseverance that does not stand out. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us greet one person we have previously overlooked. May Allah bless the perseverance of little-known servants, ease learning, and guard us against hasty judgement. May places of worship respect every member of the congregation, so those still learning hesitantly dare to attend and nurture their devotion earnestly. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: إِذَا رَأَيْتَ عَبْدًا أَقَامَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى بِوُجُودِ الْأَوْرَادِ وَأَدَامَهُ عَلَيْهَا مَعَ طُولِ الْإِمْدَادِ،
When you see a servant Allah establishes in regular devotional practice and continually sustains in it through His help,
فَلَا تَسْتَحْقِرَنَّ مَا مَنَحَهُ مَوْلَاهُ
do not belittle their Lord's gift to them
لِأَنَّكَ لَمْ تَرَ عَلَيْهِ سِيمَا الْعَارِفِينَ وَلَا بَهْجَةَ الْمُحِبِّينَ،
simply because you have not seen the signs of those knowing Him or the radiance of those loving Allah.
فَلَوْلَا وَارِدٌ مَا كَانَ وِرْدٌ.
Without an arriving spiritual gift, no regular devotional practice would be performed.

78.translation: Some people Allah has established in His service. Others He has singled out for His love. To each, these and those, We extend help from your Lord's bounty. Your Lord's bounty is not withheld.
syarahEn: Some people are strong in consistent worship and service. Others feel their hearts vividly alive in love and longing for Allah. This wisdom describes that diversity of gifts so we do not force everyone to have the same experience. Each needs Allah's help to follow their path of devotion.

Khidmah means service or devotion, while mahabbah means love. Aqamahum refers to establishing them in a particular task, and ikhtassahum to granting distinction. Numiddu means We extend help. The closing reference to Allah's giving reminds us that all paths of goodness receive strength from His bounty rather than independent human power.

Someone diligently serving in an Islamic boarding school's kitchen need not feel inferior because they cannot eloquently describe loving Allah. Honest service can be a place where love grows. Someone experiencing deep longing must still maintain obligations and other people's rights. Love does not release people from responsibility; it should deepen their earnest devotion.

Do not rush to give yourself titles or rank people by appearance. Recognize the clearest trust before you and fulfil it gratefully. If given spaciousness of heart, use it to increase compassion. If given perseverance, use it to preserve benefit. This wisdom helps us complement one another amid different abilities. We need not receive the same form of gift to work together, because devotion remains directed to Allah, who pours help upon all His servants according to His wisdom.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, may Allah honour us, when a family cares for someone ill, roles can differ. One takes them to appointments, another prepares meals, another helps with costs. An elderly relative may only be able to sit with them briefly and pray. Sometimes these differences become a contest, as though one form of assistance makes every other form meaningless.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains the diversity of gifts in devotion. Some servants are strengthened in service, others granted depth of love for Allah. All receive His help. We are not tasked with ranking people's inner lives. We can appreciate different gifts and abilities, while ensuring practical needs and obligations are responsibly met.

Dear congregation, those able to give physical effort need support rather than simply being told to stay strong. Those with limited energy need not be embarrassed either. Ask what they can still do. Prayer is valued, while work requiring hands remains clearly divided. Do not use different abilities as a reason to avoid tasks we can actually undertake.

“What if someone only says they are praying, although they could help?” Discuss needs concretely without guessing intentions. For example, ask whether they can take a particular shift. Clear answers help divide roles. We may evaluate involvement, but avoid judging someone's closeness to Allah. Managing shared work differs from believing we know every family member's entire inner state.

Dear friends, appreciation should follow every genuinely useful contribution. Name the work already helped and the needs remaining. Then people do not have to compete to appear the most self-sacrificing. Relationships feel lighter when benefits are acknowledged and responsibilities discussed. Different forms of devotion can support one another, so the person ill and their carers both feel practical attention.

Let us protect the family from competition over contributions. May Allah grant healing, bless every assistance, and strengthen those serving. May those with limits still feel appreciated, those able be willing to share burdens, and those praying continue asking sincerely. May diverse roles bring closeness to Him and warmth among relatives. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about sharing family care while appreciating prayer and physical effort meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.

Dear congregation, a saying of wisdom may be very short, yet reflection reveals how deeply it touches our long-standing habits. We are seeing that here in the matter of sharing family care while appreciating prayer and physical effort. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, those able to give physical effort need support rather than simply being told to stay strong. Those with limited energy need not be embarrassed either. Ask what they can still do. Within a family, the person taking someone to appointments feels most tired. Another contributes money, while an elderly member can only sit with them briefly. If every role becomes a competition, discussion easily turns into mutual belittling. Dear friends, we can return to needs. Who can take over a shift, and when? Who can prepare meals? Concrete questions help more than guessing intentions. Those with limited energy remain respected. Those still strong are asked to take a suitable part too. Prayer has a place for hope, while work needing hands remains clearly divided with practical support.

“What if someone hides behind saying they are praying?” We may ask willingness to help with a particular part, dear congregation. A clear answer informs the division of work without requiring a judgement about the depth of their love for Allah. Evaluating a role differs from judging an inner state. We also need to check for unknown obstacles. Those already serving should not continually carry more simply because they usually give way. This wisdom recalls diverse forms of devotion and Allah as the source of help. Every role needs His gift, leaving no reason for boasting of ability or belittling assistance suited to someone's limits.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “Which tasks need concrete discussion so that every ability can contribute?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone diligently serving in an Islamic boarding school's kitchen need not feel inferior because they cannot eloquently describe loving Allah. Honest service can be a place where love grows. Someone experiencing deep longing must still maintain obligations and other people's rights. Love does not release people from responsibility; it should deepen their earnest devotion.

Then people do not have to compete to appear the most self-sacrificing. Relationships feel lighter when benefits are acknowledged and responsibilities discussed. Different forms of devotion can support one another, so the person ill and their carers both feel practical attention.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about sharing family care while appreciating prayer and physical effort may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Do not rush to give yourself titles or rank people by appearance. Recognize the clearest trust before you and fulfil it gratefully. If given spaciousness of heart, use it to increase compassion. If given perseverance, use it to preserve benefit. This wisdom helps us complement one another amid different abilities. We need not receive the same form of gift to work together, because devotion remains directed to Allah, who pours help upon all His servants according to His wisdom.

Try making a brief division of tasks with reasonably clear times. Ask each person's ability and arrange how to request a replacement when tired. Express appropriate thanks, including to elderly relatives still wishing to show care. If neglect occurs, discuss the task without starting a contest over who is most pious. May the family cooperate more orderly, the person cared for feel safe, and every helper receive a chance to rest. We ask that service and prayer meet in compassion bringing benefit.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of sharing family care while appreciating prayer and physical effort again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about sharing family care while appreciating prayer and physical effort. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us protect the family from competition over contributions. May Allah grant healing, bless every assistance, and strengthen those serving. May those with limits still feel appreciated, those able be willing to share burdens, and those praying continue asking sincerely. May diverse roles bring closeness to Him and warmth among relatives. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: قَوْمٌ أَقَامَهُمُ الْحَقُّ لِخِدْمَتِهِ
Some people Allah establishes in His service.
وَقَوْمٌ اخْتَصَّهُمْ بِمَحَبَّتِهِ،
Others He singles out for His love.
كُلًّا نُمِدُّ هَؤُلَاءِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ مِنْ عَطَاءِ رَبِّكَ،
To each, these and those, We extend help from your Lord's bounty.
وَمَا كَانَ عَطَاءُ رَبِّكَ مَحْظُورًا.
Your Lord's bounty is not withheld.

79.translation: Spiritual gifts from Allah almost always arrive suddenly. In this way, they are protected from a servant's claim that they were obtained through personal readiness.
syarahEn: Some understanding comes unexpectedly. Advice once ordinary suddenly touches us, or an event opens an awareness long closed. This wisdom reminds us that spiritual gifts are not under human control. We can prepare ourselves, but have no right to demand when the gift should arrive.

Al-waridat al-ilahiyyah means spiritual gifts from Allah. Baghtah means suddenly. Siyanah refers to protection, while iddi'a' means a claim. A gift arriving unexpectedly protects the servant from claiming everything was obtained through personal readiness. The sentence emphasizes the way gifts commonly arrive as a surprise.

For example, someone has studied for a long time but only understands the importance of apologizing after seeing a loved one's sadness. They can appreciate that awareness without treating it as proof of having reached a particular rank. More important is responding to understanding with action, so the gift improves relationships and devotion.

Keep nurturing good means, such as learning and worship, without using them to demand an experience. Readiness is useful, but does not oblige Allah to give according to our timetable. This attitude accords with gratitude for help that cannot be entirely planned. If the heart opens one day, use it for clear goodness. If not yet, continue your responsibilities diligently. Humility protects the benefit of a gift by directing attention to the Giver of help and the responsibilities that follow.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, when good news arrives after consistent worship, we sometimes quickly conclude, “This must be because of my practice.” Gratitude can shift into feeling we possess a formula. We then offer it to others as though the same result is certain. Yet we do not know every path of Allah's giving or have power to determine anyone's form of gift.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that gifts can arrive suddenly so a servant does not feel they obtained them solely through preparation. Effort and worship continue, but the gift does not become wages we may demand according to our own calculations. This awareness protects joy from arrogance and keeps our relationship with Allah within humble servanthood.

Dear friends, suppose a family receives financial help from an unexpected source. We are grateful and thank the helper. However, do not assume those without help must worship less. Every family faces different circumstances and trials. Such a conclusion can deepen the hurt of relatives sincerely praying and trying while an urgent need remains unresolved.

“If a devotional practice makes me calmer, may I share it?” An experience may be conveyed honestly while observing guidance. Avoid guaranteeing worldly results without a basis. We can invite supplication and obedience without selling certainty that a problem will end on a particular date. Listeners deserve accurate explanations, especially when desperate and inclined to hang their hopes on a promise.

Dear congregation, when receiving goodness, ask about the responsibility accompanying it. Use assistance according to its trust, undertake a job opportunity honestly, and share ease according to your ability. Gratitude receives practical work to do. We are not merely busy recounting how a gift arrived, but ensuring it benefits others and does not create a habit of considering ourselves more loved than others.

Let us receive humbly and continue seeking guidance. May Allah bless every gift, protect worship from demanding calculations, and guard hopeful people against false promises. May unexpected goodness make us readier to thank and more sensitive to helping those whose needs remain unmet. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Once at ease, maintain obligations and attention to those still struggling. Do not turn good news into a rank that makes us feel closer than them. This wisdom guards the heart against claims, so a gift is received humbly and produces more earnest devotion.

People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. For practice, examine how you describe one good experience. Distinguish what happened from outcomes you cannot promise listeners. If inviting a practice, explain according to guidance and avoid baseless worldly certainties. Those hearing the story should still pursue needs through proper means and seek guidance if confused. May gifts increase gratitude rather than make us feel we possess a formula governing Allah's giving. We hope broadly while remaining honest about the limits of human knowledge and ability.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about receiving good news as a gift without selling a formula for results will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. What we want to nurture is a willingness to do our part properly and in an orderly way, even when the results still take time to appear.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of receiving good news as a gift without selling a formula for results that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Let us receive humbly and continue seeking guidance. May Allah bless every gift, protect worship from demanding calculations, and guard hopeful people against false promises. May unexpected goodness make us readier to thank and more sensitive to helping those whose needs remain unmet. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: قَلَّ مَا تَكُونُ الْوَارِدَاتُ الْإِلَهِيَّةُ إِلَّا بَغْتَةً،
Spiritual gifts from Allah almost always arrive suddenly.
صِيَانَةً لَهَا أَنْ يَدَّعِيَهَا الْعِبَادُ بِوُجُودِ الِاسْتِعْدَادِ.
This protects them from a servant's claim of obtaining them through personal readiness.

80.translation: If you see someone answering everything asked, expressing everything witnessed, and recounting everything known, take that behaviour as a sign of ignorance within them.
syarahEn: Wanting to appear knowledgeable can make someone answer every question, share every story, and reveal matters that should be protected. Yet breadth of knowledge also requires care about timing, need, and the consequences of speaking. This wisdom teaches that discernment appears in the ability to set limits on speech.

Mujiban means one who answers. Mu'abbiran means one who expresses, while dhakiran here means recounting what is known. The repeated word kull, every or all, is central to the warning. The issue is a habit without discernment: every question must be answered, every experience announced, and every piece of knowledge considered suitable to share with anyone.

A teacher can say they do not yet know and then check the answer. Someone entrusted with a personal story needs to protect it, however interesting it might be to share. Someone with an inner experience can also hold back if telling it would only increase pride or mislead the listener. Restraining speech in these circumstances is part of responsibility.

Before speaking, examine whether the information is true, needed, and appropriate for that listener. If other people's rights are involved, consider permission and consequences. Clarify the question before rushing to demonstrate your ability to answer. This wisdom does not invite withholding needed knowledge; it teaches the manners of conveying it. Knowledge becomes more beneficial with humility, so speech supports others' understanding and safety rather than simply enlarging the speaker's image.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, may Allah have mercy on us, questions can now arrive at any moment. A family group asks about religion, health, or a current report. Afraid of seeming uninformed, we answer immediately although our knowledge is insufficient. One confident-sounding answer can be forwarded widely, while its error travels far beyond the original conversation.

Ibn 'Ata'illah warns about someone answering every question and recounting everything known. Such behaviour can reveal a lack of discernment. Knowledge requires limits, consideration of circumstances, and willingness to admit what remains unclear. We do not need an opinion on everything. There is responsibility to restrain speech when explanation is insufficient or information unsuitable to share.

Dear congregation, if asked about something beyond your knowledge, say, “I do not know yet. Let us seek the right explanation.” That sentence can protect many people from error. If helping search, choose an authoritative source or someone competent in the field. Do not simply forward the answer best suited to our wishes, especially when the matter involves rights, health, or important decisions in another person's life.

“What if someone insists on an immediate answer?” We may explain our limits and point to a more appropriate place to ask. Pressure does not turn insufficient knowledge into enough. If an urgent situation needs help, assist in contacting those able to handle it. Our role remains useful even when we are not giving the main decision or explanation.

Dear friends, restraint is also needed with other people's private matters. Knowing something does not always give the right to announce it. Consider need, permission, and consequences. People feel safe close to us when they know their story will not automatically move elsewhere. Such discernment often matters more than the impression that we always know a great deal about everyone's lives.

Let us learn to guard speech through a simple acknowledgement. May Allah grant beneficial knowledge, courage to admit limits, and care in checking information. May we avoid embarrassing ourselves or harming others to appear clever. May every answer truly help, while what we do not understand receives a path to honest learning. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear congregation, before going further, try bringing that story closer to our own lives. We are learning about acknowledging the limits of knowledge when asked a question. Perhaps a similar event passed unnoticed because our day was too full. Now we have time to look back at it calmly. If our experience differs, take the part that fits. Children at school can picture life at home; adults can recall their responsibilities. We are not looking for whoever has made the most mistakes. We want to go home with a clearer view and one action we are able to take. So let us listen while occasionally asking our own hearts a question.
CORE WISDOM

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with acknowledging the limits of knowledge when asked a question. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, if asked about something beyond your knowledge, say, “I do not know yet. Let us seek the right explanation.” That sentence can protect many people from error. If helping search, choose an authoritative source or someone competent in the field. Do not simply forward the answer best suited to our wishes, especially when the matter involves rights, health, or important decisions in another person's life.

“What if someone insists on an immediate answer?” We may explain our limits and point to a more appropriate place to ask. Pressure does not turn insufficient knowledge into enough. If an urgent situation needs help, assist in contacting those able to handle it. Our role remains useful even when we are not giving the main decision or explanation.

A question appears in the family group and everyone waits. We once read a little about it and feel tempted to answer confidently. Dear friends, one mistaken sentence can travel far when forwarded. We can protect benefit by saying we do not yet know and pointing to a better place to ask. This admission may seem less impressive, but helps people decide from a proper explanation. If helping search, check the source and its expertise. Do not take the first answer simply because it fits an assumption. Questions involving others' lives need more care than our desire to appear universally informed.

“If I have plenty of experience, may I still share?” Experience can help, dear congregation, when distinguished from decisions requiring expertise. Explain its limits and do not apply it to every circumstance. This wisdom rebukes answering, expressing, and recounting everything without discernment. Some knowledge needs context, and private matters need protection. We do not have to prove intelligence through the number of answers. Sometimes the most useful role is clarifying a question or helping contact someone able to handle it. Benefit remains even when we are not the centre of explanation.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Do we need to be the person who answers every issue in the group?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

A teacher can say they do not yet know and then check the answer. Someone entrusted with a personal story needs to protect it, however interesting it might be to share. Someone with an inner experience can also hold back if telling it would only increase pride or mislead the listener. Restraining speech in these circumstances is part of responsibility.

Dear friends, restraint is also needed with other people's private matters. Knowing something does not always give the right to announce it. Consider need, permission, and consequences. People feel safe close to us when they know their story will not automatically move elsewhere. Such discernment often matters more than the impression that we always know a great deal about everyone's lives.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about acknowledging the limits of knowledge when asked a question may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Before speaking, examine whether the information is true, needed, and appropriate for that listener. If other people's rights are involved, consider permission and consequences. Clarify the question before rushing to demonstrate your ability to answer. This wisdom does not invite withholding needed knowledge; it teaches the manners of conveying it. Knowledge becomes more beneficial with humility, so speech supports others' understanding and safety rather than simply enlarging the speaker's image.

Try preparing one sentence for questions beyond your knowledge. Say it calmly and offer help within your ability. If you previously gave an incorrect answer, correct it in a way that can reach the earlier recipients. Do not defend a mistake for fear of losing authority. Parents admitting they do not yet know model honesty for children. May knowledge be conveyed faithfully, and may limits be accepted as reasons to continue learning and respect other people's fields of knowledge.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about acknowledging the limits of knowledge when asked a question. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of acknowledging the limits of knowledge when asked a question. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us learn to guard speech through a simple acknowledgement. May Allah grant beneficial knowledge, courage to admit limits, and care in checking information. May we avoid embarrassing ourselves or harming others to appear clever. May every answer truly help, while what we do not understand receives a path to honest learning. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَنْ رَأَيْتَهُ مُجِيبًا عَنْ كُلِّ مَا سُئِلَ،
If you see someone always answering everything asked,
وَمُعَبِّرًا عَنْ كُلِّ مَا شَهِدَ،
expressing everything witnessed,
وَذَاكِرًا كُلَّ مَا عَلِمَ،
and recounting everything known,
فَاسْتَدِلَّ بِذَلِكَ عَلَى وُجُودِ جَهْلِهِ.
take that behaviour as a sign of ignorance within them.

81.translation: He made the abode of the Hereafter the place of recompense for His believing servants because this worldly abode cannot contain what He wishes to bestow upon them. He also honoured their standing by not making a perishing abode the place of their complete reward.
syarahEn: We may feel confused when someone striving to obey still faces difficulties while wrongdoing seems to receive no immediate recompense. This wisdom reminds us that the world is not the place of life's final judgement. Complete recompense has a scope broader than the time and circumstances we see now.

Dar al-akhirah means the abode of the Hereafter. Jaza' refers to recompense, while la tasa' means unable to contain. The limited world does not encompass all Allah's giving and justice. La baqa'a laha, having no permanence, emphasizes the world's temporary nature. A servant's honour should not be measured only by something destined to end.

This lesson strengthens those doing good without immediately seeing results. A teacher may not yet witness the fruit of their teaching, and someone maintaining honesty may lose a particular profit. Goodness remains valuable even when its full reward is unseen. Hope in the Hereafter helps the heart persevere without forcing this world to fulfil every demand.

At the same time, belief in the Hereafter does not remove the obligation to seek justice now. Victims' rights remain protected and human wrongdoing still requires accountability. We do what is within our ability while entrusting what exceeds it to Allah. This wisdom broadens our assessment of life. Patience gains support, success is not excessively idolized, and devotion is not abandoned simply because the world has not shown results considered proportionate to the effort.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, some people work honestly throughout life yet remain of modest means. Some teachers educate many children without ever enjoying great ease. Seeing this, we may ask, “Where is the reward?” The question arises because we habitually judge success through what is visible now, especially measurable wealth, comfort, and human appreciation.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that the Hereafter is the place of reward for believers. The limited world cannot contain all the generosity Allah intends. Awareness of the Hereafter gives goodness a broader measure. We still seek rights and a decent life here while acknowledging that final judgement does not end with what has been received during life.

Dear friends, a teacher deserves appreciation and fair compensation according to their responsibilities. Hope in the Hereafter must not be used to withhold rights or tell people to accept harmful treatment. Those of us benefiting should instead help fulfil those rights. Faith in Allah's reward should strengthen justice rather than conceal human neglect towards those who have served.

“What if my rights are still being withheld?” Pursue them properly and safely. Seek needed support and information. During that process, guard your heart so unfair treatment does not erase belief in goodness's value. We may feel tired and disappointed. Allah knows work and circumstances that may never be recorded in human thanks.

Dear congregation, when seeing a good person living simply, do not immediately conclude they have failed. Ask what help is possible. There may be needs never voiced out of awkwardness. We can also preserve the benefit of their teaching by passing it on correctly. Respect takes form when we are present to help, rather than only praising someone after they are no longer with us.

Let us seek goodness in this world and the Hereafter with broad hope. May Allah bestow His generosity upon persevering servants, strengthen those pursuing their rights, and make us fairer towards people's contributions. May belief in the Hereafter help us persevere in goodness while becoming more responsible towards human life today. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, imagine taking this reminder home with us. We have taken off our shoes, the gathering is over, and ordinary life begins again. That is where the lesson about valuing goodness whose reward is not entirely visible now will be tested. We may still face the same situation, the same people, and old habits that have not yet changed. We need to understand the message well enough to bring it into those circumstances. Listen slowly. If a sentence speaks to our situation, keep it in mind for later. We do not have to remember every explanation. One sound understanding, put sincerely into practice, is already worth working towards today.

Dear congregation, a saying of wisdom may be very short, yet reflection reveals how deeply it touches our long-standing habits. We are seeing that here in the matter of valuing goodness whose reward is not entirely visible now. Its brevity should not make us feel that we have finished understanding it. Try expressing its meaning again in our own words. If it still seems unclear, return to the earlier example. We are not competing to memorize terminology. We want guidance we can use. In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, a teacher deserves appreciation and fair compensation according to their responsibilities. Hope in the Hereafter must not be used to withhold rights or tell people to accept harmful treatment. Those of us benefiting should instead help fulfil those rights. Faith in Allah's reward should strengthen justice rather than conceal human neglect towards those who have served.

During that process, guard your heart so unfair treatment does not erase belief in goodness's value. We may feel tired and disappointed. Allah knows work and circumstances that may never be recorded in human thanks.

A teacher returns to a modest life after years of educating. Many students already benefit from their knowledge. Dear friends, we can pray for Allah's reward while examining human obligations that remain. If rights are unfulfilled, do not close the conversation by saying the teacher should be sincere. Those benefiting should strive to show fair appreciation according to responsibility. Hope in the Hereafter broadens our view of goodness's value, but must not diminish rights here. These concerns support one another when faith encourages greater trustworthiness towards those who have served.

“If I keep being treated unjustly, is waiting for the Hereafter enough?” We may pursue our rights properly and safely, dear congregation. Seek suitable information and support. Faith in Allah's reward helps the heart avoid concluding all goodness is useless because people fail to appreciate it. We may feel tired and disappointed. The world is limited and cannot contain all His giving and justice. This understanding preserves hope without asking victims of injustice to stop trying. Supporters need to assist practical steps rather than simply request more patience while leaving their own duties delayed.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “How can hope in the Hereafter accompany the obligation to fulfil rights fairly?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

This lesson strengthens those doing good without immediately seeing results. A teacher may not yet witness the fruit of their teaching, and someone maintaining honesty may lose a particular profit. Goodness remains valuable even when its full reward is unseen. Hope in the Hereafter helps the heart persevere without forcing this world to fulfil every demand.

We can also preserve the benefit of their teaching by passing it on correctly. Respect takes form when we are present to help, rather than only praising someone after they are no longer with us.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of valuing goodness whose reward is not entirely visible now, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

At the same time, belief in the Hereafter does not remove the obligation to seek justice now. Victims' rights remain protected and human wrongdoing still requires accountability. We do what is within our ability while entrusting what exceeds it to Allah. This wisdom broadens our assessment of life. Patience gains support, success is not excessively idolized, and devotion is not abandoned simply because the world has not shown results considered proportionate to the effort.

Choose one person whose contribution has benefited your life. Examine the appreciation or rights genuinely within your responsibility. Fulfil them according to ability and proper requirements. If pursuing your own rights, prepare clear questions and seek appropriate help. In supplication, ask for steadfastness so bitter experiences do not damage honesty. May belief in the Hereafter make us fairer today, and may devotion's value be measured beyond the amount of wealth or praise received.

Now let us turn the lesson about valuing goodness whose reward is not entirely visible now into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about valuing goodness whose reward is not entirely visible now, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us seek goodness in this world and the Hereafter with broad hope. May Allah bestow His generosity upon persevering servants, strengthen those pursuing their rights, and make us fairer towards people's contributions. May belief in the Hereafter help us persevere in goodness while becoming more responsible towards human life today. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: إِنَّمَا جَعَلَ الدَّارَ الْآخِرَةَ مَحَلًّا لِجَزَاءِ عِبَادِهِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ،
He made the Hereafter the place of recompense for His believing servants,
لِأَنَّ هَذِهِ الدَّارَ لَا تَسَعُ مَا يُرِيدُ أَنْ يُعْطِيَهُمْ،
because the worldly abode cannot contain what He wishes to bestow upon them.
وَلِأَنَّهُ أَجَلَّ أَقْدَارَهُمْ عَنْ أَنْ يُجَازِيَهُمْ فِي دَارٍ لَا بَقَاءَ لَهَا.
He also honoured their standing by not making a perishing abode the place of their complete reward.

82.translation: Whoever tastes the fruit of their deeds in this world has in that an indication of their acceptance in the Hereafter.
syarahEn: Deeds can begin showing their fruits in this life. Someone learning to maintain salah becomes more orderly, someone practising honesty gains peace, and someone giving charity learns to reduce greed. This wisdom offers hope that devotion has an influence we can feel before the reward of the Hereafter arrives.

Thamarah means fruit: the result growing from a deed. 'Ajilan refers to what is immediate or in this world, while ajilan refers to what is later or in the Hereafter. Al-qabul means acceptance. This distinction in time connects present good effects with hope of later acceptance. Dalil means an indication, rather than permission to declare one's salvation certain.

The fruit of deeds needs to be understood through a good direction, such as increased submission and improved character. Smooth business or abundant praise alone is insufficient as a measure. Someone may feel comfortable because they receive recognition although their honesty has not improved. Conversely, a deed performed with a heavy heart can still train patience and faithfulness.

Notice small changes emerging after maintaining a good habit. Are we readier to apologize, more consistent in keeping promises, or more sensitive to others' needs? Appreciate those fruits and continue asking for acceptance. If none is felt yet, examine your practice and intention without immediately despairing. This wisdom nurtures humble hope. We care for emerging signs of goodness while still acknowledging that the final decision about acceptance rests in Allah's knowledge and generosity.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, after worship we often wonder whether our deeds are accepted. We certainly hope well of Allah. Yet something can also be observed daily: is worship beginning to help us treat people better? For example, while fasting we try to guard against hurtful words even when hungry and work feels difficult.

Ibn 'Ata'illah calls the felt fruit of deeds good news about acceptance. That fruit is understood as growing goodness within us, rather than simply money arriving or pleasant events. We still do not determine Allah's final judgement. We can appreciate signs of improvement and keep asking that worship be helped towards sincerity and better character.

Dear congregation, if we once readily answered shouting with shouting but can now pause, that deserves gratitude. Perhaps we do not always succeed yet. We can still learn what helps and what triggers us. Worship gives room for practice, while daily relationships reveal practical choices. Those closest to us do more than hear worship stories: they feel changes in our responses.

“What if I still often become angry after worship?” Do not immediately stop or decide all deeds are useless. Evaluate intention, understanding, and accompanying habits. Also consider rest and life's burdens. If anger is difficult to control and harms people, seek suitable help. We improve worship while taking responsibility for behaviour needing earnest attention.

Dear friends, do not use the fruit of deeds to judge others hastily. We do not know their entire struggle. Direct examination towards yourself and ask those affected for input. “Has the way I speak been better lately?” can reveal information we have overlooked. Listen humbly, because change needs evaluation through actual experience.

Let us ask for worship whose benefit reaches our relationships. May Allah accept our fasting and deeds, nurture patience our families can feel, and protect us from arrogance over believing we have changed. May every small improvement bring gratitude and greater perseverance in goodness while we keep correcting what we have not yet managed. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
talkEn: OPENING
Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, after worship we often wonder whether our deeds are accepted. We certainly hope well of Allah. Yet something can also be observed daily: is worship beginning to help us treat people better? For example, while fasting we try to guard against hurtful words even when hungry and work feels difficult.

Dear congregation, let us settle into a comfortable atmosphere for learning. Talking about bringing the practice of fasting into our speech calls for honesty, but that honesty can remain quietly within the heart. We are under no obligation to share private affairs before everyone. Simply listen, consider, and identify what can be improved. Sometimes we already know the advice, but have not made time to think about it. This gathering gives us that opportunity. We can revisit a sound understanding until it becomes clearer. Afterwards, when we face everyday situations, may we have words that help us choose our actions more calmly and responsibly.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah calls the felt fruit of deeds good news about acceptance. That fruit is understood as growing goodness within us, rather than simply money arriving or pleasant events. We still do not determine Allah's final judgement. We can appreciate signs of improvement and keep asking that worship be helped towards sincerity and better character.

Deeds can begin showing their fruits in this life. Someone learning to maintain salah becomes more orderly, someone practising honesty gains peace, and someone giving charity learns to reduce greed. This wisdom offers hope that devotion has an influence we can feel before the reward of the Hereafter arrives.

Thamarah means fruit: the result growing from a deed. 'Ajilan refers to what is immediate or in this world, while ajilan refers to what is later or in the Hereafter. Al-qabul means acceptance. This distinction in time connects present good effects with hope of later acceptance. Dalil means an indication, rather than permission to declare one's salvation certain.

Let us hold this understanding carefully, dear friends. Advice about bringing the practice of fasting into our speech should be read alongside our obligations as servants of Allah and our responsibilities towards others. Feeling peaceful after hearing a talk is certainly pleasant. Yet sound understanding also helps us act when things no longer feel peaceful. That is why explaining the words matters. We gain something to guide our direction, rather than a beautiful impression that soon fades. If we later forget how the term sounds, remember the relationship it explains: how the heart turns to Allah and how our choices touch real life.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, if we once readily answered shouting with shouting but can now pause, that deserves gratitude. Perhaps we do not always succeed yet. We can still learn what helps and what triggers us. Worship gives room for practice, while daily relationships reveal practical choices. Those closest to us do more than hear worship stories: they feel changes in our responses.

“What if I still often become angry after worship?” Do not immediately stop or decide all deeds are useless. Evaluate intention, understanding, and accompanying habits. Also consider rest and life's burdens. If anger is difficult to control and harms people, seek suitable help. We improve worship while taking responsibility for behaviour needing earnest attention.

As iftar approaches, work is unfinished and someone speaks somewhat harshly to us. A reply is almost out, but we pause. Dear friends, one successfully maintained pause deserves gratitude. Tomorrow may still be difficult, so we learn to recognize triggers and needed support. Those at home need more than stories that we are fasting. They benefit when our tone is better guarded. We also need to examine burdens and rest so worship does not become an excuse for anger. Hunger can feel hard, but other people's right to respect remains in everyday encounters.

“If I still make mistakes after worship, does that mean it is not accepted?” We do not possess certainty about acceptance, dear congregation. Keep hoping in Allah and correct what you know. The fruit of deeds can be an indication strengthening hope rather than a certificate announcing rank. Conversely, continuing mistakes must not become a reason to abandon worship. We need to evaluate understanding, intention, and accompanying habits. If anger harms people and is difficult to manage, seek proper help. Earnestness appears in continuing to learn sound worship and taking responsibility for our behaviour's consequences.

Let me ask a question, dear congregation: “What small change can our family feel from our earnest care for worship?” Take a moment to think about it. Perhaps an answer comes straight away; perhaps a difficulty comes to mind instead. Let us hear that difficulty calmly. Good advice needs to meet the reality of life, including the limitations we face. Now imagine someone we love asking that question. Would our answer help them act, or simply leave them feeling scolded? Here we learn to convey the truth in a way that can be received. We also need honesty that gives direction when speaking to ourselves, so that understanding a problem gives us courage to begin putting it right.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

The fruit of deeds needs to be understood through a good direction, such as increased submission and improved character. Smooth business or abundant praise alone is insufficient as a measure. Someone may feel comfortable because they receive recognition although their honesty has not improved. Conversely, a deed performed with a heavy heart can still train patience and faithfulness.

Dear friends, do not use the fruit of deeds to judge others hastily. We do not know their entire struggle. Direct examination towards yourself and ask those affected for input. “Has the way I speak been better lately?” can reveal information we have overlooked. Listen humbly, because change needs evaluation through actual experience.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about bringing the practice of fasting into our speech may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Notice small changes emerging after maintaining a good habit. Are we readier to apologize, more consistent in keeping promises, or more sensitive to others' needs? Appreciate those fruits and continue asking for acceptance. If none is felt yet, examine your practice and intention without immediately despairing. This wisdom nurtures humble hope. We care for emerging signs of goodness while still acknowledging that the final decision about acceptance rests in Allah's knowledge and generosity.

For practice, choose a situation that usually provokes a harsh reply. Prepare a pause and better words before it arises. If you slip, acknowledge and repair without blaming fasting. After successfully restraining yourself, be grateful without feeling superior. Family members can support one another through task sharing and polite reminders. May worship bear fruit others can feel, and may hope for Allah's acceptance nurture willingness to improve actions patiently day by day.

Dear congregation, if we want to take one task home from this discussion of bringing the practice of fasting into our speech, choose something we can truly do. There is no need to announce it now. We can decide after getting home, when we have a fuller picture of our circumstances. Make the step small enough for us to know when it will be done. If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of bringing the practice of fasting into our speech that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Let us ask for worship whose benefit reaches our relationships. May Allah accept our fasting and deeds, nurture patience our families can feel, and protect us from arrogance over believing we have changed. May every small improvement bring gratitude and greater perseverance in goodness while we keep correcting what we have not yet managed. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَنْ وَجَدَ ثَمَرَةَ عَمَلِهِ عَاجِلًا
Whoever tastes the fruit of their deeds in this world
فَهُوَ دَلِيلٌ عَلَى وُجُودِ الْقَبُولِ آجِلًا.
has in that an indication of acceptance in the Hereafter.

83.translation: If you wish to know your standing with Him, look at the state in which He has placed you.
syarahEn: We may want to know our standing with Allah through praise, special feelings, or particular experiences. Ibn 'Ata'illah directs attention to something nearer for examination: what fills this life? Our circumstances and duties can help us evaluate the direction of our devotion.

Qadraka 'indahu means your standing with Him. Yuqimuka means He places you, while fima directs the question towards the state or work in which that placement occurs. We are invited to see whether time and ability are used for obedience or continually spent in heedlessness. This assessment mainly concerns the direction of deeds rather than financial status or high office.

Someone caring for parents may be little known, yet their days are filled with valuable service. Someone leading a large activity needs to examine whether authority serves a trust or self-interest. The roles differ, but the basic question is the same: do available opportunities lead towards proper devotion?

Do not use this wisdom to rank people's honour by jobs or outward circumstances. We do not know all their responsibilities and struggles. Use it to review your own schedule. If you find heedlessness, begin changing through one upheld obligation and one reduced bad habit. If given an opportunity to obey, be grateful without feeling certainly superior. In this way, wishing to know our standing becomes earnest care for our trusts, directing attention towards work we can take responsibility for.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, sometimes we are curious about our standing with Allah. We seek extraordinary signs while neglecting clear duties. A neighbour needs help, an entrusted item remains unreturned, and preparations for a promised meeting are unfinished. The heart is busy seeking confirmation of specialness while overlooking opportunities for devotion already present in daily life.

Ibn 'Ata'illah invites those wishing to know their standing to look at where they have been placed. We apply this message to the direction of our activities and trusts. What are we doing? Is much of our time spent moving closer to obedience or further away? This wisdom gives no permission to announce our spiritual rank or judge human worth by social position.

Dear friends, a small neighbourhood administrative role can feel troublesome. Information needs passing on, residents need listening to, and activities need organizing. If fulfilled honestly, the role provides an opportunity for good. We need not wait for a high position for service to matter. Perhaps only one family benefits, but its need remains real and worthy of attention.

“What if I am in work that is wrong?” We need to evaluate and find ways to improve. Present circumstances do not justify continued violations. Learn boundaries, seek advice, and prepare responsible steps. Awareness of our place in life helps identify the next duty, including leaving harmful habits or improving how we fulfil a trust.

Dear congregation, look at the past day. Where did most attention go? Who benefited, and whose rights remain delayed? Simple answers can be more useful than guessing special signs about ourselves. We have clear material for repentance, gratitude, and improvement without knowing every secret of Allah's judgement of our lives.

Let us fulfil duties already before us. May Allah place us in obedience, grant responsibilities we can carry, and protect us from seeking spiritual recognition. May our activities bring increasing benefit, so questions about standing lead to honest service and humility to continue improving. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, simple service has practical consequences. We can maintain clarity and keep promises to provide updates. If unsure, do not invent certainty; ask the authorized person. This task may not make a name famous. Yet someone benefits because their need is considered. We learn to recognize opportunities for devotion through the use of time and ability, rather than continually seeking extraordinary experiences to confirm a special rank.

“What if my current task includes something wrong?” Circumstances do not automatically justify it, dear congregation. Examine necessary boundaries and seek suitable advice about improvement. Sometimes the trust is to refuse a violation or responsibly leave a harmful habit. This wisdom invites us to see placement through the direction of deeds rather than the size of a position. Someone in a small role can fulfil it honestly, while high office still needs examination. We cannot conclude someone's entire standing from occupation or income. We can begin by improving our actions.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “What trust is already visible before us while we search for signs of specialness?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of recognizing opportunities to serve in neighbourhood responsibilities, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Try recording one pending neighbourhood task. Determine completion steps and information needing confirmation. If ability is limited, say so early and help find an appropriate division. Do not take every task to appear important, then leave many promises neglected. Those receiving service should explain needs clearly and respect helpers. May our attention more readily find practical places of devotion, and may wanting to know our distinction not consume opportunities for goodness already available.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of recognizing opportunities to serve in neighbourhood responsibilities again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about recognizing opportunities to serve in neighbourhood responsibilities invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us fulfil duties already before us. May Allah place us in obedience, grant responsibilities we can carry, and protect us from seeking spiritual recognition. May our activities bring increasing benefit, so questions about standing lead to honest service and humility to continue improving. Amin.
