phrasesEn: إِذَا أَرَدْتَ أَنْ تَعْرِفَ قَدَرَكَ عِنْدَهُ
If you wish to know your standing with Him,
فَانْظُرْ فِيمَا ذَا يُقِيمُكَ فِيهِ.
look at the state in which He places you.

84.translation: When He grants you obedience and contentment in Him that frees you from dependence on that obedience, know that He has poured His blessings upon you outwardly and inwardly.
syarahEn: Being able to obey is a great blessing. Yet the heart may still depend on deeds wrongly, such as feeling certainly better or demanding a particular reward. This wisdom explains a fuller blessing: the ability to act accompanied by contentment in Allah, so devotion does not become a source of arrogance.

Al-ta'ah means obedience. Al-ghina bihi 'anha refers to contentment in Allah so the heart does not make deeds its absolute support. Asbagha means to pour forth or complete a gift. Zahirah wa batinah means outwardly and inwardly. The outward blessing appears in right action, while the inward blessing appears in the accompanying direction of the heart's trust.

A teacher can prepare lessons earnestly and appreciate the opportunity to help. Afterwards, they do not feel students owe unlimited respect. Someone giving charity still protects the quality of assistance without turning it into a tool to demand loyalty. Deeds are performed well while the heart acknowledges that every ability begins with Allah's help.

If a sense of deserving special credit appears, return attention to blessings preceding the work. We received life, knowledge, and resources we did not entirely build ourselves. This awareness helps us ask for acceptance humbly. This wisdom invites fuller devotion: outward action follows guidance and the inner self is not bound to pride. From there, we can more readily continue doing good without praise and remain more open to correction when work still has shortcomings.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, may Allah honour us, some days life feels ordinary. Income covers needs, activities are quiet, and people are not talking about us. Then we see others' lives and feel lacking. Yet that day we could still pray, finish work honestly, and return to family without carrying the burden of a new lie.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that joy in obedience and contentment in Allah are outward and inward blessings. We appreciate the opportunity to serve rather than constantly needing something more visible to acknowledge life's worth. This contentment does not mean considering ourselves perfect. We keep learning and correcting shortcomings while valuing the good made possible now.

Dear congregation, suppose a worker's income is still small but they fulfil their trust. They may wish to develop and improve family circumstances. However, do not let that wish erase gratitude for the ability to live honestly. Peace from not having to conceal deception has value, even though it does not look like a new possession to show neighbours or colleagues.

“If my needs remain unmet, must I be satisfied?” Real needs still require effort. Seek lawful means, ask for help if needed, and discuss responsibilities clearly. Contentment in servanthood does not command neglect of food, housing, or education. It guards the heart so the struggle to meet needs does not make every boundary seem permissible to cross.

Dear friends, we can practise gratitude by naming one act of obedience made easier today. Then consider what needs care for it to continue, perhaps a more orderly schedule or supportive friend. We need not wait for a problem-free life to appreciate the ability to do right. Some blessings remain present amid unfinished matters.

Let us seek outward sufficiency and inward spaciousness. May Allah provide enough for our families, bless lawful efforts, and help us rejoice in opportunities to obey. May gratitude not extinguish the wish to develop, and may ambition not make us belittle the simple goodness entrusted to our care today. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about being grateful for the opportunity to obey in a simple life, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us seek outward sufficiency and inward spaciousness. May Allah provide enough for our families, bless lawful efforts, and help us rejoice in opportunities to obey. May gratitude not extinguish the wish to develop, and may ambition not make us belittle the simple goodness entrusted to our care today. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَتَى رَزَقَكَ الطَّاعَةَ وَالْغِنَى بِهِ عَنْهَا،
When He grants obedience and contentment in Him freeing you from dependence on those deeds,
فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ قَدْ أَسْبَغَ عَلَيْكَ نِعَمَهُ ظَاهِرَةً وَبَاطِنَةً.
know that He has poured His blessings upon you outwardly and inwardly.

85.translation: The best thing you can ask of Him is help to fulfil what He asks of you.
syarahEn: Our supplications often contain lists of things we want. We ask for ease, success, and solutions to problems. All those needs may be brought to Allah. This wisdom reminds us of one vital request: help to fulfil our obligations and trusts, so our relationship with Allah contains more than a wish to receive.

Khayr ma tatlubuhu means the best thing to ask. Ma huwa talibuhu minka refers to what He asks of you. This arrangement of asking and being asked directs supplication towards devotion. We seek the ability to answer commands through honesty, patience, and fulfilling others' rights. Such help is needed because knowing an obligation does not always mean being able to fulfil it consistently.

Someone asking for provision can also ask for the ability to work lawfully without harming others. Someone wanting a peaceful family can ask for the ability to restrain words and listen. Supplication then does more than await external change. It also opens willingness to perform the part of responsibility we must undertake.

Try adding one request connected to your nearest trust. Ask for steadfastness in salah, courage to acknowledge mistakes, or spaciousness in serving family. After praying, determine a practical step supporting it. This wisdom improves the direction of desire, so we do more than ask what will be given: we become readier to fulfil what is commanded. Life gains direction when request and action meet in an effort to become more responsible servants.

Dear congregation, we usually make many prayers for children. We ask for health, intelligence, and a good future. All those hopes may be brought to Allah. But let us not forget one request: “O Allah, help me fulfil my responsibility as a parent.” Children need more than the outcomes we pray for; they need support we work at every day.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that the best request is help to fulfil what Allah asks of us. Supplication contains more than a list of changes we want in others. We ask for the ability to do our part. Hopes for a child need willingness to listen, educate, and model the advice we frequently give at home.

Dear friends, suppose we want a child to avoid screen addiction, but our eyes stay on the phone whenever they speak. There is an inconsistency to correct. We can begin setting aside screen-free time to talk. It need not be long; what matters is real attention. Ask about their story, let them finish, and respond without rushing to turn everything into advice.

“What if I return home exhausted?” Discuss the circumstances and choose a possible time. Presence does not always mean a big activity. It may be sharing a meal or listening for a few minutes before resting. If needed, share duties with family members. We seek an approach we can maintain rather than making lengthy promises often cancelled until the child stops hoping to be heard.

Dear congregation, this prayer also helps reduce the habit of blaming children for every relationship difficulty. Some adult behaviour can change. If you have hurt them, acknowledge it honestly. If unsure how to support them, learn. Parenthood does not mean always knowing the answer, but requires willingness to bear responsibility for continually improving our presence.

Let us add one request to family supplication: the ability to fulfil our own trust. May Allah make room in our time, soften our words, and protect our children. May hope for their future accompany practical attention today. May home be where they learn that love can be heard, seen, and felt. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

A child begins speaking, but our eyes still follow messages on the screen. They stop and leave because the timing seems wrong. Dear friends, perhaps we sincerely want to be good parents but habits have not followed. Supplication can address this: ask for the ability to listen and keep promises of time. We can put the device down and invite the child to continue if willing. Do not demand that the interrupted story be repeated immediately. Presence is built through repeated experience that adults are willing to pay attention. A child needs support they can feel alongside the great hopes we raise for their future.

We may still ask for children's health and success while seeking patience and care in our role. This prayer invites examination of our actions without making parents feel they must handle everything without help.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Do our prayers for our children's good accompany attention we actually give?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.

In the matter of asking for the ability to be a present parent, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

For practice, choose a reasonably manageable screen-free time. Ask for a child's story and let them finish before advising. If unable to listen long, state the limit and a clear time to continue. Afterwards, check whether the promise was kept. Those without children can also learn from supporting family members. May our requests produce willingness to learn, and may children feel parental supplications through warm attention, safe boundaries, and responsibilities continually pursued.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about asking for the ability to be a present parent. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about asking for the ability to be a present parent. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us add one request to family supplication: the ability to fulfil our own trust. May Allah make room in our time, soften our words, and protect our children. May hope for their future accompany practical attention today. May home be where they learn that love can be heard, seen, and felt. Amin.

phrasesEn: خَيْرُ مَا تَطْلُبُهُ مِنْهُ
The best thing you ask of Him
مَا هُوَ طَالِبُهُ مِنْكَ.
is help to fulfil what He asks of you.

86.translation: Sorrow over missed obedience without rising to perform it is a sign of self-deception.
syarahEn: We may feel sad about inconsistent worship, then stop at sadness. We talk about wanting change but arrange no possible step. This wisdom reminds us that good feelings need to continue into action. Regret left unanswered can become consolation for a habit of postponement.

Al-huzn means sadness. Fuqdan al-ta'ah refers to losing or missing obedience. Al-nuhud means rising and moving, while al-ightirar means self-deception. Someone may be deceived into considering sadness sufficient proof of earnestness. Yet the heart still needs to respond through effort suited to actual ability and circumstances.

For example, someone regrets rarely reading the Qur'an. Rather than continually setting large targets, they can arrange a short regular time and begin according to ability. Someone regretting family relationships can send an update or apologize. A small action performed gives feeling a direction, so regret does not keep circling as the same story.

Some obstacles genuinely need help to untangle, such as heavy life burdens or learning difficulties. Acknowledge them and seek a more possible approach without comparing your whole ability with others. What matters is willingness to move within your capacity. This wisdom does not demand instant change; it invites honesty about our response. After feeling the loss of goodness, determine one action possible today and ensure that step receives a place in life.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, we often repeat, “I regret rarely reading the Qur'an.” We say it sincerely, perhaps in tears. Afterwards, however, the Qur'an remains difficult to reach and the schedule unchanged. Feelings have moved, but action has not followed. Regret becomes a repeated story without clear work to do in daily life.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that sorrow over missed obedience without movement towards obedience can signal self-deception. We feel we have shown earnestness simply by being sad. Yet good feelings need a response. This does not mean everyone must immediately manage a great deal, but there are steps suited to ability, circumstances, and actual difficulties.

Dear congregation, if time is the obstacle, choose a short regular opportunity. If reading is not fluent, find a teacher and begin with a suitable passage. If small print is difficult to see, use helpful resources. We need not imitate someone else's amount of reading. The aim is a practical step, so good intention does not continually wait for ideal circumstances that may never arrive by themselves.

“What if I begin and stop again?” Examine the cause without immediately deciding you lack willpower. Perhaps the target was too large or timing unsuitable. Return with a more manageable measure. However, do not make evaluation another form of postponement. Once you identify something to change, adjust it and try again at a clearly chosen time.

Dear friends, family can help with a supportive atmosphere. Do not mock a beginner for previously reading infrequently. Offer to learn together if they wish. We want awareness to grow into habit, so support is more useful than repeating their mistakes as conversation material. Everyone needs room to begin without continually being overshadowed by shame about the past.

Let us choose one time to read or learn before today ends. May Allah accept our regret, ease our steps, and help us return whenever practice is interrupted. May sorrow over missed goodness become energy to move, so tomorrow brings a small action truly different from the habit we have long complained about. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, one change in arrangements may help. Keep it somewhere appropriate and accessible, and choose a short suitable opportunity. If reading remains difficult, the main need may be guidance. If print is hard to read, seek suitable resources. We are not measuring earnestness through the amount of regret described. We seek a way for feelings already stirred to receive action. The step may be simple and still needs care to continue.

“I once started and stopped; does that mean I lack willpower?” Examine the specific cause, dear congregation. Perhaps the target was too large or the timing unsuitable. Evaluation helps when followed by an adjustment promptly tried. Do not let planning become another reason to postpone. This wisdom warns about sadness unaccompanied by rising. Regret may be present, but does not automatically replace effort. Nor do we compare our entire ability with someone long fluent. Guidance and practice are adapted, so good intention gains a place in the life actually lived.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “What obstacle needs addressing so the intention to read does not remain only words?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

The lesson about moving regret into a practical step towards reading may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. Choose one time and passage suited to your ability. If a teacher is needed, seek information and make clear contact. Try following through before adding another target. If missed, return at the next opportunity and examine the obstacle without self-insult. Family can offer a calm atmosphere rather than embarrassing demands. May regret become courage to learn and may limited opportunity be used earnestly. We ask Allah to help improvement that no longer remains only a statement of wanting change.

Now let us turn the lesson about moving regret into a practical step towards reading into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.

If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. phrasesEn: الْحُزْنُ عَلَى فُقْدَانِ الطَّاعَةِ مَعَ عَدَمِ النُّهُوضِ إِلَيْهَا
Sorrow over missed obedience without rising to perform it
مِنْ عَلَامَاتِ الِاغْتِرَارِ.
is a sign of self-deception.

87.translation: The knower of Allah is not merely someone who, when pointing towards Him, senses Him nearer than the gesture itself. The knower is one who no longer attends to their own gesture, because attention to self has vanished, immersed in witnessing Allah.
syarahEn: Someone may speak eloquently about closeness to Allah while remaining deeply concerned with their own impression. They want their words considered profound and their experiences special. This wisdom reminds us that mature knowledge instead reduces self-absorption, directing attention more fully towards devotion.

Al-'arif is someone who knows Allah through living knowledge of the heart. Isharah means a sign or expression pointing towards Him. Fana' here describes the disappearance of self-aggrandizing attention when recognizing Allah's power. Shuhud means the heart's witnessing. These terms do not remove created existence or responsibility and do not mean union between servant and Lord.

A familiar example is someone finishing advice and thinking more about its benefit than whether they seem wise. If corrected, they are willing to improve. If another offers something better, they are grateful too. Such a direction of attention serves devotion better than displaying language supposedly demonstrating spiritual depth.

We need not claim to have experienced fana' or judge others' experiences. Care for clear work: honesty, humility, and keeping trusts. If spiritual discussion makes you feel increasingly superior, examine its purpose again. This wisdom invites knowing Allah with fruits others can feel. The more we acknowledge His gifts, the less we need to be the centre of attention, giving knowledge and worship room for quieter sincerity.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, sometimes we want to be considered spiritually deep. When speaking, we choose difficult terms and enjoy people's impressed expressions. Yet they may need a simple explanation to know what to do. Wanting to seem special can slip in even when the conversation concerns Allah, worship, and purity of heart.

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes a knower whose knowledge reduces attention to their own gestures. Fana' here refers to self-aggrandizing attention disappearing as the heart turns towards Allah. We do not understand it as union between God and human beings. The accessible lesson is to let knowing Allah nurture humility rather than increase the need to seem most knowledgeable about mysteries.

Dear friends, when asked to advise someone in difficulty, ask what they need. If they need a way to apologize, help prepare clear steps. There is no need to make them feel foolish for not understanding a term. Good explanation leads someone towards good according to ability. We may study deeply, but delivery still needs consideration of the listener and the conversation's purpose.

“What if I enjoy discussing spiritual matters?” Learn with knowledgeable teachers who observe guidance. At the same time, examine the fruit in character. Is correction easier to accept? Are people with different understanding still respected? If discussion makes us feel immune to advice, intention needs examination before adding more claims about our depth.

Dear congregation, we need not announce reaching a particular inner state. Fulfil clear trusts, guard speech, and seek guidance. If an experience is unclear, ask the right person without rushing to conclusions. Humility helps us remain learners, so knowledge does not become a wall blocking improvement through others' advice.

Let us ask for knowledge that makes the heart more submissive. May Allah guard learning against the desire for adulation, grant understandable language, and help us benefit listeners. May greater learning bring greater awareness of His generosity and less need to make ourselves the centre of attention in conversations about goodness. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Dear friends, we may appreciate the beautiful words in a saying of wisdom. Still, let us make time to understand what they mean. In discussing explaining advice in language that helps the listener, a word's meaning needs to be considered alongside the circumstances being addressed. Do not take one fragment of a sentence and use it to justify all our own wishes. Listen to it in full. Then test our understanding through a simple example. Does this explanation make our responsibilities clearer? Are other people's rights still protected? Questions like these help us read advice with a humble heart and a mind willing to learn.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, when asked to advise someone in difficulty, ask what they need. If they need a way to apologize, help prepare clear steps. There is no need to make them feel foolish for not understanding a term. Good explanation leads someone towards good according to ability. We may study deeply, but delivery still needs consideration of the listener and the conversation's purpose.

“What if I enjoy discussing spiritual matters?” Learn with knowledgeable teachers who observe guidance. At the same time, examine the fruit in character. Is correction easier to accept? Are people with different understanding still respected? If discussion makes us feel immune to advice, intention needs examination before adding more claims about our depth.

Someone asks how to apologize. We answer with many difficult terms until they simply nod without knowing where to begin. Dear friends, the explanation can return to their need. Ask what action needs repair and about the person affected. Help prepare words and safe considerations within your knowledge. For anything beyond your ability, direct them to the right person. Advice does not lose depth through simple delivery. Clarity can show willingness to attend to the listener rather than merely enjoy the impression that we possess inaccessible spiritual knowledge.

“What if I am studying profound terms?” Learning remains good, dear congregation. Follow knowledgeable guidance and maintain sound teaching. When explaining to others, consider their needs and understanding. Do not use terminology to avoid correction of wrongdoing. Fana' in this wisdom describes self-aggrandizing attention disappearing, rather than human union with Allah or the removal of responsibility. Proper understanding should help character become more orderly. If discussion instead makes us feel immune to advice, our intention deserves honest examination.

Let me ask a question, dear congregation: “Do the terms we use clarify the next step or merely make us appear impressive?” Take a moment to think about it. Perhaps an answer comes straight away; perhaps a difficulty comes to mind instead. Let us hear that difficulty calmly. Good advice needs to meet the reality of life, including the limitations we face. Now imagine someone we love asking that question. Would our answer help them act, or simply leave them feeling scolded? Here we learn to convey the truth in a way that can be received. We also need honesty that gives direction when speaking to ourselves, so that understanding a problem gives us courage to begin putting it right.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

A familiar example is someone finishing advice and thinking more about its benefit than whether they seem wise. If corrected, they are willing to improve. If another offers something better, they are grateful too. Such a direction of attention serves devotion better than displaying language supposedly demonstrating spiritual depth.

Dear congregation, we need not announce reaching a particular inner state. Fulfil clear trusts, guard speech, and seek guidance. If an experience is unclear, ask the right person without rushing to conclusions. Humility helps us remain learners, so knowledge does not become a wall blocking improvement through others' advice.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of explaining advice in language that helps the listener, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

We need not claim to have experienced fana' or judge others' experiences. Care for clear work: honesty, humility, and keeping trusts. If spiritual discussion makes you feel increasingly superior, examine its purpose again. This wisdom invites knowing Allah with fruits others can feel. The more we acknowledge His gifts, the less we need to be the centre of attention, giving knowledge and worship room for quieter sincerity.

For practice, take an explanation you often give and try expressing it in language understandable across ages. Ask whether the listener knows the next step. If not, improve the explanation without blaming them as insufficiently deep. We may admit we are still learning and seek correction from a teacher. May knowledge nurture felt benefit, and may words about humility also appear in willingness to explain patiently and respect those unfamiliar with the same terms.

Dear congregation, if we want to take one task home from this discussion of explaining advice in language that helps the listener, choose something we can truly do. There is no need to announce it now. We can decide after getting home, when we have a fuller picture of our circumstances. Make the step small enough for us to know when it will be done. If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of explaining advice in language that helps the listener. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us ask for knowledge that makes the heart more submissive. May Allah guard learning against the desire for adulation, grant understandable language, and help us benefit listeners. May greater learning bring greater awareness of His generosity and less need to make ourselves the centre of attention in conversations about goodness. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
wordsEn: and attention to self is folded away; immersed
phrasesEn: مَا الْعَارِفُ مَنْ إِذَا أَشَارَ وَجَدَ الْحَقَّ أَقْرَبَ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ إِشَارَتِهِ،
The knower of Allah is not merely someone who, when pointing towards Allah, senses Him nearer than the gesture itself.
بَلِ الْعَارِفُ مَنْ لَا إِشَارَةَ لَهُ
The knower no longer attends to their own gesture,
لِفَنَائِهِ فِي وُجُودِهِ وَانْطِوَائِهِ فِي شُهُودِهِ.
because attention to self vanishes, immersed in witnessing Allah.

88.translation: True hope is hope accompanied by action. Without action, it is only wishful thinking.
syarahEn: Hope in Allah's mercy gives strength to change. Yet hope can become wishful thinking when unaccompanied by willingness to follow the right path. We want a relationship to improve but keep hurting people, or want religious understanding but refuse to learn. This wisdom teaches us to distinguish the two through accompanying action.

Al-raja' means hope. Qaranahu 'amal means action accompanies or walks alongside it. Umniyyah means wishful thinking. The difference lies in the practical response rather than the intensity of desire. Living hope encourages effort according to ability, while wishful thinking can be enjoyed without changing daily choices.

Someone hoping for forgiveness begins leaving mistakes and restoring violated rights. Someone hoping for knowledge makes learning time, however brief. That effort is not a price forcing Allah to provide results. It shows that a request receives an earnest response while still needing His help and bounty.

If ability is limited, choose action still possible. Stopping harm, asking for help to change, or maintaining one obligation can be important steps. Do not belittle a small effort actually performed. At the same time, do not substitute grand ambitions for action. Examine one frequently voiced hope and determine a supporting step. This wisdom nurtures active, humble hope: supplication maintains direction and action shows willingness to walk towards it.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, when in debt, we naturally pray for a way to repay it. Yet we sometimes avoid a frightening step: opening the records and seeing the actual amount. We hope the problem shrinks but are unwilling to face it. Supplication is repeated while spending decisions continue as usual and promises become harder to keep.

Ibn 'Ata'illah distinguishes raja', hope accompanied by action, from wishful thinking without action. Hope in Allah nurtures willingness to do our part. It is not a tool to force results. With debt, practical steps can begin with honesty about circumstances, so requests for a way out accompany responsibility already before us.

Dear congregation, record obligations, income, and basic needs. Contact those involved to explain your ability and seek a proper arrangement. If complex, seek competent support. Avoid making new promises simply to hide momentary embarrassment. Those awaiting payment deserve honest information, even when the explanation does not bring the news they hoped for.

“What if the amount makes me more afraid?” You need not face everything alone. Choose a trustworthy person who can help arrange steps without humiliation. Facing reality to act differs from staring at numbers while continually insulting yourself. We seek decisions that can be followed: which spending can be reduced, which abilities used, and which help is needed according to circumstances.

Dear friends, family support needs reasonable firmness. Help organize needs and stop habits increasing the burden. Do not cover the problem with baseless promises of miracles. We may hope broadly in Allah while acknowledging repayment can require time, sacrifice, and orderly cooperation from those responsible.

Let us turn one hope into one action today. May Allah provide sufficient lawful provision, grant courage to communicate honestly, and ease fulfilment of rights. May those awaiting payment receive patience and a fair path to resolution. May our supplication increase earnest action, so hope stays alive alongside practical responsibility. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Choose a time to record circumstances with a safe person if necessary. Separate confirmed information from what still needs checking. Identify one expense to adjust and one conversation to conduct properly. Do not make complex decisions from general advice alone; seek support according to need. May hope in Allah strengthen us to face reality, and may honest records open a way towards more orderly responsibility. We learn to move without promising every problem will end according to our timetable.

Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about accompanying hope of repaying debts with an honest record. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

True hope is hope accompanied by action.
وَإِلَّا فَهُوَ أُمْنِيَّةٌ.
Without action, it is only wishful thinking.

89.translation: What those who know Allah ask of Allah Most High is sincerity in servanthood and the ability to fulfil the rights of His Lordship.
syarahEn: Human needs are diverse, but a heart increasingly knowing Allah begins ordering its requests. It wants help to become a true servant, meeting both blessings and trials with proper conduct. This wisdom directs attention to the quality of the relationship with Allah accompanying all life's needs.

Al-sidq fi al-'ubudiyyah means sincerity in servanthood. Sidq includes agreement between a claim and actual conduct. Al-qiyam means upholding or fulfilling, while huquq al-rububiyyah refers to the rights of Lordship acknowledged through worship, gratitude, and submission. We acknowledge Allah as Lord through a life that does not continually place our wishes above His commands.

For example, someone asks for business success while requesting not to lose honesty when profit arrives. Facing difficulty, they ask for steadfastness so they do not seize others' rights to save themselves. Supplication thus protects devotion's quality through varied outcomes rather than merely requesting external circumstances follow one wish.

Sincerity needs continual examination because good reasons can mix with self-interest. After saying you want to benefit others, notice whether you remain willing to work without the main role. After claiming gratitude, examine whether blessings are used responsibly. Ask for the ability to align words and actions, then begin with the nearest trust. This wisdom teaches a request that orders all life: becoming a servant honest in acknowledgement, diligent in obedience, and still humble because Allah's help is needed.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, when a child enters a competition or family starts a business, we often pray for victory and success. That is allowed. But another request needs to accompany it: “O Allah, preserve our honesty while trying and receiving the result.” Success benefits more when the heart still knows how to treat people and fulfil obligations accompanying the opportunity.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains that those who know Allah seek sincerity in servanthood and fulfilment of the rights of His Lordship. We acknowledge Him through obedience, gratitude, and submission. Supplication does more than ask external circumstances to follow desire. We ask to live every state as servants, so blessings and difficulties do not make us lose direction and cross understood boundaries.

Dear friends, when a child competes, explain that earnest effort and honesty remain important. If they win, respect opponents. If they lose, allow disappointment and learn from the experience. Do not demand good character from the child while adults curse organizers whenever results disappoint. Children see both our prayers and our responses to uncomfortable decisions.

“What if there really is injustice?” Concerns may be raised through proper channels with sufficient information. Maintaining servanthood does not end efforts to pursue rights. We simply try to remain fair in those efforts. Feeling right does not permit every utterance. Those we face remain human beings whose dignity deserves respect, even when their actions need examination and possible correction.

Dear congregation, before an important activity, invite the family to name values to maintain: for example, no lying for results and no belittling people in different positions. This agreement helps supplication take form in action. We seek help to make good choices, so our relationship with Allah is present in decisions, cooperation, and receiving news.

Let us broaden our requests. May Allah grant beneficial success, preserve honesty when opportunities open, and strengthen character when outcomes disappoint. May our greatest hopes always include the ability to become sincere servants. May our families grow aware that results deserve gratitude and every step still carries responsibility. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

The lesson about seeking success alongside sincerity in our methods will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

What those knowing Allah ask of Allah Most High
الصِّدْقُ فِي الْعُبُودِيَّةِ
is sincerity in servanthood
وَالْقِيَامُ بِحُقُوقِ الرُّبُوبِيَّةِ.
and ability to fulfil the rights of His Lordship.

90.translation: He expands you so you do not remain in contraction. He contracts you so you do not remain attached to expansion. He brings you beyond both so you do not become a servant of anything besides Him.
syarahEn: There are times when the heart feels spacious and worship comes easily. At other times everything feels heavy although we are still trying. This wisdom helps us understand changing spiritual states so devotion continues beyond pleasant feelings. Our relationship with Allah needs care beyond the changing feelings that come and go.

Al-bast means inner expansion, while al-qabd means contraction or apprehension of the heart in spiritual discussion. Akhrajaka 'anhuma describes the servant being brought beyond attachment to both. The aim is for the heart not to become a servant of anything besides Allah, including spacious feelings that are only one state along the journey.

When worship feels easy, we appreciate it and use it for good. When it feels dry, we maintain obligations and adapt extra practices to ability. Do not immediately assess the entire relationship with Allah through a passing feeling. Fatigue, responsibility, and bodily circumstances also deserve reasonable attention.

Examine what actions can still be performed properly today. Arrange rest, ask for help with excessive burdens, and maintain simple practices without forcing a particular experience. We may seek peace while learning faithfulness before that feeling arrives. This wisdom orders devotion's support: gifts are appreciated, difficulties faced, and obligations maintained. The heart matures when it does not treat one state as the final goal, because what we seek is Allah's pleasure in every circumstance we can live through.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, may Allah honour us, sometimes worship feels light. We attend enthusiastically, enjoy recitation easily, and feel warmth in the heart. Other times everything feels dry. We fulfil obligations while asking, “Why do I no longer feel what I used to?” This change can frighten someone into believing their whole relationship with Allah has vanished because one feeling has not returned.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains expansion and contraction on the heart's journey. Both come and go, while devotion is directed beyond enslavement to either. We learn obedience without demanding a particular feeling always be present. Expansion is appreciated, contraction met with suitable effort, and obligations retain a place in daily decisions according to guidance and ability.

Dear congregation, if the heart feels empty, begin with what is clear. Maintain obligations and simplify extras according to circumstances. Examine whether the body is exhausted or an unspoken burden exists. We need not force ourselves into every activity to chase the same experience. Sometimes rest, renewed learning, or support is needed so life becomes more orderly and worship calmer.

“Does emptiness mean I am bad?” Do not rush to a verdict. Feelings can be influenced by many things needing understanding. If the state persists and disrupts daily functioning, seek suitable support. We can care for ourselves while continuing to pray. Asking for help does not diminish sincere faith; it can help us fulfil our responsibilities with greater capacity.

Dear friends, avoid forcing someone losing enthusiasm to describe inner experiences so we can judge. Offer gentle companionship and practical help. People often need safe room to reorder their steps. We do not know their whole heart, so helping maintain good is more appropriate than amplifying fear through baseless accusations.

Let us ask for steadfastness when feelings change. May Allah expand constricted hearts, give rest to the tired, and help maintain obligations. May happiness not make us forget ourselves and loneliness not extinguish hope. May devotion continue sincerely through the circumstances within our ability today. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We want to go home with a clearer view and one action we are able to take. So let us listen while occasionally asking our own hearts a question.

Notice its connection with maintaining obligations when warmth in worship changes. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.

Recitation once felt easy to enjoy. Now someone stands fulfilling an obligation while feeling dry. They compare every occasion with an old experience and grow more disappointed. Dear friends, we can allow room for changing feelings without immediately deciding the whole relationship has gone. Begin with clear guidance and suitable extra practice. Examine a tired body and unsupported burdens too. We need not pursue every activity to force a particular feeling back. Earnestness can appear through quiet actions, including maintaining obligations while seeking guidance when circumstances confuse us.

“What if that emptiness lasts a long time?” Seek suitable support, especially if daily life is disrupted, dear congregation. We need not face everything alone or accuse ourselves of insufficient faith. Some circumstances need further explanation and help. The wisdom about inner expansion and contraction invites the heart beyond servitude to feelings. It does not ask us to ignore our condition. We care for our ability to live while continuing to ask Allah. Do not make others' experiences a target that must be copied. Each person's circumstances need attentive understanding, and advice should give possible direction.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Can we continue what is clear even when our mood is not as it once was?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

The lesson about maintaining obligations when warmth in worship changes may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Examine what actions can still be performed properly today. Arrange rest, ask for help with excessive burdens, and maintain simple practices without forcing a particular experience. Choose one obligation to maintain consistently and one self-care need requiring attention. If extra practice feels too heavy, seek guidance for proper adjustment. Share your circumstances with a safe person if support is needed. Family can accompany without forcing immediate cheerfulness. May the heart receive help in varied states, and may we learn to turn honestly towards Allah even before warmth returns. Willingness to continue can be nurtured through suitable guidance and help.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about maintaining obligations when warmth in worship changes. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of maintaining obligations when warmth in worship changes. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us ask for steadfastness when feelings change. May Allah expand constricted hearts, give rest to the tired, and help maintain obligations. phrasesEn: بَسَطَكَ كَيْ لَا يُبْقِيَكَ مَعَ الْقَبْضِ،
He expands you so you do not remain in contraction.
وَقَبَضَكَ كَيْ لَا يَتْرُكَكَ مَعَ الْبَسْطِ،
He contracts you so you do not remain attached to expansion.
وَأَخْرَجَكَ عَنْهُمَا حَتَّى لَا تَكُونَ لِشَيْءٍ دُونَهُ.
He brings you beyond both so you do not become a servant of anything besides Him.

91.translation: Those who know Allah fear expansion more than contraction. Few can maintain the boundaries of proper conduct in expansion.
syarahEn: Difficulty often makes us careful, while ease sometimes makes boundaries feel loose. With money, influence, or a pleasant mood, we more readily assume every choice is safe. This wisdom reminds us that spacious circumstances still need watchfulness so blessings do not lead to heedlessness.

Busitu means being expanded, and qubidu means being contracted in inner experience. Hudud al-adab means boundaries of proper conduct protecting servanthood. Akhwaf means more fearful or watchful. Someone who knows personal weakness understands comfort can reduce attention to limits, so expansion needs gratitude and self-control.

For example, someone newly appointed feels free to speak however they wish because everyone respects them. That situation actually demands greater care. Someone whose worship feels easy must also avoid belittling those still struggling. Gifts should refine character rather than increase immunity to correction.

Before using ease, examine the rights attached to it. If you have time, who needs company? If wealth, what obligations remain unfulfilled? If your heart is joyful, is speech still guarded? These questions give blessings direction. This wisdom does not invite suspicion of every happiness; it teaches responsible enjoyment. Watchfulness keeps ease beneficial, so pleasure does not take the wheel and devotion continues within proper bounds.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, new authority can make life feel easier. People answer messages quickly, consider our opinions, and immediately fulfil some requests. Amid that comfort, something needs checking: are we still willing to hear refusal? Or does every objection begin to feel insulting because we have grown used to being given priority?

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that those who know Allah are more watchful in expansion, because maintaining conduct when happy is not always easy. Ease can reduce the perceived need for caution. Feeling capable and respected, we forget limits. The blessing of authority therefore needs awareness of people's rights, entrusted work, and our possibility of mistaken decisions.

Dear friends, suppose a manager sends tasks late at night about matters that could wait. Because everyone answers, the habit seems normal to them. Yet staff may fear saying they are with family. Power makes boundaries difficult for some to state. Whoever holds authority needs to protect time first and make room for colleagues to voice needs without threats.

“What if work really is urgent?” Explain the need's degree, choose appropriate people, and observe applicable requirements and rights. Distinguish urgency from habitual delay until everyone must panic. Evaluate the process so sudden requests do not continually recur. A leader's responsibility also includes making work more orderly for those they lead.

Dear congregation, seek input in ways allowing honesty. Do not ask whether you are too harsh and immediately defend yourself when someone answers. Listen, examine, and make needed changes. Authority used humbly makes an environment safer. People need not guess a superior's mood to know whether their rights will be respected that day.

Let us maintain conduct when circumstances favour us. May Allah bless every leadership trust, protect against arbitrariness, and grant courage to accept correction. May ease make us more sensitive to people's needs, so received honour does not become a habit of demanding everyone sacrifice comfort and rights to personal wishes. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.

A task message arrives late at night. Everyone answers immediately, but some leave family time for fear of seeming uncommitted. The leader sees quick replies as proof the habit causes no problem. Dear friends, authority requires greater sensitivity to reasons for silence. We can distinguish urgency from work that could be planned. State needs and deadlines clearly. Allow obstacles to be voiced without threats. Managing involves more than distributing tasks: it includes arranging work so it does not continually consume rights that deserve respect. Comfort from always being served actually requires greater watchfulness.

“If I allow too much flexibility, work will not finish.” Order still matters, dear congregation. Agree on timing, quality, and ways to report obstacles. Hearing limits does not mean accepting every neglect without evaluation. However, leaders also need to examine whether sudden requests result from their inadequate preparation. The wisdom about expansion recalls proper boundaries when the heart feels comfortable. Power that eases affairs can make refusal feel insulting. We learn to receive explanations and correction, so a trust does not become a habit of demanding everyone adapt to personal wishes.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “Do those we lead feel safe stating boundaries and legitimate concerns?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of maintaining good conduct after receiving authority, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Try reviewing one pattern of assigning tasks. Examine timing and explain what is truly urgent. Ask the team about obstacles previously difficult to voice, then respond without humiliation. If arrangements were mistaken, acknowledge and improve the process. Those receiving tasks should explain ability honestly and fulfil agreements. May authority become a place of service, and may received ease accompany gratitude and willingness to protect the rights of people depending on our decisions.

Now let us turn the lesson about maintaining good conduct after receiving authority into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about maintaining good conduct after receiving authority, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

phrasesEn: الْعَارِفُونَ إِذَا بُسِطُوا أَخْوَفُ مِنْهُمْ إِذَا قُبِضُوا،
Those knowing Allah fear expansion more than contraction.
وَلَا يَقِفُ عَلَى حُدُودِ الْأَدَبِ فِي الْبَسْطِ إِلَّا قَلِيلٌ.
Few maintain the boundaries of proper conduct in expansion.

92.translation: In expansion, the lower self receives its share of joy. In contraction, it receives no such share.
syarahEn: Pleasant circumstances are easily liked because they satisfy the self. We want them to last and may feel disappointed when they change. This wisdom helps explain why expansion can pose greater danger to the heart's attention: the lower self receives pleasure that can make it forget devotion's purpose.

Al-bast is expansion and al-qabd contraction in spiritual experience. Hazz means a share or portion received. Al-farah refers to joy. The lower self has a share in expansion because it enjoys its pleasure. In contraction, that satisfaction is not available in the same way, making personal weakness and need easier to feel.

For example, we enthusiastically undertake a lively, warmly received activity. When the task becomes quiet work still needed, enthusiasm falls. This may show that some previous energy came from enjoyment of the atmosphere. Recognizing this helps care for intention without hating permissible pleasures.

Happiness may still be enjoyed and appreciated. What needs training is faithfulness to a trust even when pleasant elements decrease. Complete one useful part without waiting for ideal conditions, then evaluate honestly. Nor should we deliberately seek difficulty to feel more pious. This wisdom teaches recognition of the lower self's movements, so we receive expansion gratefully and meet contraction patiently while maintaining devotion's direction beyond complete dependence on comfort.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, may Allah have mercy on us, a reunion with old friends can make time fly. Stories flow, laughter grows, and we feel young again. Enjoyment leads us to ignore messages from home and forget a promise to return. When a spouse reminds us, we become offended. Good happiness begins taking over attention until agreed responsibilities feel like intrusions on pleasure.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains that the lower self receives its share in expansion through enjoyable happiness. Because that pleasant share exists, expansion needs care. We may enjoy ourselves within proper limits. Yet comfort does not always indicate every choice is right. Rights, promises, and capacity still require examination when the atmosphere is especially pleasant.

Dear congregation, before leaving, discuss timing and household needs. If plans change, provide updates and listen to the situation. Do not assume a short message is enough if an urgent need remains unaddressed. Friends can also remind one another without mocking someone who wants to leave. Company becomes healthier when it respects each person's life, including responsibilities awaiting them afterwards.

“What if I occasionally want freedom from routine?” The need for rest and friendship can be discussed. Allow balanced opportunities for other family members. We do not want one person's break always paid for by extra burdens never agreed by those at home. Enjoyment is easier with responsibilities arranged and loved ones included in decisions.

Dear friends, also examine the jokes arising in a lively atmosphere. Do not reveal a spouse's secrets or embarrass a friend to keep laughter going. Someone laughing may not agree; perhaps they simply do not want to spoil the mood. Set conversational limits before anyone is hurt, because joy still needs attention to the dignity of people present.

Let us enjoy gatherings with proper conduct. May Allah bless friendship, grant balance between company and family responsibility, and guard our tongues when happy. May we return with warmth to share at home rather than leaving loved ones with work and feelings long overlooked. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
