Dear friends, at home there may be needs discussed before we left. We can update and listen rather than merely announce we will stay longer. If someone needs to leave, friends should not mock them as though family responsibility reduces closeness. Meetings feel better when each life is respected. Joy may still be enjoyed, while changes to agreements are discussed with those affected. We do not make those at home automatically responsible for every decision made while happy.

“Sometimes I want a break from routine.” That need may be expressed, dear congregation. Arrange reasonable opportunities for other family members too. Examine whether one person's rest always means another works harder without agreement. The explanation of the lower self's share in expansion helps examine joy beginning to dominate attention. It does not prohibit good gatherings. We simply guard against pleasure making obligations appear hostile. Considering boundaries beforehand makes enjoyment more possible without leaving a pile of problems on returning home.

Let me ask a question, dear congregation: “Does our enjoyment accompany agreed arrangements for responsibilities?” Take a moment to think about it. Perhaps an answer comes straight away; perhaps a difficulty comes to mind instead. Let us hear that difficulty calmly. Good advice needs to meet the reality of life, including the limitations we face. Now imagine someone we love asking that question. Would our answer help them act, or simply leave them feeling scolded? Here we learn to convey the truth in a way that can be received. We also need honesty that gives direction when speaking to ourselves, so that understanding a problem gives us courage to begin putting it right.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

For example, we enthusiastically undertake a lively, warmly received activity. When the task becomes quiet work still needed, enthusiasm falls. This may show that some previous energy came from enjoyment of the atmosphere. Recognizing this helps care for intention without hating permissible pleasures.

Dear friends, also examine the jokes arising in a lively atmosphere. Do not reveal a spouse's secrets or embarrass a friend to keep laughter going. Someone laughing may not agree; perhaps they simply do not want to spoil the mood. Set conversational limits before anyone is hurt, because joy still needs attention to the dignity of people present.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about enjoying a reunion without forgetting family agreements may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Happiness may still be enjoyed and appreciated. What needs training is faithfulness to a trust even when pleasant elements decrease. Complete one useful part without waiting for ideal conditions, then evaluate honestly. Nor should we deliberately seek difficulty to feel more pious. This wisdom teaches recognition of the lower self's movements, so we receive expansion gratefully and meet contraction patiently while maintaining devotion's direction beyond complete dependence on comfort.

Before the next gathering, agree on timing and household needs. If plans change, make sincere contact and listen to the response. A host can help keep time without pressuring everyone to stay late. After returning, fulfil responsibilities still yours. We may also evaluate what to arrange better next time. May reunions strengthen friendship and provide healthy refreshment, while family continues feeling attention and respect that remain when we are enjoying ourselves.

Dear congregation, if we want to take one task home from this discussion of enjoying a reunion without forgetting family agreements, choose something we can truly do. There is no need to announce it now. We can decide after getting home, when we have a fuller picture of our circumstances. Make the step small enough for us to know when it will be done. If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, choose one sentence from our discussion of enjoying a reunion without forgetting family agreements that we want to remember tomorrow. Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Let us enjoy gatherings with proper conduct. May Allah bless friendship, grant balance between company and family responsibility, and guard our tongues when happy. May we return with warmth to share at home rather than leaving loved ones with work and feelings long overlooked. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: الْبَسْطُ تَأْخُذُ النَّفْسُ مِنْهُ حَظَّهَا بِوُجُودِ الْفَرَحِ،
In expansion, the lower self receives its share of joy.
وَالْقَبْضُ لَا حَظَّ لِلنَّفْسِ فِيهِ.
In contraction, it receives no such share.

93.translation: Sometimes He gives to you, yet the gift withholds you from goodness. Sometimes He withholds something from you, yet that withholding is a gift.
syarahEn: Not everything pleasant benefits the heart's journey. A fulfilled desire can make us more heedless. Conversely, something delayed may prevent a mistake or open attention to another trust. This wisdom broadens how we assess gifts, so goodness is not measured only by immediate liking and disappointment.

A'taka means He gives you, while mana'aka means He withholds from you. Their repetition with reversed relationships shows reality can be broader than our first assessment. Rubbama means sometimes, so we are not asked to consider every blessing dangerous or every loss easy to understand.

Someone may receive abundant attention, then begin neglecting family and refusing advice. That outward gift turns out to accompany a decrease in more important goodness. Another misses a deeply desired opportunity, then finds room to improve skills and discover a more suitable task. These examples invite learning without determining Allah's particular purpose in every event.

When receiving something, examine its fruit in obligations and character. When held back, allow time for sadness, then seek possible steps. Do not rush to call every outcome a sign of honour or rejection. Our knowledge does not encompass every consequence. This wisdom nurtures clarity: blessings are used responsibly, difficulties faced with effort, and the heart remains open to goodness arriving in a form not initially pleasant.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, an offer can look like an answer to every prayer. The income is large, the location attractive, and people praise us for accepting. Yet once undertaken, the working methods damage health, neglect family, or require crossing boundaries. Something initially felt as a gift can bring losses visible only after we are inside it.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that sometimes a gift includes withholding from goodness, while something withheld may itself become a gift. We are trained to assess beyond passing delight and disappointment. This message does not enable certainty about Allah's purpose in every event. We simply learn caution in judging outcomes and openness to possibilities not yet fully visible.

Dear friends, before accepting an opportunity, examine accompanying obligations. What is required, who is affected, and can we undertake it properly? Ask important details. If something clearly harms or conflicts with guidance, do not justify it because profits look large. We may pass over an opportunity unsuited to our responsibilities and intended boundaries.

“What if I refuse and regret it?” Regret may arise from imagining the enjoyable part. Return to reasons honestly considered. If new information appears, evaluate reasonably. However, do not compare your actual life with imagined gains. We may not see all the burdens accompanying a choice that now looks more beautiful from afar.

Dear congregation, if already in a difficult situation, seek improvement. Discuss needs, ask advice, and arrange change according to ability. Every problem cannot be left immediately, but some steps can begin. We need not force ourselves to call every difficulty a gift. Simply allow room to learn while seeking protection and more responsible future decisions.

Let us ask for goodness Allah knows, including when our preferences do not yet understand it. May He protect us from harmful opportunities, calm the heart when refusal is necessary, and guide the next choice. May we receive blessings watchfully and face withholding without hastily concluding every door of goodness is closed. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
talkEn: OPENING
Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, advice sometimes feels distant because we think it applies only to people who are already very righteous. Yet the lesson about weighing an opportunity through its accompanying obligations meets us in ordinary matters. We may arrive with questions, with experiences we have not yet worked through, and even with confusion. In this gathering we learn together. I, too, need to practise what I share. When a part touches us, let us not immediately think of the neighbour who ought to hear it. Give ourselves a chance to receive it. Perhaps a problem that has long seemed stuck will begin to show a way forward once we are willing to pause and listen.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with weighing an opportunity through its accompanying obligations. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

However, do not compare your actual life with imagined gains. We may not see all the burdens accompanying a choice that now looks more beautiful from afar.

The offer arrives when we badly want change. Its gains are easy to imagine, while work details seem boring. Dear friends, those details need time precisely now. What is required daily, and who will be affected? Ask about unclear terms. If something clearly violates a boundary, do not justify it because the reward is large. We may desire ease while preserving limits. An opportunity good for one person may not suit another's responsibilities. Decisions need understanding of our ability and circumstances rather than simply following outside praise.

“What if I refuse and someone else succeeds?” We may see only part of their outcome, dear congregation. Return to reasons honestly considered. If new information comes, evaluate reasonably. Yet do not compare actual life with a picture containing only enjoyment. This wisdom uses sometimes to show giving and withholding may be understood more broadly than our first assessment. We are not asked to suspect every blessing or immediately understand every loss. We seek responsible judgement and willingness to learn from choices without feeling we know all Allah's arrangements.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “What must we undertake behind the gains that look attractive?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone may receive abundant attention, then begin neglecting family and refusing advice. That outward gift turns out to accompany a decrease in more important goodness. Another misses a deeply desired opportunity, then finds room to improve skills and discover a more suitable task. These examples invite learning without determining Allah's particular purpose in every event.

Dear congregation, if already in a difficult situation, seek improvement. Discuss needs, ask advice, and arrange change according to ability. Every problem cannot be left immediately, but some steps can begin. We need not force ourselves to call every difficulty a gift. Simply allow room to learn while seeking protection and more responsible future decisions.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of weighing an opportunity through its accompanying obligations, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

When receiving something, examine its fruit in obligations and character. When held back, allow time for sadness, then seek possible steps. Do not rush to call every outcome a sign of honour or rejection. Our knowledge does not encompass every consequence. This wisdom nurtures clarity: blessings are used responsibly, difficulties faced with effort, and the heart remains open to goodness arriving in a form not initially pleasant.

For practice, write visible benefits and accompanying obligations of one opportunity. Seek explanations for decisive points. Discuss effects with those actually involved, then assess ability without forcing an image. If refusing, keep your reasons to recall when passing regret arises. If accepting, uphold understood limits. May Allah guide towards beneficial choices, and may enticing gains not make us forget safety, trusts, and the rights of those sharing the consequences.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of weighing an opportunity through its accompanying obligations again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about weighing an opportunity through its accompanying obligations invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us ask for goodness Allah knows, including when our preferences do not yet understand it. May He protect us from harmful opportunities, calm the heart when refusal is necessary, and guide the next choice. May we receive blessings watchfully and face withholding without hastily concluding every door of goodness is closed. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: رُبَّمَا أَعْطَاكَ فَمَنَعَكَ،
Sometimes He gives to you, yet the gift withholds you from goodness.
وَرُبَّمَا مَنَعَكَ فَأَعْطَاكَ.
Sometimes He withholds something from you, yet that withholding is a gift.

94.translation: When He opens for you the door of understanding His withholding, that withholding becomes the gift itself.
syarahEn: When a desire is withheld, disappointment can narrow all attention to the loss. We see no benefit yet. This wisdom explains that opened understanding can transform the experience of waiting. Something felt as withholding can become a gift when the heart gains a lesson guiding devotion.

Bab al-fahm means the door of understanding. Al-man' refers to withholding, while 'ayn al-'ata' means the gift itself or the very essence of giving. The change occurs in how the heart understands and responds to circumstances. We do not need to know Allah's entire plan to begin taking clear lessons and fulfilling responsibilities still available.

For example, a planned activity receives less support than hoped. Evaluation reveals preparations were inadequate and implementation would burden many people. Delay provides an opportunity to improve arrangements. Elsewhere, the emerging understanding may be awareness of personal limits or the importance of appreciating help once taken for granted.

Remain careful not to make lessons a demand upon someone hurting. Understanding may take time, and sadness can be acknowledged. For yourself, ask for clarity while continuing to seek a good path. Ask what needs improving, what needs accepting, and what assistance is needed. This wisdom preserves hope without forcing quick answers. As the heart grows through the experience, we may discover a gift deeper than fulfilment of the one desire we initially held most tightly.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, delay sometimes hurts because we have already taken pride in a plan. A family wants to renovate, drawings are ready, but funds are insufficient. We feel disappointed and behind our neighbours. Yet recalculation reveals safety needs or important costs omitted. An unwanted pause can open an opportunity to improve before losses grow.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that when the door of understanding withholding opens, withholding can become a gift. The change is in how the heart reads circumstances and responds. We need not know Allah's entire plan to gain a lesson. Some things clearly can improve, even while disappointment remains and the final result is unseen today.

Dear congregation, use a renovation pause to seek competent explanation, examine needs, and calculate honestly. Separate the wish for decoration from what is truly necessary. Do not decide merely to appear to have started quickly. A house serves family life, so affordability and safety matter far more than seeming to keep up with neighbours.

“What if I have not found any benefit in the delay?” There is no need to force a story. We may say we remain disappointed and do not understand. Lessons sometimes take time. What matters is continuing to assess choices and seek possible steps. Some circumstances cannot be explained in one sentence, yet can still be lived through with help, planning, and maintained supplication.

Dear friends, when accompanying someone whose plans are delayed, avoid rushing to say something better must be coming without hearing their need. Offer help arranging steps. Understanding often grows when someone feels safe enough to face circumstances, rather than forced to feel grateful immediately. We make room for hope while respecting the process of accepting an unwanted reality.

Let us use the pause for work still available. May Allah clear our judgement, provide housing needs, and protect families from decisions beyond their means. May delay give room to learn without extinguishing enthusiasm. May our next steps carry better calculations, calmer hearts, and clearer responsibility. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Those who are older can still discover a new understanding, and children can still bring serious questions. Let us listen with an open heart. If an example does not match our circumstances exactly, notice the attitude being discussed. Often, beneath differences in work or age, there is a habit of the heart that many of us recognize.

House drawings have already been shown to several people. When funds prove insufficient, embarrassment appears because the plan has not visibly moved. Dear friends, wanting to seem underway can encourage careless decisions. We can use the pause to ask competent people and distinguish safety needs from appearance. Calculate costs honestly according to circumstances. Do not add burdens simply to end neighbours' comments. The family will live in the house for years, while others' attention may last briefly. Care now can bring benefit even while the delay itself remains disappointing.

Lessons can begin with what is clear, such as reviewing calculations. When an issue has no answer yet, we can still fulfil available responsibilities. Seek suitable help and choices without forcing every circumstance to appear beautiful immediately. Honesty with oneself is also part of learning the process.

Now try answering silently, dear friends: “What can be examined while the plan cannot yet begin?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. May a gathering like this send us home with the courage to learn, rather than merely the ability to comment on other people's lives.

Try reviewing the plan with family. Mark what requires expert explanation and what merely follows pride. Discuss adjustments before promising others. May the pause provide thinking space, and may we continue praying without knowing the benefit of every delay. A responsibly prepared home is more likely to become a safe place for shared life.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about using a renovation delay to clarify needs will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. What we want to nurture is a willingness to do our part properly and in an orderly way, even when the results still take time to appear.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about using a renovation delay to clarify needs, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us use the pause for work still available. May Allah clear our judgement, provide housing needs, and protect families from decisions beyond their means. phrasesEn: مَتَى فَتَحَ لَكَ بَابَ الْفَهْمِ فِي الْمَنْعِ
When He opens for you the door of understanding His withholding,
عَادَ الْمَنْعُ عَيْنَ الْعَطَاءِ.
that withholding becomes the gift itself.

95.translation: The world has an attractive exterior and an interior containing lessons. The lower self looks at its outward attraction, while the heart looks at its inward lesson.
syarahEn: The world presents many things attracting attention. Beauty, possessions, and position easily make us want more. This wisdom invites a deeper look, because every experience also contains lessons about change, limitation, and human responsibility before Allah.

Ghirrah means an attraction that can deceive. 'Ibrah means a lesson gained through reflection. Zahir refers to the visible side, while batin refers to meaning not immediately apparent. The similar sounds of ghirrah and 'ibrah emphasize two directions of sight: the lower self stops at enjoyable appearances, while the heart seeks lessons in the same reality.

Seeing a beautiful house, for example, can awaken desire to own it. Deeper reflection reminds us that a home also brings responsibilities, expenses, and an opportunity to protect family. Seeing someone's success can provoke envy, but can also encourage learning while acknowledging different life paths. What changes is how we read reality, so attention is not simply dragged by the wish to possess.

We may enjoy lawful beauty. Include awareness of its purpose and limits of use. Before pursuing something, ask about benefits, responsibilities, and effects on obligations. When seeing change or separation, take lessons without losing compassion. This wisdom guides the heart to make the world a place of learning. We remain present in it, yet increasingly able to use blessings as provision, so visible attraction does not conceal meaning that should strengthen devotion.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, wedding photographs often show beauty. Clothes are neat, decorations lovely, and everyone smiles. We may enjoy and appreciate that. But a long life follows the photograph: discussing money, managing a home, facing illness, and learning to listen through disagreements. Outward beauty needs attention to trusts not always included in the picture.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that the world has outward attraction and lessons behind it. The lower self is easily captivated by pleasure, while the heart seeks 'ibrah. We learn to read more deeply. A celebration may be enjoyable, but do not let appearances absorb all energy while preparation for the relationship receives very little attention.

Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, wedding photographs often show beauty. Clothes are neat, decorations lovely, and everyone smiles. We may enjoy and appreciate that. But a long life follows the photograph: discussing money, managing a home, facing illness, and learning to listen through disagreements. Outward beauty needs attention to trusts not always included in the picture.

Dear congregation, before going further, try bringing that story closer to our own lives. We are learning about preparing married life beyond the beauty of the celebration. Perhaps a similar event passed unnoticed because our day was too full. Now we have time to look back at it calmly. If our experience differs, take the part that fits. Children at school can picture life at home; adults can recall their responsibilities. We are not looking for whoever has made the most mistakes. We want to go home with a clearer view and one action we are able to take. So let us listen while occasionally asking our own hearts a question.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that the world has outward attraction and lessons behind it. The lower self is easily captivated by pleasure, while the heart seeks 'ibrah. We learn to read more deeply. The world presents many things attracting attention. Beauty, possessions, and position easily make us want more. This wisdom invites a deeper look, because every experience also contains lessons about change, limitation, and human responsibility before Allah.

Ghirrah means an attraction that can deceive. 'Ibrah means a lesson gained through reflection. Zahir refers to the visible side, while batin refers to meaning not immediately apparent. The similar sounds of ghirrah and 'ibrah emphasize two directions of sight: the lower self stops at enjoyable appearances, while the heart seeks lessons in the same reality.

Let us hold this understanding carefully, dear friends. Advice about preparing married life beyond the beauty of the celebration should be read alongside our obligations as servants of Allah and our responsibilities towards others. Feeling peaceful after hearing a talk is certainly pleasant. Yet sound understanding also helps us act when things no longer feel peaceful. That is why explaining the words matters. We gain something to guide our direction, rather than a beautiful impression that soon fades. If we later forget how the term sounds, remember the relationship it explains: how the heart turns to Allah and how our choices touch real life.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, those preparing for marriage should discuss daily life openly. How will needs be managed, tasks shared, and concerns expressed? Learn rights and obligations from competent sources. Everything cannot be settled once, but honest conversation needs to begin. Useful preparation helps a couple recognize reality, so hope grows alongside the ability to face problems after the event.

What matters is the approach and ability to live responsibly, including protecting rights and avoiding unbearable burdens. Families need conversation without imposed pride. Happiness should not be measured by comments from guests present a few hours who do not carry the life afterwards.

The wedding preparation list is long, but the couple has scarcely discussed life after the guests leave. Expressing concerns and managing household needs are treated as matters for later. Dear friends, those conversations deserve a place. We need not control every possibility, but honesty needs practice. Learn rights and obligations from competent people. Discuss affordability without forcing each other to please family comments. A beautiful event deserves gratitude, and the life afterwards needs earnest attention. A couple will face one another on ordinary days without photographers or applause to support the atmosphere.

“Is a simple wedding certainly happier?” We cannot judge an entire life by a celebration's size, dear congregation. What matters is preparation and the ability to live properly. Do not belittle different choices. For ourselves, examine whether costs suit circumstances and rights remain protected. This wisdom invites lessons behind captivating appearances. A good picture shows only part of time. We may enjoy beauty while remembering invisible trusts. Families should help couples prepare for reality rather than add demands whose later burden they will not share.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Which conversations need time alongside choosing clothes and decorations?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Seeing a beautiful house, for example, can awaken desire to own it. Deeper reflection reminds us that a home also brings responsibilities, expenses, and an opportunity to protect family. Seeing someone's success can provoke envy, but can also encourage learning while acknowledging different life paths. What changes is how we read reality, so attention is not simply dragged by the wish to possess.

Dear congregation, those already married should stop comparing daily life with others' photographs. We only see what they share. If the relationship has needs, express them and seek a path together. For severe or safety-related problems, ask appropriate help. Real life needs action, so prolonged attention to appearances of others' relationships rarely helps problems at home.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of preparing married life beyond the beauty of the celebration, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

We may enjoy lawful beauty. Include awareness of its purpose and limits of use. Before pursuing something, ask about benefits, responsibilities, and effects on obligations. When seeing change or separation, take lessons without losing compassion. This wisdom guides the heart to make the world a place of learning. We remain present in it, yet increasingly able to use blessings as provision, so visible attraction does not conceal meaning that should strengthen devotion.

Those preparing for marriage can choose one daily-life conversation not yet held. Find a quiet time and hear each other's hopes without rushing to blame. If something is unclear, learn through suitable guidance. Supporting families should ask the couple's needs before imposing event demands. May outward beauty accompany readiness to fulfil rights, and may marriage become a place to learn compassion long after photographs are stored and guests return home.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about preparing married life beyond the beauty of the celebration. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about preparing married life beyond the beauty of the celebration. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us see beauty as an opportunity to learn. May Allah bless the congregation's marriages, protect families from burdensome pride, and grant honest communication. May celebrations bring good joy while preparation for responsibilities receives sufficient attention. May home nurture safety, respect, and compassion continually cared for. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: الْأَكْوَانُ ظَاهِرُهَا غِرَّةٌ وَبَاطِنُهَا عِبْرَةٌ،
The world has an attractive exterior and an interior containing lessons.
فَالنَّفْسُ تَنْظُرُ إِلَى ظَاهِرِ غِرَّتِهَا
The lower self looks at its outward attraction,
وَالْقَلْبُ يَنْظُرُ إِلَى بَاطِنِ عِبْرَتِهَا.
while the heart looks at its inward lesson.

96.translation: If you desire honour that does not perish, do not seek honour by relying on what will perish.
syarahEn: People's respect can change quickly. Positions end, wealth diminishes, and opinions do not always remain. If our entire worth hangs on these, the heart rises and falls with circumstances. This wisdom invites honour through devotion to Allah, so dignity is not traded for temporary recognition.

'Izz means honour, dignity, or strength of standing. La yafna means does not perish. Tasta'izzanna describes seeking a sense of honour through reliance on something. The warning concerns dependence on what will end. Possessions and positions remain useful, but should not be the sole basis for self-assessment or treatment of people.

Someone losing a job still has obligations and opportunities for good. Someone receiving office remains a human being who must be honest and accept correction. Upholding principles in both states gives the heart a steadier measure. We respect people for their humanity and responsibility rather than only the power they currently hold.

Examine what makes us feel higher or lower than others. If possessions alone are the measure, return attention to trustworthiness and character. Use a position to benefit others while available, and prepare to accept change. Honour growing through obedience does not require belittling people. This wisdom helps preserve dignity through remaining upright, so loss of attention does not erase life's direction and outward success does not make us forget our limits.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, after retirement some people feel life suddenly quiet. Messages once arrived constantly and people addressed them by title. Now schedules are emptier and some people rarely call. The change can make the heart ask, “Am I still valuable?” We need to support this transition respectfully, because a long-held identity is taking a new form.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us not to seek lasting honour through what will end. Positions, possessions, and attention can change. We may still use a role beneficially while available. Yet human dignity and devotion to Allah do not end with an appointment letter. Ways to do good remain open even when a title no longer precedes our name.

Dear congregation, life after work can be arranged according to health and needs. Perhaps share experience, help neighbours, or study something postponed. There is no need immediately to create a major activity to cover loss. Allow adjustment time. Discuss new habits with family, including personal space and household task sharing, so changed schedules do not create tensions that could be discussed.

“What if people stop respecting me?” Poor treatment may still be addressed and boundaries protected. At the same time, distinguish sincere respect from habits of following authority. We cannot preserve every old form of attention. We can nurture more equal relationships, acceptance of change, and willingness to be present without constantly demanding treatment formerly accompanying office.

Dear friends, families can invite involvement without making someone feel they are merely assigned work to keep busy. Listen to experience, ask about preferred activities, and respect decisions still within their rights. Do not assume ability disappears immediately with age or changed work status. People still need opportunities to choose and feel useful according to actual circumstances.

Let us value people beyond their positions. May Allah bless retirement, provide sufficient needs, and open devotion suited to ability. May families receive gentleness in supporting change. May we find honour through honest life and benefit still possible, so an ending position does not extinguish hope of continued good. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

The first day without a work routine can feel strange. The phone is quieter and home has a rhythm we rarely followed before. Dear friends, this change need not be immediately covered by a major activity. We may allow adjustment time. Discuss space needs and tasks with family. If wanting to share experience, find a place genuinely needing it and listen to circumstances. We can still benefit others without always controlling things. Human honour does not end with office. More equal relationships may need learning, including how to be present when others are no longer obliged to follow every request.

“If people call less often, does it mean I am useless?” Attention accompanying authority can indeed change, dear congregation. Loss needs acknowledgement. Yet do not immediately interpret every distance as lost worth. Build relationships willing to listen mutually and activities suited to health. If mistreatment occurs, maintain boundaries. This wisdom reminds us that honour relying entirely on something ending is easily shaken. A position is useful as a means, but not the whole basis for viewing people. We still have opportunities to worship and treat others faithfully in new circumstances.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “What remains meaningful when an old position and attention begin to diminish?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.

The lesson about accepting change after retirement while preserving self-respect may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

For practice, choose one simple routine helping the day feel orderly. Ask family how to live through changed schedules together. Find useful activities according to ability without forcing proof of busyness. Those supporting retired parents should listen to feelings and avoid degrading jokes. May transition give room to warmer relationships, and may we find ways to benefit others that do not always depend on a title or how many people seek our attention.

Now let us turn the lesson about accepting change after retirement while preserving self-respect into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about accepting change after retirement while preserving self-respect invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us value people beyond their positions. May Allah bless retirement, provide sufficient needs, and open devotion suited to ability. May families receive gentleness in supporting change. May we find honour through honest life and benefit still possible, so an ending position does not extinguish hope of continued good. Amin.

phrasesEn: إِذَا أَرَدْتَ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَكَ عِزٌّ لَا يَفْنَى،
If you desire honour that does not perish,
فَلَا تَسْتَعِزَّنَّ بِعِزٍّ يَفْنَى.
do not seek honour by relying on what will perish.

97.translation: The true shortening of distance is to fold the world's distance out of your heart until you see the Hereafter nearer to you than your own self.
syarahEn: We may spend much energy thinking about our worldly future while treating the return to Allah as very distant. Yet we do not fully know life's limit. This wisdom discusses the most useful shortening of distance: reducing the Hereafter's remoteness in the heart's attention, giving today's choices clearer direction.

Al-tayy means folding or shortening distance. Masafat al-dunya refers to the world's distance seeming long in our imagination. Al-haqiqi means true or real. The metaphor redirects attention from wanting extraordinary abilities towards a changed view of life. What is shortened is heedlessness, making the Hereafter more present in daily considerations.

For example, someone delays restoring another's right because they feel there is plenty of time. Remembering life's limits, they begin now. Someone too busy increasing possessions can also rearrange time so family and worship are not continually left with leftovers. Awareness of the Hereafter improves priorities rather than extinguishing worldly responsibility.

List responsibilities that should not remain postponed, then begin with the clearest. We may still plan education, business, and the family's future. Include readiness to account for the means used. This wisdom helps us live more presently. Time is valued because limited, relationships cared for because they may end, and blessings used as provision. The Hereafter then does more than appear in conversation: it helps guide actual decisions.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, a promise to return an item keeps being moved. Busy today, rain tomorrow, another day feels available afterwards. We know the owner waits but assume opportunity always remains. Only news of a loss suddenly brings time close. Awareness of death often arrives abruptly, while many small trusts have long awaited attention.

Ibn 'Ata'illah calls true shortening of distance the Hereafter's nearness in the heart's attention. What is folded is our imagined remoteness of returning. We learn that preparing accountability need not wait until it feels close. Worldly life continues, but important matters gain a place now, before ability and opportunity change against our wishes.

Dear friends, begin with obligations possible to complete today. Contact an item's owner, send promised information, or explain delay honestly. If unable to fulfil everything, explain circumstances and a realistic plan. Do not disappear hoping people forget. A trust still concerns human rights, even when the matter feels small and many other affairs occupy us.

“If I keep thinking about the Hereafter, what about worldly work?” Worldly responsibility can actually become more orderly. Awareness of limited time helps choose priorities. Some arguments need not continue; some promises need settling. We still work and plan ahead while recognizing today also needs right action and cannot be entirely exchanged for tomorrow's plans.

Dear congregation, before sleeping, choose one matter involving another person still in our care. Ask the nearest possible step. No need to await great enthusiasm or a moving atmosphere. One honest message and one proper return can begin improving a habit. The person waiting gains clarity while we learn to respect their time and rights.

Let us bring the Hereafter closer through more practical responsibility. May Allah help fulfil promises, forgive neglect, and grant courage to contact those we have avoided. May remembering our return make life more orderly and relationships more honest. May today's opportunity not disappear simply because we assume later is certain. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

List responsibilities that should not remain postponed, then begin with the clearest. We may still plan education, business, and the family's future. Include readiness to account for the means used. This wisdom helps us live more presently. Time is valued because limited, relationships cared for because they may end, and blessings used as provision. The Hereafter then does more than appear in conversation: it helps guide actual decisions.

For practice, examine one unfinished promise or entrusted item. Determine the right step and take it at a clear time. If ability remains insufficient, explain without false promises. Families can remind respectfully rather than announcing shortcomings publicly. May remaining opportunities fulfil trusts, and may hope of long life not make us forget actions already due. We ask for a good ending while improving today's responsibilities.

Dear congregation, if we want to take one task home from this discussion of fulfilling rights before opportunities keep being postponed, choose something we can truly do. There is no need to announce it now. We can decide after getting home, when we have a fuller picture of our circumstances. Make the step small enough for us to know when it will be done. If there are obstacles, consider what reasonable help we need. We may also ask a trusted person to remind us respectfully. Change requires our involvement, as well as a heart that feels inspired. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

Dear friends, we can pause before answering a question that feels close to home. Sometimes our first answer comes from a habit of defending ourselves. Given time, we can hear the advice more clearly. We do not have to make everyone speak immediately. Some people think more easily in silence, while others are helped by asking questions. What matters is making room to understand, then choosing a step sincerely. We want to learn in a way that preserves good manners and makes our responsibilities clearer.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of fulfilling rights before opportunities keep being postponed. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us bring the Hereafter closer through more practical responsibility. May Allah help fulfil promises, forgive neglect, and grant courage to contact those we have avoided. May remembering our return make life more orderly and relationships more honest. May today's opportunity not disappear simply because we assume later is certain. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: الطَّيُّ الْحَقِيقِيُّ
The true shortening of distance
أَنْ تَطْوِيَ مَسَافَةَ الدُّنْيَا عَنْكَ
is folding the world's distance out of your heart,
حَتَّى تَرَى الْآخِرَةَ أَقْرَبَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْكَ.
until you see the Hereafter nearer than your own self.

98.translation: A gift from creation can be a deprivation. Withholding from Allah can be kindness.
syarahEn: Human help can mean much in need. Yet some gifts nurture excessive dependence or make principles difficult to maintain. Conversely, withheld desires can teach the heart to rely on Allah again. This wisdom asks us to examine a gift's inner influence beyond immediately felt outward benefit.

'Ata' al-khalq means a gift from created beings. Hirman refers to deprivation or loss of deeper benefit. Al-man' min Allah means withholding from Allah, while ihsan means kindness. Understand the sentence with attention to the heart's state. Receiving lawful assistance remains permissible and can be a means of compassion; we examine reliance and consequences.

For example, someone receives help and then feels obliged to follow all the helper's wishes, including those contrary to a trust. Outward benefit accompanies harmful attachment. Improvement means expressing proper thanks while maintaining boundaries. Meanwhile, help not yet arriving may encourage learning skills and opening avenues of effort previously overlooked.

Do not reject every assistance to appear independent. Human life involves cooperation. Accept what is good, clarify responsibilities, and remember the helper is also a means. If a need remains unmet, seek lawful paths without immediately accusing Allah of abandoning us. This wisdom trains the heart's freedom in social relationships. We can appreciate human goodness while maintaining devotion to Allah, so help brings benefit and delay remains bearable with hope.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, receiving help can bring relief. But some assistance later carries a demand: “I helped before; now every decision must follow me.” Refusal becomes difficult even when the request is wrong. A contribution meant to strengthen becomes a tether. The recipient feels no room remains to uphold principles and choose calmly.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that gifts from creation can become deprivation, while withholding from Allah may contain goodness. Read the message through the heart's state and consequences. Lawful help may still be accepted and its giver appreciated. Yet gratitude must not make people absolute supports requiring unlimited obedience.

Dear congregation, if help has conditions, discuss them clearly before acceptance. Ask about responsibilities and your ability to fulfil them. Do not be ashamed to request explanation simply because you need help. Helpers should state intentions openly too, so recipients do not discover demands only after becoming dependent. Honesty keeps assistance a relationship both sides can take responsibility for.

“What if I have already accepted and am pressured?” Seek safe support and understand available options. Express appreciation without agreeing to violating demands. With threats or complex rights issues, seek competent assistance. We need not resolve pressure alone. Maintaining boundaries does not erase gratitude, because past kindness grants no permission to demand everything afterwards.

Dear friends, givers should examine their hearts when recipients disagree. Do we still respect them? If assistance was a gift, do not quietly turn it into control. We may reasonably arrange future help, but people's honour remains protected. Help is healthier when strengthening responsible independence rather than keeping someone afraid of losing permission to choose.

Let us ask for help that brings spaciousness and wisdom to receive properly. May Allah protect people in need against pressure, guard givers against misuse of power, and guide fair relationships. May gratitude remain alive alongside boundaries, so assistance truly eases burdens without taking the recipient's dignity. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

We guard against need making boundaries seem permissible to cross, and against help controlling every recipient's choice.

Dear congregation, some questions look simple, but we only feel their weight when living through them: “How can we give thanks without agreeing to a demand that violates a boundary?” Let us give ourselves time to consider this. We may picture ourselves or someone who needs support. We are learning to answer in words that can be put into practice. Avoid an answer that makes every problem seem resolved in a single breath. Some matters need time and support. Even so, that process can begin with a small decision. Try finding that decision in the earlier example. This is where our conversation becomes useful for life after the gathering ends.

We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Try examining one form of help to receive or give. Ask important conditions and avoid hidden expectations. If pressure has occurred, record issues factually and seek support suited to circumstances. Thanks may still be expressed respectfully. Givers should allow disagreement without bringing up contributions. May helping relationships grow through honesty, and may those in need receive benefit strengthening dignity and responsible agency in their lives.

Dear friends, test our plan against everyday situations. When we face the matter of maintaining boundaries when help becomes pressure again, what will change in our actions? Choose an answer we can recognize, such as having a conversation or stopping a habit. If the answer is still too general, make the step smaller. We are not writing a beautiful promise for others. We are preparing help for ourselves when we encounter an old habit. After doing it, give thanks and keep learning. If it has not worked yet, examine the reason honestly, then try again with preparation better suited to the situation.

Let us leave room for questions that remain unresolved, dear congregation. If confusion remains after the gathering, write down the issue clearly. Then ask someone who understands the subject and knows the circumstances involved. We may learn gradually. A little accurate understanding is more helpful than a rushed decision made simply because we want to feel that everything is settled. Meanwhile, continue fulfilling our clear obligations and respect the rights of those around us.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about maintaining boundaries when help becomes pressure. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us ask for help that brings spaciousness and wisdom to receive properly. May Allah protect people in need against pressure, guard givers against misuse of power, and guide fair relationships. phrasesEn: الْعَطَاءُ مِنَ الْخَلْقِ حِرْمَانٌ
A gift from creation can be a deprivation.
وَالْمَنْعُ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِحْسَانٌ.
Withholding from Allah can be kindness.

99.translation: Exalted is our Lord above receiving a servant's devotion in immediate payment while rewarding it only as a deferred debt.
syarahEn: We easily view worship as work whose reward comes only far in the future. Obedience then feels merely like a burden to finish. This wisdom invites recognition that the ability to serve and the relationship with Allah already contain gifts, even before the complete reward of the Hereafter.

Naqdan means immediate payment, while nasi'ah means deferred or like a debt. This metaphor does not portray Allah as indebted to people. Jalla affirms His exaltedness beyond a degrading understanding. We are reminded that Allah's generosity exceeds awaited results; help to do good is itself a gift preceding our hopes.

Someone helped to leave deception has already gained a great benefit in life's direction. Someone able to apologize has an opportunity to repair a relationship. Obedience can also nurture order, self-control, and closeness in supplication. These benefits do not always arrive as strong comfort, yet still deserve grateful recognition.

Do not turn this wisdom into a promise that every worship immediately produces money or worldly ease. Allah's recompense is far broader. When a deed feels difficult, remember the opportunity to answer a command is no small gift. Fulfil obligations properly and seek acceptance. The heart grows more spacious when it does more than calculate what remains unreceived, recognizing help already present within devotion itself.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, someone regularly supporting children's learning may begin with a simple wish to help. Over time, they notice their own change: greater patience explaining, more attentive listening, and more appreciation of schooling once taken for granted. Goodness is already present within service, even without any recognition from others.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that Allah is Most Generous, never leaving all reward as though merely a deferred debt. We learn to recognize generosity already accompanying deeds. Opportunities to obey and good growth can be appreciated now, while still hoping for the Hereafter's reward. We do not turn worship into a promise that every deed immediately produces material gains in our desired amount.

Dear friends, suppose we help a neighbour understand a lesson. Preparation may be tiring, but we also train our ability to explain. Seeing a child dare to ask brings joy without awaiting an award ceremony. Recognize this benefit without forgetting the supporter's rights. If the activity is paid work by agreement, those rights still need fair fulfilment rather than replacement with praise for sincerity.

“What if I only feel tired and see no benefit yet?” Fatigue needs attention. Arrange burdens, ask for help, and evaluate working methods. We need not force happiness from every activity. Sometimes benefit appears later or quietly. What matters is proper service without continually neglecting those performing it to maintain an image of constant strength.

Dear congregation, occasionally ask what we have learned through service. Answer honestly, including newly recognized shortcomings. Perhaps we understand others' difficulties better. That awareness can help relationships outside the activity. Deeds provide resources for life, so we count more than what we gave: we acknowledge help received while performing them.

Let us appreciate goodness already growing while continuing broad hope in Allah. May He accept our service, protect community workers' rights, and help recognize gifts present amid work. May helping make us humbler, more patient learners, and more responsible in caring for entrusted benefits. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Yet do not demand every activity always feel pleasant. Preparation can still tire and require support. If compensation was agreed, fulfil that right. We appreciate it while still seeking help, without erasing rest needs and fair treatment for those serving.

Now try answering silently, dear friends: “What good change do we also learn while helping a child study?” There is no need to hurry. People may give different answers because their circumstances also differ. We listen while holding to the guidance that is already clear. If someone is new to learning, give them a chance to ask. If someone has made a mistake, do not make their experience a joke. A safe conversation gives us courage to examine our own habits. Then we can choose a reasonable improvement. May a gathering like this send us home with the courage to learn, rather than merely the ability to comment on other people's lives.

Let us arrange a step that fits our lives, dear congregation. The lesson about recognizing benefits growing while supporting others will be easier to remember when connected with a time or activity that already exists. We do not need to add burdens without considering our ability. Choose a reasonable place to begin, and respect other people's rights as we act. Children may ask for their parents' support; adults can also seek advice when struggling. We do not have to face everything alone. Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.

Repeat its meaning silently in our own words. We do not need the sentence that sounds most impressive. Choose what helps most when facing real circumstances. Then ask Allah to enable us to put it into practice. We also pray for those struggling in similar circumstances. May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

phrasesEn: جَلَّ رَبُّنَا
Exalted is our Lord above
أَنْ يُعَامِلَهُ الْعَبْدُ نَقْدًا فَيُجَازِيَهُ نَسِيئَةً.
receiving a servant's devotion in immediate payment while rewarding it only as a deferred debt.

100.translation: It is sufficient as His reward for your obedience that He has chosen you as someone fit to perform it.
syarahEn: We may consider the opportunity for worship entirely available through our own ability. Yet health, knowledge, and the wish to obey are not present in every circumstance. This wisdom invites gratitude that help to fulfil Allah's command is already part of His reward and generosity.

Kafa means sufficient, emphasizing a gift's greatness. Jaza'uhu means His reward. Radiyaka laha ahlan indicates that He chooses or approves of us as fit to perform that obedience. This fitness is received as a gift, never used to feel purer or determine our standing compared with others.

Someone reading the Qur'an, for example, has received learning opportunities, bodily ability, and time to use. Someone serving family is also given capacity to help. Remembering these foundations helps us stop seeing deeds solely as sacrifices indebting others. We may still appreciate hard work while acknowledging the help preceding it.

After doing good, make a habit of thanking Allah for the opportunity and asking forgiveness for shortcomings. If circumstances reduce ability, undertake forms of devotion still possible according to guidance. Do not belittle yourself for no longer maintaining the same measure of deeds. This wisdom improves how we enjoy obedience. We rejoice in being helped, becoming gentler towards others struggling and more diligent in protecting the gift from arrogance and demands for recognition.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, have we ever found going to the mosque difficult because we take it for granted? The distance is short and body healthy, yet reasons to delay always appear. Then we see someone arriving slowly or with family assistance. We need not compare rewards, but it can remind us that current ability is an opportunity that may not always remain the same.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that being helped to perform obedience is already Allah's generosity. We appreciate an opened path rather than feeling deserving, as though Allah needed our deeds. This awareness gives humbler joy. Health, time, and willingness deserve care so opportunities to obey do not continually pass unnoticed.

Dear congregation, if able to attend, arrange time and prepare reasonably. Do not rely only on passing enthusiasm. If other responsibilities or special circumstances exist, learn suitable guidance. We do not assess someone's entire devotion by visible attendance. Absentees may have circumstances unknown to us, so invitations remain polite and free from humiliation.

“If I already attend regularly, what should I examine?” Look at how other congregants are treated. Are we friendly to newcomers? Does worship feel safe for learners? Attendance should not make us entitled to belittle. Routine experience can instead help someone find space, understand arrangements, and feel accepted for gradual improvement.

Dear friends, family can support through small assistance. Offer company to someone needing it, arrange safe travel, or help with tasks so a relative has an opportunity to worship. We need not force everyone into the same method. The aim is mutual ease within proper boundaries, so obedience's opportunities are cared for together rather than becoming a competition in judgement.

Let us thank Allah for one act of obedience made easier today. May He preserve health, grant room for worship, and accept efforts still full of shortcomings. May the mosque's doors remain open through its congregation's friendliness. May attendance make us humbler and more willing to help those whose journey towards goodness remains difficult. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
