Dear congregation, before going further, try bringing that story closer to our own lives. We are learning about using the opportunity to attend the mosque humbly. Perhaps a similar event passed unnoticed because our day was too full. Now we have time to look back at it calmly. If our experience differs, take the part that fits. Children at school can picture life at home; adults can recall their responsibilities. We are not looking for whoever has made the most mistakes. We want to go home with a clearer view and one action we are able to take. So let us listen while occasionally asking our own hearts a question.
CORE WISDOM

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that being helped to perform obedience is already Allah's generosity. We appreciate an opened path rather than feeling deserving, as though Allah needed our deeds. This awareness gives humbler joy. Health, time, and willingness deserve care so opportunities to obey do not continually pass unnoticed.

We may consider the opportunity for worship entirely available through our own ability. Yet health, knowledge, and the wish to obey are not present in every circumstance. This wisdom invites gratitude that help to fulfil Allah's command is already part of His reward and generosity.

Kafa means sufficient, emphasizing a gift's greatness. Jaza'uhu means His reward. Radiyaka laha ahlan indicates that He chooses or approves of us as fit to perform that obedience. This fitness is received as a gift, never used to feel purer or determine our standing compared with others.

Let us slow down for a moment, dear congregation. The terms in these sayings help us recognize the movements of the heart, but we need not feel intimidated by the terminology. Notice its connection with using the opportunity to attend the mosque humbly. Once we understand the meaning, examine the actions we can see: what words are spoken, what decisions are made, and who experiences the consequences. That is where understanding begins to take shape. If it is not yet clear, go through the explanation again. Learning our religion requires patience. We can also ask respectfully when a sentence seems confusing, so that eagerness to practise is accompanied by sound understanding.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear congregation, if able to attend, arrange time and prepare reasonably. Do not rely only on passing enthusiasm. If other responsibilities or special circumstances exist, learn suitable guidance. We do not assess someone's entire devotion by visible attendance. Absentees may have circumstances unknown to us, so invitations remain polite and free from humiliation.

“If I already attend regularly, what should I examine?” Look at how other congregants are treated. Are we friendly to newcomers? Does worship feel safe for learners? Attendance should not make us entitled to belittle. Routine experience can instead help someone find space, understand arrangements, and feel accepted for gradual improvement.

The mosque is near and time sufficient, yet preparation is postponed because opportunity seems constant. Then someone arrives slowly with family help. Dear friends, this can remind us of blessings without comparing rewards. We can arrange available time. Regular attendees have opportunities to make the atmosphere welcoming. Greet newcomers and explain needs politely. Do not turn small mistakes into humiliating experiences. We appreciate worship's opportunity through preparation and attention to others seeking a place to learn and improve their steps.

“How do we invite someone rarely seen?” Speak respectfully without assuming unknown reasons, dear congregation. Perhaps responsibilities or special circumstances exist. Offer assistance according to need rather than announcing judgement publicly. This wisdom calls the ability to obey a great gift. Understanding protects against feeling purer simply because a habit is visible. We still learn guidance suited to circumstances and seek attendance when able. Recipients of invitations need to feel respected as people, so gatherings and worship spaces provide safe room to begin.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Does our ability to attend make us friendlier towards congregants still learning?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone reading the Qur'an, for example, has received learning opportunities, bodily ability, and time to use. Someone serving family is also given capacity to help. Remembering these foundations helps us stop seeing deeds solely as sacrifices indebting others. We may still appreciate hard work while acknowledging the help preceding it.

Dear friends, family can support through small assistance. Offer company to someone needing it, arrange safe travel, or help with tasks so a relative has an opportunity to worship. We need not force everyone into the same method. The aim is mutual ease within proper boundaries, so obedience's opportunities are cared for together rather than becoming a competition in judgement.

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about using the opportunity to attend the mosque humbly may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

After doing good, make a habit of thanking Allah for the opportunity and asking forgiveness for shortcomings. If circumstances reduce ability, undertake forms of devotion still possible according to guidance. Do not belittle yourself for no longer maintaining the same measure of deeds. This wisdom improves how we enjoy obedience. We rejoice in being helped, becoming gentler towards others struggling and more diligent in protecting the gift from arrogance and demands for recognition.

Choose one simple preparation supporting orderly attendance. Ask the right person about anything unclear. After arriving, observe how you treat others and shared facilities. Do not demand equal ability from everyone. Family can support according to circumstances without threats or mockery. May available opportunity not be wasted, and may the ability to worship nurture gratitude and friendliness that help the environment welcome those wanting improvement.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about using the opportunity to attend the mosque humbly. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of using the opportunity to attend the mosque humbly. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us thank Allah for one act of obedience made easier today. May He preserve health, grant room for worship, and accept efforts still full of shortcomings. May the mosque's doors remain open through its congregation's friendliness. May attendance make us humbler and more willing to help those whose journey towards goodness remains difficult. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: كَفَى مِنْ جَزَائِهِ إِيَّاكَ عَلَى الطَّاعَةِ
It is sufficient as His reward for your obedience
أَنْ رَضِيَكَ لَهَا أَهْلًا.
that He chooses you as fit to perform it.

101.translation: It is sufficient reward for those who act that He opens their hearts in obedience to Him and brings intimacy with Him into their hearts.
syarahEn: Obedience can bring the gift of a heart opened to understanding, gratitude, and having somewhere to return to Allah. Others may not see this gift, but it gives devotion meaning. This wisdom reminds us that the relationship growing within deeds is already a great gift.

Fatihuhu refers to Him opening the servant's heart. Mu'anasah means intimacy or tranquillity in closeness. Muriduhu 'alayhim describes something He brings to them. The wording emphasizes that enjoyment of devotion is received as a gift, rather than treated as a result we can command or demand whenever we worship.

Someone may begin feeling more honest in supplication. They can acknowledge fear without maintaining an impression of strength. Another finds room to forgive after long nursing resentment. Such experiences deserve gratitude through changed action, rather than merely remembrance as a mood we want repeated.

If intimacy is not yet felt, do not conclude worship lacks value. Maintain obligations and improve practice through knowledge and perseverance. Consider bodily needs and burdens affecting attention too. We may seek peace while learning faithfulness before feeling accompanies it. This wisdom directs joy towards relationship with Allah, so deeds are more than tasks to finish. Within them is an opportunity to know the Giver, acknowledge weakness, and receive help to live better.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, some days we return with minds full. Work conversations remain unfinished, household needs await, and the heart struggles to explain its weight. Worship offers a moment away from people's demands to bring our circumstances to Allah. We need not appear constantly strong. Honesty can be expressed in supplication even with very simple words.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us of reward through the heart opening in obedience and intimacy with Allah. Mu'anasah describes tranquillity in closeness. This gift deserves gratitude without being forced into every act of worship. We keep fulfilling commands while hoping for guidance. Calm is not an item we can demand after completing a particular number of recitations.

Dear friends, if supplication brings spaciousness, use the opportunity to seek guidance. Afterwards, examine one problem needing attention. Perhaps a conversation needs repair or work needs sharing. Closeness to Allah can strengthen our return to life, so worship does more than offer temporary escape from responsibilities still awaiting resolution.

“What if I still feel burdened after salah?” Do not immediately assume Allah is distant or worship useless. Feelings can be influenced by many circumstances. Maintain obligations, learn meanings, and consider personal needs. If burdens persist, speak with someone trustworthy or seek suitable support. We care for relationship with Allah while using available help to face problems more orderly.

Dear congregation, do not compare inner experiences. Someone readily crying is not automatically closer, and someone calm without expression may be no less sincere. We do not know every heart. Better to encourage obedience and help practical needs. A safe environment can also help someone learn supplication without fear that public appearance measures sincerity.

Let us bring tiredness to Allah with simple hope. May He open hearts, guide steps after prayer, and grant tranquillity supporting responsibilities. May those not yet feeling spaciousness receive steadfastness and support. May worship be a place of return strengthening relationship with Him and improving our presence with others. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

That is where the lesson about bringing a difficult day into supplication and returning to our responsibilities will be tested. We may still face the same situation, the same people, and old habits that have not yet changed. We need to understand the message well enough to bring it into those circumstances. Listen slowly. If a sentence speaks to our situation, keep it in mind for later. We do not have to remember every explanation. One sound understanding, put sincerely into practice, is already worth working towards today.

In this way, a word that once sounded unfamiliar can help us recognize a mistaken step before the habit makes life harder for us or for others.

After work, someone cannot explain their full heart. Household needs also await. In supplication, they can finally say they are tired without composing impressive sentences. Dear friends, such honesty is welcome. If spaciousness appears, appreciate it as help. Afterwards, identify one matter to discuss more calmly. Perhaps tasks need sharing or earlier words need repair. Worship offers a place to turn towards Allah, and received strength can return to life. We need not resolve every issue at once, but can choose one sufficiently clear, responsible step.

“What if I feel no spaciousness after salah?” Do not immediately pass judgement, dear congregation. Feelings have many influences and we cannot command a particular experience always to come. Maintain obligations and learn meaning through sound guidance. Consider support needs when burdens persist. This wisdom explains devotion's sweetness as a gift, received gratefully when it comes. It does not make someone without that feeling distant from Allah. Family and friends can accompany without forcing immediate calm. Suitable help supports responsibilities with better capacity.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “After supplication, which problem still needs our action?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone may begin feeling more honest in supplication. They can acknowledge fear without maintaining an impression of strength. Another finds room to forgive after long nursing resentment. Such experiences deserve gratitude through changed action, rather than merely remembrance as a mood we want repeated.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of bringing a difficult day into supplication and returning to our responsibilities, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. If intimacy is not yet felt, do not conclude worship lacks value. Maintain obligations and improve practice through knowledge and perseverance. This wisdom directs joy towards relationship with Allah, so deeds are more than tasks to finish. Within them is an opportunity to know the Giver, acknowledge weakness, and receive help to live better.

For practice, allow a chance to pray honestly. Then choose one issue needing action and possible assistance. If needing to share, find someone safe and trustworthy. Do not carry everything simply to appear strong. Listeners should allow room without rushing to lecture. May worship help hearts acknowledge need before Allah, and may granted peace become provision for improving relationships and work awaiting us daily.

Now let us turn the lesson about bringing a difficult day into supplication and returning to our responsibilities into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about bringing a difficult day into supplication and returning to our responsibilities, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us bring tiredness to Allah with simple hope. May He open hearts, guide steps after prayer, and grant tranquillity supporting responsibilities. May those not yet feeling spaciousness receive steadfastness and support. May worship be a place of return strengthening relationship with Him and improving our presence with others. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: كَفَى الْعَامِلِينَ جَزَاءً
It is sufficient reward for those who act
مَا هُوَ فَاتِحُهُ عَلَى قُلُوبِهِمْ فِي طَاعَتِهِ،
that their hearts open in obedience to Him
وَمَا هُوَ مُورِدُهُ عَلَيْهِمْ مِنْ وُجُودِ مُؤَانَسَتِهِ.
and intimacy with Him comes into their hearts.

102.translation: Whoever worships Him solely for something hoped for from Him, or to ward off punishment through obedience, has not fully fulfilled the right of His divine attributes.
syarahEn: When beginning to learn, we may worship hoping for reward and fearing punishment. Both have a place in religious teaching. This wisdom invites devotion to grow deeper, until the heart also knows Allah deserves worship because of His Lordship and generosity, rather than solely the benefit desired for oneself.

'Abadahu means worshipped Him. Li-shay'in yarjuhu refers to something hoped for from Him, while li-yadfa'a means to ward off a feared consequence. Haqq awsafih directs attention to the right of His divine attributes. The warning concerns worship stopping at calculations of self-interest, without removing hope for Paradise and fear of punishment taught by religion.

A child first learns to help because they want a gift. As they mature, they are expected to understand compassion and responsibility. This simple analogy helps us read the growth of intention without equating Allah with human beings. Our devotion too can develop from initial motivations towards gratitude, love, and livelier acknowledgement of Allah's greatness.

When asking for good reward, include a request for help towards greater sincerity. While fulfilling obligations, remember blessings received before the deed. We need not claim to have gone beyond needing reward or feel higher than others. Simply care for intention so it does not entirely revolve around personal wants. This wisdom trains mature servanthood, allowing hope and fear to accompany love, gratitude, and humble willingness to fulfil commands.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, may Allah honour us, early in obedience we often need encouragement. We want reward, fear punishment, and hope needs become easier. All have a place in religious teaching. Yet the heart's journey needs continued growth. We learn Allah deserves worship through His Lordship and generosity, so worship is not always filled with questions about what we will immediately receive.

Ibn 'Ata'illah challenges devotion stopping at obtaining something or avoiding feared consequences. He invites deeper fulfilment of Allah's right of Lordship. We do not erase taught hope for Paradise and fear of punishment. What we improve is treating worship as though the whole relationship were an exchange always required to benefit personal calculations.

Dear congregation, suppose we pray hoping business improves. When time passes without change, we want to stop obeying. Then purpose needs examination. We may still seek ease, but Allah remains the Lord worshipped in busy and quiet circumstances. An obligation does not lose meaning because one request has not arrived in the worldly form we desire.

“Must I claim complete sincerity without hoping for anything?” No need to claim beyond your state. We can ask for increasing ikhlas while still seeking goodness. Improving intention is a process. Whenever demanding calculations appear, return attention to blessings received and guidance directing life, beyond results still awaited.

Dear friends, family can learn through simple habits. Invite children to worship with suitable explanations while nurturing gratitude and love. Initial encouragement can help, but avoid pricing every good deed with a prize until they feel no need to act when prizes stop. Adult example matters, helping children see worship as a relationship cared for rather than simply a condition for obtaining something.

Let us ask for hearts increasingly knowing Allah's generosity. May He accept worship with mixed intentions, guide hope and fear towards obedience, and nurture sincere love. May we keep asking hopefully while learning that devotion means far more than gains measurable today. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

May this gathering make us more willing to support others with understanding while continuing to improve our own actions. Let us close this lesson with good hope and sincere supplication.

Let us ask for hearts increasingly knowing Allah's generosity. May He accept worship with mixed intentions, guide hope and fear towards obedience, and nurture sincere love. May we keep asking hopefully while learning that devotion means far more than gains measurable today. Amin.

104.translation: His withholding pains you because you have not yet understood Allah's purpose within it.
syarahEn: When a desire remains unfulfilled, pain often increases because we feel no goodness exists in the situation. Our view narrows and every possibility closes. This wisdom explains the connection between hurt and limited understanding, so we can allow room for insight not yet present.

The expression invites acknowledgement that a servant's knowledge does not encompass every consequence. Broader understanding can reduce inner resistance, even while human sadness remains part of the process.

We need not force every loss to have an immediately beautiful replacement story. Some circumstances can only be lived through gradually with patience and help.

Therefore, do not use this wisdom to blame a grieving person for insufficient knowledge of Allah. Begin with yourself through supplication, evaluation, and willingness to hear gentle advice. Distinguish what can improve from what needs acceptance. Understanding grows when one withheld desire does not close our entire view. From there, pain can gain a direction of devotion, allowing continued care for responsibilities without understanding every wisdom accompanying the journey.

Dear friends, losing a job can make the world feel narrow. Bills, self-esteem, and family explanations await. Amid confusion, someone sometimes brings quick advice: “Something better is certainly coming; do not be sad.” Perhaps they mean encouragement, but the listener may be unready. Avoid comparison with someone supposedly worse off. That does not automatically reduce burdens. People can arrange steps more easily when understood and not required to defend their right to sadness before us.

“What if I am the one losing a job?” Allow space to settle, then examine immediate needs. Record skills, essential expenses, and people to contact. If rights need investigation, seek competent information and support. We need not solve the whole future in one day. Focusing on a sufficiently clear step can reduce the feeling of everything arriving at once.

Dear friends, do not rush to treat one rejection as judgement of all your abilities. Evaluate what needs evaluation while preserving fairness. Business conditions and job requirements may be beyond personal control. We keep trying and seeking guidance without making an unreceived result a reason to close every hope in Allah and opportunities still possible.

Let us pray for families losing income. May Allah meet needs, bring lawful work, and strengthen hearts through the process. May supporters receive gentle language and useful actions. May understanding grow in its time, while compassion is present now to help carry difficult days. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

105.translation: Sometimes He opens the door of obedience for you without opening the door of acceptance. Sometimes He decrees that you slip into sin, and it becomes a cause of your returning and drawing near to Him.
syarahEn: Apparently good obedience can be damaged by arrogance, while someone who slips can return with deep remorse. This wisdom reminds us to consider an experience's effect on the heart. Outward form alone is insufficient without examining the attitude growing afterwards.

Bab al-ta'ah means the door of obedience, while bab al-qabul means the door of acceptance. They are distinguished so we keep asking for acceptance rather than feeling safe through abundant deeds alone. Al-wusul refers to closeness in the heart's knowledge of Allah. Sin becoming a cause of closeness is understood through repentance, humility, and subsequent change rather than the value of sin itself.

Someone regularly helping may begin belittling recipients. They need to improve intention and behaviour although the work remains useful. Someone who hurt others can later acknowledge wrongdoing, restore rights, and learn gentleness. In both circumstances, attention goes to the response nurturing or damaging servanthood.

This wisdom gives no reason to seek wrongdoing for an experience of repentance. Obligations remain observed and sins avoided. If you fall, return immediately without waiting to feel worthy; if you obey successfully, ask that pride not damage it. Nor should one event determine who Allah accepts or rejects. The lesson is primarily personal: appreciate deeds, fear arrogance, and turn regret into repair. Every experience then receives practical responsibility, while acceptance is entrusted to Allah's generosity and knowledge.

Dear congregation, may Allah have mercy on us, some people regularly do good but struggle greatly to admit a mistake. When corrected, they present their whole list of contributions. Others have slipped, then remorse makes them humbler and more careful. We see that outward action needs attention alongside the heart's subsequent direction, without believing we can determine Allah's final judgement of anyone.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains that obedience's door is not necessarily followed by acceptance if damaged by the heart's state. He also reminds us that wrongdoing can cause a return through repentance. This does not make sin a sought choice. What brings goodness is the response afterwards: remorse, restoration of rights, and submission making someone genuinely willing to improve.

Dear friends, suppose a coordinator speaks harshly to volunteers. When reminded, they say everyone should be grateful because they have worked so much. Yet contributions do not remove people's right to respect. The needed step is acknowledging the words, apologizing, and improving instructions. Good service is more than the number of successful activities.

“What if I once did wrong and now feel close to Allah?” Appreciate the prompting to return and maintain its responsibilities. Do not make the past a story for admiring yourself as changed. Rights may still need restoration. Others may need time too. Humility helps accept that process without demanding immediate praise for a new direction.

Dear congregation, examine deeds' fruits with a simple question: after doing good, is apologizing easier or do we feel more immune to correction? If arrogance exists, seek forgiveness and improve actions. We need not stop good because intentions are mixed. Continue while correcting the heart, protecting goodness and ending justifications for what damages it.

Let us seek acceptance beyond the ability to add activities. May Allah protect deeds from arrogance, strengthen those repenting, and grant courage to repair wrongdoing's effects. May every success bring gratitude and every recognized mistake lead to responsibility. May loved ones feel a heart increasingly willing to listen and improve. Amin.

If we later forget how the term sounds, remember the relationship it explains: how the heart turns to Allah and how our choices touch real life.
EXAMPLES AND CONVERSATION WITH THE CONGREGATION

Dear friends, suppose a coordinator speaks harshly to volunteers. When reminded, they say everyone should be grateful because they have worked so much. Yet contributions do not remove people's right to respect. The needed step is acknowledging the words, apologizing, and improving instructions. Good service is more than the number of successful activities.

“What if I once did wrong and now feel close to Allah?” Appreciate the prompting to return and maintain its responsibilities. Do not make the past a story for admiring yourself as changed. Rights may still need restoration. Others may need time too. Humility helps accept that process without demanding immediate praise for a new direction.

A coordinator speaks harshly to volunteers because preparations are unfinished. When reminded, they explain all the work already handled. Dear friends, that effort is real, but harsh speech still needs examination. We can acknowledge both without making contributions erase responsibility. Apologize clearly and improve future instructions. Volunteers need guidance and respect beyond successful events. If the coordinator's burden is excessive, discuss sharing too. We need not conceal tiredness with conceit or repay sacrifices through a right to belittle helpers.

“If a mistake made me humbler, was the sin actually good?” Wrongdoing still needs leaving, dear congregation. The good direction comes through repentance and subsequent change. This wisdom distinguishes obedience's door from acceptance so we keep asking rather than feeling certain of safety through many deeds. Nor should we deliberately seek mistakes hoping for humility. We can learn submission through sound guidance. The past need not become a story admiring our own change. Rights still need restoring and people need time. Humility makes room to respect that process.

Dear congregation, let us imagine a short conversation. I ask, “Do past contributions make us feel we need not apologize?” Then imagine someone here answering from everyday experience. We do not need to guess the most impressive answer. An honest answer helps this discussion more. If a part is difficult, name the difficulty without dismissing the wisdom's message. Then look for one step that is still possible. Conversation often becomes more useful when we stop trying to defeat one another and begin asking about real needs. In that way, advice can accompany us when facing a problem, instead of becoming an extra burden that merely sounds good in a gathering.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Someone regularly helping may begin belittling recipients. They need to improve intention and behaviour although the work remains useful. Someone who hurt others can later acknowledge wrongdoing, restore rights, and learn gentleness. In both circumstances, attention goes to the response nurturing or damaging servanthood.

Dear congregation, examine deeds' fruits with a simple question: after doing good, is apologizing easier or do we feel more immune to correction? If arrogance exists, seek forgiveness and improve actions. We need not stop good because intentions are mixed. Continue while correcting the heart, protecting goodness and ending justifications for what damages it.

Dear congregation, try looking at our own journey with both honesty and compassion. In the matter of maintaining humility after doing much good, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

This wisdom gives no reason to seek wrongdoing for an experience of repentance. Obligations remain observed and sins avoided. If you fall, return immediately without waiting to feel worthy; if you obey successfully, ask that pride not damage it. Nor should one event determine who Allah accepts or rejects. The lesson is primarily personal: appreciate deeds, fear arrogance, and turn regret into repair. Every experience then receives practical responsibility, while acceptance is entrusted to Allah's generosity and knowledge.

For practice, recall one correction rejected by listing contributions. Separate the corrected issue from good deeds genuinely performed. If words were wrong, acknowledge and improve next time. Request task sharing if genuinely needed. After good deeds, ask Allah for acceptance. May perseverance nurture character ready to listen, and may slipping teach greater care through repentance without reducing earnest obedience and respect for others' rights.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about maintaining humility after doing much good. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, before we close, silently recall the lesson we most want to take home. Today we have spoken about maintaining humility after doing much good. We do not have to feel accomplished after a single meeting. A clearer understanding and a willingness to begin are enough. If we later forget, we can open our notes or ask again. Do not be embarrassed to repeat a good lesson. Life gives us opportunities to practise many times. May each repetition make our actions a little more orderly and our hearts more aware of our need for Allah's help. Let us keep that willingness to learn after leaving this gathering.

Let us seek acceptance beyond the ability to add activities. May Allah protect deeds from arrogance, strengthen those repenting, and grant courage to repair wrongdoing's effects. May every success bring gratitude and every recognized mistake lead to responsibility. May loved ones feel a heart increasingly willing to listen and improve. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: رُبَّمَا فَتَحَ لَكَ بَابَ الطَّاعَةِ
Sometimes He opens the door of obedience for you,
وَمَا فَتَحَ لَكَ بَابَ الْقَبُولِ،
without opening the door of acceptance.
وَرُبَّمَا قَضَى عَلَيْكَ بِالذَّنْبِ
Sometimes He decrees that you slip into sin,
فَكَانَ سَبَبًا فِي الْوُصُولِ.
and it becomes a cause of returning and drawing near to Him.

106.translation: Disobedience followed by humility and need for Allah is better than obedience followed by conceit and arrogance.
syarahEn: A mistake can awaken someone to acknowledge weakness and return to Allah. Conversely, successful worship can make someone feel higher and resistant to advice. This wisdom compares those inner fruits so we understand arrogance's great danger and humility's importance in devotion.

Dhull means humility before Allah. Iftiqar is a sense of needing His help. Conversely, 'izz in this warning refers to self-importance accompanied by conceit, and istikbar means arrogance. Awrathat means producing or bequeathing a consequence. The focus is what grows after an action and how that state directs the next step.

Someone acknowledging a mistake may become readier to apologize and repair relationships. Someone believing they have done much good may reject correction as though always right. This comparison does not make disobedience the better choice. What is praised is humility following repentance, while conceit damaging obedience is strongly rebuked.

Undertake goodness earnestly and keep examining your view of others. If worship achievements make contempt easy, correct intention and stop hurtful actions. If you have slipped, use regret for responsibility rather than an identity of permanent ruin. This wisdom guards two doors: repentance stays open and arrogance remains watched. The heart learns devotion knowing Allah's help is needed before, during, and after every deed.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, when someone with a troubled past attends religious learning, our response can matter greatly. Some welcome normally; others continually bring up the past. We may feel we are protecting goodness while actually enjoying being the cleaner person. Someone wanting change then feels no place remains to begin rightly.

Ibn 'Ata'illah compares wrongdoing producing humility and need for Allah with obedience producing arrogance. This is no invitation to choose disobedience. Repentance and submission are praised, while conceit is rebuked even after good deeds. We apply this message to self-examination rather than declaring any particular person certainly nobler than another.

Dear congregation, welcoming a learner does not mean ignoring safety or the rights of those harmed. Necessary boundaries remain. However, humiliation and ridicule are not needed to maintain them. We can allow participation under clear rules while supporting the responsibility and repair still required by circumstances.

“What if I find trust difficult?” Trust need not be given all at once. Observe actions and use reasonable arrangements. Avoid assuming the past permits continual embarrassment. People can learn although change needs time and evidence. We also have shortcomings, so caution should accompany humility and hope for human improvement.

Dear friends, those returning need not await everyone's trust to begin obedience. Fulfil obligations, find a trustworthy guide, and accept necessary boundaries. If words hurt, seek good support. We need not retaliate with contempt. The journey can continue through honest actions and willingness to improve what still harms self and others.

Let us make learning environments protect dignity and responsibility together. May Allah accept repentance, protect those hurt, and cleanse arrogance from our hearts. May regular practitioners remain humble and beginners receive strength. May we never obstruct someone sincerely trying to return to Him. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

What matters is being willing to learn sincerely, examine our understanding, and follow sound guidance when seeking to change our daily habits.

Welcome someone wanting to learn and explain applicable rules. If repair responsibilities remain, respect that process. Those harmed need not be forced into closeness or immediate trust. Goodness can be protected through clarity and boundaries without perpetual humiliation. We are opening a chance to take proper steps rather than announcing every past consequence instantly settled.

“If I remain suspicious, is that arrogance?” Caution may be necessary, dear congregation. Examine actions and facts, using appropriate arrangements. Watch for enjoying a cleaner self-image until ridicule closes someone else's learning opportunity. This wisdom highlights actions' inner consequences: humility and need for Allah, or self-importance with arrogance. We do not know final judgement of people. Therefore maintain rules while remaining willing to hope for improvement. Such an attitude supports return without sacrificing safety or the dignity of those affected.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “How can we welcome change while protecting other people's rights and safety?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.
PERSONAL REFLECTION

Dear friends, before moving to practical steps, let us give ourselves room to absorb this. The lesson about making learning space for someone returning may touch an experience that is still unresolved. We do not have to force all our feelings into order tonight. Simply recognize one part that now seems clearer. Perhaps we need to apologize, seek an explanation, or change how we make decisions. Perhaps we first need rest so that we can think clearly. We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Try reviewing how newcomers or returning congregants are welcomed. Stop comments making the past entertainment. Discuss needed boundaries appropriately with responsible people. We can provide learning information without demanding someone's entire history of wrongdoing. Those changing should follow rules and responsibilities earnestly. May gatherings help improve steps, and may caution accompany humility so hope for people is not lost through enjoying the position of judge too much.

Now let us turn the lesson about making learning space for someone returning into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Let us recall the direction of today's discussion, dear congregation. The lesson about making learning space for someone returning invites us to examine our own choices and improve what is our responsibility. After returning home, things may feel ordinary again. That is where a good intention needs attention. We can remind ourselves gently while remaining firm about our obligations. If we need to begin again one day, let us begin. The opportunity to learn is not exhausted because one attempt has not gone smoothly. While we have the ability and opportunity, let us keep seeking goodness and asking Allah to guide our hearts and accept our deeds.

Let us make learning environments protect dignity and responsibility together. May Allah accept repentance, protect those hurt, and cleanse arrogance from our hearts. May regular practitioners remain humble and beginners receive strength. May we never obstruct someone sincerely trying to return to Him. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: مَعْصِيَةٌ أَوْرَثَتْ ذُلًّا وَافْتِقَارًا
Disobedience followed by humility and need for Allah
خَيْرٌ مِنْ طَاعَةٍ أَوْرَثَتْ عِزًّا وَاسْتِكْبَارًا.
is better than obedience followed by conceit and arrogance.

107.translation: There are two blessings from which no created being is separate. Every created being necessarily needs both: the blessing of being brought into existence and the blessing of being sustained by His help.
syarahEn: We often count blessings through newly acquired things, such as income or an opportunity. Yet more fundamental blessings continually accompany us: being brought into existence and sustained to continue living. This wisdom invites sight of that foundation, so gratitude appears beyond fulfilment of additional desires.

Ni'mat al-ijad means the blessing of creation or being brought into existence. Ni'mat al-imdad means the blessing of continual sustaining help and care. Mawjud refers to something existing as creation, while la budda emphasizes an inseparable need. All creatures need creation and do not become independent afterwards. Their continuation still depends on Allah's sustaining care.

A day can unfold because much works without our constant awareness: bodily functions, resources in the environment, and people helping one another. We try to maintain life but do not create every foundation making effort possible. This awareness restrains arrogance in success and strengthens a sense of need when facing limitations.

Try beginning gratitude with what is nearest, then continue through action. Care for the body as a trust, use opportunities for good, and do not damage others' rights for momentary interests. We need not feel satisfied with every circumstance to acknowledge remaining blessings. This wisdom broadens sight so life is assessed beyond additions we lack. Beneath all change, fundamental gifts continually invite remembrance of Allah and thoughtful use.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, a baby has no achievements, earns nothing, and cannot repay attention. Yet their needs still deserve care. Their presence reminds us that human worth does not begin only after usefulness by a particular measure. We too once received life and help before being able to say thanks or do anything considered impressive.

Ibn 'Ata'illah explains two blessings creatures continually need: being brought into existence and supported through sustaining care. Ijad refers to creation, and imdad to accompanying help. We do not create life's foundations ourselves. This awareness teaches gratitude more fundamental than delight at a new item or news of achievement to announce.

Dear friends, at home we can learn through viewing vulnerable relatives. Children, people ill, and elders still deserve respect. Do not measure love only by the ability to repay. When someone needs much help, burdens do need fair sharing. But dividing tasks does not diminish the dignity of someone cared for who cannot yet do much.

“What if I feel useless because I have not succeeded?” Allow room for a broader view. Development can still be pursued, but self-worth need not await major achievement. We can still guard speech, learn, and accept help. If worthlessness remains burdensome, speak to someone trustworthy or seek support for a fairer view of circumstances.

Dear congregation, gratitude for life also appears in care. Look after the body within ability, use learning opportunities, and respect others' lives. We need not prove high productivity daily to deserve rest. The entrusted body requires care. Effort and rest can both serve responsibility when arranged according to actual needs and trusts.

Let us remember we received long before producing. May Allah help us appreciate life, provide for families caring for vulnerable members, and protect every person's dignity. May achievements bring gratitude without becoming the sole measure of worth. May remaining life be used for goodness suited to ability and others' needs. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Perhaps an answer comes straight away; perhaps a difficulty comes to mind instead. Let us hear that difficulty calmly. Let us accompany a good intention with preparation that makes it easier to carry out.

phrasesEn: نِعْمَتَانِ مَا خَرَجَ مَوْجُودٌ عَنْهُمَا
There are two blessings from which no created being is separate.
وَلَا بُدَّ لِكُلِّ مُكَوَّنٍ مِنْهُمَا،
Every created being necessarily needs both:
نِعْمَةُ الْإِيجَادِ وَنِعْمَةُ الْإِمْدَادِ.
being created and being sustained by His help.

108.translation: First, He blesses you by creating you. Second, He blesses you by continually sustaining and providing for you.
syarahEn: Life does not end with birth. Every day we need food, bodily capacity, and resources to survive and fulfil responsibilities. This wisdom continues the discussion of two basic blessings, inviting recognition that Allah's gifts appear at existence's beginning and in its continually renewed continuation.

Awwalan means first, while thaniyan means second. Al-ijad refers to creation, and tawali al-imdad means continuous sustaining assistance. Tawali conveys successive arrival. Sustaining blessings often escape attention precisely because they recur, making something vital seem guaranteed.

For example, we realize walking's value when a foot hurts. We notice family help when managing everything alone. Such changes open understanding of blessings previously used without much gratitude. We can learn to remember before loss through more conscious attention to daily life.

109.translation: Your need for Allah is inherent in your very being. Events merely remind you of a need you had not recognized. That inherent poverty does not disappear with changing circumstances; those circumstances affirm it.
syarahEn: We sometimes feel we need Allah only when business is threatened or the body weakens. When circumstances run smoothly, that dependence fades from awareness. This wisdom reminds us that our need for Allah never disappears. Difficulty merely makes clearer to the heart what a sense of ability had concealed.

Faqatuka means your need or poverty. Dhatiyyah indicates something inherent in one's very being rather than an occasional addition. Al-'awarid means temporary circumstances, such as ease or difficulty. Tu'akkiduha means affirming it. Changed circumstances reveal an existing need; abundant resources do not make people independent of Allah.

Someone well provided for still needs health, knowledge, and sustaining care they cannot guarantee. Someone lacking resources still has dignity and responsibilities not determined by wealth. Poverty in this wisdom primarily concerns the creature's position before the Creator, applying to every social circumstance.

Practise supplication when life feels smooth too. Appreciate working ability without treating it as an unchangeable guarantee. If a trial arrives, acknowledge need honestly and seek suitable help. We need not wait for weakness to become overwhelming before returning to Allah. This wisdom preserves continuity in devotion, because dependence is awakened beyond danger alone. In ease and constraint, the heart learns its position as a recipient continually needing guidance and help.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

We begin assuming others are anxious because they manage badly, forgetting that many circumstances cannot be controlled by planning and saved money alone.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that need for Allah belongs to our very being. Events merely recall something often forgotten. We need Him while strong, rather than only when savings diminish. Wealth and preparation are means used responsibly. Neither turns people into independent creatures free of every limit of life.

Dear friends, still prepare needs according to ability. Keep records, plan spending, and learn important decisions properly. Afterwards, maintain humility. If someone struggles, hear circumstances before judging. Some burdens are unfamiliar to us. Planning advice can help when it understands reality rather than announcing our life is more orderly and therefore certainly safer.

“If everything still depends on Allah, why prepare?” Preparation is part of our possible work. We use given ability while acknowledging limits. Like locking the front door, we try to protect without assuming a key guarantees every event. Tawakkul places effort in its proper measure, so we neither become idle nor claim control of all results.

Dear congregation, a simple practice when circumstances are good is continued prayer, learning, and openness to input. Do not await problems before appreciating human support. Nurture relationships sincerely, because friendship is not a reserve sought only in urgent need. We live through Allah's sustaining care and help often arriving through people working and walking with us.

Let us appreciate preparation without idolizing its security. May Allah bless family savings, provide for those unable to save, and protect us from arrogance. May ease preserve humility and constraint preserve hope. May awareness of needing Him accompany daily decisions rather than arrive only after plans are disrupted. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

110.translation: The best of your times is when you recognize your need for Allah and are returned to awareness of your lowliness before Him.
syarahEn: The most valuable time is not always the most pleasant. Sometimes we honestly recognize weakness, stop pretending to control everything, and return to ask Allah's help. This wisdom directs attention to that awareness's value, because humbler and more earnest devotion can grow from it.

Khayr awqatik means the best of your times. Tashhadu refers to witnessing or living awareness of the heart. Faqatuka is your need, while dhulluka means your lowly position as a servant before Allah. This humility does not erase human dignity. It frees us from conceit that makes help difficult to request and advice difficult to accept.

Someone may find such a time in a sincere apology. They acknowledge self-defence does not repair damage and choose responsibility. Another experiences it by admitting inability to solve a problem alone and accepting help. Its value lies in honesty and the direction of return to Allah rather than the severity of difficulty.

Therefore, we need not deliberately seek suffering to feel closer. Use present circumstances to nurture awareness of need. In success, remember preceding help. In failure, acknowledge limits and improve what remains possible. Time becomes precious when the heart accepts its teaching. This wisdom helps us see that clarity and humility can benefit more deeply than merely feeling strong, allowing every circumstance to offer guidance and reordered steps.

We can examine all of this calmly. Turn our attention towards an action we can manage today, then ask Allah for help with the next stage of the process.

Dear congregation, try practising that answer in our own words. Imagine a family member asking while we are relaxing. We do not need to give a long sermon. Begin by listening, then share what we truly understand. If something remains unclear, say that we will learn more. A simple conversation like this helps us check our own understanding while ensuring that advice is given respectfully. We learn together, without needing to appear as people who have already resolved every problem.
PRACTICAL STEPS TO TRY

Therefore, we need not deliberately seek suffering to feel closer. Use present circumstances to nurture awareness of need. In success, remember preceding help. In failure, acknowledge limits and improve what remains possible. Time becomes precious when the heart accepts its teaching. This wisdom helps us see that clarity and humility can benefit more deeply than merely feeling strong, allowing every circumstance to offer guidance and reordered steps.

Try preparing one sufficiently clear request for help. State need and timing, then allow the other person to explain capacity. If unable, do not immediately judge the entire relationship. Families can arrange conversation when reasonably calm. Listen without humiliating someone admitting difficulty. May honesty open better shared responsibility, and may we learn to ask people with proper manners while placing highest hope in Allah, who knows our deepest needs.

Dear congregation, may Allah honour us, before the inspiration of this lesson passes, let us choose a practical exercise about acknowledging need for help while respecting others' limits. We do not all have to choose the same step. Our families, work, and abilities differ. What matters is that our choice follows the wisdom's message and respects the obligations we already have. Allow a reasonable time to try it. If a change affects others, listen to their views. We are learning to develop habits we can practise in real life. Advice then begins to shape how we handle our responsibilities, instead of remaining something we agree with during the gathering.

Dear friends, take a moment to connect this explanation with a decision we once made. If we could go through that experience again, what would we want to improve? Of course, we cannot turn back time. But what we learned can still help us face the next situation. Keep one clear lesson. If someone's rights still need to be fulfilled, consider a proper way to fulfil them. Reflection becomes useful when it helps us move forward in the life we are living now.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear friends, our problems may not be resolved immediately after this lesson. Yet may we gain a clearer way of seeing the matter of acknowledging need for help while respecting others' limits. That clarity can help us take the next step more responsibly. Carry a sound understanding, then make room for the process of learning. If help is needed, seek it properly. If we can already begin, act without waiting for every circumstance to become perfect. We have an opportunity to make an effort today, and we continue asking Allah for help. With that hope, let us bring this meeting to a close with supplication and a willingness to put the lesson into practice.

Let us bring needs to Allah without shame in admitting limits. May He grant a way out, bring trustworthy support, and soften family hearts to share burdens. May humility ease receiving and giving help, so difficult times begin a more honest and responsible life together. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
phrasesEn: خَيْرُ أَوْقَاتِكَ وَقْتٌ تَشْهَدُ فِيهِ وُجُودَ فَاقَتِكَ،
The best of your times is when you recognize your need for Allah
وَتُرَدُّ فِيهِ إِلَى وُجُودِ ذِلَّتِكَ.
and are returned to awareness of your lowliness before Him.

111.translation: When He makes your heart no longer find comfort in dependence on His creatures, know that He wishes to open for you the door of intimacy with Him.
syarahEn: Sometimes those we usually rely on cannot give what we hope. This can feel lonely and painful. This wisdom invites the heart to see devotion's possibility within it: limited creaturely help can encourage more honest knowledge of a place of return to Allah.

Awhashaka means making you feel estranged or unsettled. Al-khalq refers to creatures, while al-uns means intimacy and tranquillity. Bab al-uns bihi describes closeness with Allah through supplication and the heart's knowledge. The sequence does not command ending social relationships; it orders reliance when human limitations appear.

For example, a friend cannot yet understand our problem. We may seek a more suitable listener and explain needs more clearly. At the same time, we learn that no person can perfectly hold our entire inner life. Supplication gives room to acknowledge weakness without waiting for everyone to understand.

If loneliness feels heavy, keep paths to healthy relationships open and seek needed support. Do not use this wisdom to withdraw or reject help. What needs adjustment is expecting creatures always to meet every inner need. Closeness to Allah should help us return more calmly, appreciate help, and accept others' limits. From loneliness, the heart can learn broader trust while maintaining compassion and responsibility in shared life.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, when sad, we sometimes expect one friend always ready to listen. A slow reply or visible tiredness feels like abandonment. Yet they have problems and limits too. Our need for company is real, but one person cannot always fill every inner space asking for attention and certainty.

Ibn 'Ata'illah reminds us that when comfort in dependence on creatures decreases, the heart can gain opportunity for intimacy with Allah. This does not tell us to end relationships or reject help. We learn proper reliance so human limits do not immediately collapse all hope. Supplication and healthy relationships can work together in caring for ourselves.

Dear friends, if a friend cannot listen, ask for a better time. Explain needs clearly, perhaps wanting a brief hearing without immediate advice. We can seek other safe support, including family or a suitable supporter. Sharing places to talk avoids burdening a relationship with demands that one person always be available for everything daily.

“What if I feel extremely lonely?” Acknowledge it without facing it alone. Contact trustworthy people and activities allowing healthy encounters. If feelings remain heavy and disrupt daily life, professional support may help. Pray simply. We need not wait for calm before bringing loneliness to Allah and seeking help towards good steps.

Dear congregation, listeners can state boundaries kindly too. Explain when you can listen and what exceeds your capacity. Avoid disappearing without explanation if an update remains possible. Relationships are easier to care for when needs and ability are discussed. We help as limited human beings, so closeness does not become an obligation always to be strong and have answers.

Let us maintain hope in Allah while caring for friendships more honestly. May He comfort lonely hearts, bring good support, and help us respect others' limits. When people cannot yet listen, may we retain courage to seek help. May relationships gain growing room through sincere attention and more reasonable expectations. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

Friendship is likelier preserved without demanding one person hold everything. We still deserve company, and friends retain rights over limited time and energy.

Supporters should not dismiss loneliness by simply demanding more gratitude without listening.

Dear friends, if we sat in a circle after the lesson, someone might raise this question: “Are we demanding one friend always be available for every burden?” That question deserves to be heard. We should not rush to answer before understanding the difficulty. We can begin by restating the issue in simple language, then consider the available choices. If we do not know the whole answer, we can admit it and continue learning. What matters is that the conversation leads towards a good action. Now think about the answer we would give a friend. Choose words that are clear and gentle, without promising an outcome beyond human ability.

In the matter of caring for friendship when friends have limits too, we may have made small progress for which we have never given thanks. There may also be a mistake we keep wanting to hide. Both can teach us without being put on display. Give thanks for the help that has already come, then examine what needs improving. Do not compare our whole journey with a fragment of someone else's life. We have real responsibilities today. Recognizing our part allows reflection to move into action, so regret need not remain a thought circling endlessly without direction.

We learn hope in Allah without closing ourselves to human assistance that can support daily life.

Now let us turn the lesson about caring for friendship when friends have limits too into a simple plan, dear friends. Choose one action with a reasonably clear time for doing it. Do not immediately promise to change our whole life. Ask when we can begin and what needs preparing. If other people are involved, speak with them properly; do not make decisions on their behalf in a passing burst of enthusiasm. After trying, notice what helped and what still got in the way. We may adjust our approach while keeping the right aim. A small exercise gives us a chance to learn from real circumstances, so a good intention takes a form we can actually carry out.

Dear congregation, if we wish to respond, sharing the general lesson is enough. We do not need to name anyone or reveal anybody's private affairs. Listen calmly to different responses. There may be circumstances we have never considered. After listening, return to the message we are studying and consider the most appropriate action. Learning together can broaden our understanding, provided the conversation respects people's dignity and does not become a place for judging their experiences.
REINFORCING THE MESSAGE AND CLOSING SUPPLICATION

Dear congregation, after hearing this explanation about caring for friendship when friends have limits too, keep one insight that is closest to our circumstances. We can recall it on the journey home or discuss it with our family without talking down to them. Ask ourselves which part we have understood and which part needs further study. In this way, the conversation continues naturally beyond the gathering. We do not need to monitor other people's inner states. It is enough to care for the responsibilities already before us. May this little knowledge help us choose a step pleasing to Allah when we face the matter in real life.

Let us maintain hope in Allah while caring for friendships more honestly. May He comfort lonely hearts, bring good support, and help us respect others' limits. phrasesEn: مَتَى أَوْحَشَكَ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ
When He makes your heart no longer find comfort in dependence on His creatures,
فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَفْتَحَ لَكَ بَابَ الْأُنْسِ بِهِ.
know that He wishes to open the door of intimacy with Him.

112.translation: When He frees your tongue to ask, know that He intends to give to you.
syarahEn: When the heart is moved to ask earnestly, we receive a precious opportunity. We acknowledge need and choose return to Allah although circumstances have not changed. This wisdom nurtures hope that an opened tongue for supplication is already part of a gift inviting closeness.

Atlaqa means to free or release. Lisanaka bi al-talab refers to the tongue being eased in expressing requests. An yu'tiyaka means to give to you. The relationship between request and gift teaches hopeful supplication. However, the form and timing remain according to Allah's will, as explained in Wisdom 6.

Someone facing family problems can begin praying simply. They need not wait to compose beautiful expressions. Afterwards, they still fulfil their part, such as listening, apologizing, or seeking advice. An honest request can open readiness to accept improvements previously avoided.

Do not measure supplication only by how quickly one wish is fulfilled. Notice courage to acknowledge weakness and willingness to follow the right path too. If unsure what to ask, express need for guidance and goodness. We may ask clearly while entrusting results. This wisdom makes supplication a living doorway of relationship, so waiting contains more than demands. Devotion continues through honest asking, diligent effort, and trust in Allah's generosity.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear friends, may Allah honour us, someone wants to pray but feels ashamed of lacking eloquence. Hearing another's beautiful words, they compare their own simple language. Needs remain suppressed. Yet the wish to ask Allah is itself an opportunity to welcome rather than delay until we feel fluent enough to sound suitable before people.

Ibn 'Ata'illah teaches that when the tongue is freed to ask, the heart is invited to hope in Allah's giving. We still understand answers within His will and timing. This encourages closeness through honest requests. We do not control results, but need not close supplication's opportunity because we cannot compose supposedly beautiful, moving words.

Dear congregation, in difficulty we can say, “O Allah, I am confused. Show me what is good and help me follow it.” We may learn taught supplications and understand their meaning. Yet learning need not stop us asking. Allah knows circumstances not yet neatly explained, including mixed feelings and needs named only gradually.

“What if I do not know what to ask?” Ask for guidance and goodness. Afterwards, notice a possible step: seeking explanation, pausing, or contacting the right person. Supplication need not make us wait without action. Earnest asking can increase readiness for guidance through knowledge, advice, and choices emerging as thought becomes more orderly.

Dear friends, do not mock someone praying hesitantly. We do not know the heart's struggle. Safety helps people dare to learn. If asked to guide, explain gently without making them feel far from Allah for memorizing few recitations. We want understanding opened, so knowledge helps devotion and preserves hope.

Let us welcome the wish to pray while opportunity remains. May Allah ease good requests, accept honest acknowledgement, and guide subsequent steps. May learners receive ease and safety. May supplication become daily life, bringing needs humbly to Him while effort continues according to available ability. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.

When He frees your tongue to ask,
فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يُعْطِيَكَ.
know that He intends to give to you.

113.translation: The knower of Allah never loses a profound sense of needing Him. Their heart does not settle in comfort through dependence on anything besides Allah.
syarahEn: Someone knowing Allah does more than ask when every path feels closed. In success and abundant resources, they still recognize fundamental need. This wisdom describes that maturity, so smooth circumstances do not make the heart feel sufficient through personal ability or created help.

Idtirar means profound need and inability to stand independently. Qarar means settling or finding comfort in a support. The heart of an 'arif, one knowing Allah, never loses awareness of needing Him. Its highest peace does not depend on anything besides Allah, although it still uses means and appreciates helpers.

Someone earning well still maintains supplication, honesty, and willingness to learn. They know working ability can change and much lies beyond control. That awareness makes success easier to appreciate without arrogance. When human help arrives, they give thanks while recognizing it as a provided means.

Practise remembering Allah on ordinary days too. Seek protection before problems and use ease to fulfil unfinished rights. If one support is lost, allow sadness and seek a good path. Need for Allah does not conflict with courage to act. It directs action away from making means absolute. This wisdom builds deeper steadfastness because relationship with Allah lives through ease and constraint, rather than only when no other choice seems available.
shortEn: Assalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh. Alhamdulillah, all praise belongs to Allah. May blessings and peace be upon Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

Dear congregation, sometimes work goes well, family is healthy, and needs are met. Gratitude is fitting. Yet smooth circumstances can weaken habitual supplication. We begin feeling we know how to live and need little advice. Only disruption sends us seeking support again. Awareness of Allah seems summoned only when life stops following our confidently arranged plans.

Ibn 'Ata'illah describes a knower never losing need for Allah or relying absolutely on anything besides Him. Need remains in ease. We learn awareness so success does not make the heart claim independence. Means are used well and people appreciated, while acknowledgement of Allah's sustaining care accompanies daily decisions.

Dear friends, in good circumstances keep learning about your trusts. Do not reject input because of past success. Change can occur and abilities need renewal. We can also help others within ability without feeling their saviour. Help respectfully, because we ourselves still receive much assistance not entirely visible or individually nameable.

“If I always feel need, will I lose confidence?” We can still use abilities firmly. Acknowledging limits makes decisions more honest. We know what we understand and what needs asking. Healthy confidence does not require denying Allah's help or others' work. Ability can be appreciated and developed while remaining open to improvement.

Dear congregation, smooth family circumstances offer good time to build habits. Pray together as appropriate, discuss trusts, and practise fair task sharing. Do not wait for crisis to begin listening. Relationships cared for in calm can help face difficulty more orderly. We prepare beyond knowing when problems come: today's trust already deserves care.

Let us humble our hearts when life is easy. May Allah preserve beneficial ease, protect against self-sufficiency, and guide blessings' use. May success increase willingness to learn and sensitivity to help. May need for Him remain recognized in calm, so supplication appears before every relied-upon method reveals its limits. Amin.
Wassalamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh.
